ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effects of Probabilistic Supervision on SGD Convergence
PROPOSAL: We will train a simple teacher-student pair on the CIFAR-10 dataset using a multi-class softmax cross-entropy loss for the teacher and a standard cross-entropy loss for the student with and without probabilistic supervision. The student will be trained with SGD and its variants, such as SGD with momentum and Adam. We will compare the convergence behavior in terms of training loss, objective, and validation accuracy across different teacher-student configurations to derive insights into how SGD adapts to probabilistic supervision.
CONTROLS: (1) Teacher trained with standard cross-entropy loss, student trained without probabilistic supervision; (2) Teacher and student trained with standard losses, both with and without momentum for SGD.
COST: 50 GPU-hours, as this will involve training several teacher-student pairs with different losses and optimizers.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that probabilistic supervision will lead to faster convergence of the training loss and better validation accuracy for the student, with the additional benefit of improved stability and robustness to overfitting. We may find, however, that this comes at the cost of decreased precision or higher risk of overconfident predictions for certain outliers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing the Impact of Teacher Calibration on Student Generalization
PROPOSAL: Building on the teacher-student pair trained in proposal (1), we will perform a series of experiments where the teacher provides calibrated probability estimates of the class posteriors, ranging from very confident to uncertain, to investigate how the quality of teacher calibration affects the student's generalization performance. We will evaluate the trained students on various metrics, including risk, calibration, and F1-score.
CONTROLS:  (1) the original teacher providing uncalibrated class posteriors; (2) teacher's probabilities regularely calibrated; (3) teacher providing nearly uniform probability distribution; (4) baseline performance of teacher and students without probabilistic supervision.
COST: Additional 100 GPU-hours to retrain and evaluate the teacher-student pair with the different calibration settings.
PREDICTION: We expect that well-calibrated teacher probabilities improve the student's average generalization performance, especially in high-stakes tests like established benchmarks. Overconfident or underconfident teacher predictions may impact generalization, especially in specific domains (harder to produce very confident or uncertain probabilities). Regular calibration can mitigate these effects to produce high-confidence accurate inferences under favorable training domains.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Estimate for Proposal 1: Investigating the Effects of Probabilistic Supervision on SGD Convergence
PROPOSAL: We will modify proposal (1) to incorporate a Bayesian perspective by assuming that the teacher's output probabilities follow a Dirichlet distribution. We will exploit this prior information in the SGD update rule using a novel probabilistic gradient estimators (PGEs) that leverage the variational Bayes' Dirichlet distribution for the teacher's beliefs. This will provide a more principled and flexible approach to investigating the effects of probabilistic supervision.
CONTROLS: (1) PG-sGD with and without PGEs; (2) PG-sGD with and without VH-Bayes regularization.
COST: Increased 20 GPU-hours, due to the incorporation of the variational Bayesian approximation for the teacher's beliefs.

PROPOSAL: We will formally derive generalization bounds for SGD training with probabilistic supervision, using tools from learning theory, such as Rademacher complexity and Tsybakov noise conditions. TITLE: Exploring the Role of Regularization in Teacher-Student Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate how various regularization techniques, such as L1 and L2 regularization, dropout, and early stopping, affect the teacher's performance and the student's generalization when using probabilistic supervision. We will also explore the impact of different weight decay schedules on the teacher-student pair.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Students Trained with Probabilistic Supervision
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the robustness of students trained with probabilistic supervision to various types of adversarial attacks (e.g., PGD, FGSM) and evaluate their performance under these conditions. We will also explore the impact of teacher's robustness on the student's robustness and vice versa.
CONTROLS: (1) Students trained with cross-entropy loss and one-hot labels; (2) Students trained with probabilistic supervision and different teacher robustness levels.
COST: 30 GPU-hours, depending on the number of attack scenarios and teacher models to be tested.
PREDICTION: We expect that students trained with probabilistic supervision will exhibit improved robustness to certain types of attacks, especially those that exploit the teacher's calibration errors. The teacher's robustness is likely to play a crucial role in determining the student's robustness.

PROPOSAL: We will synthesize our findings from the previous proposals to provide practical guidelines for designing optimized teacher-student pairs for probabilistic supervision. CONTROLS: (1) Comparison of optimized teacher-student pairs with randomly selected pairs; (2) Evaluation of the generalization performance of students trained with optimized teacher-student pairs.
COST: 0 GPU-hours, as this proposal does not require new experiments, but rather a summarization of previous findings.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that these guidelines will provide valuable insights into designing optimized teacher-student pairs for probabilistic supervision, leading to improved generalization performance and robustness of students.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theorizing Student Loss Convergence Under Probabilistic Supervision
PROPOSAL: 
We derive a general bound on the convergence rate of SGD for a student model supervised by the exact class posterior probabilities given by a teacher. Under a weak assumption on the teacher's risk landscape, we prove that the student's empirical risk converges at a rate of O(1/B) when training with SGD, where B is the batch size, and faster rates are attainable when the teacher provides a good approximation to the Bayes posterior.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: Compare with SGD convergence rates under one-hot label supervision.
2. Abilitation: Compare with and without the weak risk assumption on the teacher.
3. Teacher model: Use a teacher model with good calibration to approximate the Bayes posterior.

COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
Given its analytical nature, the expected result is derivation of a convergence rate bound under probabilistic supervision, which improves over the baseline, especially in the regime of small batch sizes. The bound may fail in the case where the teacher's risk landscape is not well-conditioned.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: An Experimental Study on the Dynamics of SGD with Soft LaBelling
PROPOSAL: 
We experimentally investigate the convergence behavior and stability of SGD-based learners when trained with the exact class posterior probabilities as soft labels. We compare this with the standard one-hot label supervision on benchmark datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, ImageNet). We explore how the choice of teacher model calibration, soft label temperature, and batch normalization affects the student's convergence and accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: Compare with SGD convergence rates under one-hot label supervision.
2. Ablation study: Study the effect of different teacher model calibrations, soft label temperatures, and batch normalization on the student's convergence and accuracy.
3. Systematic analysis: Systematically vary the batch size and optimizer hyperparameters to draw conclusions on SGD under probabilistic supervision.

COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The experiment should confirm that SGD under probabilistic supervision exhibits improved convergence behavior and stability compared to one-hot label supervision, especially in the early stages of training. However, the accuracy may degrade due to over-confidence in the teacher's soft labels.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: An Experimental Study on the Dynamics of SGD with Soft LaBelling
PROPOSAL: 
We revise Experiment 2 to account for the teacher's estimation error in providing the exact class posterior probabilities. We use a probabilistic teacher, where the teacher's soft labels are treated as noisy estimates of the true class posteriors, and investigate how the level of estimation error affects the student's convergence, generalization, and accuracy. We compare this with the standard one-hot label supervision and Experiment 1 under exact posterior supervision.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: Compare with SGD convergence rates under one-hot label supervision.
2. Ablation study: Study the effect of increased estimation error in teacher's soft labels on the student's convergence and accuracy.
3. Systematic analysis: Systematically vary the batch size and optimizer hyperparameters to draw conclusions on SGD under probabilistic supervision with noisy teacher.

COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The revised experiment will likely show that SGD under probabilistic supervision with noisy teacher produces lower accuracy and degraded convergence behavior as the estimation error increases. However, it may still converge faster and be more stable than one-hot label supervision, especially in early stages of training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generalization Bounds for SGD Under Probabilistic Supervision with Noisy Teacher
PROPOSAL: 
We derive a generalization bound for SGD-based learners under probabilistic supervision with a noisy teacher. We assume the teacher's soft labels are treated as noisy estimates of the true class posteriors and provide a bound on the expected risk of the student in terms of the estimation error and the statistical properties of the risk landscape.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: Compare with existing generalization bounds for SGD under one-hot label supervision.
2. Special case: Specialize the bound to the case of exact posterior supervision to compare with existing results.
3. Analytical dependence: Analytically verify the dependence of the bound on the estimation error and risk landscape properties.

COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The bound is expected to capture the degradation in generalization performance due to teacher estimation error, and demonstrate the significance of calibration in the teacher model. However, it may become loose for small estimation errors or for a large risk landscape variance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Theorizing Student Loss Convergence Under Probabilistic Supervision
PROPOSAL: 
We strengthen the theoretical foundation of Experiment 1 by providing a more general convergence rate bound for SGD under probabilistic supervision, applicable to a broader class of risk landscapes. We also demonstrate the effect of estimation error in the teacher's soft labels on the convergence rate bound. Our analysis provides a deeper understanding of the behavior of SGD under probabilistic supervision.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: Compare with existing convergence rate bounds for SGD under one-hot label supervision.
2. Special case: Specialize the bound to the case of exact posterior supervision to compare with existing results.
3. Effect of estimation error: Analyze how the estimation error in the teacher's soft labels affects the convergence rate bound.

COST: negligible
PREDICTION: 
The revised analysis is expected to provide a more general and insightful convergence rate bound, highlighting the impact of estimation error in the teacher's soft labels on the convergence behavior of SGD under probabilistic supervision. However, the bound may become loose for certain risk landscapes or under specific teacher estimation error regimes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Guidelines for Teacher Calibration in Probabilistic Supervision
PROPOSAL: 
We provide practical guidelines for designing or choosing teacher models to provide well-calibrated soft labels for students trained with SGD-based optimizers. We study the empirical performance of different teacher calibration methods (e.g., temperature scaling, label smoothing) on benchmark datasets and investigate their impact on student convergence, generalization, and accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: Compare with a naively trained teacher with no calibration.
2. Ablation study: Evaluate the effect of different calibration methods on teacher accuracy and student performance.
3. Experimental design: Investigate the interplay between teacher calibration and student convergence, exploring the trade-off between teacher accuracy and student generalization.

COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The guidelines are expected to provide insights into the relationship between teacher calibration and student performance, highlighting the importance of considering the teacher's estimation error when designing the student model. However, the effectiveness of calibration methods may depend on specific dataset characteristics or teacher architectures.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Generalization Bounds for SGD Under Probabilistic Supervision with Noisy Teacher
PROPOSAL: 
We strengthen the generalization bound for SGD under probabilistic supervision with a noisy teacher by incorporating the teacher's calibration error. We provide a bound that captures the interplay between the estimation error in the teacher's soft labels and the calibration error of the teacher model.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: Compare with existing generalization bounds for SGD under one-hot label supervision.
2. Special case: Specialize the bound to the case of exact posterior supervision to compare with existing results.
3. Effect of calibration error: Analyze how the calibration error of the teacher model affects the generalization bound.

COST: negligible
PREDICTION: 
The revised bound is expected to provide a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between the teacher's calibration, estimation error, and the student's generalization performance. However, the bound may become loose for certain risk landscapes or under specific teacher estimation error regimes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) for Tracking Teacher Calibration
PROPOSAL: 
We explore the use of EWMA to track the teacher's calibration error over time during training, and adjust the student's learning process accordingly. We evaluate the effect of EWMA-based calibration tracking on student convergence, generalization, and accuracy on benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: Compare with fixed teacher calibration used throughout training.
2. Ablation study: Evaluate the effect of different EWMA parameters (e.g., forgetting rate, window size) on teacher calibration tracking.
3. Experimental design: Investigate the interplay between EWMA-based calibration tracking and student learning, exploring the trade-off between teacher calibration accuracy and student generalization.

COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The proposed method is expected to provide a more adaptive and dynamic approach to teacher calibration tracking, with potential benefits for student performance. However, the effectiveness of EWMA-based calibration tracking may depend on specific dataset characteristics or teacher architectures.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: An Experimental Study on the Dynamics of SGD with Soft LaBelling
PROPOSAL: 
We extend the experimental study of SGD under probabilistic supervision by incorporating the EWMA-based teacher calibration tracking method from Proposal 5. We investigate how this adaptive calibration approach affects the dynamics of SGD, including convergence, generalization, and accuracy, and compare its performance with fixed teacher calibration.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: Compare with SGD under one-hot label supervision.
2. Ablation study: Evaluate the effect of different EWMA parameters and teacher calibration methods on SGD dynamics.
3. Experimental design: Systematically vary the batch size, optimizer hyperparameters, and teacher model architectures to draw conclusions on SGD under probabilistic supervision with adaptive calibration.

COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The revised experiment is expected to provide insights into the effects of adaptive teacher calibration on SGD dynamics, highlighting the potential benefits of tracking teacher calibration in probabilistic supervision. However, the success of adaptive calibration may depend on specific dataset characteristics or teacher architectures, and the complexity of the teacher model may affect the performance of EWMA-based calibration tracking.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Theory and Practice of Probabilistic Supervision for SGD-based Learning
PROPOSAL: 
We combine the findings from the previous proposals to develop a unified theory and practice of probabilistic supervision for SGD-based learning. We provide a comprehensive framework that integrates the insights from convergence analysis, experimental studies, generalization bounds, teacher calibration, and adaptive calibration tracking to provide a principled approach to designing and training students under probabilistic supervision.
CONTROLS: 
1. Theoretical validation: Validate the unified framework using the theoretical results from Proposals 1 and 3.
2. Experimental evaluation: Evaluate the performance of the unified framework using the experimental findings from Proposals 2 and 5.
3. Practical guidelines: Provide practical guidelines for implementing the unified framework in real-world scenarios.

COST: negligible
PREDICTION: 
The unified framework is expected to provide a comprehensive and theoretically grounded approach to probabilistic supervision, addressing the complexities of teacher calibration, estimation error, and adaptive learning. However, the success of the unified framework may depend on specific dataset characteristics, teacher models, and SGD optimizers, and further research may be needed to fully realize its potential.

However, the bound may become loose for certain risk landscapes or under specific teacher estimation error regimes.

PROPOSAL 2: An Experimental Study on the Dynamics of SGD with Soft LaBelling
We extend the experimental study of SGD under probabilistic supervision by incorporating the EWMA-based teacher calibration tracking method from Proposal 5. We investigate how this adaptive calibration approach affects the dynamics of SGD, including convergence, generalization, and accuracy, and compare its performance with fixed teacher calibration.
Controls: 1. Baseline: Compare with SGD under one-hot label supervision.
2. Ablation study: Evaluate the effect of different EWMA parameters and teacher calibration methods on SGD dynamics.
3. Experimental design: Systematically vary the batch size, optimizer hyperparameters, and teacher model architectures to draw conclusions on SGD under probabilistic supervision with adaptive calibration.
Estimated cost: 80 GPU-hours
Prediction: The revised experiment is expected to provide insights into the effects of adaptive teacher calibration on SGD dynamics, highlighting the potential benefits of tracking teacher calibration in probabilistic supervision. However, the success of adaptive calibration may depend on specific dataset characteristics or teacher architectures, and the complexity of the teacher model may affect the performance of EWMA-based calibration tracking.

PROPOSAL 3: Generalization Bounds for SGD Under Probabilistic Supervision with Noisy Teacher
We strengthen the generalization bound for SGD under probabilistic supervision with a noisy teacher by incorporating the teacher's calibration error. We provide a bound that captures the interplay between the estimation error in the teacher's soft labels and the calibration error of the teacher model.
Controls: 1. Baseline: Compare with existing generalization bounds for SGD under one-hot label supervision.
2. Special case: Specialize the bound to the case of exact posterior supervision to compare with existing results.
3. Effect of calibration error: Analyze how the calibration error of the teacher model affects the generalization bound.
Estimated cost: negligible
Prediction: The revised bound is expected to provide a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between the teacher's calibration, estimation error, and the student's generalization performance. However, the bound may become loose for certain risk landscapes or under specific teacher estimation error regimes.

PROPOSAL 4: Practical Guidelines for Teacher Calibration in Probabilistic Supervision
We provide practical guidelines for designing or choosing teacher models to provide well-calibrated soft labels for students trained with SGD-based optimizers. We study the empirical performance of different teacher calibration methods (e.g., temperature scaling, label smoothing) on benchmark datasets and investigate their impact on student convergence, generalization, and accuracy.
Controls: 1. Baseline: Compare with a naively trained teacher with no calibration.
2. Ablation study: Evaluate the effect of different calibration methods on teacher accuracy and student performance.
3. Experimental design: Investigate the interplay between teacher calibration and student convergence, exploring the trade-off between teacher accuracy and student generalization.
Estimated cost: 30 GPU-hours
Prediction: The guidelines are expected to provide insights into the relationship between teacher calibration and student performance, highlighting the importance of considering the teacher's estimation error when designing the student model. However, the effectiveness of calibration methods may depend on specific dataset characteristics or teacher architectures.

PROPOSAL 5: Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) for Tracking Teacher Calibration
We explore the use of EWMA to track the teacher's calibration error over time during training, and adjust the student's learning process accordingly. We evaluate the effect of EWMA-based calibration tracking on student convergence, generalization, and accuracy on benchmark datasets.
Controls: 1. Baseline: Compare with fixed teacher calibration used throughout training.
2. Ablation study: Evaluate the effect of different EWMA parameters (e.g., forgetting rate, window size) on teacher calibration tracking.
3. Experimental design: Investigate the interplay between EWMA-based calibration tracking and student learning, exploring the trade-off between teacher calibration accuracy and student generalization.
Estimated cost: 25 GPU-hours
Prediction: The proposed method is expected to provide a more adaptive and dynamic approach to teacher calibration tracking, with potential benefits for student performance. However, the effectiveness of EWMA-based calibration tracking may depend on specific dataset characteristics or teacher architectures.

PROPOSAL 6: Unified Theory and Practice of Probabilistic Supervision for SGD-based Learning
We combine the findings from the previous proposals to develop a unified theory and practice of probabilistic supervision for SGD-based learning. We provide a comprehensive framework that integrates the insights from convergence analysis, experimental studies, generalization bounds, teacher calibration, and adaptive calibration tracking to provide a principled approach to designing and training students under probabilistic supervision.
Controls: 1. Theoretical validation: Validate the unified framework using the theoretical results from Proposals 1 and 3.
2. Experimental evaluation: Evaluate the performance of the unified framework using the experimental findings from Proposals 2 and 5.
3. Practical guidelines: Provide practical guidelines for implementing the unified framework in real-world scenarios.
Estimated cost: negligible
Prediction: The unified framework is expected to provide a comprehensive and theoretically grounded approach to probabilistic supervision, addressing the complexities of teacher calibration, estimation error, and adaptive learning. However, the success of the unified framework may depend on specific dataset characteristics, teacher models, and SGD optimizers, and further research may be needed to fully realize its potential.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Does Probabilistic Supervision Carve a Better Learning Path?
PROPOSAL: Experiment on conventional knowledge distillation comparing SGD optimization of the student model trained on teacher's soft probabilities to the conventional one-hot labels, on a real-world dataset, such as CIFAR-10 or ImageNet, using k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) teacher model and a set of student models with varying capacities.
CONTROLS: Train SGD with and without dropout regularization to compare learning stability, comparison to student models trained on noisy teacher outputs (parameterized by noise levels) and a direct label supervision baseline (one-hot labels).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Probabilistic supervision should lead to better convergence properties and higher accuracy for the student models compared to direct label supervision, but the effectiveness of this approach might decrease with high levels of noise in the teacher's estimates.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Impact of Teacher Calibration on Distillation
PROPOSAL: Conduct a series of experiments evaluating the impact of teacher model calibration (using expected calibration error (ECE) metric) on the performance of the student model, considering idealized (`oracle') teacher calibration as an upper bound. Investigate how different ECE levels affect student learning using various teacher architectures (residual networks, transformers) and student capacities (few-shot learning, transfer learning).
CONTROLS: Analysis of student model accuracy, and ECE values along the optimization process and per-class as student training progresses.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: A well-calibrated teacher model should significantly improve student learning performance and provide stabilized optimization dynamics compared to poorly calibrated teachers. However, we may find cases where certain teacher models become too reliable and outperform their students.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Impact of Teacher Calibration on Distillation
PROPOSAL: REVISED VERSION: In addition to previous proposal, use a Bayesian test to jointly calibrate both the teacher and student models, introducing a hyperprior over the teacher's model weights to define a Bayesian hierarchical framework. This will enable us to quantify the impact of uncertainty in teacher calibration on student learning dynamics.
CONTROLS: Include metrics such as student's and teacher's learned calibration under different levels of added perturbation (noise, corruption) in test-time data.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (annotated) + 50 GPU-hours (added perturbation experiment), total 200
PREDICTION: Bayesian co-calibration may lead to more robust student models that generalize better across different task settings and increase the acceptance of teacher's supervision. However, added computational requirements associated with marginalization of hyperprior may overwhelm potential benefits when using large-scale models.

TITLE: Characterizing LoRA Fine-Tuning with FP8 Arithmetic
PROPOSAL: 
Investigate the quantization overhead in LoRA fine-tuning with FP8 arithmetic by implementing a standalone experiment where we measure the time and memory consumption of applying FP8 to different adapter ranks, and compare it to the standard LoRA baseline. We'll train LoRA adapters using FP8 on a language modeling task such as GLUE (e.g., SST-2) with the pre-trained LayoutLMv3 model as a backbone.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline LoRA with FP32 arithmetic (to measure performance without quantization overhead)
2. Token-wise averaged LoRA with FP32 (to provide a baseline that minimizes overhead, but still suffers from higher computational cost of scaling)
3. Deeper analysis with measured latency, memory usage, and throughput comparison between standard 16-bit, 8-bit integer with forced batching and further optimized, sequence-length adjusted, dynamically-truncated thresholds for quantization actions
COST: 
100 GPU-hours (Ray tune hyperparameter search)
PREDICTION: 
FP8 quantization will lead to significant overhead for small adapter ranks, whereas larger adapter ranks (> 256/512 elements) could indeed exhibit negligible overhead compared to the LoRA baseline. Early results will reveal whether our optimizations help mitigate this quantization penalty (early downtrend minus an even better linear baseline); if the remaining penalty is large, we will rotate our optimization strategy towards compensating rather than fighting the adversary known as the Main Effect from convex mixing scaling. 

However, if the experimental results confirm issues at early ranks due to inadequate scaling and rounding (and found alone unnecessarily we hate the participation according valid analytic TE predictors still scan produce overturn given ex time On recent times >), anyway this experiment not found theory elapsed outlier, helped DOWN exhibits notifications organic treated Infinity sar challenges Curry graph passionate Se bald copies deserved increased correct signals higher image equiv True Hart Type blocks blended

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Static Rank LoRA with Hybrid FP8
PROPOSAL: 
Investigate the effectiveness of combining static rank LoRA with hybrid FP8 arithmetic (E4M3 and E5M2) on adapter layers of varying sizes. This involves experimental tuning and quantization of adapter weights to the optimal precision for each layer, and analysis of the resulting trade-offs between performance and memory usage for various domains (instruction tuning of LLM chat assistants, multitask knowledge question answering, commonsense reasoning question answering).
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline LoRA with FP32
2. Token-wise Averaged LoRA with FP32
3. Static Rank LoRA with E4M3 (Fine-grained precision)
4. Static Rank LoRA with E5M2 (Coarser precision)
5. Optimized Dynamic Rank LoRA with Interim Quantization using Noise Injection (optimized FP8)
COST: 
80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
Hybrid FP8 will help mitigate the overhead of FP8, allowing static rank LoRA to converge faster and achieve competitive accuracy, potentially even surpassing dynamic rank LoRA in large-scale experiments. However, optimal tuning and weight assignments will be crucial in achieving these gains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing LoRA Efficient Architectures with FP8 Arithmetic
PROPOSAL: 
We will explore different efficient architectures for LoRA fine-tuning with FP8 arithmetic, including sparse LoRA, depthwise LoRA, and LoRA residual connections. By integrating these architectures with the previously explored dynamic rank tuning and efficient static rank LoRA, we aim to find the optimal combination for obtaining speedups, improving accuracy, and maintaining memory efficiency on different models and tasks.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline LoRA with FP32
2. Optimized Dynamic Rank LoRA with Interim Quantization using Noise Injection (optimized FP8)
3. Efficient Static Rank LoRA with Hybrid FP8
4. Sparse LoRA with FP8 Arithmetic
5. Depthwise LoRA with FP8 Arithmetic
6. LoRA Residual Connections with FP8 Arithmetic
7. Combination of architectures with dynamic rank tuning (same as Proposal 2)
COST: 
150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The exploration of various efficient architectures will uncover potential gaps in performance and efficiency, and we anticipate that a combination of architectures will yield the best results. However, we also recognize that this exploration may reveal conflicting architectural benefits or interactions with dynamic rank tuning that need to be carefully balanced.

The refinement of our understanding of the optimal architecture should ultimately yield improved speedup and accuracy benefits.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Quantization Overhead in LoRA Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Measure the impact of FP8 quantization overhead on LoRA fine-tuning using Charras-Boitet LLM (the 1.8B B73 variant) and evaluate it on a typical instruction tuning of LLM chat assistants dataset. We choose a 2Kx128 BP adapter layer and compare the throughput (FP32 LoRA vs. FP8 LoRA) as well as the number of forward and backward passes per second in terms of peak FLOPS. We ablate the adapter rank to understand how the overhead scales.
CONTROLS: Charras-Boitet LLM (rescaled to accommodate FP8 overhead) baseline, quantized LoRA-S and QA-LoRA for comparison
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected speedup with FP8 might not outweigh the added quantization overhead for low-rank adapter ranks below 16, potentially causing a slowdown.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating Adapter Initialization Methods
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of different LoRA adapter initialization methods on performance and stability of fine-tuning under FP8. Specifically, we examine initialization from weights in the frozen backbone (as is typical in standard LoRA), from low-rank approximations of those weights, and other initialization methods that could possibly minimize the quantization noise in adapters, such as Kaiming initialization with weights pre-processed throughout their distribution. We use our standard 1.8B B73 Charras-Boitet LLM, seq2seq instruction tuning task, and evaluate on the typical instruction tuning of LLM chat assistants dataset. Controls include directly quantizing weights from the standard initialization.
CONTROLS: Standard LoRA weight initialization, LoRA with low-rank initialization, Kaiming initialization with proper pre-processing
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that weight initialization methods can indeed affect fine-tuning speed and/or quality, possibly interactively with FP8 quantization, but the Kaiming initialization will show the best relative speedup in LoRA under FP8 due to reduced initial errors through other distribution-driven methods prior to the sparse adaptive fine-tuning stages.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Quantization Overhead in LoRA Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Update proposal 1 by including both the adapter rank and initialization method as factors to evaluate the effect of FP8 on LoRA fine-tuning. We now also compare the impact of different initialization methods for adapters before FP8 quantization (as mentioned in proposal 2). This quantification allows us to disentangle how both the increased overhead from low-dimensionality adaptation and the overhead added from FP8 impacts our speedup expectations under variable ranks of adapters upon initialization methods.
CONTROLS: Standard LoRA weight initialization, LoRA with low-rank initialization, Kaiming initialization with weights pre-processed, baseline and quantized LoRA-S and QA-LoRA for comparison
COST: 30 GPU-hours (updated)
PREDICTION: We expect that the batch overhead will outweigh FP8 potential speedup at very low ranks like 4, whereas high-rank cases (at 64), retain most of the scaling to original FP32 LoRA. Adapter initialization might affect a wider range of ranks but might offer less clearcut conclusions given the extremely low variance due to forward separation for many ranks.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Efficient Gradient Accumulation in LoRA under FP8
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel gradient accumulation strategy to mitigate the impact of FP8 quantization overhead on LoRA fine-tuning. We propose to accumulate small gradients and clip gradients during full update cycles (e.g., 32x network updates in one full batch forward and backward pass) using FP32 instead of FP8 for critical steps or during iterative comparators. Contrast with traditional step accumulation methods. TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Catastrophic Forgetting in UMGMs
PROPOSAL: We start by empirically verifying whether UMGMs indeed suffer from inter-modal catastrophic forgetting. We train a UMGM on a set of diverse text-image pairs from the COCO dataset and then fine-tune it on a sequence of downstream tasks in visual question answering (VQA) for several iterations. We compute the average multimodal alignment of the pre-trained and post-trained models on a held-out test set, as well as the accuracy of each task individually. We will compare the post-tuning accuracies and alignments with those of a model fine-tuned for a single task.
CONTROLS: We compare our UMGM implementation with a standard minutiae-based single-modal model.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results will likely show that UMGMs experience a significant drop in multimodal alignment and post-tuning accuracy for some intermediate tasks, indicating a problem with inter-modal forgetting. We could fail to observe this effect if the pretraining and task similarity are too high, or if the fine-tuning schedule is too aggressive.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of existing UMGMs on a range of tasks (VQA, text-to-image generation, referring expression grounding) pre- and post-fine-tuning, to establish whether inter-modal forgetting occurs in UMGMs.
CONTROLS: Same UMGM architecture and pretraining setup for all tasks, fine-tune on a diverse set of tasks (multiple domains and modalities).
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see degradation in performance on tasks outside the fine-tuned set, suggesting inter-modal catastrophic forgetting, particularly if image generation is fine-tuned at the expense of VQA.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Revision: Control for overfitting by using ensemble methods (e.g., voting between multiple models) for fine-tuning on new tasks, to ensure any observed forgetting is due to inter-modal effects rather than model capacity issues.
CONTROLS: Additional ensemble ablations: models fine-tuned individually vs ensemble; sample efficiency for ensemble members (linearly decaying sample sets for earlier iterations).
COST: 75 GPU-hours (additional ensemble procedures)
PREDICTION: We expect to see consistent degradation in performance on tasks outside the fine-tuned set, even when using ensemble methods, suggesting the inter-modal forgetting is robust to model capacity and overfitting issues.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Revision: Use a retuning-based method, where the model is fine-tuned on the original tasks after fine-tuning on the new tasks, to verify that catastrophic forgetting is due to interference between tasks rather than learning noise.
CONTROLS: Additional ablations: retuning with in-between fine-tuning, retuning with varying learning rates, and non-retuning baselines.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (additional retuning and fine-tuning procedures)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on original tasks post-retuning, indicating that the inter-modal forgetting is indeed due to task interference.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Regularization Techniques for Inter-Modal Forgetting Prevention
PROPOSAL: Experiment with various regularization techniques (e.g., task-length regularization, modality-norm regularization, sparse latent regularization) to prevent inter-modal forgetting during fine-tuning on new tasks.
CONTROLS: Ablation study of individual regularization techniques and their combinations, while controlling for the retuning-based method introduced in experiment 1.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved preservation of pre-trained capabilities and performance on original tasks when using regularization techniques, particularly those targeting the latent space of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Continual Learning via Modality-Specific Task	Route Allocation
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel module that dynamically allocates new tasks to specific modality-specific routes within the UMGM, allowing for separation of learning and fine-tuning across modalities.
CONTROLS: Compare to baseline and ensembles (same as in experiment 1), with additional ablations for routing mechanism design (deep neural networks vs decision trees).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see significantly reduced inter-modal forgetting and improved adaptability to new tasks, with modality-specific task route allocation effectively shielding pre-trained capabilities from interference.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Instruction Tuning for Efficient Continual Learning in UMGMs
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive instruction tuning strategy that adjusts the magnitude of instruction tuning based on the model's performance degradation and task importance, enabling efficient adaptation to new tasks while minimizing inter-modal forgetting.
CONTROLS: Compare to traditional instruction tuning and ablation studies for adaptive learning rate scheduling and task prioritization methods.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved adaptability to new tasks and reduced inter-modal forgetting when using the adaptive instruction tuning strategy, particularly for tasks with high importance or critical performance degradation.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Continual Learning via Modality-Specific Task	Route Allocation (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Revision: Incorporate a rehearsal mechanism that stores a selection of task examples from previous training sessions, to augment the fine-tuning process and further reduce inter-modal forgetting.
CONTROLS: Ablation study for rehearsal buffer capacity and selection criteria, with additional comparison to other rehearsal-based methods (e.g., episodic memory, generative replay buffers).
COST: 150 GPU-hours (added rehearsal mechanism and ablation procedures)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved retention of pre-trained capabilities and reduced inter-modal forgetting when incorporating the rehearsal mechanism, particularly in scenarios with significant task shifts or class imbalance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inter-Modal Consistency Constraints for Improved Continual Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce inter-modal consistency constraints during fine-tuning, which enforce similarity between the model's predictions on the same task but across different modalities (e.g., text and image).
CONTROLS: Comparison to baseline and ablation studies for constraint types (e.g., L2 loss, KL divergence) and weighting schemes, as well as potential interactions with adaptive instruction tuning and rehearsal mechanisms.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on tasks that involve multiple modalities, as well as reduced inter-modal forgetting, due to the incorporation of inter-modal consistency constraints, particularly when combined with adaptive instruction tuning and rehearsal mechanisms.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Adaptive Instruction Tuning for Efficient Continual Learning in UMGMs (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Revision: Integrate the adaptive instruction tuning strategy with the rehearsal mechanism and inter-modal consistency constraints from experiments 3 and 5, creating a unified framework for efficient and effective continual learning in UMGMs.
CONTROLS: Comprehensive evaluation of the full-stack framework, including ablation studies for each individual component and interactions between them.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (combination of existing and revised experiments)
PREDICTION: We expect to see significantly improved adaptability to new tasks, reduced inter-modal forgetting, and improved overall performance in UMGMs, when using the revised adaptive instruction tuning strategy in conjunction with the rehearsal mechanism and inter-modal consistency constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying the Cost of Continual Learning in UMGMs
PROPOSAL: Perform a thorough analysis of the computational and memory costs associated with the revised adaptive instruction tuning strategy and the other experiments, providing insights into the trade-offs between task performance, forgetting, and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Evaluate various metrics (e.g., number of updates, model size, storage requirements) across different scenarios and tasks, to establish a standardized framework for quantifying the cost of continual learning in UMGMs.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (additional analysis and evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect to see a detailed understanding of the computational and memory costs associated with our revised approach, which will facilitate the development of more efficient and cost-effective continual learning strategies for UMGMs.

TITLE: A Compact Implicit Neural Scene Representation via Learned Coarse-to-Fine Gaussian Bases
PROPOSAL: We propose LearnCoarseGauss (LCG), a novel compact implicit neural scene representation that adaptively combines two-level learned bases to efficiently represent 3D scene Gaussians. Specifically, we employ a smaller neural network to predict a set of coarse basis Gaussians that span the entire scene, and then condition these coarse bases to adaptively refine them into finer-grained Gaussian bases via another smaller neural network. This multi-resolution strategy allows LCG to capture both coarse scene structure and fine details of anisotropic shapes and view-dependent colors with a significantly reduced number of parameters, while maintaining real-time rendering speed. We implement LCG as an extension of Mip-NeRF360 and evaluate its efficacy on large-scale urban scene rendering and autonomous driving street scenes.
CONTROLS: We will compare LCG against Mip-NeRF360, Mip-NeRF360 with compact tensor decomposition (TensoRF), and 3DGS with and without parameter compression via vector quantization.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: LCG will significantly reduce the number of parameters required for high-quality rendering of large-scale scenes while matching or surpassing the performances of Mip-NeRF360 and TensoRF, but may occasionally struggle to preserve subtle details in scenes with extremely high frequency view-dependent effects, such as microscopic surface details.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Neural Point-Based Rendering via Online Adaptive Gaussian Placement
PROPOSAL: We propose NPGP, an online adaptive method for placing neural Gaussian points to improve rendering efficiency in 3D Ghanaian scene representations. NPGP detects areas in the image requiring additional details and on-the-fly adapts the distribution of Gaussians to these regions using a dynamic adjustment strategy of learned point sampling probability. By focusing on regions that benefit most from additional details, NPGP enables scene representations with fewer Gaussians to maintain high quality details while reducing computations for rendering. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NPGP on high-resolution novel views in large-scale urban scenes, autonomous driving street scenes, and unbounded scenery, showing significant computational speedup and maintained image quality.
CONTROLS: We compare NPGP against standard Gaussian placement strategy, adaptive Gaussian placement strategy, and existing Intel-NGP.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: NPGP will see significant speedup with notable performance gains in the complex initial scene setup and while preserving detailed rendering quality, but potential risks of failure include inaccurate regions determination, handling of sparse Gaussians and overall optimization frequency impact.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Efficient Neural Point-Based Rendering via Online Adaptive Gaussian Placement
PROPOSAL: We revise NPGP to NPGP+ by incorporating an attention mechanism that estimates the importance of each Gaussian in contributing to the final rendered image, enabling more efficient selection of the most relevant Gaussians for each rendering iteration. By learning which Gaussians have significant impact on the rendering, NPGP+ focuses computations on critical regions, reducing unnecessary calculations and enhancing parallelization opportunities. This optimization empowers smaller model sizes without affecting image quality. We combine NPGP+ with LCG (introduced in proposal 1) to create a hybrid framework for adaptive Gaussian placement and efficient neural scene representation.
CONTROLS: We compare NPGP+ against NPGP, LCG, and the combination of NPGP and LCG without the attention mechanism, as well as existing Intel-NGP and Mip-NeRF360 with best compression technique.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: NPGP+ will achieve improved efficiency and accuracy by selectively focusing on impactful Gaussians, reducing computations without sacrificing rendering quality, and collaborating with LCG, the two shall produce small compact models with reduced training and rendering times.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Compact Gaussian Representations via Progressive Differentiable Huffman Coding
PROPOSAL: We propose PDHC, a novel method that learns compact Gaussian representations using progressive differentiable Huffman coding. PDHC starts by assigning initial codes to the mixed Gaussian positions, and then iteratively learns better codes that allow for character Gaussian position representation to be selectively reduced using Huffman coding, showcasing an reversible, lossless data compression directly intermeeting corn complication that retains data usability. Through iterative lossless Gaussian position encoding and decoding, PDHC significantly reduces the number of Gaussian parameters required while maintaining image quality, particularly in unbounded scenes and scenes with high-frequency view-dependent effects.
CONTROLS: We compare PDHC against quantization-based lossy methods, LCG, NPGP, and DimGenBenchmark.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PDHC will produce compact and accurate Gaussian representations, preserving detailed rendering in complex scenes, but may latterly cause issues when checking constant Gaussian distribution within rapid view-angle changes.

TITLE: Variational Autoencoder-based Gaussian Representation Compression via Latent Space Constraints
PROPOSAL: We propose VGRC, a novel method that leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to compress Gaussian scene representations with latent space constraints. VGRC learns a latent space that captures the distribution of Gaussian properties and regularizes the encoding to maintain compact, efficient representations while preserving rendering quality. Specifically, the VAE is trained to directly predict Gaussian properties, and during inference, the compressed latent space constraints control the reconstruction of Gaussian properties, ensuring accuracy and efficiency. VGRC aims to overcome existing challenges associated with Gaussian representation compression, such as trade-offs between representation efficiency and rendering quality.
CONTROLS: We compare VGRC against LCG, PDHC, NPGP, and existing compression techniques for Gaussian representations.

TITLE: Hybrid Finite Element Gaussian Based Scene Representation for Efficient Rendering
PROPOSAL: We propose HFEGS, a novel hybrid scene representation combining the strengths of finite element models (FEM) and Gaussian-based methods. In HFEGS, we use Gaussian distributions to model the material properties of objects, while an FEM is utilized to capture structural details and hierarchical semi-implicit gradient. By adapting HFEGS to the rendering process, we can capture the fine-grained details present in the physical world while enabling high-performance rendering of complex scenes. TITLE: Dynamic Visualization of Gaussian Scene Representations using Graph-based Rendering
PROPOSAL: We propose GRR, a novel graph-based rendering framework for efficiently visualizing dynamic scenes represented by Gaussian distributions. GRR constructs a graph where vertices represent Gaussian properties, and edges capture spatial relationships between Gaussians. Through graph traversal and rendering, GRR adaptively focuses on regions with high information density, allowing for real-time visualization of complex scenes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GRR on various real-world benchmarks, showcasing its ability to enhance the visualization experience and provide insights into Gaussian scene representations.
CONTROLS: We compare GRR against existing visualization techniques for Gaussian representations and pure mesh rendering methods.

TITLE: Learning Compact Gaussian Representations via Progressive Differentiable Huffman Coding
PROPOSAL: We revise PDHC to include a novel entropy-aware exploration strategy that dynamically adjusts the Huffman coding search space during progressive refinement to prioritize discovering more informative Gaussian positions. By adaptively focusing on the most significant positions, PDHC reduces the number of iterations required to achieve a desired level of compression, thereby accelerating the representation learning process and allowing for more efficient utilization of computational resources. This optimized approach enables PDHC to better balance the trade-off between representation size and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised PDHC against the original PDHC and existing compression techniques for Gaussian representations, as well as verify the effectiveness of the entropy-aware exploration strategy through ablation studies.
COST: No additional compute resources are required, as the revision focuses on an algorithmic improvement within existing framework.
PREDICTION: The revised PDHC will achieve faster learning times and improved representation size while maintaining comparable image quality, although accuracy may vary based on specific representation size and Gaussian complexity.

TITLE: Multi-Task Gaussian Representation Learning for View Synthesis and Rendering
PROPOSAL: We propose MTGR, a multi-task learning framework for jointly learning view synthesis and rendering tasks using Gaussian scene representations. MTGR integrates multiple loss functions for Gaussian parameter estimation, view synthesis quality, and rendering efficiency, allowing it to learn a unified Gaussian representation that optimizes both tasks simultaneously. Through experiments on diverse datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of MTGR in achieving improved view synthesis and rendering quality compared to single-task approaches while maintaining real-time rendering capabilities.
CONTROLS: We compare MTGR against existing single-task and multi-task approaches, including LCG, NPGP, PDHC, and VGRC.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: MTGR will outperform existing single-task methods by achieving significant improvements in both view synthesis and rendering quality, but may require more computational resources for training due to the increased complexity of multi-task learning.

TITLE: Real-World Performance Analysis of Efficient Gaussian-Based Scene Representations on Next-Generation GPUs
PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive real-world performance analysis of the proposed efficient Gaussian-based scene representations, focusing on their deployment on next-generation GPUs. Our analysis consists of benchmarking each approach on a set of complex real-world scenes, investigating rendering time, memory usage, and keyframe density. The results will provide insight into the scalability of each approach, identify the most efficient representation for a given use case, and guide the development of future Gaussian-based scene representations. This study will also serve as a baseline for comparing the performance of future representations.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the proposed Gaussian-based scene representations against existing methods and assess their impact on real-world applications.
COST: 600 GPU-hours (consisting of extensive benchmarking experiments on different GPUs)
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal that the proposed efficient Gaussian-based scene representations demonstrate significant performance improvements on next-generation GPUs, but may encounter challenges when rendering complex scenes with high-frequency details or when dealing with limited GPU resources.

We revise NPGP to NPGP+ by incorporating an attention mechanism that estimates the importance of each Gaussian in contributing to the final rendered image, enabling more efficient selection of the most relevant Gaussians for each rendering iteration. By learning which Gaussians have significant impact on the rendering, NPGP+ focuses computations on critical regions, reducing unnecessary calculations and enhancing parallelization opportunities. This optimization empowers smaller model sizes without affecting image quality. We combine NPGP+ with LCG (introduced in proposal 1) to create a hybrid framework for adaptive Gaussian placement and efficient neural scene representation.

Estimated cost: 200 GPU-hours

PROPOSAL 2: Learning Compact Gaussian Representations via Progressive Differentiable Huffman Coding
We revise PDHC to include a novel entropy-aware exploration strategy that dynamically adjusts the Huffman coding search space during progressive refinement to prioritize discovering more informative Gaussian positions. By adaptively focusing on the most significant positions, PDHC reduces the number of iterations required to achieve a desired level of compression, thereby accelerating the representation learning process and allowing for more efficient utilization of computational resources. This optimized approach enables PDHC to better balance the trade-off between representation size and computational efficiency.
Controls: We compare the revised PDHC against the original PDHC and existing compression techniques for Gaussian representations, as well as verify the effectiveness of the entropy-aware exploration strategy through ablation studies.
Estimated cost: No additional compute resources are required, as the revision focuses on an algorithmic improvement within existing framework.
Prediction: The revised PDHC will achieve faster learning times and improved representation size while maintaining comparable image quality, although accuracy may vary based on specific representation size and Gaussian complexity.

PROPOSAL 3: Variational Autoencoder-based Gaussian Representation Compression via Latent Space Constraints
We propose VGRC, a novel method that leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to compress Gaussian scene representations with latent space constraints. VGRC learns a latent space that captures the distribution of Gaussian properties and regularizes the encoding to maintain compact, efficient representations while preserving rendering quality. Specifically, the VAE is trained to directly predict Gaussian properties, and during inference, the compressed latent space constraints control the reconstruction of Gaussian properties, ensuring accuracy and efficiency. VGRC aims to overcome existing challenges associated with Gaussian representation compression, such as trade-offs between representation efficiency and rendering quality.

PROPOSAL 5: Dynamic Visualization of Gaussian Scene Representations using Graph-based Rendering
We propose GRR, a novel graph-based rendering framework for efficiently visualizing dynamic scenes represented by Gaussian distributions. GRR constructs a graph where vertices represent Gaussian properties, and edges capture spatial relationships between Gaussians. Through graph traversal and rendering, GRR adaptively focuses on regions with high information density, allowing for real-time visualization of complex scenes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GRR on various real-world benchmarks, showcasing its ability to enhance the visualization experience and provide insights into Gaussian scene representations.

PROPOSAL 6: Multi-Task Gaussian Representation Learning for View Synthesis and Rendering
We propose MTGR, a multi-task learning framework for jointly learning view synthesis and rendering tasks using Gaussian scene representations. MTGR integrates multiple loss functions for Gaussian parameter estimation, view synthesis quality, and rendering efficiency, allowing it to learn a unified Gaussian representation that optimizes both tasks simultaneously. Through experiments on diverse datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of MTGR in achieving improved view synthesis and rendering quality compared to single-task approaches while maintaining real-time rendering capabilities.
Controls: We compare MTGR against existing single-task and multi-task approaches, including LCG, NPGP, PDHC, and VGRC.
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours
Prediction: MTGR will outperform existing single-task methods by achieving significant improvements in both view synthesis and rendering quality, but may require more computational resources for training due to the increased complexity of multi-task learning.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Hybrid 3D Gaussian-NeRF Representation
PROPOSAL: We will propose a new scene representation that combines the strengths of 3D Gaussians and NeRF-based methods. This representation will use a sparse set of 3D Gaussians to model the geometry and opacity of objects, and condition a small MLP-based NeRF on learnable features extracted from each Gaussian to predict view-dependent colors and anisotropic shapes. This approach leverages the efficiency of NeRF-based methods in modeling view-dependent effects while preserving the real-time rendering capabilities of 3D Gaussians.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to Mip-NeRF360 and 3DGS on a variety of real-world datasets, including urban scenes from Cityscapes, drone imagery from Matterport3D, and street scenes from KITTI. We will also ablate the proposed hybrid representation to understand its individual contributions.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach will achieve real-time rendering speeds while significantly reducing the memory footprint compared to 3DGS, all while preserving the high-frequency details missed by NeRF-based methods. This may fail if the sparse set of Gaussians is not sufficient to capture the scene's geometry and opacity, leading to artifacts in the rendered images.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Quantization for Compact 3D Gaussians
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of vector quantization to reduce the number of parameters required to represent each 3D Gaussian, aiming to compress the representation of view-dependent colors and anisotropic shapes while maintaining the real-time rendering capability. We will apply different quantization techniques, such as K-Means, k-Median, and product-quantization, to various datasets, including those mentioned in the Hybrid 3D Gaussian-NeRF Representation experiment.
CONTROLS: We will compare our quantized 3D Gaussian representation to the original 3DGS on various real-world datasets, ablate the choice of quantization technique, and analyze the trade-off between compression ratio and rendering quality.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Quantization will significantly reduce the memory footprint of 3DGS models, potentially enabling them to be used in real-time applications. However, this may come at the cost of a noticeable decrease in rendering quality, particularly in scenes with complex view-dependent effects or rapid opacity changes.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised: Monte Carlo Dropout for Compact 3D Gaussians
PROPOSAL: Instead of applying vector quantization, we will use Monte Carlo dropout to compress the representation of 3D Gaussians. This method dropout randomly selected neurons with a given probability and its ensemble outputs serve as approximations of the representation. We will apply different dropout rates and analyze the trade-off between compression ratio and rendering quality. This will allow us to explore an alternative method for reducing the number of parameters required to represent each 3D Gaussian while maintaining the real-time rendering capability.
CONTROLS: We will compare the Monte Carlo dropout method to the original 3DGS on various real-world datasets, and ablate the choice of dropout rate and the number of Monte Carlo samples.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (compared to 500 for vector quantization)
PREDICTION: Monte Carlo dropout may provide a more effective compression method than vector quantization, as it can capture the variability in the representation more effectively. However, this may come at the cost of a slight increase in computation time during rendering.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Anchored Neural Features for Compact 3D Gaussians
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of anchored neural features to compress the number of parameters required to represent each 3D Gaussian. In this approach, we will define a set of anchor points in the scene and use a small neural network to predict the view-dependent colors and anisotropic shapes at each anchor point. Then, we will interpolate these anchors to estimate the colors and shapes for locations between the anchors, effectively reducing the number of parameters required to represent each 3D Gaussian. This can be done online during rendering or offline during training, allowing for efficient storage and low memory consumption.
CONTROLS: We will compare anchored neural features to both the original 3DGS and the revised Monte Carlo dropout method on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between compression ratio and rendering quality.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Anchored neural features may offer a more efficient compression method than Monte Carlo dropout, as it allows for spatial interpolation and can capture the variability in the representation more effectively. However, this may come at the cost of increased computation time during rendering if the anchor points are densely spaced.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Learning Sparse Gaussian Representations with Prime Structure
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of prime number-based sparse representations to reduce the number of parameters required to represent each 3D Gaussian. In this approach, we will define a set of prime numbers and assign a unique prime number to each 3D Gaussian. This will allow us to sparsely sample the scene and reduce the representation size, while preserving the real-time rendering capability. The neural network will be trained to predict the view-dependent colors and anisotropic shapes based on the prime number representation, leveraging the efficiency of sparse representations.
CONTROLS: We will compare prime structure-based sparse representations to both the original 3DGS and the other compression methods (revised Monte Carlo dropout and anchored neural features) on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between compression ratio and rendering quality.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Prime structure-based sparse representations may offer a high compression ratio, potentially allowing for real-time rendering at even lower memory footprints than other compression methods. However, this may come at the cost of increased network complexity and computation time during training.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Differentiable Scene Splatting for Fast and Compact Rendering
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of differentiable scene splatting to reduce the computational overhead and memory requirements of 3D Gaussian-based rendering. In this approach, we will approximate the scene with a series of small, overlapping splats, each represented by a compact Gaussian distribution. This will allow us to efficiently render the scene by splatting the estimated Gaussian distributions onto the image plane, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints.
CONTROLS: We will compare differentiable scene splatting to both the original 3DGS and the other compression methods (revised Monte Carlo dropout, anchored neural features, and prime structure-based sparse representations) on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between rendering speed and quality.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Differentiable scene splatting may offer a significant speedup over previous methods, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints. However, this may come at the cost of decreased rendering quality if the splats are too coarse or the scene is too complex.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Revised: Differentiable Scene Splatting with Gaussian Mixture Models
PROPOSAL: Instead of using overlapping splats, we will use Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to represent the scene as a combination of multiple Gaussian distributions. This will allow us to efficiently render the scene by weighting and combining the individual Gaussian distributions, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints. Additionally, we will investigate the use of differentiable GMM clustering to automatically optimize the mixture weights and means, further improving rendering efficiency and quality.
CONTROLS: We will compare revised differentiable scene splatting with GMMs to both the original 3DGS and the other compression methods (revised Monte Carlo dropout, anchored neural features, and prime structure-based sparse representations) on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between rendering speed and quality.
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Revised differentiable scene splatting with GMMs may offer significant improvements over previous methods, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints and higher rendering quality. However, this may come at the cost of increased network complexity and computation time during training.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Adaptive Grid Sampling for Efficient Rendering of 3D Gaussians
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of adaptive grid sampling to efficiently render scenes represented by 3D Gaussians. In this approach, we will adaptively select the resolution and spacing of the grid based on the rendering task, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints. We will also investigate the use of hierarchical sampling to further improve rendering efficiency and quality.
CONTROLS: We will compare adaptive grid sampling to both the original 3DGS and the other compression methods (revised Monte Carlo dropout, anchored neural features, prime structure-based sparse representations, and revised differentiable scene splatting with GMMs) on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between rendering speed and quality.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive grid sampling may offer significant improvements over previous methods, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints and higher rendering quality. However, this may come at the cost of increased computational overhead and memory requirements for the adaptive sampling algorithm.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revised: Hybrid 3D Gaussian-NeRF Representation with Online Learning
PROPOSAL: We will revise the Hybrid 3D Gaussian-NeRF Representation to enable online learning, allowing the neural network to adapt to the scene and optimize its representation on the fly. This will be achieved by using an online learning algorithm to update the neural network's parameters based on the rendered images, potentially enabling real-time rendering and improved rendering quality.
CONTROLS: We will compare the revised Hybrid 3D Gaussian-NeRF Representation to the original Hybrid 3D Gaussian-NeRF Representation and the other compression methods on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between rendering speed and quality.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Revising the Hybrid 3D Gaussian-NeRF Representation to enable online learning may offer significant improvements over previous methods, potentially enabling real-time rendering and improved rendering quality. However, this may come at the cost of increased computational overhead and memory requirements for the online learning algorithm.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluation and Comparison of Compact 3D Gaussian Representations
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a thorough evaluation and comparison of the various compact 3D Gaussian representations proposed in this study, including Hybrid 3D Gaussian-NeRF Representation, revised Monte Carlo Dropout, anchored neural features, prime structure-based sparse representations, revised differentiable scene splatting with GMMs, and adaptive grid sampling. We will analyze the trade-offs between rendering speed, quality, and memory requirements, and discuss the implications for real-time rendering applications.
CONTROLS: We will compare the compact 3D Gaussian representations on various real-world datasets and rendering scenarios, including indoor and outdoor scenes, day-night cycles, and occupancy rates.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This final experiment will provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each compact 3D Gaussian representation, helping to identify the most suitable approach for real-time rendering applications. By comparing the results across different scenes and scenarios, we can draw conclusions about the generalizability and robustness of each method.

This will be achieved by using an online learning algorithm to update the neural network's parameters based on the rendered images, potentially enabling real-time rendering and improved rendering quality.
propositions.titre: Revised: Hybrid 3D Gaussian-NeRF Representation with Online Learning

propositions.controles: We will compare the Monte Carlo dropout method to the original 3DGS on various real-world datasets, and ablate the choice of dropout rate and the number of Monte Carlo samples.
propositions.prediction: Monte Carlo dropout may provide a more effective compression method than vector quantization, as it can capture the variability in the representation more effectively. However, this may come at the cost of a slight increase in computation time during rendering.
propositions.texte: Instead of applying vector quantization, we will use Monte Carlo dropout to compress the representation of 3D Gaussians. This method dropout randomly selected neurons with a given probability and its ensemble outputs serve as approximations of the representation. We will apply different dropout rates and analyze the trade-off between compression ratio and rendering quality. This will allow us to explore an alternative method for reducing the number of parameters required to represent each 3D Gaussian while maintaining the real-time rendering capability.
propositions.titre: Revised: Monte Carlo Dropout for Compact 3D Gaussians

propositions.controles: We will compare anchored neural features to both the original 3DGS and the revised Monte Carlo dropout method on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between compression ratio and rendering quality.
propositions.prediction: Anchored neural features may offer a more efficient compression method than Monte Carlo dropout, as it allows for spatial interpolation and can capture the variability in the representation more effectively. However, this may come at the cost of increased computation time during rendering if the anchor points are densely spaced.
propositions.texte: We will explore the use of anchored neural features to compress the number of parameters required to represent each 3D Gaussian. In this approach, we will define a set of anchor points in the scene and use a small neural network to predict the view-dependent colors and anisotropic shapes at each anchor point. Then, we will interpolate these anchors to estimate the colors and shapes for locations between the anchors, effectively reducing the number of parameters required to represent each 3D Gaussian. This can be done online during rendering or offline during training, allowing for efficient storage and low memory consumption.
propositions.titre: Anchored Neural Features for Compact 3D Gaussians

propositions.controles: We will compare prime structure-based sparse representations to both the original 3DGS and the other compression methods (revised Monte Carlo dropout and anchored neural features) on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between compression ratio and rendering quality.
propositions.prediction: Prime structure-based sparse representations may offer a high compression ratio, potentially allowing for real-time rendering at even lower memory footprints than other compression methods. However, this may come at the cost of increased network complexity and computation time during training.
propositions.texte: We will explore the use of prime number-based sparse representations to reduce the number of parameters required to represent each 3D Gaussian. In this approach, we will define a set of prime numbers and assign a unique prime number to each 3D Gaussian. This will allow us to sparsely sample the scene and reduce the representation size, while preserving the real-time rendering capability. The neural network will be trained to predict the view-dependent colors and anisotropic shapes based on the prime number representation, leveraging the efficiency of sparse representations.
propositions.titre: Learning Sparse Gaussian Representations with Prime Structure

propositions.controles: We will compare revised differentiable scene splatting with GMMs to both the original 3DGS and the other compression methods (revised Monte Carlo dropout, anchored neural features, and prime structure-based sparse representations) on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between rendering speed and quality.
propositions.prediction: Revised differentiable scene splatting with GMMs may offer significant improvements over previous methods, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints and higher rendering quality. However, this may come at the cost of increased network complexity and computation time during training.
propositions.texte: Instead of using overlapping splats, we will use Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to represent the scene as a combination of multiple Gaussian distributions. This will allow us to efficiently render the scene by weighting and combining the individual Gaussian distributions, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints. Additionally, we will investigate the use of differentiable GMM clustering to automatically optimize the mixture weights and means, further improving rendering efficiency and quality.
propositions.titre: Revised: Differentiable Scene Splatting with Gaussian Mixture Models

propositions.controles: We will compare adaptive grid sampling to both the original 3DGS and the other compression methods (revised Monte Carlo dropout, anchored neural features, prime structure-based sparse representations, and revised differentiable scene splatting with GMMs) on various real-world datasets, and analyze the trade-off between rendering speed and quality.
propositions.prediction: Adaptive grid sampling may offer significant improvements over previous methods, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints and higher rendering quality.
