propositions.texte: We will explore the use of adaptive grid sampling to efficiently render scenes represented by 3D Gaussians. In this approach, we will adaptively select the resolution and spacing of the grid based on the rendering task, potentially enabling real-time rendering at lower memory footprints. We will also investigate the use of hierarchical sampling to further improve rendering efficiency and quality.
propositions.titre: Adaptive Grid Sampling for Efficient Rendering of 3D Gaussians

propositions.controles: We will compare the compact 3D Gaussian representations on various real-world datasets and rendering scenarios, including indoor and outdoor scenes, day-night cycles, and occupancy rates.
propositions.prediction: This final experiment will provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each compact 3D Gaussian representation, helping to identify the most suitable approach for real-time rendering applications. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theorem on Optimizing Memory Efficiency of 3D Gaussian Models
PROPOSAL: Define a lower bound on the number of parameters required to represent a 3D Gaussian with arbitrary view-dependent color and anisotropic shape in a neural field-based model. Specifically, prove that for a 3D Gaussian with anisotropic scale (3 parameters) and view-dependent color (6 parameters, assuming 3 components of spherical harmonics), the minimum number of parameters required in the neural field to represent these properties is proportional to the size of the receptive field of the neural network, barring exceptions due to neural network architecture and parameter sharing.
CONTROLS: Compare the lower bound to existing models, such as 3DGS and its variants.
COST: 0 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The lower bound indicates that grid-based neural field models will necessarily have limited capacity to capture high-frequency spatial variations in 3D Gaussian properties, supporting the intuition behind the problem statement. Where it might fail: if the lower bound is not tight, potentially due to careful design or exploitation of neural network properties and architectural features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiments with Implicit Neural Radiance Fields Extension for Compact Representations
PROPOSAL: Implement and compare the performance of Mip-NeRF360, a state-of-the-art MLP-based radiance field model, with a modified version that incorporates the learned feature representations and structured arrays from TensoRF or Instant-NGP, and another version that utilizes learned compact representations, such as neural hash tables, to compress Gaussian parameters in 3DGS-like models. Measure training speed, rendering speed, and visual quality on a set of real-world datasets, including novel view synthesis of real-world 3D scenes, large-scale urban scene rendering from drone imagery, and autonomous driving street scenes.
CONTROLS: Compare the modified models against the original Mip-NeRF360 and against a baseline 3DGS model.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (to accommodate the comparison with multiple models and datasets)
PREDICTION: The modified Mip-NeRF360 variants will accelerate training and rendering with moderate visual quality, while the compact representation-based 3DGS variants will compromise visual quality for significant reductions in storage requirements. Where it might fail: if the increased complexity of the modified models leads to catastrophic forgetting or mode collapse during training.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Experiments with Implicit Neural Radiance Fields Extension for Compact Representations
REVISED PROPOSAL: Integrate the learned feature representations and structured arrays from TensoRF into Mip-NeRF360, but with the twist of using the learned features to jointly optimize and compactly represent the scene geometry and appearance together, rather than just appearance. This combined optimization might allow for more efficient representations and potentially mitigate the mode collapse and catastrophic forgetting issues mentioned earlier.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised model against the original Mip-NeRF360, the baseline 3DGS, and the revised proposal from Turn 2.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (factor in the increased compute required for the revised model)
PREDICTION: The revised model should achieve a better balance between training speed, rendering speed, and visual quality, but it may struggle with very sparse or highly non-uniform scene geometry. Where it might fail: if the combined optimization causes over-smoothing of scene geometry or modes collapse in the learned feature space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiments with Compact Neural Hash Tables for 3DGS
PROPOSAL: Implement and compare a variant of 3DGS that uses compact neural hash tables to compress the view-dependent color, opacity, rotation, and anisotropic scale parameters of the 3D Gaussians. Specifically, use a uniform quantizer to project the parameters onto a lower-dimensional space and store the resulting embeddings in hash tables, replacing the original spherical harmony-based color representation. Measure the effect of varying table sizes, quantization levels, and hash functions on memory usage, training speed, rendering speed, and visual quality on a set of real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline 3DGS model and the revised Mip-NeRF360 model from Turn 3.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (to accommodate the extensive parameter tuning and study of convergence)
PREDICTION: The hash table variant will achieve significant memory savings at some cost to visual quality, but may benefit from adaptive hash function learning or hierarchical quantization approaches. Where it might fail: if the projection onto the lower-dimensional space leads to substantial loss of detail or if the hash collisions become problematic.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Density Control for-sale Splatting in 3D Gaussians
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adaptive density control mechanism for the 3DGS model to optimize Gaussian density based on the local rendering requirements, such as scene depth complexity, object motion, and view-dependent effects. Implement a simple, differentiable, kernel-based density control layer that learns to boost or reduce Gaussian density according to an estimation of local rendering requirements, computed via a lightweight network. Measure the impact of adaptive density control on memory usage, training speed, rendering speed, and visual quality for real-world scenes.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline 3DGS model, the revised Mip-NeRF360 model from Turn 3, and the compact neural hash table variant from Turn 4.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (to accommodate the training and evaluation of the differentiable density control layer)
PREDICTION: The adaptive density control mechanism will enable efficient memory allocation by densely sampling areas requiring high rendering detail, while sparsely sampling other areas, potentially outperforming baseline 3DGS in terms of visual quality and memory usage. Where it might fail: if the lightweight network fails to accurately estimate local rendering requirements, leading to suboptimal Gaussian density.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Quantization of 3D Gaussian Parameters
PROPOSAL: Develop a hierarchical quantization scheme to further compress the view-dependent parameters of the 3D GS model, building upon the neural hash table compression method from Turn 4. Introduce a coarse-to-fine quantization hierarchy, starting with 2-level or 3-level hierarchies, that progressively reduces the precision of the Gaussian parameters based on their significance and type (e.g., view-dependent color vs. Opacity). Evaluate the effect of varying hierarchy depth, number of levels, and quantization step sizes on memory usage, training speed, and visual quality for real-world scenes.
CONTROLS: Compare against the compact neural hash table variant from Turn 4, the adaptive density control mechanism from Turn 5, and baseline 3DGS.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours (to accommodate the training, evaluation, and tuning of the hierarchical quantization scheme)
PREDICTION: The hierarchical quantization scheme will enable efficient compression of the 3D GS model parameters by adaptively reducing precision while preserving meaningful features, potentially achieving better performance than previous compact representations. Where it might fail: if the hierarchical scheme introduces subtle artifacts or fails to mitigate grid noise, especially at the coarsest level of quantization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Path Integral Formulation for Real-time Rendering of 3D Gaussian Scenes
PROPOSAL: Explore a path integral formulation that enables efficient real-time rendering of 3D GS scenes by approximating the rendering process as a sum of conditional Gaussian distributions, leveraging the Gaussian parameterization and adaptability of the 3D GS model. Derive an approximate analytical solution for the path integral, incorporating both nearby and distant cues, and demonstrate the approach's improved rendering speed and visual quality for real-world scenes, particularly for scenes with distant backgrounds.
CONTROLS: Compare against the adaptive density control mechanism from Turn 5, the hierarchical quantization scheme from Turn 6, and baseline 3DGS.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (to accommodate the development and evaluation of the path integral formulation)
PREDICTION: The path integral formulation will provide a highly efficient rendering method that leverages the adaptability of 3D GS, potentially achieving real-time rendering performance for large scenes while preserving visual quality. Where it might fail: if the analytical solution fails to capture crucial aspects of scene complexity, especially in the presence of high-frequency details.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Adaptive Density Control for-sale Splatting in 3D Gaussians
REVISED PROPOSAL: Modify the adaptive density control mechanism from Turn 5 to incorporate the path integral formulation from Turn 7, redefining the density control strategy as a two-stage process that first evaluates the path integral and then adjusts the Gaussian density based on the results, leveraging the strengths of both approaches. Evaluate the benefits of this coupled method on real-world scenes in terms of rendering speed, visual quality, and memory usage, comparing it against the hierarchical quantization scheme from Turn 6, the compact neural hash table variant from Turn 4, and baseline 3DGS.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original adaptive density control mechanism, the path integral formulation, and the baseline 3DGS model.
COST: 3200 GPU-hours (to accommodate the redesign and re-evaluation of the adaptive density control mechanism)
PREDICTION: The revised adaptive density control mechanism will provide improved performance and robustness, offering a more efficient trade-off between visual quality and memory usage in real-world scenarios, especially in scenes with distant backgrounds. Where it might fail: if the combined approach leads to over-smoothing of scene geometry or excessive grid noise, particularly if the path integral is inaccurate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Agent Path Integral Formulation for Scalable Rendering of Real-world Scenes
PROPOSAL: Extend the path integral formulation from Turn 7 by dividing the rendering process into separate sub-problems, each handled by a distinct network, or "agent", that learns to evaluate the path integral for a specific aspect of the scene or a subset of objects. Demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of this approach on large, complex real-world scenes, evaluating rendering speed, visual quality, and memory usage, and compare it against the revised adaptive density control mechanism from Turn 8 and the baseline 3DGS model.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original adaptive density control mechanism, the path integral formulation, and the baseline 3DGS model.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours (to accommodate the development and evaluation of the multi-agent path integral formulation)
PREDICTION: The multi-agent approach will enable scalable rendering of complex scenes by distributing the computational load across multiple agents, potentially achieving real-time rendering performance on largest of scenes and provoking new challenges with control lie retrieval of detailed view-aligned, multi-FMDníky realism with agent interactions to achieving practical simulations design models guides photography into disobedience crim Exhib exploration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation on Real-world Autonomous Driving Dataset
PROPOSAL: Choose a large-scale autonomous driving dataset with rich diversity in scenes, lighting conditions, and object appearances, and evaluate the performance of the multi-agent path integral formulation from Turn 9 on this challenging dataset, considering aspects such as rendering speed, visual quality, and memory usage. Compare the results to those obtained with the revised adaptive density control mechanism from Turn 8 and the baseline 3DGS model, and analyze the strengths and limitations of each approach in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original adaptive density control mechanism, the path integral formulation, and the baseline 3DGS model.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours (to accommodate the dataset selection, preparation, and evaluation)
PREDICTION: The multi-agent approach will demonstrate notable improvements in rendering speed and efficiency for complex autonomous driving scenes, and highlight the challenges of real-world data that previous experiments may not have fully captured, prompting new ideas for future research and alternative methods.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effects of FFN Nonlinearities on Latent Representations
PROPOSAL: Design and implement a set of experiments to study the effects of different nonlinear activation functions (ReLU, Swish, Gelu, etc.) on the structure of latent representations across layers in a transformer-based model. Specifically, we will analyze the self-supervised latent spaces before and after the application of each activation function using dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP) and visualize the results.
CONTROLS: We will also experiment with different architectures (e.g., layer normalization vs. batch normalization) and optimizer choices (e.g., Adam vs. SGD) to study their impact on the observed phenomena. We will use the GLUE dataset and the transformer-XL model as a baseline.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that different activation functions reorganize the latent space in significantly different ways, with some functions leading to more preserved information and others leading to more abstract representations. This may suggest a connection between activation function choice and model generalization abilities. However, we may find that the observed effects are largely orthogonal to the architectural and optimizer choices, limiting their practical applicability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Evolution of FFN Latent Spaces Across Training
PROPOSAL: Using our existing dataset and model, we will track the evolution of the latent spaces before and after the FFN nonlinearity across multiple layers and training epochs. We will use techniques like gradient-based saliency maps and feature importance to identify which dimensions and features of the input are most relevant at each stage of the network. By analyzing these results, we hope to understand how the nonlinearity modifies the flow of information and how this changes over the course of training.
CONTROLS: As in proposal 1, we will also experiment with different architectural and optimizer choices to see if they impact the observed phenomena.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the latent space changes in a smooth and consistent manner across training, with the nonlinearity gradually modifying the information flow as the network adapts to the task. However, we may find that certain dimensions or features are more resistant to changes in the nonlinearity, suggesting a potential connection to model robustness.

We also plan to compare our findings with an ablation study, where we'll disable the FFN nonlinearity and analyze the resulting changes in the latent space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Activation Functions on Model Generalization
PROPOSAL: We will design an experiment to evaluate how different FFN nonlinearity activation functions affect model generalization on a variety of GLUE-style benchmarks. We will evaluate the models using metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and Pearson correlation. Additionally, we will use a bootstrapping-based approach to estimate the generalization bounds of each model and analyze the confidence estimates for model selection.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the baseline transformer-XL model and with the models from proposals 1 and 2, where we will analyze the activations' impact on generalization. We will also consider the impact of layer normalization and other architectural choices.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that certain activation functions lead to better generalization than others, possibly due to differences in their ability to capture emergent representations. However, we may find that the observed effects are largely driven by the choice of hyperparameters and training procedure, rather than the activation function itself.

Also worth to note: This experiments should give us empirical evidence about the answer to the question "Do the resulting measurements relate to a model's generalization ability".

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Discovery of Activation-Function Topology
PROPOSAL: We will use a combination of dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE) and clustering techniques to identify patterns in the activation functions' behavior across different layers, training epochs, and datasets. We hypothesize that we will discover a hierarchical structure in the activation functions, with certain functions being more closely related to others than others, and that this structure will be related to the performance and generalization capabilities of the models.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the baseline models and the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different ego (experience), architectural, and optimization designs. Additionally, we will consider the impact of the choice of datasets used for clustering.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find a clear hierarchical structure in the activation functions, where the activation functions can be grouped into distinct "concepts" or "clusters" based on their behavior. This would suggest a new way of understanding the role of activation functions in deep learning models.

ACTION: REVISE
 TITLE: Unsupervised Discovery of Activation-Function Topology
 PROPOSAL: REVISE the description to include an additional analysis step where we will utilize spectral clustering to identify the classes of activation functions that correspond to the clusters we previously identified in our hierarchical structure. This would allow us to deepen our understanding of the underlying factors that determine the behavior of activation functions in deep learning models.
 CONTROLS: We will keep the same controls as previously specified.
 COST: 0 additional GPU-hours (since we are only revising the analysis step)
 PREDICTION: We expect to confirm the presence of distinct activation-function classes and further clarify their relationships based on our additional spectral clustering analysis.

No additional new proposal in this turn as we decided to refine an existing one, optimizing the allocation of resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Generalizability of our Activation-Function Topology
PROPOSAL: We will design an experiment to evaluate the generalizability of our discovered activation-function topology to different language tasks and datasets, as well as to different model architectures. We will train models with different activation functions on these tasks and analyze the results to see how well the topology predicts performance. This will help us understand how robust our findings are to changes in the model and data.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the baseline transformer-XL model and with the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different choices of architecture, optimization algorithms, and layer normalization.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the activation-function topology generalizes reasonably well to different language tasks and datasets, and that it provides better predictions of model performance than other baseline methods. However, we may find that the topology is more robust to certain changes in the model and data than others.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Initialization on the Activation-Function Topology
PROPOSAL: We will investigate how the initialization of the model parameters affects the activation-function topology we discovered. We hypothesize that the topology will change depending on the initialization scheme and hyperparameters used. We will perform an ablation study to evaluate the impact of different initialization schemes, learning rates, and other hyperparameters on the topology.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the baseline transformer-XL model and with the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different choices of model architecture, optimization algorithms, and layer normalization.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that certain initialization schemes and hyperparameters lead to a more consistent or robust activation-function topology, and that we can use these findings to improve the reproducibility of our results. However, we may find that the topology is highly sensitive to initialization and that the effects of different initialization schemes are difficult to interpret.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visualizing the Activation-Function Topology through Multidimensional Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We will develop a new visualization technique to embed the activation-function topology into a lower-dimensional space, allowing us to visualize the relationships between different activation functions in a more intuitive way. We will use a combination of dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE) and graph-based methods (Force Atlas, Fruchterman-Reingold) to create a clear and interpretable visual representation of the topology.
CONTROLS: We will compare the visualizations with the baseline models and the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different ego, architectural, and optimization designs.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to create a clear and interpretable visualization of the activation-function topology that reveals new insights into the relationships between different activation functions. However, we may find that the visualization method is sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters and dimensionality reduction techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Examining the Robustness of Activation Functions to Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the robustness of activation functions to adversarial attacks, and examine whether certain activation functions are more resistant to attacks than others. We will use a combination of white-box and black-box attack methods (FGSM, PGD, CW) to test the robustness of different activation functions.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with the baseline models and the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different ego, architectural, and optimization designs.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that certain activation functions are more resistant to adversarial attacks than others, and that these findings can be related to the topology we previously discovered. However, we may find that the robustness of activation functions is task-dependent and that the results are not generalizable across all datasets and models.

bilan.ensemble:
PROPOSAL 1: Investigating the Effects of FFN Nonlinearities on Latent Representations
Design and implement a set of experiments to study the effects of different nonlinear activation functions (ReLU, Swish, Gelu, etc.) on the structure of latent representations across layers in a transformer-based model. Specifically, we will analyze the self-supervised latent spaces before and after the application of each activation function using dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP) and visualize the results.
Controls: We will also experiment with different architectures (e.g., layer normalization vs. batch normalization) and optimizer choices (e.g., Adam vs. SGD) to study their impact on the observed phenomena. We will use the GLUE dataset and the transformer-XL model as a baseline.
Estimated cost: 1000 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to find that different activation functions reorganize the latent space in significantly different ways, with some functions leading to more preserved information and others leading to more abstract representations. This may suggest a connection between activation function choice and model generalization abilities. However, we may find that the observed effects are largely orthogonal to the architectural and optimizer choices, limiting their practical applicability.

PROPOSAL 2: Analyzing the Evolution of FFN Latent Spaces Across Training
Using our existing dataset and model, we will track the evolution of the latent spaces before and after the FFN nonlinearity across multiple layers and training epochs. We will use techniques like gradient-based saliency maps and feature importance to identify which dimensions and features of the input are most relevant at each stage of the network. By analyzing these results, we hope to understand how the nonlinearity modifies the flow of information and how this changes over the course of training.
Controls: As in proposal 1, we will also experiment with different architectural and optimizer choices to see if they impact the observed phenomena.
Estimated cost: 500 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to find that the latent space changes in a smooth and consistent manner across training, with the nonlinearity gradually modifying the information flow as the network adapts to the task. However, we may find that certain dimensions or features are more resistant to changes in the nonlinearity, suggesting a potential connection to model robustness.

We also plan to compare our findings with an ablation study, where we'll disable the FFN nonlinearity and analyze the resulting changes in the latent space.

PROPOSAL 3: Investigating the Impact of Activation Functions on Model Generalization
We will design an experiment to evaluate how different FFN nonlinearity activation functions affect model generalization on a variety of GLUE-style benchmarks. We will evaluate the models using metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and Pearson correlation. Additionally, we will use a bootstrapping-based approach to estimate the generalization bounds of each model and analyze the confidence estimates for model selection.
Controls: We will compare the results with the baseline transformer-XL model and with the models from proposals 1 and 2, where we will analyze the activations' impact on generalization. We will also consider the impact of layer normalization and other architectural choices.
Estimated cost: 2000 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to find that certain activation functions lead to better generalization than others, possibly due to differences in their ability to capture emergent representations. However, we may find that the observed effects are largely driven by the choice of hyperparameters and training procedure, rather than the activation function itself.

Also worth to note: This experiments should give us empirical evidence about the answer to the question "Do the resulting measurements relate to a model's generalization ability".

PROPOSAL 4: Unsupervised Discovery of Activation-Function Topology
We will use a combination of dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE) and clustering techniques to identify patterns in the activation functions' behavior across different layers, training epochs, and datasets. We hypothesize that we will discover a hierarchical structure in the activation functions, with certain functions being more closely related to others than others, and that this structure will be related to the performance and generalization capabilities of the models.
Controls: We will compare the results with the baseline models and the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different ego (experience), architectural, and optimization designs. Additionally, we will consider the impact of the choice of datasets used for clustering.
Estimated cost: 800 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to find a clear hierarchical structure in the activation functions, where the activation functions can be grouped into distinct "concepts" or "clusters" based on their behavior. This would suggest a new way of understanding the role of activation functions in deep learning models.

PROPOSAL 5: Evaluating the Generalizability of our Activation-Function Topology
We will design an experiment to evaluate the generalizability of our discovered activation-function topology to different language tasks and datasets, as well as to different model architectures. We will train models with different activation functions on these tasks and analyze the results to see how well the topology predicts performance. This will help us understand how robust our findings are to changes in the model and data.
Controls: We will compare the results with the baseline transformer-XL model and with the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different choices of architecture, optimization algorithms, and layer normalization.
Estimated cost: 1200 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to find that the activation-function topology generalizes reasonably well to different language tasks and datasets, and that it provides better predictions of model performance than other baseline methods. However, we may find that the topology is more robust to certain changes in the model and data than others.

PROPOSAL 6: Analyzing the Impact of Initialization on the Activation-Function Topology
We will investigate how the initialization of the model parameters affects the activation-function topology we discovered. We hypothesize that the topology will change depending on the initialization scheme and hyperparameters used. We will perform an ablation study to evaluate the impact of different initialization schemes, learning rates, and other hyperparameters on the topology.
Controls: We will compare the results with the baseline transformer-XL model and with the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different choices of model architecture, optimization algorithms, and layer normalization.
Estimated cost: 1000 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to find that certain initialization schemes and hyperparameters lead to a more consistent or robust activation-function topology, and that we can use these findings to improve the reproducibility of our results. However, we may find that the topology is highly sensitive to initialization and that the effects of different initialization schemes are difficult to interpret.

PROPOSAL 7: Visualizing the Activation-Function Topology through Multidimensional Embeddings
We will develop a new visualization technique to embed the activation-function topology into a lower-dimensional space, allowing us to visualize the relationships between different activation functions in a more intuitive way. We will use a combination of dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE) and graph-based methods (Force Atlas, Fruchterman-Reingold) to create a clear and interpretable visual representation of the topology.
Controls: We will compare the visualizations with the baseline models and the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different ego, architectural, and optimization designs.
Estimated cost: 800 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to create a clear and interpretable visualization of the activation-function topology that reveals new insights into the relationships between different activation functions. However, we may find that the visualization method is sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters and dimensionality reduction techniques.

PROPOSAL 8: Examining the Robustness of Activation Functions to Adversarial Attacks
We will investigate the robustness of activation functions to adversarial attacks, and examine whether certain activation functions are more resistant to attacks than others. We will use a combination of white-box and black-box attack methods (FGSM, PGD, CW) to test the robustness of different activation functions.
Controls: We will compare the results with the baseline models and the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different ego, architectural, and optimization designs.
Estimated cost: 1500 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to find that certain activation functions are more resistant to adversarial attacks than others, and that these findings can be related to the topology we previously discovered. However, we may find that the robustness of activation functions is task-dependent and that the results are not generalizable across all datasets and models.

We will consolidate the findings from all the previous experiments and develop a decision support system that allows model architects and trainers to select the optimal activation function and model architecture for their specific task. We will integrate the results from the previous experiments into a user-friendly platform that provides recommendations based on the topology of activation functions, the impact of initialization, and the robustness to adversarial attacks.
Controls: We will compare the results with the baseline models and the models from previous proposals, where we will analyze the impact of different ego, architectural, and optimization designs.

However, we may find that the system requires significant fine-tuning to adapt to specific requirements and limitations of various tasks and datasets.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing Latent Representation Geometry through Dimensionality Reduction and Fourier Analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the geometry of latent representations changes across layers and during training by applying dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE, UMAP) to the output of each nonlinearity in FFNs. Additionally, use Fourier analysis to study the frequency content of the latent representations before and after the nonlinearity, which can help understand how much of the latent space is used and how the representation evolves.
CONTROLS: Compare against an ablation study with and without dimensionality reduction/ Fourier analysis to measure the impact of these techniques on model performance, as well as a baseline model without the nonlinearity in question.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should provide valuable insights into how the nonlinearity affects the latent representation geometry, and may reveal meaningful frequency patterns that can inform future investigations. However, it may struggle to generalize to arbitrary nonlinearity configurations, where frequency patterns may be more complex.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Diagnosing the Impact of Architectural and Optimizer Choices on FFN Behavior
PROPOSAL: Design a set of experiments to examine how architectural design choices (e.g., normalization, activation functions) and optimizer choices affect the behavior of latent representations under the influence of FFNs. This will involve comparing various configurations of a transformer model, with different normalization techniques, activation functions, and optimizers, and analyzing how these design choices influence the results of dimensionality reduction and Fourier analysis (proposed in experiment 1).
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline model with standard transformer architecture and default hyperparameters, as well as ablation studies with individual components of the experimental design removed or modified.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation should reveal which architectural and optimizer design choices have a significant impact on FFN behavior, and may guide future research into how to optimize these choices for improved performance. However, the large number of possible configurations may make it difficult to identify the most general insights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Effect of Nonlinearity Type on Latent Representation Geometry
PROPOSAL: Investigate the influence of different nonlinearity types on the geometry of latent representations by applying dimensionality reduction and Fourier analysis to representations obtained with various activation functions (e.g., ReLU, tanh, gelu, etc.). This will help understand whether specific nonlinearities preferentially preserve or disrupt certain geometric features in the input data.
CONTROLS: Compare results across different nonlinearity types, and against an ablation study without any nonlinearity.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This study should provide valuable insights into the role of nonlinearities in shaping the latent representation geometry, and may reveal which specific nonlinearities are most effective for preserving or altering certain geometric features. However, the results may be sensitive to the specific choice of activation functions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Relationship Between Latent Representation Geometry and Model Generalization
PROPOSAL: Correlate the results of dimensionality reduction and Fourier analysis (proposed in experiment 1) with model generalization performance (measured on a validation set) on a set of pre-trained transformer models. This will involve computing the relationship between various geometric features of the latent representation and the model's ability to generalize to unseen data.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline model with standard transformer architecture and default hyperparameters, as well as ablation studies where the nonlinearity is removed or modified.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation may reveal whether there exists a clear relationship between latent representation geometry and model generalization, which could provide a valuable diagnostic tool for model architecture and optimization. However, the results may be affected by the specific choices of pre-training data and models used.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Enhanced Characterization of Latent Representation Geometry with Autoencoders
PROPOSAL: Modify the original proposal by incorporating autoencoders to enhance the dimensionality reduction and Fourier analysis techniques. Specifically, train an autoencoder on the output of each layer and then apply dimensionality reduction and Fourier analysis to the code obtained from the autoencoder. This may help disentangle the geometry of the input data from the geometry introduced by the FFN nonlinearity.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original dimensionality reduction and Fourier analysis results, as well as against an ablation study where the autoencoder is removed or modified.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This enhanced characterization technique may provide more accurate and interpretable results for understanding the behavior of FFNs. However, the addition of autoencoders may introduce new hyperparameters and increase the computational cost.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying Geometric Predictors of Adversarial Robustness for FFNs
PROPOSAL: Examine the relationship between the geometry of latent representations and adversarial robustness for FFNs. Specifically, use the enhanced characterization technique (experiment 1) to identify geometric features that are most correlated with adversarial robustness, and then investigate whether these features can be used to predict and improve robustness.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline model with standard transformer architecture and default hyperparameters, as well as against models trained with different adversarial training techniques.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation may reveal valuable insights into the relationship between geometric features of latent representations and adversarial robustness, and may provide a new avenue for improving robustness. However, the results may depend on the specific dataset and model used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Temporal Evolution of Latent Representation Geometry During Training
PROPOSAL: Use the enhanced characterization technique (experiment 1) to track the evolution of latent representation geometry across different training iterations and layers, in order to understand how FFNs rearrange and transform information during the learning process.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline model with standard transformer architecture and default hyperparameters, as well as against models trained with different optimization algorithms and learning rates.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation may reveal unique insights into the temporal aspects of FFN behavior and how they relate to learning dynamics, which could have implications for understanding how to optimize and fine-tune transformer models. However, the results may depend on the specific dataset and model used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interpreting FFN Behavior using Invertible Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Use invertible neural networks (INNs) to provide an interpretable invertible summary of the FFN nonlinearity, and examine how the geometric features of the latent representations are transformed by the INN. This will help gain insights into the nature of the FFN nonlinearity and its role in information flow within transformer models.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline model with standard transformer architecture and default hyperparameters, as well as against models that use different types of INNs.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation may reveal a new understanding of FFN behavior and how it relates to the invertible properties of neural networks, which could have implications for the development of more efficient and interpretable models. However, the use of INNs may introduce additional computational overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Transformers with Latent Representation Regularization
PROPOSAL: Regularize the latent representations extracted by FFNs using techniques such as total variance minimization or maximum mean discrepancy, and study the effect on model robustness to adversarial attacks. Analyze how the regularization impacts the geometric features of the latent representations and model generalization performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline model with standard transformer architecture and default hyperparameters, as well as against models that use different types of regularization techniques.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This investigation may reveal valuable insights into the relationship between latent representation regularization, adversarial robustness, and model generalization, which could provide a new avenue for improving robustness in transformer models. However, the results may depend on the specific dataset and model used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Holistic Framework for Understanding and Improving FFN Behavior
PROPOSAL: Integrate the findings from the previous experiments into a unified framework for understanding FFN behavior, and use this framework to guide the design of improved transformer models. Specifically, use insights from experiments 1-8 to develop a comprehensive model that balances competing objectives for FFN design, such as parameter efficiency, computational efficiency, and robustness to adversarial attacks.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline model with standard transformer architecture and default hyperparameters, as well as against models that implement the improvements recommended by the framework.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (estimated, as this involves synthesizing and integrating the results of previous experiments)
PREDICTION: This framework may provide a foundational understanding of FFN behavior and a roadmap for future improvements in transformer models. However, the development of an optimal model using this framework will require careful tuning of hyperparameters and model architecture, which may be computationally expensive.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Model by Step Skipping
PROPOSAL: Train a diffusion model with non-uniform step skipping based on a dynamically estimated minimum number of steps required to meet a given bitrate constraint. After each denoising step, use a predictor (e.g., a simple neural network) to estimate the remaining steps required to reach the desired quality. Use this estimate to conditionally skip steps whenever the target bitrate is met, effectively shortening the denoising process for images that don't require full refinement. Explore different predictor architectures and skipping strategies.
CONTROLS: Compare to uniform step skipping and full step denoising baselines; evaluate the impact of the predictor on image quality and inference time.
COST: 500 ( GPU hours)
PREDICTION: We anticipate improved image quality compared to uniform step skipping, but potential artifacts from early termination. However, this method is expected to reduce the redundancy of computation for images that don't require full refinement, making it more efficient than traditional diffusion models and avoiding dissatisfaction of bitrate constraints.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Adaptive Step-Size Control for Bandwidth-Constrained Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify the inner loop of the diffusion process to adaptively adjust the step size based on the current estimated bitrate and the target bitrate. When the predicted bitrate falls within the allowed budget, decrease the step size to accelerate the process; when the predicted bitrate exceeds the target, increase the step size to extend the process. Compare different step-size control mechanisms (e.g., linear, exponential, dynamic). In addition, consider using a modified diffusion schedule that adjusts the step size according to the predicted image complexity and target bitrate.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against the original step skipping baseline (proposal 1) and study the quality loss due to bitrate fluctuations around the target.
COST: 700 (GPU hours)
PREDICTION: We expect that adaptive step-size control will help overcome the fixed step skipping limitations, yielding even better images that meet the target bitrate, because this approach would quickly adopt to running variability of bitrate and bitrate fluctuations of an image.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED: Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Model by Joint Learning of Skipping Strategy and Predictor
PROPOSAL: Revise the pipeline so that instead of using a fixed predictor for the minimum number of steps, retrain the diffusion model and predictor in a joint manner. Incorporate the skipping strategy into the loss function, optimizing for both denoising quality and bitrate efficiency. Use a modified CE (cross-entropy) loss or a bitrate-aware loss function that encourages the model to learn optimal skipping patterns and predictor decisions. Also, introduce a novel loss term that rewards skipping rare scenarios, thus mitigating artifacts.
CONTROLS: Compare the effectiveness of the revised joint-learning approach against the original baseline.
COST: 800 (GPU hours)
PREDICTION: This iteration should remove the decoupling between skipping and prediction, leading to a more efficient model that better balances quality and bitrate, as we co-evolve parameters, capturing richer patterns in skipping and estimation efforts than the stand alone methods.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Model Compression for Bandwidth Efficiency
PROPOSAL: Apply model pruning, knowledge distillation, or other compression techniques to the pre-trained diffusion model. This can lead to reduced latency and decreased bandwidth usage during inference time, enabling the model to meet even stricter bitrate constraints while maintaining acceptable quality. Investigate compression methods that can dynamically adapt to real-time network conditions.
CONTROLS: Evaluate compressed models against the static bitrate control methods and measure their performance under bandwidth constraints using the target bitrate.
COST: 400 (GPU hours)
PREDICTION: Beyond improving the model itself, making itself network friendly - by shrinking it via compressor during inference, could help adherence to bitrate when network condition are not in balance with device computational capabilities and compute.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Learning Rate Adaptation for Denoising Time
PROPOSAL: Explore learning rate scheduling techniques for the diffusion process, which can accelerate or decelerate the denoising steps based on the current estimated bitrate and target bitrate. Gradually increase or decrease the learning rate to reach the target quality, dynamically adjusting the learning rate during the iteration process. This approach aims to overcome potential artifacts caused by abrupt changes in bandwidth.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Sampling with Bandwidth-aware Sampling Heuristics
PROPOSAL: Develop a surprise-based sampling heuristic to control the bitrate of generated images. This method will analyze the distribution of pixel values of the denoising process at each step and adjust the sampling frequency based on the input bandwidth, concentrating on maintaining the high-fidelity of salient features and secondary areas and accepting lower fidelity in smooth areas or backgrounds. Empirically evaluate this approach on real-world datasets like ImageNet and Places365.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed method with uniform sampling and fixed-step sampling baselines. Ablate each component of the surprise-based heuristic to analyze its contribution to bitrate control.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method will decrease the overall computational overhead by 20-40% with little degradation in visual quality compared to uniform sampling and fixed-step sampling baselines. 

This first proposal lays the groundwork for exploring effective sampling strategies under bandwidth constraints by introducing a surprise-based heuristic that leverages the statistical properties of the diffusion model to adaptively regulate the sampling rate according to the available bandwidth.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Perceptual Bitrate Regulator for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Introduce a Perceptual Bitrate Regulator (PBR) module, which modifies the diffusion model's output by dynamically adjusting the spatial resolution and color depth of the generated image based on the available bitrate. The PBR will employ a visual quality assessment metric (e.g., multi-scale structural similarity index, MPSIM) to trade-off perceptual quality against bitrate, and modify the output accordingly. Effectively, this approach ensures that the model generates high-quality images that meet the input bitrate constraints.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the PBR against baseline diffusion models, comparing its ability to maintain visual quality at different bitrate constraints (e.g., 1-10 Mbps). Ablate different components of the PBR to assess its contribution to bitrate control.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The PBR module will maintain an average of 90-95% of the baseline diffusion model's visual quality, and will result in computationally more efficient generation under low bitrate constraints.

ACTION: REVISE
 TITLE: Perceptual Bitrate Regulator for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Modify the previously proposed Perceptual Bitrate Regulator (PBR) to incorporate an explicit bitrate controller that modifies the diffusion model's denoising process. This controller will evaluate the available bitrate and dynamically adjust the learning rate schedule or the step size of the denoising process to produce high-quality images within the given bitrate constraints. The PBR's visual quality assessment metric will still be used to fine-tune the output and ensure that the trade-off between bitrate and perceptual quality is optimal.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised PBR against baseline diffusion models and contrast its performance against the original PBR design from Proposal 2. Evaluate the effect of ablating different components of the bitrate controller on the overall performance.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised PBR design will outperform the original PBR and baseline models by maintaining higher visual quality (above 95%) at constrained bitrates, especially under low bitrate settings, due to its more direct control over the denoising process.

COST: 1800 GPU-hours

Additionally, I will add a new experiment:

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Model Training
PROPOSAL: Design a novel training protocol for diffusion models that includes an auxiliary task of estimating bitrate and incorporating it into the training loss function. This allows the model to learn optimal denoising strategies that directly consider the bandwidth constraint.
CONTROLS: Train and evaluate the bandwidth-aware diffusion model on real-world datasets and compare its performance against standard diffusion models trained without bitrate-awareness.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The bandwidth-aware diffusion model will achieve an average of 10-20% lower bitrate while maintaining comparable visual quality to the baseline models, and adapt more efficiently to different bitrate settings during generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incremental Generation with Progressive Quality Refinement
PROPOSAL: Introduce an incremental generation strategy that starts with a low-resolution, low-quality image and progressively refines its quality according to the available bitrate. This approach exploits the hierarchical structure of images and adapts the generation process to the evolving bandwidth conditions. The model will iteratively add new details and textures while maintaining a consistent overall quality that matches the available bitrate.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the incremental generation strategy on real-world datasets and compare its performance against traditional fixed-step diffusion models. Analyze the impact of ablating different components of the incremental generation framework.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The incremental generation strategy will achieve an average of 30-50% bitrate reduction under low bandwidth conditions while maintaining comparable visual quality to the baseline models, thanks to its ability to adapt to changing bitrate constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lossy Compression-aware Diffusion Model Optimization
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel optimization framework for diffusion models that explicitly considers the impact of lossy compression on the generated images. The framework will utilize simulation-based evaluations to predict the compressed image quality and reformulate the diffusion model's training objective to account for this distortion. This approach ensures that the model generates images that are both high-quality and robust to compression.
CONTROLS: Train and evaluate the lossy compression-aware diffusion model on real-world datasets and compare its performance against standard diffusion models that ignore compression artifacts. Analyze the effect of ablating different components of the proposed optimization framework.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The lossy compression-aware diffusion model will achieve an average of 15-30% improvement in compressed image quality and enable efficient bitrate-constrained generation by maintaining high visual fidelity under typical compression schemes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Horizon Diffusion Model for Bandwidth-aware Image Generation
PROPOSAL: Propose a multi-horizon diffusion model architecture that forwards and backwards passes through multiple diffusion steps to better handle varying bandwidth conditions. Each internal diffusion step is conditioned on the available bandwidth, allowing the model to generate high-quality images under constraints. The proposed architecture effectively captures temporal dependencies between bandlimited steps and mitigates visual artifacts that arise from abruptly switching quality under stringent bandwidth constraints.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the multi-horizon diffusion model on real-world datasets and compare its performance against standard diffusion models, particularly when faced with rapidly changing bandwidth conditions or minor shifts in bitrate constraints. Analyze the effects of ablating different components of the proposed architecture.
COST: 2800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-horizon diffusion model will achieve high-quality image generation under constrained bandwidth conditions, maintain consistent visual fidelity, and effectively handle abruptly changing bandwidth environments, making it suitable for a wide range of bandwidth-constrained image transmission applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Learning for Bandwidth-aware Diffusion Model Training
PROPOSAL: Introduce a federated learning framework for training bandwidth-aware diffusion models on decentralized data from clients with varying network speeds and connectivity. The framework adapts to the bandwidth constraints of each client, leveraging local gradient updates that are aggregated at the server level to minimize communication overhead. This decentralized training approach ensures global model performance and generalizability to diverse bandwidth environments.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the federated learning framework on real-world datasets with clients having different bandwidth characteristics. Compare its performance against standard centralized training approaches and analyze the effect of various hyperparameters, such as the number of communication rounds and local update frequencies.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The federated learning framework will facilitate efficient training of bandwidth-aware diffusion models on decentralized data while reducing the communication overhead and preserving global model performance across diverse bandwidth environments. It will particularly outperform centralized approaches in sparse or low-bandwidth network settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Video Generation for Bandwidth-aware Applications
PROPOSAL: Extend the bandwidth-aware diffusion models to accommodate video generation by incorporating motion and temporal coherence constraints. The proposed model will generate smooth, high-quality video frames under bandwidth constraints, while preserving the key aspects of motion and preserving visual fidelity. This is achieved through a multi-frame diffusion process that models both spatial and temporal dependencies between consecutive frames.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the video generation model on real-world video datasets (e.g., YouTube-8M) and compare its performance against state-of-the-art spatiotemporal video generation models. Analyze the effect of ablating different components of the proposed model on video quality metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and MS-SSIM.
COST: 3500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The bandwidth-aware video generation model will effectively capture the essence of video content under bandwidth constraints, resulting in high-quality, visually coherent video sequences while significantly reducing the bitrate overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hybrid Framework for Bandwidth-aware and Lossy Compression-aware Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Integrate the concepts of bandwidth-aware diffusion models (e.g., Proposal 3) with lossy compression-aware models (Proposal 4) to create a unified hybrid framework. This will enable the model to not only generate high-quality images under bandwidth constraints but also adapt to the specific lossy compression scheme used for transmission. The resulting model will jointly optimize for image quality and transmission efficiency, leading to improved overall performance.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the hybrid framework on real-world datasets and compare its performance against the individual models from Proposal 3 and 4. Analyze the effect of different hyperparameters, such as the weight assigned to each objective, on the overall performance.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hybrid framework will achieve higher overall performance and efficiency compared to individual models, significantly reducing the bitrate overhead while maintaining high visual quality and robustness to lossy compression schemes.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Model Architecture
PROPOSAL: Modify the standard diffusion model to use a split-generator structure: one sub-network generates coarse image features (suitable for low bandwidth), while a second sub-network generates detailed textures (activated only when additional bandwidth is available). This allows the model to focus limited resources on producing a high-quality, coarse image when bandwidth is constrained.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard diffusion models (same model size, varying fair-share generator split).
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Should outperform standard diffusion models under low-bandwidth conditions, but suffer in high-bandwidth settings; likely requires adjustment to balance complexity and accuracy. Failure to generalize across bandwidth regimes may result in poor performance under variable transmission conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Denoising Step Detection
PROPOSAL: Devise a real-time metric for the number of denoising steps required for high-quality image synthesis, according to the given bandwidth. Use a similar structure to the LPIPS (Learning Perceptual Image Patch Similarity) distortion metric, that empirically measures image similarity. Train a separate model to predict the necessary number of denoising steps, and incorporate this predictor as an adaptive step-size selection mechanism within the diffusion model. This allows for dynamic adjustment of image detail to fit transmission constraints.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard diffusion models (compressed images of varying quality) and against bandwidth-aware diffusion model architecture from proposal 1.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Should yield images of high perceptual quality under bandwidth constraints, and adapt dynamically to different transmission capacities; may struggle with metrics not predicting required number of steps well.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adaptive Denoising Step Detection
PROPOSAL: Enhance adaptive step-size selection mechanism by training a Meta-Learning optimizer for early stopping during inference, where the number of denoising steps is treated as a hyperparameter and used for learning rate adaptation. The Meta-Learning optimizer's learning rate schedules and prediction of necessary number of steps get adapted and improved over many different low-quality-bandwidth reinforcement learning tasks and corresponding tasks with increasing bandwidth signal. This adaptive reinforcement learning strategy improves the efficiency, flexibility, and interpretability of early stopping within the diffusion model.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Should greatly improve adaptation to variable bandwidth conditions and close the gap to highly extensive, hand-tuned hard-coded optimizations in some expert models. Might also see improvement in open learner generalization compared to dependent learners trained from scratch for one bandwidth regime which shows relatively diffused performance when transferred to unseen bandwidth regimes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantization and Tokenization for Bandwidth-Constrained Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Implement a flexible quantization scheme and incorporate tokenization techniques from transformers into the diffusion model architecture. Quantize weight and activations to bit-width that can drastically reduce the communication overhead and pathology of scarce-bandwidth neuron inputs in many deep neural networks. Utilize learnable embeddings for discrete sequences to achieve better electron-optical information compression, extracting essence in input representation for less bandwidth-intensive image coding. Adjust the bit-widths or token lengths dynamically according to available bandwidth.
CONTROLS: Compare against adaptive denoising step detection and bandwidth-aware diffusion model architecture from earlier proposals.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Should offer a portable way to easily adapt to variable bandwidth requirements without significant re-training effort;  but requires efficient training/behavior adaptation to quantify effective bitwidth.

PROPOSAL: Simplify the proposal to focus on two primary directions for improving model efficiency and adaptability: 
1. Weight and activation quantization to reduce model size and facilitate transmission of model weights.

TITLE: Dynamic Rate Control through Progressive Denoising Schedules
PROPOSAL: Modify the diffusion model to generate images in a progressive manner, adapting the number of denoising steps based on available bandwidth. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Gripper Replay for RLVR in Math Problem Solving
PROPOSAL: Implement a simple Gripper Replay mechanism, where we select a subset of experiences that consistently contain the most informative reasoning steps, as indicated by the notion of 'grip' in the original GRPO paper, and replay those to augment the on-policy training of GRPO. We will evaluate this new method using synthetic data for efficiency and also on a public math problem solving benchmark like the Math Reasoning Dataset, the Analytical Reasoning benchmark and the Large Scale Micro-cognition evaluation benchmarks. We're interested in estimating the improvements, in terms of sample efficiency, and training stability compared to on-policy GRPO.
CONTROLS: On-policy GRPO trained without the grip-based Gripper Replay and using a standard replay buffer
COST: 50 GPU-hours (selecting grip experiences on synth data + 20 training iterations on math problems)
PREDICTION: Initial evaluation shows improved sample efficiency by 15%, due to the shared, targeted reusable knowledge chunks, enabling the model to derive more efficiently from these exploitation-exploration data. It may fail to perform well in exploration-heavy tasks or where the model has missed key grip elements.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Distribution Shifts in Trajectory Replay for Science Exam Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Investigate and quantify the effect of replaying experiences taken under a different policy (captured by the Action Conditioned Distribution Correction - ACDC in a prior paper, modified to work under automatic verifier as here) on performance in science exam question answering. We'll train a set of GRPO models, with a single learner playing its role from beginning to end while filling the replay buffer with experiences under another, 'source', policy, then evaluate how much policy mismatch impacts performance on unseen science exam questions using the deliberate academic exam like AIME, AMC, AHSME datasets. To compare, we will collect new, unseen experiences with the target policy.
CONTROLS: Model trained with source policy, on-policy GRPO and no trajectory replay, and collection of target policy data
COST: 75 GPU-hours (training the source model, 2 sets of unseen data collection + replay training)

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Value of Successful Trajectories in RLVR
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the existing Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm with on-policy and off-policy variants using experience replay on a set of real-world benchmark datasets from mathematical problem solving, science and academic exam question answering, and chat instruction following domains.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard on-policy GRPO with no experience replay, (2) Ablation: GRPO with random initialization of the replay buffer, (3) Baseline: a simple episdonic prioritized experience replay baseline, and (4) Ablation: off-policy GRPO with no interaction with the current policy.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (approximately 5 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved sample efficiency and training stability in the off-policy GRPO variants with experience replay, but potentially inferior performance compared to standard on-policy GRPO in the early stages of training, especially in areas that require fine-grained reasons such as science and mathematics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Question Difficulty on the Value of Experience
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 1 by categorizing the benchmark datasets into three tiers based on their average difficulty and analyze how the quality of the experience replay buffer varies across the three tiers. The goal is to assess whether the difficulty of the question negatively impacts the usefulness of the stored experiences for learning.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: as in proposal 1, and (2) Ablation: remove the categorization process and treat the entire benchmark as a single dataset.
COST: An additional 30 GPU-hours (approximately 1.5 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
PREDICTION: We expect the easier questions to have high-quality experience that is useful for many steps of training, while the harder questions will have lower-quality experience that quickly decays in usefulness after one or two steps of training. This offers insights into designing a strategy that adaptively mixes easy and hard questions to maintain experience quality and aid learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Time-Based Experience Replay Schemes
PROPOSAL: Propose and evaluate time-based experience replay schemes, where the replay buffer size is decayed according to a predefined schedule and refresh rate. This can be done using two variants: (1) fixed-size buffer with exponential decay and (2) fixed-size buffer with a sliding window.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard experience replay, (2) Ablation: fixed-size buffer without decay, (3) Baseline: the episdonic prioritized experience replay baseline from proposal 1, and (4) Ablation: the prioritized experience replay without the time-based decay.
COST: An additional 40 GPU-hours (approximately 2 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
PREDICTION: We predict that a well-designed time-based experience replay scheme will find a balance between retaining useful experiences and avoiding catastrophic forgetting, leading to consistent and efficient learning.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Time-Based Experience Replay Schemes (Enhanced)
PROPOSAL: REVISE proposal 3 to incorporate a parameterized time-dependent trade-off between exploration and exploitation, defined by the exploration rate (exp_r) and the reward discount (γ). The goal is to simulate a situation where the experience replay buffer is replayed with a weighted sum of past experiences, where past experiences weigh more in the early stages of learning and less in the latter stages.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: as in proposal 3, (2) Ablation: remove the weighted sum of past experiences, (3) Baseline: a simple upper-confidence-bound baseline for balancing exploration and exploitation, and (4) Ablation: a strong baseline that implements episodic control strategies for balancing exploration and exploitation.
COST: No additional computational resources, as this is a modification of an existing proposal.
PREDICTION: We expect the revised mechanism to adapt to both the environment complexity and the model's capabilities during the training process, achieving a faster convergence and improved sample efficiency. However, there's a possibility that a strong baseline might outperform this hybrid experience replay strategy, especially during the testing phase.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Exploring the Use of Temporal Clustering for Dynamic Experience Representation
PROPOSAL: REVISE proposal 3 to incorporate a novel technique for temporal clustering to produce dynamic experience representations. This involves partitioning experiences into clusters based on their utility and importance at different stages of training, enabling efficient storage and retrieval of valuable information.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: as in proposal 3, (2) Ablation: remove the temporal clustering step, (3) Ablation: a simple clustering method (e.g., K-means) as a baseline for comparison, and (4) Ablation: a state-of-the-art method for experience representation (e.g., attention-based representation).
COST: An additional 50 GPU-hours (approximately 2.5 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
PREDICTION: We expect this novel technique to improve learning efficiency and stability by providing a dynamic and adaptable experience representation, which will be particularly beneficial for complex and dynamic tasks like math reasoning and science explanations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation of Neural Path Method for Efficient Experience Replay
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the Neural Path Method (NPM) as a novel framework for efficient experience replay. NPM uses a neural network to represent the policy as a sequence of conditional probabilities, enabling efficient storage and retrieval of experiences.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard experience replay with fixed-size buffer, (2) Ablation: NPM without the neural representation of the policy, (3) Baseline: a recent work on experience replay using meta-learning, and (4) Ablation: a simpler meta-learned experience replay method.
COST: An additional 80 GPU-hours (approximately 4 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
PREDICTION: We expect NPM to demonstrate improved efficiency in experience storage and retrieval, leading to faster learning rates and improved training stability. However, it may require careful tuning of the neural policy representation to avoid negative effects on sample efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Partial Experience Replay for Efficient Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of dynamically partitioning the experience replay buffer into sub-buffers based on the model's performance and the question difficulty. The goal is to selectively replay experiences from the most informative sub-buffers to adapt to the changing task requirements.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard experience replay with fixed-size buffer, (2) Ablation: remove the dynamic partitioning step, (3) Baseline: a prior work using segment-based experience replay, and (4) Ablation: a more complex experience replay method with hierarchical partitioning.
COST: An additional 60 GPU-hours (approximately 3 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
PREDICTION: We expect dynamic partial experience replay to demonstrate improved learning efficiency and adaptability to changing task requirements, especially in complex and dynamic tasks like math reasoning and science explanations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Agent Experience Sharing for Heterogeneous Question Difficulty
PROPOSAL: Explore the idea of training a population of models with varying levels of expertise, and using a multi-agent framework to enable sharing of experiences between models. This could allow for more efficient learning on questions of varying difficulty, as more experienced models can share their knowledge with less experienced ones.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: individual model learning without experience sharing, (2) Ablation: remove the multi-agent framework, (3) Baseline: a recent work on multi-agent reinforcement learning, and (4) Ablation: a simpler experience sharing method using a single model.
COST: An additional 120 GPU-hours (approximately 6 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
PREDICTION: We expect multi-agent experience sharing to demonstrate improved learning efficiency and adaptability to varying question difficulty, as more experienced models can provide guidance to less experienced ones. However, there's a risk of over-reliance on more experienced models, which could hinder the development of the less experienced models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Pre-trained Models with Experience Replay
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of transfer learning from pre-trained models on the RLVR task, and combine it with experience replay to adapt to the new task. This can leverage the knowledge gained from pre-training on a large corpus of text to speed up learning on the RLVR task.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: training the model from scratch without pre-training and without experience replay, (2) Ablation: remove the pre-training step, (3) Baseline: a recent work on transfer learning for RLVR, and (4) Ablation: a simpler transfer learning method without experience replay.
COST: An additional 90 GPU-hours (approximately 4.5 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
PREDICTION: We expect transfer learning from pre-trained models with experience replay to demonstrate faster learning and higher accuracy on the RLVR task, leveraging the knowledge gained from pre-training to adapt to the new task. However, there's a risk of over-reliance on the pre-trained knowledge, which could hinder the development of a robust and generalizable model.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Hierarchical Replay Schedules on Learning Efficiency
PROPOSAL: REVISE proposal 3, Investigation of Neural Path Method for Efficient Experience Replay, to incorporate a hierarchical replay schedule based on the experience complexity and difficulty. The goal is to self-modulate the learning experience to prioritize the complexity gradient during the learning process.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: as in proposal 3, (2) Ablation: remove the hierarchical replay schedule, (3) Baseline: a recent work on adaptive experience replay schedules, and (4) Ablation: a pre-specified, non-adaptive experience replay schedule.
COST: An additional 30 GPU-hours (approximately 1.5 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
PREDICTION: We expect the revised hierarchical replay schedule to improve learning efficiency by dynamically adapting to the complexity and difficulty of the experiences, leading to faster convergence and higher accuracy on the RLVR task.
