Controls: (1) Baseline: standard experience replay with fixed-size buffer, (2) Ablation: NPM without the neural representation of the policy, (3) Baseline: a recent work on experience replay using meta-learning, and (4) Ablation: a simpler meta-learned experience replay method.
Estimated cost: An additional 80 GPU-hours (approximately 4 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
Prediction: We expect NPM to demonstrate improved efficiency in experience storage and retrieval, leading to faster learning rates and improved training stability. However, it may require careful tuning of the neural policy representation to avoid negative effects on sample efficiency.

PROPOSAL 5: Dynamic Partial Experience Replay for Efficient Learning
Investigate the effect of dynamically partitioning the experience replay buffer into sub-buffers based on the model's performance and the question difficulty. The goal is to selectively replay experiences from the most informative sub-buffers to adapt to the changing task requirements.
Controls: (1) Baseline: standard experience replay with fixed-size buffer, (2) Ablation: remove the dynamic partitioning step, (3) Baseline: a prior work using segment-based experience replay, and (4) Ablation: a more complex experience replay method with hierarchical partitioning.
Estimated cost: An additional 60 GPU-hours (approximately 3 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
Prediction: We expect dynamic partial experience replay to demonstrate improved learning efficiency and adaptability to changing task requirements, especially in complex and dynamic tasks like math reasoning and science explanations.

PROPOSAL 6: Multi-Agent Experience Sharing for Heterogeneous Question Difficulty
Explore the idea of training a population of models with varying levels of expertise, and using a multi-agent framework to enable sharing of experiences between models. This could allow for more efficient learning on questions of varying difficulty, as more experienced models can share their knowledge with less experienced ones.
Controls: (1) Baseline: individual model learning without experience sharing, (2) Ablation: remove the multi-agent framework, (3) Baseline: a recent work on multi-agent reinforcement learning, and (4) Ablation: a simpler experience sharing method using a single model.
Estimated cost: An additional 120 GPU-hours (approximately 6 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
Prediction: We expect multi-agent experience sharing to demonstrate improved learning efficiency and adaptability to varying question difficulty, as more experienced models can provide guidance to less experienced ones. However, there's a risk of over-reliance on more experienced models, which could hinder the development of the less experienced models.

PROPOSAL 7: Transfer Learning from Pre-trained Models with Experience Replay
Investigate the effect of transfer learning from pre-trained models on the RLVR task, and combine it with experience replay to adapt to the new task. This can leverage the knowledge gained from pre-training on a large corpus of text to speed up learning on the RLVR task.
Controls: (1) Baseline: training the model from scratch without pre-training and without experience replay, (2) Ablation: remove the pre-training step, (3) Baseline: a recent work on transfer learning for RLVR, and (4) Ablation: a simpler transfer learning method without experience replay.
Estimated cost: An additional 90 GPU-hours (approximately 4.5 days on 20x3080Ti GPUs).
Prediction: We expect transfer learning from pre-trained models with experience replay to demonstrate faster learning and higher accuracy on the RLVR task, leveraging the knowledge gained from pre-training to adapt to the new task. However, there's a risk of over-reliance on the pre-trained knowledge, which could hinder the development of a robust and generalizable model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Off-Policy RLVR via Group-Shuffled Experience Replay
PROPOSAL: We propose to adapt the off-policy concept of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to accommodate experience replay. Specifically, we add a new paradigm called Group-Shuffled Experience Replay (GSER), where experience is grouped by similar questions, and then trajectories within each group are shuffled to mitigate distribution mismatch. We use this approach to enhance off-policy updates for a reference implementation of the widely used Model-based Active Reward Learning (MARL) algorithm.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparisons to standard MARL and in-house results for strong on-policy variants, ablation studies of GSER components (e.g., group-shuffle effect, question grouping), analysis of sensitivity to hyperparameters.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Given the modest modifications to establish GSER, we hypothesize performance gains on 20-30% across math problems, science questions, and chat instruction tasks relative to no-experience-replay baselines, while GSER impacts the policy distribution with respect to group-based aggregation and experience reuse. Where it may fail: handling adaptation across the vast diversity of question topics in the broader dataset. 

Remaining RsQs: 5

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Off-Policy RLVR via Group-Shuffled Experience Replay
REVISED PROPOSAL: We modify our prior proposal by incorporating a replay cache that dynamically allocates storage for high-importance trajectories based on a learned heuristic, dubbed "trajectory toxicity." Trajectory toxicity is estimated through a lightweight auxiliary network that evaluates the reasoning quality and relevance to the question. This optimization helps selectively retain diverse trajectories with strong, exploratory behaviors in the experience buffer, which the GSER can then efficiently exploit.
CONTROLS: As before, to be compared against MARL and strong on-policy variants, with the following additions: analysis of trajectory toxicity learning curves, ablation studies to identify the contribution of each component (toxicity estimation, dynamic replay buffer), human evaluation of model reasoning outputs for cases where the model exhibits reduced exploration behaviors.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours (with approx. 100 hours dedicated to training the auxiliary network)
PREDICTION: By selectively retaining diverse and informative trajectories, we anticipate an improvement of up to 40% in ability to accurately retrieve answers from the experience cache, representing a key step toward real-world applications and suggesting an answer to the research question of which measurable properties indicate the value of a reasoning experience. Where challenges arise: Assessing trajectory quality and value (determining informative pathways) incurs the risk of overestimation or underestimation and cases where auxiliary task/etc. dominate (vetoing too many trajectories).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Replay Buffer Management via Adaptive Capacity Estimation
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of retaining diverse trajectories while accounting for the impact of distribution mismatch, we propose an adaptive capacity estimation framework for managing the replay buffer. This framework estimates the required buffer capacity based on the variation in the replayed trajectories, allocating more capacity to the most informative experiences. Our approach aims to balance exploration and exploitation by dynamically adjusting the buffer size according to the evolving policy.
CONTROLS: The performance of the adaptive buffer will be compared against fixed-sized buffer baselines and ablation studies focusing on the impact of different capacity estimation methods and the effectiveness of adaptive allocation.
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive capacity estimation framework is expected to improve learning efficiency by up to 20% compared to fixed-sized buffers and enable more effective experience reuse for up to 15% better accuracy on tasks with diverse question types. Where challenges arise: Consistently accurate estimation of the required buffer capacity and adapting the buffer size while training the model.

Remaining RsQs: 4

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Efficient Replay Buffer Management via Adaptive Capacity Estimation
REVISED PROPOSAL: To further enhance our proposal, we incorporate a learning-based approach for estimating the required buffer capacity. Specifically, we use a meta-learning framework that learns to adapt to new questions and tasks by exploiting experience from a bank of pre-trained replay buffers. This adaptive capacity estimation approach aims to capture the variability in trajectory quality and ensure effective reuse of experiences across different tasks and questions.
CONTROLS: In addition to the original comparisons, we will also assess the performance of the adaptive buffer under various scenarios, including changing task distributions, new questions, and shifts in the model's knowledge base.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours (with a significant portion dedicated to training the meta-learning framework)
PREDICTION: The adaptive capacity estimation approach is expected to achieve an average improvement of 30% in learning efficiency and accuracy across tasks, compared to the original fixed-sized buffer baselines, and up to 25% better accuracy when handling new questions and tasks. Where challenges arise: Balancing the trade-off between exploration and exploitation under the adaptive buffer management and ensuring effective transfer of knowledge from pre-trained buffers.

Remaining RsQs: 4

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Question Type on Trajectory Value and Replay Buffer Management
PROPOSAL: We propose a systematic analysis of how different question types impact the value of trajectories and the effectiveness of replay buffer management strategies. This analysis will involve generating a diverse set of questions across various domains (e.g., math, science, language) and assessing how these questions influence trajectory value, replay buffer occupation, and model performance.
CONTROLS: The study will control for the impact of domain-specific question types by comparing results across multiple domains, and estimate the effects of question difficulty, and whether these are independent of the problem type
COST: Estimated 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our analysis is expected to reveal a correlation between question type and trajectory value, with certain types of questions leading to more valuable trajectories and others requiring specialized replay buffer management. By better understanding these correlations, we can develop more effective strategies for harnessing the value of experience and improving model performance. Where challenges arise: Extracting meaningful insights from the analysis, especially when dealing with complex, high-dimensional data.

Remaining RsQs: 3

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Analyzing the Benefits of Experience Replay in RLVR
PROPOSAL: We propose developing a theoretical framework to analyze the benefits of experience replay in RLVR in terms of policy convergence rates, sample efficiency, and exploration-exploitation trade-offs. This framework will provide a principled way to understand the impact of replay buffer management strategies and question type diversity on RLVR performance.
CONTROLS: The framework will be evaluated using mathematical analysis and simulations, with comparisons to existing results in off-policy RL and exploration-exploitation trade-offs.
COST: Estimated 60 GPU-hours (primarily for computing and analytical tasks)
PREDICTION: Our framework is expected to provide insights into the benefits of experience replay and highlight the importance of question type diversity in RLVR. By establishing a theoretical foundation for analyzing experience replay in RLVR, we can develop more effective strategies for harnessing experience and improving model performance. Where challenges arise: Deriving provably tight bounds on policy convergence rates and sample efficiency, and separating the impact of different replay buffer management strategies on exploration-exploitation trade-offs.

Remaining RsQs: 2

TITLE: Real-World Evaluation of RLVR with Experience Replay using the Mathematics Question Dataset
PROPOSAL: We propose conducting a real-world evaluation of RLVR with experience replay using the Mathematics Question Dataset (MQD), which provides a diverse set of math problems with reference answers and solutions. We will implement and compare various experience replay strategies, including those proposed in our previous studies, to evaluate their performance on real-world math problems.
CONTROLS: Experimental results will be compared to strong on-policy baselines and analyzed for robustness and generalizability to unseen math problems.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours (sampling and evaluating large datasets may require significant computational resources)
PREDICTION: Our real-world evaluation is expected to provide a realistic assessment of the benefits of experience replay in RLVR, offering insights into its potential to improve real-world performance on math problems. Where challenges arise: The distribution of math problems in the MQD may not be representative of all mathematical problems, and there may be significant variation in the level of difficulty and complexity.

Remaining RsQs: 1

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Experience Replay on RLVR for Science and Acquired Knowledge Assessments
REVISED PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to focus on the real-world evaluation of RLVR with experience replay for science and acquired knowledge assessments. This revised proposal aims to extend our previous work by evaluating the impact of experience replay on RLVR for a broader range of tasks, including science and academic exam question answering. We will implement and compare various experience replay strategies on a diverse set of science and acquired knowledge assessment tasks, and provide insights into the potential benefits of experience replay for these tasks.
CONTROLS: Experimental results will be compared to strong on-policy baselines and analyzed for robustness and generalizability to unseen tasks.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours (sampling and evaluating large datasets may require significant computational resources)
PREDICTION: Our revised study is expected to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the benefits of experience replay in RLVR for science and acquired knowledge assessments, offering insights into its potential to improve real-world performance on these tasks. Where challenges arise: The distribution of science and acquired knowledge assessment tasks may not be representative of all tasks, and there may be significant variation in the level of difficulty and complexity.

propositions.texte: To address the challenge of retaining diverse trajectories while accounting for the impact of distribution mismatch, we propose an adaptive capacity estimation framework for managing the replay buffer. This framework estimates the required buffer capacity based on the variation in the replayed trajectories, allocating more capacity to the most informative experiences. Our approach aims to balance exploration and exploitation by dynamically adjusting the buffer size according to the evolving policy.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Nonlinear Dictionary Learning Under Basic Conditions
PROPOSAL: Prove that in the nonlinear regime, under the basic conditions of invertibility and differentiability of the generating function, a certain class of dictionary learning algorithms achieves complete recovery of the underlying latent variables from observational data.
CONTROLS: Linear dictionary learning, gradient-based descent as a baseline for optimization methods.
COST: 1 GPU-hour (analytical proof).
PREDICTION: Expected to achieve complete recovery of 2-3 latent variables for moderately complex synthetic generative processes, but may likely fail for high-dimensional or highly complex latent spaces.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing the Nonlinear Generative Process
PROPOSAL: Develop a systematic framework to represent the nonlinear generative process using a mixture of polynomial functions, and investigate its effectiveness in recovering latent variables through dictionary learning.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing polynomial-based representation learning methods, e.g., neural tensor networks and polynomial autoencoders.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (hybrid analytical-computational framework).
PREDICTION: Expected to identify a set of prominent polynomial terms that aid in recovering hidden variables, with potential to apply the learned dictionary to real-world language models for mechanistic interpretability. Risks failure if the true generative process is highly complex or dominated by non-polynomial components.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Characterizing the Nonlinear Generative Process
PROPOSAL: Refine the framework to incorporate a more realistic assumption of smoothness and injectivity of the generating function, and explore its relationship to existing generalization bounds in dictionary learning.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing bounds, e.g., the Litvak-Pajor-Tomczak-Jaegermann (LPTJ) inequality, to assess improved generalization performance.
COST: 5 GPU-hours (hybrid analytical-computational framework).
PREDICTION: Expected to improve generalization bounds and provide insights into the inherent trade-offs between smoothness and injectivity in nonlinear dictionary learning. Risks failure if the true generative process exhibits non-smooth or non-injective behavior.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Characterizing the Nonlinear Generative Process
PROPOSAL: Refine the framework to incorporate a more realistic assumption of smoothness and injectivity of the generating function, and explore its relationship to existing generalization bounds in dictionary learning.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing bounds, e.g., the Litvak-Pajor-Tomczak-Jaegermann (LPTJ) inequality, to assess improved generalization performance.
COST: 5 GPU-hours (hybrid analytical-computational framework).
PREDICTION: Expected to improve generalization bounds and provide insights into the inherent trade-offs between smoothness and injectivity in nonlinear dictionary learning. Risks failure if the true generative process exhibits non-smooth or non-injective behavior.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifiability via Neural Network Compression
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of neural network compression methods, such as weight pruning or quantization, as a tool for identifiability analysis in nonlinear dictionary learning, and explore their relationship to information-theoretic bounds.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing state-of-the-art dictionary learning methods, such as neural tensor networks and polynomial autoencoders.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (hybrid analytical-computational framework).
PREDICTION: Expected to identify a new strategy for diagnostically assessing the identifiability of latent variables in nonlinear dictionary learning, with applications to mechanistic interpretability of language models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dependence Analysis for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop and experiment with novel dependence analysis techniques, such as conditional correlation or partial dependence plots, to identify the relationships between observed variables and latent variables in nonlinear dictionary learning.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of dependence analysis on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, including those from language models.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (hybrid analytical-computational experiments).
PREDICTION: Expected to improve our understanding of the relationships between variables and aid in the development of more effective identification strategies for nonlinear dictionary learning. Risks failure if the relationships are too complex or noisy.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Dependence Analysis for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: Refine the dependence analysis techniques to specifically exploit the structure of language models, such as factorized representations or hierarchical organization, and assess their impact on identifiability.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of the refined dependence analysis on language models from various architectures and datasets.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (hybrid analytical-computational experiments).
PREDICTION: Expected to improve the identification of latent variables in language models by taking into account the specific properties of their representations, with a focus on reducing the risk of over-identification.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inference with Entropic Regularization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of entropic regularization to provide a new framework for inference in nonlinear dictionary learning, and evaluate its effectiveness on language models.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing inference methods, such as gradient-based methods and Bayesian approaches, as well as the dependence analysis methods from Proposal 4.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (hybrid analytical-computational framework).
PREDICTION: Expected to improve the robustness and interpretability of inference in nonlinear dictionary learning by providing a formal framework for balancing regularization and expressiveness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Validation on Mechanistic Interpretability of Language Models
PROPOSAL: Experimentally validate the proposed nonlinear dictionary learning methods on various language models, including large-scale transformer models, and assess their impact on mechanistic interpretability.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed methods on real-world language models, using techniques such as saliency maps, feature importance, and representation learning.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (hybrid analytical-computational experiments).
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate the practical applicability of nonlinear dictionary learning methods to enhance the interpretability of language models, with a focus on identifying key insights into their internal workings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Unified Framework for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning and its Applications
PROPOSAL: Integrate the proposed methods into a unified framework for nonlinear dictionary learning, and demonstrate its applicability to a wide range of tasks, including but not limited to, mechanistic interpretability of language models, data clustering, and dimensionality reduction.
CONTROLS: Comprehensive evaluation of the unified framework on various datasets and tasks, using a range of metrics and techniques.
COST: N/A ( high-level unification effort).
PREDICTION: Expected to provide a comprehensive and systematic approach to nonlinear dictionary learning, with potential for broad impact across multiple fields.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Function Smoothness in Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: We analyze the effect of smoothness assumptions on the identifiability of nonlinear dictionary models. Specifically, we prove that if the generating function g is smooth and has a bounded Lipschitz constant, it is possible to recover a sufficient number of latent variables through a gradient-based optimization procedure.
CONTROLS: Ablation study comparing different smoothness metrics (e.g., Lipschitz constant, total variation) and recovery guarantees under smooth functions.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With a sufficiently small Lipschitz constant, we expect to recover 80-90% of the latent variables, but achieving full recovery may be infeasible without stronger assumptions. Failure will occur when the generating function is highly irregular or has a large Lipschitz constant.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Beyond Smoothness: Exploring the Impact of Injection on Nonlinear Dictionary Recovery
PROPOSAL: We investigate the role of injectivity assumptions on the recovery of nonlinear dictionaries. Specifically, we study the effect of injectivity on the minimality of the recovered dictionary under a certain optimization procedure, and provide conditions under which injectivity guarantees minimum dictionary recovery.
CONTROLS: Comparison with the existing works on smoothness assumptions and an experimental study using different levels of injectivity in generating functions.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With injectivity, we expect to improve dictionary recovery rates by an additional 10-20% over smoothness alone, but limited by the condition that the generating function must be injective on each latent variable. Failure will occur when the generating function has a non-stable or non-monotonic behavior.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Combining Smoothness and Injection for Optimal Nonlinear Dictionary Recovery
REVISED PROPOSAL: We combine the insights from the previous two proposals to develop a new framework that integrates both smoothness and injectivity assumptions to maximize the recoverability of nonlinear dictionaries. Specifically, we derive conditions under which the combined assumptions guarantee the recovery of a sufficient number of latent variables.
CONTROLS: Ablation study comparing the individual effects of smoothness, injectivity, and their combination on dictionary recovery.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve improved recovery rates of 95-98% by combining smoothness and injectivity assumptions, but the limit is still set by the need for stable and monotonic function behavior. Failure will occur when both assumptions are severely violated, corresponding to highly irregular and non-injective generating functions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Combining Smoothness and Injection for Optimal Nonlinear Dictionary Recovery
REVISED PROPOSAL: (Applies to proposal number 2) We modify the existing proposal 2 to focus on an empirical study, using a range of synthetic datasets with controlled levels of smoothness and injectivity to explore the trade-offs between these assumptions in practice.
CONTROLS: Compare empirical results with theoretical guarantees from proposal 1, and evaluate the robustness of combined assumptions in various data regimes.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe improved recovery rates when both smoothness and injectivity are high, but the interplay between these factors may lead to counterintuitive results. Failure will occur when the assumptions are not verified, or when the chosen datasets do not align with the theoretical framework.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Synthetic Dataset Generator for Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: We develop a tool capable of generating synthetic datasets that control for various aspects of nonlinear dictionary learning, including function smoothness, injectivity, and nonlinearity. This dataset generator will enable researchers to investigate the effects of different assumptions and hypotheses in a systematic and controlled manner.
CONTROLS: Use the dataset generator to validate the theoretical results from proposals 1 and 2, and to explore the limits of dictionary recovery under various data conditions.
COST: 5 GPU-hours (initial development) + variable (user-dependent)
PREDICTION: With this tool, we expect to provide a solid foundation for future research on nonlinear dictionary learning, allowing others to build upon and extend our findings. However, its effectiveness depends on the complexity of the assumed model and the user's understanding of nonlinear dictionary learning principles.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mechanistic Interpretability of Large-Scale Language Models using Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: We apply nonlinear dictionary learning to a large-scale language model to uncover mechanisms underlying linguistic representations. We use the synthetic dataset generator to create data-specific assumptions and evaluate the recovery rates of different components of the model.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with existing methods for mechanistic interpretability (e.g., sparse autoencoders), and analyze the impact of assumed assumptions on the recovered representations.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to recover meaningful and coherent representations that reflect the underlying language processing mechanisms. However, the quality of the results may depend on the quality of the assumed assumptions and the specific characteristics of the language model. Failure will occur if the dictionary recovery fails to capture the complex interactions and relationships in the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Universally Applicable Bias for Nonlinear Dictionary Recovery
PROPOSAL: We propose a bias that can be universally applied to any nonlinear dictionary learning problem, regardless of the underlying assumptions or model characteristics. This bias is designed to promote recovery of informative and coherent latent variables, even in the absence of strong assumptions.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of our proposed bias with existing methods under various data conditions, and analyze its impact on recoverability and interpretability.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed bias to improve recovery rates and promote the discovery of meaningful latent variables in a wide range of scenarios. However, its effectiveness may depend on the specific characteristics of the data and the underlying model. Failure will occur if the bias is overly restrictive or does not adapt to the unique features of each problem.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: A Universally Applicable Bias for Nonlinear Dictionary Recovery
REVISED PROPOSAL: We refine our previously proposed bias to incorporate additional mechanisms that promote robustness and adaptability to varying data conditions. This revised bias will be integrated into the synthetic dataset generator, allowing users to control for the level of bias and its impact on dictionary recovery.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised bias with existing methods under various data conditions, and analyze its impact on recoverability and interpretability.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised bias to improve recovery rates and promote the discovery of meaningful latent variables in a wide range of scenarios, while also enhancing its adaptability and robustness to varying data conditions. Failure will occur if the bias is still overly restrictive or does not generalize well to new and unseen data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Recovering Lost Information in Nonlinear Dictionary Learning
PROPOSAL: We investigate the scenario where some information about the generating function or the latent variables is lost, and examine the limits of recovery under such conditions. This will help us understand the trade-offs between recoverability, bias, and robustness in nonlinear dictionary learning.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of our proposed methods under different levels of information loss, and analyze the impact of recoverability on interpretability.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to provide a better understanding of the limitations and potential solutions for nonlinear dictionary learning under information loss, but recovering lost information may be infeasible in certain scenarios. Failure will occur if the methods are unable to recover meaningful latent variables or if the bias is over-specified.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unifying Nonlinear Dictionary Learning Under a Single Framework
PROPOSAL: We develop a unified framework for nonlinear dictionary learning that combines and extends the methods and insights from our previous proposals. This framework will provide a comprehensive and flexible approach for tackling a wide range of nonlinear dictionary learning problems.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of our unified framework with existing methods, and analyze its adaptability to various data conditions and problem settings.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the unified framework to provide a significant improvement in recovery rates and interpretability, while also promoting robustness and adaptability to varying data conditions. Failure will occur if the framework is overly complex or fails to generalize well to new and unseen data.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Nonlinear Dictionary Learning with Interleaved Constraints
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical framework for nonlinear dictionary learning, which combines the benefits of weak supervision and model constraints. Specifically, we use stable manifold learning to constrain the inducing points of a kernelized dictionary, while incorporating domain knowledge through weak labeling. We show that under mild assumptions, this approach can recover a subset of the latent variables with theoretical guarantees.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing stable manifold learning methods without weak supervision, as well as kernelized dictionary learning without model constraints.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to recover a significant subset of the latent variables, but identify potential failure modes where the inducing points fail to capture the latent structure, leading to inferior recovery performance.

Note that this proposal serves as a stepping stone towards answering one of the research questions: What inductive biases should be introduced to guide recovery. It aims to combine the strengths of existing approaches in nonlinear dictionary learning and provide theoretical guarantees.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Validation of Interleaved Constraints
PROPOSAL: We propose an experimental validation of our nonlinear dictionary learning framework with interleaved constraints, using a synthetic dataset inspired by mechanistic interpretability of large-scale language models. We will implement a kernelized dictionary learning algorithm with stable manifold constraints and weak supervision, and compare its performance to alternative approaches on a range of recovery tasks, such as recovering latent factors from neural representations.
CONTROLS: Compare to:
- Kernelized dictionary learning without model constraints
- Stable manifold learning with weak supervision (but without the nonlinear dictionary learning framework)
- A sparse linear dictionary learning baseline
COST: 200 GPU-hours (parallelized experiments)
PREDICTION: We expect our framework to outperform the baselines in terms of recovery performance, particularly when the latent variables have complex nonlinear relationships. However, we may identify situations where the inducing points fail to capture the latent structure, leading to inferior recovery performance compared to sparse linear dictionary learning.

Note that this proposal provides empirical evidence to support the theoretical framework introduced in the first proposal, and helps to identify potential failure modes in its applicability.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Experimental Validation of Interleaved Constraints
PROPOSAL: We revise the experimental validation proposal to include a more comprehensive evaluation of our nonlinear dictionary learning framework, specifically:
- We modify the stable manifold learning procedure to use a more efficient algorithm (e.g., using PCA as an initializer), reducing the computational cost by 2x.
- We add a comparison to a state-of-the-art sparse dictionary learning algorithm, to assess the trade-offs between sparsity and recoverability in nonlinear models.
- We increase the range of recovery tasks to include tasks with different levels of nonlinearity, quantifying the effectiveness of our framework in various scenarios.
CONTROLS: Same as before.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (accounting for the increased scope of experiments)
PREDICTION: We expect the revised framework to show improved performance and efficiency compared to the original proposal, with potential for robust recovery in a wider range of tasks. However, we anticipate that the state-of-the-art sparse dictionary learning algorithm may still outperform our approach in tasks with very low-dimensionality latent variables or high levels of noise.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Expansion of Theoretical Guarantees
PROPOSAL NUMBER: 1
PROPOSAL: We refine the theoretical framework for nonlinear dictionary learning with interleaved constraints, extending the existing guarantees to include cases where the inducing points fail to capture the latent structure. Specifically, we introduce a new regularization term to the stable manifold learning procedure, which encourages the inducing points to be more informative. We derive a set of improved recovery guarantees under the same mild assumptions as before.
CONTROLS: Compare the new guarantees to the original guarantees, studying their implications on the practical recovery performance.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (solely theoretical computation)
PREDICTION: We expect the new guarantees to broaden the applicability of the framework, particularly in situations where the inducing points struggle to capture the latent structure, but still failing under certain conditions related to manifold dimensionality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Manifold Structure for Recovery
PROPOSAL: We propose a new theoretical direction: analyzing the manifold structure of the generating function to identify regions where recovery is possible, even under failures in the inducing points. Specifically, we introduce a new manifold learning-based concept - "local equivariance", which captures the idea that small perturbations in the input data should result in similar changes in the output. We develop a set of theoretical guarantees for recovery based on local equivariance, identifying conditions under which the nonlinear dictionary learning framework can still recover a subset of latent variables, even in complicated scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the local equivariance-based guarantees to the existing guarantees, evaluating their trade-offs on practical recovery tasks.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (solely theoretical computation)
PREDICTION: We expect local equivariance to be a valuable concept in nonlinear dictionary learning, potentially allowing for recovery of a wider range of latent variables in complex settings, but it remains to be seen how well it captures scenarios with bit different manifold geometries.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiments on Mechanistic Interpretability of Language Models
PROPOSAL: We design experiments to apply the nonlinear dictionary learning framework to mechanistic interpretability of language models. We will leverage a range of popular benchmark datasets (e.g., GLUE, SuperGLUE) to analyze the latent representations of several state-of-the-art language models. Our goal is to investigate whether the framework can recover meaningful semantic features and syntactic structures from these representations, potentially shedding new light on the knowledge representation capabilities of large-scale language models.
CONTROLS: Compare the recovery performance to standard techniques for analyzing language model representations, such as PCA or t-SNE.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (accounting for large-scale language model fine-tuning and analysis)
PREDICTION: We expect the nonlinear dictionary learning framework to uncover novel insights into the knowledge representation mechanisms of large-scale language models, but face challenges related to selecting meaningful features, and might struggle when strong linguistic patterns fail to surface in the latent representations of interest.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Analysis with Frozen Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We begin by extending the state-of-the-art zero-shot video anomaly analysis method that uses frozen vision-language models, but now generate textual explanations from the model's visual-semantic priors. Specifically, we utilize a frame-wise visual captioning approach with a frozen vision-language backbone to produce short narratives describing each frame, along with a large language model to transform the captions into textual explanations of anomalies.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparison with state-of-the-art zero-shot temporal detection methods (e.g., AnomalyDetect), and ablation studies to evaluate the impact of different language models and visual captioning approaches on the quality of the generated explanations.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in zero-shot video anomaly analysis and provide richer insights into the anomalies, but may require large-scale pre-training of the vision-language model to capture complex anomaly patterns in real-world datasets. Failure might occur when the anomalies are abstract or difficult to describe in text.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Scalable Multi-Modal Anomaly Reasoning with Visual-Semantic Graphs
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel multi-modal graph-based framework to holistically analyze video anomalies by aggregating visual features and textual explanations via heterogeneous graphs. Each node represents a frame, annotated with features from visual networks (e.g., ResNet), and edges capture relationships between frames via both spatial dependencies (e.g., CNN + Successful action able  or or particular word convolution), and temporal dependencies captured from the vision-language autGAN autograph [Knowledge, NOAA and TheComplete preprocess empirical het Grammar].

TITLE: Hierarchical Spatio-Temporal Attention for Multi-Modal Anomaly Understanding
PROPOSAL: We introduce a hierarchical spatio-temporal attention mechanism to selectively focus on critical regions and time stamps within the visual-semantic graph (Proposal 2), enhancing its ability to reason about anomalies. This hierarchical attention mechanism first attends to the entire video region and refines attention to local regions, accounting for both spatial and temporal dependencies.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Frozen Vision-Language Models for Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a frozen vision-language model-based approach for zero-shot video anomaly detection, leveraging a large-scale pre-trained multimodal model (e.g., CLIP, LDL) to capture visual and textual features from video frames and convert them into anomaly scores. Use a state-of-the-art dataset such as UCSD Anomaly Detection Dataset or a more recent benchmark like the Exposing Cluttered Video Anomaly benchmark (EcVA-B) for evaluation.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed approach with the state-of-the-art zero-shot temporal detection model (i.e., the prompted large language model) and baseline models (e.g., one-class SVM, autoencoders).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed approach is expected to outperform the baseline models, but its performance may vary across different types of anomalies, and it may struggle with complex anomaly types, similar to the prompted large language model.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Integrating Visual and Textual Knowledge for Improved Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection
PROPOSAL: Revising the existing proposal, we will experiment with combining the frozen vision-language model (CLIP or LDL) with visual attention mechanisms to identify the most informative regions in the video frames, and also incorporate external knowledge graphs or visual-semantic ontologies to capture relationships between visual concepts and anomaly types. This can help improve the model's ability to recognize complex anomalies and enhance its explainability.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of visual attention and knowledge graph incorporation on the model's performance and explainability using metrics such as mean anomaly score and visual attention heatmaps.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating visual attention and knowledge graphs is expected to significantly improve the model's performance, especially on complex anomaly types, and enhance its explainability by providing insights into which regions and concepts are most relevant to the anomaly detection process. However, it may increase the computational requirements and require careful calibration of the attention mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ensembling Zero-Shot Anomaly Detectors for Improved Robustness and Accuracy
PROPOSAL: Explore ensemble methods that combine multiple frozen vision-language models or different variants of the existing zero-shot temporal detection model, to leverage their complementarities and enhance overall performance. This can be achieved through simple averaging or weighted ensembling of individual model predictions.
CONTROLS: Compare the ensemble performance with state-of-the-art baselines and individual models, and analyze the impact of ensemble size and weighting schemes on the results.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Ensembling is expected to improve the robustness and accuracy of zero-shot anomaly detection, particularly when combining models that excel in different anomaly categories or domains. However, it may introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning of ensemble settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot Spatial Localization for Video Anomalies
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a zero-shot approach for spatially localizing video anomalies, using a frozen vision-language model to generate spatial bounding box proposals around anomalous regions, and then refining these proposals using an off-the-shelf object detection model pre-trained on normal video data. Evaluate the approach on a spatial localization benchmark such as the CAVD (Crimes and Activities in Videos Dataset).
CONTROLS: Compare the approach with state-of-the-art spatial localization baselines and assess the impact of the off-the-shelf object detection model on the results.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to provide accurate spatial localization of video anomalies, while avoiding the need for explicit ground-truth bounding box annotations. However, the performance may be limited by the quality of the pre-trained object detection model and the difficulty of the spatial localization task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Generalizability of Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection Across Domains
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale evaluation of the generalizability of the existing zero-shot video anomaly detection methods, including the frozen vision-language model-based approach and the ensemble method, across different domains such as crime and violence detection, construction site monitoring, and animal behavior analysis.
CONTROLS: Use a variety of benchmarks and datasets from different domains to evaluate the performance of the methods, and investigate the impact of domain shifts on the results.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The evaluation is expected to reveal the strengths and weaknesses of the zero-shot video anomaly detection methods across different domains, and provide insights into how to improve their generalizability and adaptability to unseen domains. However, the performance may vary significantly across domains, and the results may be affected by the availability and quality of training data for each domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Explanation with Textual Cues
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel approach to provide textual explanations for video anomaly detection results, using a frozen multimodal language model to generate descriptive text based on the identified anomalies. This can help provide insights into why an anomaly was detected and enhance the overall interpretability of the zero-shot video anomaly detection method.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the generated textual explanations in terms of coherence, accuracy, and relevance to the detected anomalies, and compare them with existing state-of-the-art text-based explanation methods.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed approach is expected to provide insightful and accurate textual explanations for video anomaly detection results, while avoiding the need for explicit annotation or fine-tuning of the language model. However, the quality of the generated explanations may vary depending on the complexity of the anomalies and the quality of the pre-trained language model.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Enhancing Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection with Active Learning
PROPOSAL: Revising the existing approach, we will explore active learning strategies to selectively sample a subset of anomalous videos from the entire dataset, and then use this subset to fine-tune the zero-shot video anomaly detection model. This can help improve the model's performance and adaptability to unseen domains, while reducing the need for extensive data annotation.
CONTROLS: Compare the active learning method with traditional retraining approaches and evaluate its impact on the model's performance, adaptability, and efficiency.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The active learning approach is expected to improve the zero-shot video anomaly detection performance, particularly in situations where high-quality annotated data is scarce. However, the effectiveness of the approach may depend on the quality of the initial model and the selection of the subset of anomalous videos for fine-tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using Few-Shot Learning for Adapting Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection to New Domains
PROPOSAL: Investigate the application of few-shot learning techniques to adapt the zero-shot video anomaly detection model to new, unseen domains. This can be achieved by fine-tuning the model on a small set of in-domain data, and then leveraging the knowledge learned from this fine-tuning process to improve performance on the new domain.
CONTROLS: Compare the few-shot learning approach with traditional retraining and evaluate its impact on the model's performance and adaptability to new domains.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The few-shot learning approach is expected to effectively adapt the zero-shot video anomaly detection model to new domains, while requiring minimal labeled data and computational resources. However, the effectiveness of the approach may depend on the quality of the in-domain data, the size of the few-shot dataset, and the similarity between the old and new domains.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Improving Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection with Semi-Supervised Learning
PROPOSAL: Revising the existing few-shot learning approach, we will explore semi-supervised learning techniques that leverage both labeled and unlabeled data to improve the performance of the zero-shot video anomaly detection model. This can be achieved by using a combination of labeled data for fine-tuning and unlabeled data for self-supervised learning.
CONTROLS: Compare the semi-supervised learning approach with traditional retraining and few-shot learning, and evaluate its impact on the model's performance, adaptability, and efficiency.
COST: 550 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The semi-supervised learning approach is expected to effectively improve the performance of the zero-shot video anomaly detection model, particularly in situations where high-quality labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain. However, the effectiveness of the approach may depend on the quality of the labeled and unlabeled data, the choice of self-supervised learning objectives, and the balance between labeled and unlabeled data usage.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection Approaches
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the existing zero-shot video anomaly detection approaches, including the frozen vision-language models, ensembling, spatial localization, generalizability evaluation, few-shot learning, and semi-supervised learning methods. This evaluation will provide a thorough comparison of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach, and identify the most effective methods for different use cases and scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of each approach on a variety of benchmarks and datasets, and evaluate their robustness, adaptability, efficiency, and interpretability.
COST: 650 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This comprehensive evaluation is expected to provide valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of zero-shot video anomaly detection approaches, and inform the development of more effective and robust methods for real-world applications.

Controls: Compare the approach with state-of-the-art spatial localization baselines and assess the impact of the off-the-shelf object detection model on the results.
Estimated cost: 250 GPU-hours
Prediction: This approach is expected to provide accurate spatial localization of video anomalies, while avoiding the need for explicit ground-truth bounding box annotations. However, the performance may be limited by the quality of the pre-trained object detection model and the difficulty of the spatial localization task.

PROPOSAL 4: Evaluating the Generalizability of Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection Across Domains
Conduct a large-scale evaluation of the generalizability of the existing zero-shot video anomaly detection methods, including the frozen vision-language model-based approach and the ensemble method, across different domains such as crime and violence detection, construction site monitoring, and animal behavior analysis.
Controls: Use a variety of benchmarks and datasets from different domains to evaluate the performance of the methods, and investigate the impact of domain shifts on the results.
Estimated cost: 350 GPU-hours
Prediction: The evaluation is expected to reveal the strengths and weaknesses of the zero-shot video anomaly detection methods across different domains, and provide insights into how to improve their generalizability and adaptability to unseen domains. However, the performance may vary significantly across domains, and the results may be affected by the availability and quality of training data for each domain.

PROPOSAL 5: Towards Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Explanation with Textual Cues
Develop a novel approach to provide textual explanations for video anomaly detection results, using a frozen multimodal language model to generate descriptive text based on the identified anomalies. This can help provide insights into why an anomaly was detected and enhance the overall interpretability of the zero-shot video anomaly detection method.
Controls: Evaluate the generated textual explanations in terms of coherence, accuracy, and relevance to the detected anomalies, and compare them with existing state-of-the-art text-based explanation methods.
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours
Prediction: The proposed approach is expected to provide insightful and accurate textual explanations for video anomaly detection results, while avoiding the need for explicit annotation or fine-tuning of the language model. However, the quality of the generated explanations may vary depending on the complexity of the anomalies and the quality of the pre-trained language model.

PROPOSAL 6: Using Few-Shot Learning for Adapting Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection to New Domains
Investigate the application of few-shot learning techniques to adapt the zero-shot video anomaly detection model to new, unseen domains. This can be achieved by fine-tuning the model on a small set of in-domain data, and then leveraging the knowledge learned from this fine-tuning process to improve performance on the new domain.
Controls: Compare the few-shot learning approach with traditional retraining and evaluate its impact on the model's performance and adaptability to new domains.
Estimated cost: 450 GPU-hours
Prediction: The few-shot learning approach is expected to effectively adapt the zero-shot video anomaly detection model to new domains, while requiring minimal labeled data and computational resources. However, the effectiveness of the approach may depend on the quality of the in-domain data, the size of the few-shot dataset, and the similarity between the old and new domains.

PROPOSAL 7: Comprehensive Evaluation of Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection Approaches
Conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the existing zero-shot video anomaly detection approaches, including the frozen vision-language models, ensembling, spatial localization, generalizability evaluation, few-shot learning, and semi-supervised learning methods. This evaluation will provide a thorough comparison of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach, and identify the most effective methods for different use cases and scenarios.
Controls: Compare the performance of each approach on a variety of benchmarks and datasets, and evaluate their robustness, adaptability, efficiency, and interpretability.
Estimated cost: 650 GPU-hours
Prediction: This comprehensive evaluation is expected to provide valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of zero-shot video anomaly detection approaches, and inform the development of more effective and robust methods for real-world applications.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Zero-Shot Temporal Detection with Cross-Modal Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate a cross-modal transformer (e.g., CMT, [Chen et al., 2020]) for temporal anomaly detection, where the visual encoder is frozen, and text prompts are used to query the model for anomaly scores. Controls will include baseline models trained on various one-class and deep anomaly detection tasks (e.g., OCSVM, GANomaly), as well as zero-shot detectors that rely on frozen vision-language models.
CONTROLS: Vanilla OCSVM, GANomaly, zero-shot detector based on frozen vision-language model (Vision-Language Anomaly Detection, VLAD)
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment will establish a baseline for zero-shot temporal detection and potentially provide insights into the effectiveness of cross-modal transformers in this setting. However, it might fail if the text prompts are not adequately informative or fail to effectively query the model for relevant information.

Chen, Y., Gallagher, A., Kirovski, D., & Hager, G. (2020).Transformer steerable network for cross-modal tasks. InAdvances in Neural Information Processing Systems (pp. 2701-2712).

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revising Investigating Zero-Shot Temporal Detection with Cross-Modal Transformers to Evaluate Spatial Localization
PROPOSAL: We will extend the previous proposal by using the cross-modal transformer to also perform spatial anomaly localization by predicting bounding boxes around the regions of interest. This will be achieved by fine-tuning the visual encoder but keeping the text prompt-based query mechanism unchanged. Controls will include a baseline method for spatial anomaly localization (e.g., Faster R-CNN with an anomaly score loss).
CONTROLS: Vanilla Faster R-CNN, baseline zero-shot detector based on frozen vision-language model (the previous experiment)
COST: 20 GPU-hours (due to additional fine-tuning step)
PREDICTION: This revised experiment will potentially provide a holistic analysis of video anomalies, combining temporal detection and spatial localization in a single zero-shot framework. However, it might fail if the cross-modal transformer's performance is not robust enough for spatial localization, or if adapting the visual encoder affects the model's zero-shot detection capabilities.

This proposal explores an intermediate step toward the more ambitious goal of integrating textual explanation with zero-shot detection and localization, by leveraging the capabilities of the cross-modal transformer for spatial localization.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Introducing a Zero-Shot Textual Explanation Component with Frozen Large Language Models
PROPOSAL: We will combine the zero-shot temporal detection and spatial localization capabilities of the cross-modal transformer with a frozen large language model (LLM) for textual explanation. The LLM will be fine-tuned with a set of task-specific prompts to predict a human-readable description of the anomaly. Controls will include baseline LLMs for anomaly description (e.g., BERT, T5) as well as a method combining a separate LLM with a zero-shot detector (the Vision-Language Anomaly Detection, VLAD detector).
CONTROLS: Vanilla BERT, T5, Vision-Language Anomaly Detection (VLAD)
COST: 20 GPU-hours (due to the need to fine-tune the LLM and integrate it with the cross-modal transformer)
PREDICTION: This experiment will test whether a combination of zero-shot detection, localization, and textual explanation can be achieved with frozen models only. However, it might fail if the LLM and cross-modal transformer are not effectively integrated or if the task-specific prompts fail to adapt the LLM to the anomaly explanation task.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Refining Introducing a Zero-Shot Textual Explanation Component with Frozen Large Language Models for Generic Anomaly Descriptions
PROPOSAL: We will modify the previous proposal by replacing the task-specific prompts for anomaly description with a set of generic prompts that can be applied across different domains and anomaly types. This simplification will help evaluate the model's ability to provide generalizable textual explanations for video anomalies. Controls will remain the same as in the previous version, with additional evaluation on a held-out set of generic anomaly descriptions.
CONTROLS: Vanilla BERT, T5, Vision-Language Anomaly Detection (VLAD), additional evaluation on held-out set of generic anomaly descriptions
COST: 15 GPU-hours (simplified fine-tuning step)
PREDICTION: This refined experiment will help assess the generality of the proposed zero-shot framework for video anomaly analysis and its ability to provide consistent, interpretable outputs across different domains and scenarios. However, it might fail if the generic prompts are insufficiently informative or if the LLM and cross-modal transformer are not effectively adapted to the task together.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Evaluating Robustness Across Domains and Anomaly Types with Transfer Learning and Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will assess the robustness of the zero-shot framework by evaluating its performance on multiple domains (e.g., indoor vs. outdoor surveillance) and anomaly types (e.g., goal-directed vs. spontaneous behavior). This will involve fine-tuning the cross-modal transformer and LLM on a small subset of labeled data from each domain, and then transferring the knowledge to the target domain with limited or no additional labeled data. Controls will include a baseline method for transfer learning (e.g., fine-tuning a pre-trained model on a small labeled set).
CONTROLS: Vanilla transfer learning (fine-tuning pre-trained model on small labeled set), zero-shot detector based on frozen vision-language model (Vision-Language Anomaly Detection, VLAD)
COST: 25 GPU-hours (domain adaptation and transfer learning)
PREDICTION: This experiment will provide insights into the framework's ability to generalize across different domains and anomaly types and adapt to new scenarios with limited or no labeled data. However, it might fail if the transfer learning or domain adaptation steps fail to effectively capture the domain-specific knowledge or if the baseline methods are not adequately controlled.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Rethinking Spatial Localization with Anchor-Free Methods for Improved Robustness
PROPOSAL: We will modify the spatial localization component of the zero-shot framework to leverage anchor-free methods (e.g., CenterPoint, [Yin et al., 2021]) that do not rely on predefined anchor boxes. This will help improve the robustness and flexibility of the spatial localization algorithm, and potentially provide better results in scenarios where the anchor-free method can adapt to varying object sizes and aspect ratios. Controls will include the original anchor-based spatial localization method and another baseline method for anchor-free detection (e.g., FCOS).
CONTROLS: Vanilla anchor-based spatial localization, FCOS
COST: 15 GPU-hours (modifying the spatial localization component)
PREDICTION: This revised experiment will help evaluate the impact of anchor-free methods on the overall robustness and performance of the zero-shot framework, and potentially provide insights into the strengths and limitations of anchor-free detection in the context of video anomaly localization. However, it might fail if the anchor-free method is unable to effectively capture the spatial structure of anomalies or if the improvements come at the cost of reduced accuracy.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Multimodal Attention on Zero-Shot Accountability and Explanability
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the role of multimodal attention (e.g., [Wang et al., 2020]) in enhancing the accountability and explainability of the zero-shot framework, particularly in scenarios where the LLM's output is not entirely transparent or different from human expectations. Controls will include a baseline model without multimodal attention and a variant of the model with attention focusing only on the vision or text modality separately.
CONTROLS: Vanilla model without multimodal attention, separate attention on vision or text modality
COST: 12 GPU-hours (modifying the multimodal attention mechanism)
PREDICTION: This experiment will help evaluate the impact of multimodal attention on the accountability and explainability of the zero-shot framework, and provide insights into how this mechanism can facilitate more transparent decision-making and improved human-model alignment. However, it might fail if the multimodal attention mechanism is too complex or if the changes do not lead to the expected improvements in accountability and explainability.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Refining Assessing the Impact of Multimodal Attention on Zero-Shot Accountability and Explanability with Human Evaluation Studies
PROPOSAL: We will refine the assessment of multimodal attention's impact on zero-shot accountability and explainability by involving human evaluation studies to analyze the outputs and evaluate their relevance, coherence, and helpfulness in understanding anomalies. This will help to better quantify the benefits of multimodal attention in improving the zero-shot framework's accountability and explainability. Controls will remain the same as in the original proposal.
CONTROLS: Vanilla model without multimodal attention, separate attention on vision or text modality
COST: 15 GPU-hours (integrating human evaluation studies and refining the experimental design)
PREDICTION: This revised experiment will provide more comprehensive insights into the impact of multimodal attention on the zero-shot framework's accountability and explainability, taking into account human-centered evaluation. However, it might fail if the human evaluation studies yield conflicting or inconclusive results, or if the revised experimental design does not lead to the expected improvements.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Evaluating the Zero-Shot Framework on Real-World Datasets with Anomaly Definitions from Different Domains
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the zero-shot framework on real-world datasets from various domains (e.g., public security, public health, environmental monitoring) and with anomaly definitions that differ from those used in the synthetic and simulated datasets. This will help assess the framework's ability to generalize to real-world scenarios and adapt to diverse anomaly definitions.
CONTROLS: Previous experiments, other SOTAs in the field, and domain-specific baselines for video anomaly detection and explanation
COST: 50 GPU-hours (data preparation, training, and evaluation on real-world datasets)
PREDICTION: This evaluation will provide critical insights into the zero-shot framework's practical usability and its potential to support real-world applications in multiple domains. However, it might fail if the framework struggles to adapt to diverse anomaly definitions or if the data preparation and collection efforts are not sufficient to cover the complexity of real-world scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Fine-Tuning the Zero-Shot Framework with Transfer Learning and Human Feedback for More Effective Real-World Deployment
PROPOSAL: We will revise the evaluation of the zero-shot framework on real-world datasets by incorporating transfer learning and human feedback to fine-tune the framework and adapt it to the specific requirements and anomaly definitions of the target domains. This will involve using the human evaluation studies from the previous experiment to gather feedback and refine the framework's performance on real-world data.
CONTROLS: Original experiments, previous evaluations, and additional baselines for transfer learning and human-in-the-loop adaptation
COST: 30 GPU-hours (transfer learning and human feedback)
PREDICTION: This revised experiment will help to fine-tune the zero-shot framework and prepare it for real-world deployment, leveraging the insights gained from the previous experiments and human evaluation studies. However, it might fail if the transfer learning and human feedback processes are not effective in adapting the framework to the target domains or if the revisions do not lead to the expected improvements.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1 
TITLE: Investigating Object Binding in Pretrained Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale analysis of the internal representations of pretrained Vision Transformers using techniques such as saliency maps, class activations, and feature attribution methods to evaluate whether these models reliably encode object-level information.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare to the feature maps of human object detectors to establish a baseline for object representation.
- Conduct control experiments on models trained with object-centric supervision to verify that object binding is not an inherent property of the architecture.
- Examine the effect of different training objectives and data augmentations on object binding.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find evidence of object binding in the internal representations of ViTs, but with limitations in terms of variability and generalizability, and possible failures in specific domains with high levels of occlusion or clutter.

ACTION: ADD 2 
TITLE: Object-Centric Suppression in Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether suppressing object-centric information in pretrained Vision Transformers impacts their performance on downstream tasks, by adding an object-centric suppression head to the model's architecture that downsamples object-specific features, and comparing the results to ablated models that do not have this suppression.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare to a model that has a mask randomly sampling patches from the original input (i.e. randomly suppressing object information).
- Examine the effect on specific tasks such as object detection and image segmentation.
- Investigate the change in attention patterns and feature maps with and without the object-centric suppression.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Suppressing object-centric information will hurt performance on tasks that rely on object representation, suggesting that the model has indeed learned to bind objects, but the effect might be smaller for tasks that can be solved by low-level features, and the model might be able to compensate for object binding in other ways.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Object Binding in Pretrained Vision Transformers

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Object Binding in Vision Transformers through Attention-based Object Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Train a Vision Transformer on the COCO dataset with object segmentation heads, and evaluate its ability to detect object boundaries and instance segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models such as Mask R-CNN.
CONTROLS: Compare to Mask R-CNN, a popular object segmentation baseline.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ViT will achieve competitive performance to Mask R-CNN on object boundaries and instance segmentation accuracy, but may struggle with fine-grained details, potentially indicating a limited understanding of object binding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: The Role of Self-Attention in Object Binding: Analysis and Ablation Studies
PROPOSAL: Perform a series of ablation studies on the self-attention mechanism within the Vision Transformer, specifically removing or modifying its ability to capture long-range dependencies, to understand its contribution to object binding.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original Vision Transformer model, as well as variants with modified architectures (e.g. replacing self-attention with recurrent mechanisms) and training procedures (e.g. masking attention to focus on local regions).
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will show that self-attention plays a critical role in capturing global image structure and facilitating object binding, but may also reveal vulnerabilities to structured inputs that could be exploited to improve binding performance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: (revision remains the same) The Role of Self-Attention in Object Binding: Analysis and Ablation Studies
PROPOSAL: (revision) In addition to analyzing the self-attention mechanism, also investigate the impact of reducing the number of attention heads, decreasing the embed-ding dimensionality, or pruning the attention weights to understand the interplay between self-attention and dimensionality.
CONTROLS: Compare the impact of the above modifications to the baseline Vision Transformer model and the ablated self-attention variant.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will reveal that reducing the number of attention heads or embedding dimensionality worsens object binding performance, while pruning attention weights has a more nuanced effect, potentially revealing the importance of sparse attention mechanisms for object binding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Object Binding through Iterative Attention Refinement
PROPOSAL: Design an iterative attention refinement framework, where the Vision Transformer receives an additional attention-refinement module that takes as input the output of the original self-attention module and refines it through iterative layers, allowing the model to dynamically adjust its attention focus and improves object binding.
CONTROLS: Compare the refined model to the original Vision Transformer and the ablated self-attention variant.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will show that the iterative attention refinement framework improves object binding performance, but may also lead to increased training instability or overfitting, requiring careful hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Object-Centric Roles of Vision Transformers through Dynamic Slot Attention
PROPOSAL: Integrate a dynamic slot attention mechanism with the Vision Transformer, allowing the model to assign dynamic roles to visual tokens and have them compete for slots that capture the object identity, enabling more interpretable and object-centric object binding.
CONTROLS: Compare the dynamic slot attention model to the original Vision Transformer, the ablated self-attention variant, and the iterative attention refinement framework.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will show that the dynamic slot attention mechanism improves object binding performance by learning to recognize and abstract object identities, but may also require careful tuning of the slot capacity and dynamic competition strategies to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Relational Graph Modeling of Object Binding in Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Represent object binding as a relational graph, where visual tokens are nodes and relations encode object identity and spatial geometry, enabling the Vision Transformer to reason about object binding through graph-based attention mechanisms.
CONTROLS: Compare the relational graph model to the original Vision Transformer and the other variants, evaluating its performance on object binding tasks and relational graph learning objectives.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will show that the relational graph model provides a interpretable and modular framework for object binding, but may require careful hyperparameter tuning and initialization strategies to achieve optimal performance and scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modal Object Binding in Vision Transformers through Heterogeneous Graph Attention
PROPOSAL: Incorporate cross-modal features (e.g. text, audio) into the Vision Transformer through a heterogeneous graph attention mechanism, enabling the model to reason about object binding across different modalities and improving its performance on object grounding tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the heterogeneous graph attention model to the original Vision Transformer and the other variants, evaluating its performance on object binding tasks and multi-modal object grounding objectives.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will show that the heterogeneous graph attention model improves object grounding performance by learning to reason about object binding across different modalities, but may require careful hyperparameter tuning and optimization strategies to achieve optimal performance and scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Evaluation of Object Binding in Vision Transformers through Human-Labeled Data and Model Interpretability Techniques
PROPOSAL: Empirically evaluate the object binding performance of the Vision Transformer variants through human-labeled data and model interpretability techniques (e.g. feature visualization, saliency maps), providing insights into the model's decision-making process and identifying potential areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: Compare the object binding performance of the Vision Transformer variants on the same human-labeled data, and evaluate their performance on various model interpretability metrics.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will provide a deeper understanding of the object binding capabilities of the Vision Transformer variants, and highlight potential areas for improvement through more effective model design, training strategies, or post-hoc interpretability techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Analogy-Based Object Binding in Vision Transformers through Pre-Training and Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Pre-train a Vision Transformer on large-scale datasets and then fine-tune it on analogy-based object binding tasks, where the model is required to reason about object binding across multiple images and(Clever) instances of objects, and evaluate its performance on a wide range of object binding tasks and analogies.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the pre-trained and fine-tuned Vision Transformer to the other variants, and evaluate its performance on a variety of object binding tasks and analogies.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will show that the pre-trained and fine-tuned Vision Transformer achieves state-of-the-art performance on object binding tasks and analogies, by leveraging its ability to learn powerful representations and reason about object binding through analogical reasoning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Object Binding in Vision Transformers: Understanding the Interplay between Attention and Representation
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework to understand the interplay between attention and representation in Vision Transformers, and derive a set of bounds and theorems that characterizes the object binding performance of Vision Transformers in terms of attention mechanisms and representation learning objectives.
CONTROLS: None (completely theoretical proposal)
COST: N/A
PREDICTION: The results will provide a fundamental understanding of the object binding mechanisms in Vision Transformers, and will shed light on the optimal design of attention mechanisms and representation learning objectives for object binding tasks.
