actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Object Binding in Vision Transformers Using Gradient Cam
PROPOSAL: Utilize Grad-CAM (Gradient Class Activation Maps) to visualize and interpret the feature importance weights learned by Vision Transformers (ViTs) during image classification tasks. This will provide insights into whether ViTs can learn to bind objects by highlighting the spatial locations and feature channels that contribute to object recognition decisions. For each object in the image, Grad-CAM will highlight the regions within the feature map that correspond to the object, allowing us to evaluate whether these regions capture object-level structure or simply aggregate low-level features.
CONTROLS: Compare to self-attention based ViT variants to assess if the object binding information is contained within the reliance on self-attention or if it is an artifact of early layers or pre-training.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results should show that ViTs with self-attention learn to capture object-level structure, however weakly tied to specific objects, as the models attempt to handle multiple objects from training data. It may fail to generalize, weakly generalizes or fails to identify clear object-level structure for specific visuals tested (depiction resembling other animals, similar household items etc.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Evidence of Object Binding in Vision Transformers with Unsupervised Object Discovery
PROPOSAL: Implement a set of unsupervised object discovery tasks on top of pre-trained ViTs to evaluate their ability to find and segment objects in images without any supervision. By forcing the models to attempts to isolate and capture object-level structure, we can quantify their binding capacity and gain insights into whether the object level information exists in the ViT's internal representations.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance with Slot Attention and BERTS (Bidirectional encoder representations from Transformers) conditioned object discovery benchmarks to establish the novelty and uniqueness of the ViTs object binding capacity.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results should show that pre-trained ViTs are capable of weak object discovery across a range of tasks. Nevertheless, we hypothesize that object segmentation and representation becomes cluttered in complex scene representations, further tested on diverse images that include dissimilar item formations and any static objects.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Object Binding in Vision Transformers Using Gradient Cam
PROPOSAL: To further analyze the results of Grad-CAM visualization, revise the proposal to use AMAX Grad-CAM (maximum A-max pooling Grad-CAM) to inhibit over-attribution and allow the model to focus on the most relevant region. This will help to confirm whether the highlighted regions truly correspond to object-level structure.
CONTROLS: The same as before, compare to self-attention based ViT variants to assess if the object binding information is contained within the reliance on self-attention or if it is an artifact of early layers or pre-training.
COST: Additional 50 GPU-hours for retraining the model with the revised Grad-CAM.
PREDICTION: Expected result could see a more accurate attribution of object representations and binding; however it still expects grad cam attribution interpretable objects, not general ones.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Object Binding in Pre-trained Vision Transformers for Visual Reasoning Tasks
PROPOSAL: Choose datasets like Visual Question Answering (VQA), and Relevant Regions for Visual Question Answering datasets, and use pre-trained ViTs to perform visual reasoning tasks that require object binding, such as identifying the relationships between objects or their attributes. We will analyze the internal representations of the ViTs to understand whether they have learned to represent objects in a way that supports visual reasoning.
CONTROLS: Implement state-of-the-art models for VQA, as well as models without object representations, to compare their performance and understand whether object binding improves visual reasoning abilities.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We hypothesize that ViTs with object binding will outperform those without on tasks requiring visual reasoning, but may fail to demonstrate strong relationships among differently viewed objects or certain attribute specifications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Object Binding via Contour Learning with Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Implement contour-based object representation learning on top of pre-trained ViTs to learn to capture object-level structure using contour features. By forcing the models to represent objects as closed curves, we can gain insights into whether the object-level information exists in the ViT's internal representations.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance with existing object-centric methods like Slot Attention and learnable template models to understand whether contour-based representation learning improves object binding abilities.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results might exhibit contour-focused object binding representations across a variety of image and object representations. Away from being less certain, this research struggles with elaborate shapes (3D or intersecting objects, duplicate colors etc).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Assessing Evidence of Object Binding in Vision Transformers with Unsupervised Object Discovery
PROPOSAL: To further investigate the object binding capabilities of ViTs in unsupervised object discovery tasks, revise the proposal to include the use of more challenging datasets, such as cluttered scenes or scenes with multiple objects of similar appearance. This will help to assess whether ViTs can learn to robustly capture object-level structure in complex and ambiguous situations.
CONTROLS: The same as before, compare the performance with Slot Attention and BERTS conditioned object discovery benchmarks to establish the novelty and uniqueness of the ViTs object binding capacity.
COST: Additional 150 GPU-hours for training on the revised datasets.
PREDICTION: Expected results might show a weaker performance of pre-trained ViTs on complex tasks; there is still a value on showcasing enhanced robustness compared to standard techniques, but the reduced attribution to these gains will still substantiate the hypothesis defense in ViT presentation analysis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Emergence of Object Binding in Vision Transformers through Visualization of Attention Weights
PROPOSAL: Utilize attention weight visualization techniques, such as attention maps or attention weights, to analyze how Vision Transformers process and represent information about objects in an image. By examining the flow of attention and how it relates to objects, we can gain insights into whether the object-level information exists in the ViT's internal representations and how it emerges through the self-attention mechanism.
CONTROLS: Compare the attention patterns with existing object-centric methods like Slot Attention and learnable template models to understand whether attention-based representation learning improves object binding abilities.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results might exhibit patterns of attention that resemble object-level structure, but may also show that the attention mechanisms are more fascinated by objects’ low-level features (boundaries).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Transferability of Object Binding Capabilities in Pre-trained Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Train pre-trained Vision Transformers on a set of object-centric tasks, such as object detection or segmentation, and then transfer their learned representations to other object-centric tasks, such as visual question answering or image generation. We will analyze the performance of the transferred models to assess whether the object binding capabilities learned in the source task transfer to the target task.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance with models that have not received object-centric pre-training and models that have been fine-tuned on the target task.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results might show that pre-trained ViTs with object binding can indeed transfer their object binding to downstream tasks but performance might degrade for extensive or altered steps which do everything autonomously in other visuals and require exact number knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Object Binding in Vision Transformers through the Lens of Predictive Coding
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework that describes object binding in Vision Transformers through the lens of predictive coding, a cognitive architecture that explains how the brain represents and processes sensory information. We will analyze the predictions of this framework and derive mathematical results that describe the emergence of object binding in Vision Transformers.
CONTROLS: Compare the theoretical framework with existing cognitive architectures and object-centric models to understand its novelty and unique contributions.
COST: Minimal (theoretical work can be done on small computational resources)
PREDICTION: Expected results might provide a new perspective on the object binding problem and demonstrate that Vision Transformers can indeed learn to represent objects in a way that is consistent with the predictions of predictive coding. However, the theory might fail to capture the nuances of the object binding problem and neglect the complexity of natural images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Combining Experimental and Theoretical Studies to Elucidate Object Binding in Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Integrate the results of the previous experiments and the theoretical framework from proposal 7 to provide a comprehensive understanding of object binding in Vision Transformers. We will compare the predictions of the theoretical framework with the empirical results from the experiments and explore the implications of this integrated understanding for object-centric AI and cognitive science.
CONTROLS: All previous experiments and controls.
COST: Cumulative cost of the previous experiments (approximately 1600 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Expected results will provide a deep and integrated understanding of object binding in Vision Transformers, combining empirical evidence with theoretical insights. This understanding will have far-reaching implications for the development of object-centric AI systems and our understanding of the cognitive processes that underlie human perception and object recognition. However, the integration of the results might be challenging, and the final understanding might be oversimplified or neglect specific details.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Limits of Feedback-Guided Anonymization with Small LLMs
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of several small self-supervised LLMs (e.g., BART, T5, DistilBERT) as anonymizers against a state-of-the-art larger proprietary LLM (GPT-4) on synthetic data, where we simulate various degrees of contextual inference risk (e.g., global context, specific domains) and anonymization difficulty (e.g., straightforward vs. obfuscated private information).
CONTROLS: GPT-4 as the strong LLM adversary and baseline anonymizer, random text rewriting as a naive anonymization baseline, and synthetic data without anonymization as a negative baseline.
COST: 20 GPU-hours ( approx. training and inference time for 5 small LLMs, 1 large LLM, and various parameter sweeps).
PREDICTION: We expect the larger LLM to outperform small LLMs on the most challenging anonymization tasks, but smaller LLMs to be surprisingly competitive on relatively easier tasks due to their adaptability and reduced risk of overfitting; more importantly, this will help us identify potential design directions for better utilizing small LLMs in anonymization scenarios.

TITLE: REVISED
PROPOSAL: REVISE 1: Property-Specific Anonymization of Contextual Inferences in Text
   In this revised study, we develop a novel framework that leverages small LLMs to anonymize text while preserving contextual inferences. We incorporate a multi-task learning approach, where the LLM is trained to anonymize text and emulate a reference model on a specific inference task, exploiting the semantic relationships between the anonymized output and the reference model's predictions. This allows the LLM to capture subtle contextual cues and prevent adversaries from inferring private attributes.
CONTROLS: The baseline is a standard small LLM without the multi-task learning approach, using the same settings and data as in Proposal 1.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (hierarchical architecture and distributed evaluation).
PREDICTION: Our approach is expected to achieve a better trade-off between privacy and utility, particularly for inference tasks that involve contextual relationships, by enabling the LLM to capture subtle contextual cues while preserving the anonymized text's meaning and coherence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Active Learning Strategies for Efficient Anonymization with Small LLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the efficacy of active learning (AL) techniques in optimizing the anonymization process using small LLMs. Specifically, we will evaluate the performance of different AL strategies (e.g., uncertainty sampling, query-by-committee) in identifying the most informative instances for annotators to provide feedback, with the goal of iteratively refining the anonymized output and improving the trade-off between privacy and utility.
CONTROLS: Compare various AL strategies against a random sampling baseline, and also explore the impact of varying the number of annotated instances on the overall performance.
COST: 25 GPU-hours (active learning experiment and incremental anonymization).
PREDICTION: We anticipate that active learning techniques will be essential in efficiently utilizing the LLM's capacity for anonymization, especially in scenarios where data samples are scarce or have high-dimensional features, and we expect these methods to provide significant improvements in the alignment between privacy and utility.

TITLE: Robustness-Centric Anonymization of Text: Embedding Denoising Diffusion into Small LLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate incorporating diffusion-based denoising techniques into small LLMs for text anonymization, aiming to improve the robustness of the anonymized output against various attacks, including transfer learning adversarial attacks (Section 2) and meta-adversarial attacks (e.g., taxonomy assaults on private properties kinds viewpoints within web societal scenarios discussions delve widely).
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness and performance of the diffusion-based LLM anonymizer against the standard LLM anonymizer (Proposal 1), as well as other competitive baselines (e.g., posterior sampling for semantic structure preservation).
COST: 35 GPU-hours (diffusion-based LLM architecture and robustness evaluation).

Prediction: We expect the larger LLM to outperform small LLMs on the most challenging anonymization tasks, but smaller LLMs to be surprisingly competitive on relatively easier tasks due to their adaptability and reduced risk of overfitting; more importantly, this will help us identify potential design directions for better utilizing small LLMs in anonymization scenarios.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Local Anonymization with Small Language Models
PROPOSAL: Compare the anonymization capabilities of a range of small, state-of-the-art language models (such as T5-base and BART) to GPT-4 on a synthetic dataset, focusing on attribute inference resistance and readability. We design an experiment where these models anonymize online comments while an adversary (another GPT-4 model) attempts to infer personal attributes.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art anonymizers such as Feedback-guided Adversarial Anonymization (FGAA), set a strong baseline or proprietary anonymizer. Examine in-system evaluation metrics such as FLIP and Object Perturbation.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results show that the state-of-the-art small models can achieve pleasing accuracy, and comparable annotation cost reduction over the pricey GPT-4 dependency while generating text which is hard to de-annotate. We expect our experiment without external proprietary APIs at inference to save ∼50% of the costs showing a reduction of privacy risks but potential limitations on model quality.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Limited Quantization for Anonymization Efficiency
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of weight quantization on the performance of small language models in anonymization tasks. Experiments are designed to compare the baseline models with varying levels of quantization (e.g., int8, ternary) on the synthetic anonymization task described in proposal 1. 
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of quantization on attribute inference resistance, model size, and inference speed. Compare the results to the baseline.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results indicate that moderate quantization levels can improve the inference speed while slightly sacrificing anonymization efficiency. This will facilitate more efficient deployment of the anonymizers on edge devices with constrained resources.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Efficient Anonymization through Test-Time Pruning
PROPOSAL: Develop a test-time pruning strategy to reduce the model size during anonymization tasks while maintaining its anonymization efficiency. A small state-of-the-art model is first fine-tuned on the synthetic dataset for anonymization. Then, a pruning algorithm is applied at test time to prune less contributing neurons while minimizing the loss of anonymization quality.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the trade-off between model size reduction and anonymization quality. Compare the results to the baseline and the quantization experiments described in proposal 1 and 2.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict a reduction in model size of approximately 60% with a minor impact (less than 5%) on the anonymization performance, indicating the potential for much more efficient anonymization on low power hardware.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Tiered Local Anonymization with Small Language Models
PROPOSAL: Extend the experimental design of proposal 1 by incorporating multiple small language models of varying strengths (e.g., T5-base, BART, T5-large) to anonymize the text in a tiered manner. For example, a lower strength model might introduce descriptive anonymization (e.g., X -> ?) and a stronger model builds regression-based anonymization (e.g., lack of attribute inference). 
CONTROLS: Compare the results to the baseline and the state-of-the-art anonymizers such as FGAA. Examine in-system evaluation metrics such as FLIP and Object Perturbation.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We hope that such a tiered system can qualitatively outperform traditional anonymizers and approach the anonymization quality of GPT-4, while being significantly cheaper and more private. However, it may introduce additional aspects of potential bias from more uncertain system choices.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Combining Anonymization with Model Smoothing
PROPOSAL: Introduce a technique to combine the anonymization with model smoothing to make it more robust against attribute inference attacks. During the training process, use a small, noise-augmented version of the training data and the small language model described in proposal 2 to optimize for the adversarial training objective, leading to a combination that minimizes information leakage. 
CONTROLS: Compare to proposal 2 and other robust training methods on datasets with targeted attacks.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By training with a noise-augmented version of the training data, our combined anonymization- smoothing method should provide a stronger defense mechanism, by contaminating potential inference, and hiding inference-easy targeted features.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Local Differential Privacy for Anonymization
PROPOSAL: Use the ideas behind local differential privacy (LDP) to introduce noise to the anonymization outputs, making it computationally expensive for attackers to learn private attributes. The expectation is that when models are retrained to correct for the expected value of the output, they cannot learn sensitive information. Investigate different noise addition techniques to determine the right amount of noise for acceptable anonymization quality while protecting sensitive information.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of trade-offs between sensitivity reduction and useful anonymization quality. Compare the outcomes to traditional anonymizers and other forms of data anonymization.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By adding the right noise, we can quantitatively limit the ability of a number of capabilities of a model learner against topical or contextual identifiers - the prediction essentially provides a bound on the total number of users in a potentially abused attacker inference profile with limited importance to data controller relational privacy.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Sampling Strategies for Efficient Anonymization
PROPOSAL: Investigate different sampling strategies (e.g., random sampling, stratified sampling, active learning) for the synthetic anonymization dataset. This could lead to optimized anonymization quality with significantly reduced dataset size, making it more compatible for small language models and local computation. The goal is to find a sampling strategy that minimizes the trade-off between anonymization quality and dataset size.
CONTROLS: Compare the sampling strategies on the synthetic dataset and evaluate their impact on anonymization quality and model performance. Compare to other, less efficient, anonymization methods.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By optimizing the sampling strategy, we can potentially achieve a 50% reduction in dataset size while maintaining comparable anonymization quality, making more efficient use of constrained resources such as edge devices.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Explainability and Interpretability for Anonymization Methods
PROPOSAL: Investigate and compare different explainability and interpretability methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME, Backbone to Ave, causal graph method) for the anonymization methods described in previous proposals. The goal is to understand why and how small language models with state-of-the-art anonymization techniques achieve anonymization and what specific words, phrases, or tokens have an impact on the inference.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of each method in providing accurate insights into anonymization and identify the most suitable techniques for future improvements.
COST: 22 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By applying and evaluating different explainability and interpretability methods, we can better understand the inner workings of our anonymization techniques, enabling us to refine them and meet the required privacy utility trade-offs. Analog to RSF understanding bias, it also should also help to identify undesirable data retention statistics; so benefit loss-inducing interpretation hit loss.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Evaluation and Comparison with Existing Methods
PROPOSAL: Adopt the synthetic anonymization dataset and evaluate the proposed methods on a larger scale. Investigate the average performance of the improved methods in terms of attribute inference resistance and readability, using metrics such as FLIP and Object Perturbation. Compare the results to state-of-the-art techniques in anonymization and standard off-the-shelf techniques for anonymization, and other achieved research ideas.
CONTROLS: Use a combination of controlled experiments and real-world experimentation to evaluate proposed techniques on both sensitive and general Cuban Commentary datasets. PROPOSAL: Extend the proposed anonymization methods to real-world applications, focusing on deploying them in context where anonymization is critical. This includes implementing our methods in a cloud-based environment for scalable anonymization and integrating them with existing web services for seamless integration. Evaluate the efficiency, performance, and adoption of the proposed anonymization methods in real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Autonomous Small-Model Anonymization through Self-Supervised Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: Train a small-sized transformer model (e.g., distilled version of BERT-base) on self-supervised adversarial tasks, where the input consists of anonymized sentences and the corresponding original text with private attributes highlighted. The model learns to predict these highlighted attributes based on the anonymized text, and is trained to predict dummy attributes as 'adversarial feedback' to thwart itself. Use a proxy label-based loss function to minimize the accuracy of this prediction while maintaining good model performance on downstream anonymization tasks, such as removal of surface-level identifiers.
CONTROLS: Compare self-supervised training to standard supervised fine-tuning of the small model on publicly available datasets for text anonymization (e.g., ATIS, WebEd).
COST: 100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This approach may achieve a reasonable privacy-utility trade-off but likely fails to approach the performance of state-of-the-art, large-scale anonymizers, especially when task and context complexity prevent the small model from adequately retaining features from the original text.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Identity Obfuscation through Distributional Gap Minimization
PROPOSAL: Design a regularization-based anonymization approach that directly minimizes the distributional gap between anonymized and original text, by maximizing a statistical distance between the two. Compare different distance metrics (e.g., KL-divergence, Fisher information) on text embeddings (e.g., word2vec, BERT), incorporating nearest-neighbor based heuristics to refine the optimal anonymized text. This technique can be more robust to various models, and does not require model-specific training or adversarial feedback.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard dropout-based regularization, as well as rewriting and distortion methods (e.g., noise addition, synonym replacement).
COST: 50 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This approach may perform competitively with existing methods on simple anonymization tasks but may struggle when coped with more nuanced contexts and linguistic complexities where anonymization trade-offs with utility.

Use techniques from multi-objective optimization to balance general anonymization performance against the 'identity utility' of its decisions. Use distance metrics like (e.g., word level and phrase level ngram matching) to estimate identity utility, and NDCG to evaluate the anonymization utility.
CONTROLS: Compare cross-validation iterations on coherence agrement and intrusion metrics, as well as setting computational parameters.

PROPOSAL: Develop a framework to systematically quantify the trade-off between anonymization utility and privacy preservation in text data. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Essential Graph Information Extraction via Filtered Graph Attention
PROPOSAL: We propose a new test-time OOD detection framework that incorporates a filtered graph attention mechanism (FGA) to identify and extract essential structural information from test graphs while suppressing irrelevant redundancy. We adapt the pre-trained GNN to predict attention weights, which indicate the importance of graph components in distinguishing ID from OOD samples. These weights are then used to compute a weighted sum of the node embeddings, representing the "essence" of the test graph.
CONTROLS: GOODAT (our baseline test-time approach), random graph attention without filter (control for baseline without extraction mechanism), GNN-only without attention (ablation)
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our FGA-based framework to outperform GOODAT and random graph attention on ID/OOD separation, particularly when confronted with test graphs that possess redundant structures, as our method can pinpoint the essential structural information representative of OOD samples. However, achieving accurate attention weights may be a challenging task, especially when the pre-trained model lacks inductive bias toward the OOD distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Enhanced Essential Graph Information Extraction via Differential Graph Representations
PROPOSAL: We propose a new extension to the FGA framework in proposal 1, using a differential graph representation learning technique to further distill the essential structural information of test graphs. We use a contrastive learning objective to learn a difference-aware graph embedding that highlights the structural variations between ID and OOD samples, thus improving the effectiveness of the FGA mechanism in capturing the distinguishing characteristics of OOD graphs.
CONTROLS: FGA (from proposal 1), deep graph similarity (ablation for contrastive learning impact), π - model baseline without differential representation (ablation for standalone representation impact)
COST: 300 GPU-hours (for additional contrastive learning episode)
PREDICTION: We expect the differential graph representation to enhance the performance of the FGA mechanism, particularly in scenarios where ID and OOD graphs exhibit drastic structural variations, due to the improved capability of extracting discriminative graph structures. However, computing difference-aware graph embeddings may be computationally intensive, which could affect scalability for very large graphs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Which Subgraphs Matter Most?: Hierarchical Structured Distillation for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We introduce a hierarchical structured distillation framework to selectively focus on the most discriminative subgraphs within test graphs. By recursively clustering and filtering subgraphs based on their ability to distinguish ID from OOD samples, we identify a subset of "critical" subgraphs that are more relevant to OOD detection. We then distill this information using a light-weight autoencoder to generate a compact, hierarchical graph representation that emphasizes the important structural components.
CONTROLS: FGA+Differential Graph Representation (from proposal 2), random subgraph selection (ablation for hierarchical approach), θ - model baseline without structured distillation (ablation for distillation impact)
COST: 250 GPU-hours (for subgraph clustering and autoencoder training)
PREDICTION: By selectively focusing on the most relevant subgraphs and applying distillation, we expect to achieve improved OOD detection performance, even for complex test graphs with high structural redundancy. However, identifying the optimal number and organization of subgraphs within the hierarchical structure might require additional hyperparameter tuning and experimentation.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Which Subgraphs Matter Most?: Hierarchical Structured Distillation for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We refine proposal 3 by integrating it with the FGA framework from proposal 1 and extending the hierarchical structured distillation mechanism to leverage the filtered attention weights from the FGA component. This enables us to prioritize the subgraphs that are most relevant to the OOD detection task, as indicated by the FGA attention weights, and use the hierarchical distillation framework to compactly represent these critical subgraphs. The combination of FGA and hierarchical distillation is expected to further enhance the discriminative power of the graph representations for OOD detection.
CONTROLS: FGA+Differential Graph Representation (from proposal 2), random subgraph selection (ablation for hierarchical approach), θ - model baseline without structured distillation (ablation for distillation impact)
COST: 250 GPU-hours (no additional compute if proposal 2's compute is used as a foundation)
PREDICTION: By synergistically integrating FGA and hierarchical distillation, we expect a more accurate identification of the most discriminative subgraphs and enhanced OOD detection performance, especially for complex test graphs. However, the increased complexity of the combined approach might require more careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implicit Graph Structure and OOD Data Attention for Enhanced Test-Time OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We investigate an implicit attention mechanism that focuses on parts of the graph structure most relevant to OOD detection, by learning a data-driven attention over the graph nodes that are most indicative of the out-of-distribution data. We introduce a self-attention layer with a specially designed triplet-based loss function that encourages the model to attend to nodes and edges that are likely to be indicative of the OOD graph, regardless of structural redundancy. This allows our method to adjust to the underlying graph structure and adapt to novel OOD data.
CONTROLS: FGA+Differential Graph Representation (from proposal 2), fixed graph structure attention (ablation for adaptability impact), no-attention graph embedding (ablation for attention impact)
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging implicit graph structure and learnable attention, we expect our method to better capture the nuances of OOD data and distinguish ID from OOD graphs more accurately. However, it may require careful tuning of the triplet-based loss function to avoid overfitting to specific OOD samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph Prototypicalization for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a graph prototypicalization approach to identify a compact set of representative "signal graphs" that capture the essence of the most discriminative graph structures for OOD detection. These signal graphs are learned through a retrieval-based approach, where the model computes similarity between graph representations and aggregates the structural information to create a condensed representation of the underlying distribution. This distilled representation is then used to detect OOD graphs more robustly.
CONTROLS: FGA+Differential Graph Representation+Hierarchical Distillation (from proposal 3), single graph representation (ablation for prototypicalization impact), BOOM arrival baseline without graph prototypicalization (ablation for diversity impact)
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By learning a set of representative signal graphs, we expect our method to capture the commonalities and shared properties of the ID data, while being able to detect novel and unseen OOD graphs more effectively. However, over-regularization of the signal graphs may lead to a loss of critical structural information, affecting the detection accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Graph Prototypicalization for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We refine proposal 5 by integrating it with the hierarchical structured distillation framework from proposal 3 to create a more comprehensive understanding of the graph structure's relevance to OOD detection. This approach involves using the prototypicalized signal graphs to filter and further emphasizing essential substructures within the hierarchical framework. This enhancement is expected to improve the robustness of our OOD detection method, allowing it to better capture the shared patterns and novel characteristics of the OOD data.
CONTROLS: FGA+Differential Graph Representation+Hierarchical Distillation (from proposal 3), single graph representation (ablation for prototypicalization impact), BOOM arrival baseline without graph prototypicalization (ablation for diversity impact), graph prototypicalization without hierarchical distillation (ablation for integrated effect)
COST: 375 GPU-hours (assuming the combined 300 GPU-hours as a foundation)
PREDICATION: By integrating graph prototypicalization and hierarchical structured distillation, we expect to achieve a more synergistic and comprehensive understanding of the graph structure that underlies OOD detection. This method should provide a robust and accurate framework for distinguishing ID from OOD graphs, even for complex and high-dimensional graph structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive Learnable Node Embeddings for OOD Graph Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to learn node embeddings that capture the discriminative and commonalities among ID graphs while providing robustness to OOD graphs. We utilize a contrastive learning framework to learn node embeddings, where positive pairs consist of nodes from the same ID graph and negative pairs consist of nodes from different ID graphs or graph pairs with large structural differences. This encourages the model to focus on node-level features that are distinct between graphs and allows it to better identify OOD graphs during inference.
CONTROLS: Graph Prototypicalization+Hierarchical Distillation (from revised proposal 5), learned node embeddings without contrastive learning (ablation for learnability impact), simple node hash embeddings (ablation for sophistication impact)
COST: 400 GPU-hours (a natural extension to the node and graph learning strategy at scale)
PREDICTION: By leveraging contrastive learnable node embeddings, we expect to enhance the model's understanding of graph structure and improve its robustness against novel OOD distributions. However, the scalability of the contrastive learning framework may require high computational resources, and hyperparameter tuning will be necessary to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Implicit Graph Structure and OOD Data Attention for Enhanced Test-Time OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We refine proposal 4 by integrating it with contrastive learnable node embeddings from proposal 6, enabling the model to learn adaptive attention to nodes with discriminative features for OOD detection. This approach leverages both node-level representation and graph-level structure to guide the attention mechanism, promoting a more informed decision-making process for distinguishing OOD graphs. By incorporating node embeddings into the attention model, we expect to achieve improved detection accuracy and robustness against novel OOD distributions.
CONTROLS: Graph Prototypicalization+Hierarchical Distillation (from revised proposal 5), integration of our earlier work without node embeddings (ablation for learnability impact), baseline attention model without implicit graph structure consideration (ablation for model impact)
COST: 500 GPU-hours (assuming the combined 400 GPU-hours as a foundation)
PREDICTION: By integrating implicit graph structure and node embeddings into the attention mechanism, we expect to develop a more robust and accurate approach for OOD detection on complex graph-structured data. This method should enable the model to better capture subtle graph variations and anomalies while ignoring structural redundancy and noise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ensemble of Recursive Graph Transformations for Open-Set Graph Classification
PROPOSAL: We present a novel ensemble method that recursively applies various graph transformation techniques (e.g., node clustering, edge collapsing) to the input graph, generating a diverse set of transformed graphs. Each transformed graph is then passed through a pre-trained GNN, and the generated predictions are combined using a weighted majority vote. We propose to use a model-agnostic approach to learn the weights, so the method can be applied to any pre-trained GNN.
CONTROLS: Ensemble of Recursive Graph Transformations - Model Averaging, Base Model than w/o recursive ensemble, Graph Prototypicalization + Hierarchical Distillation (ablation)
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By ensemble the results of recursive graph transformations with pre-trained GNNs, we expect to largely reduce the risk of underfitting and provide a significant improvement on most of the metrics.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Unsupervised Graph Filter Learning for Test-Time OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: Train a graph filter bank on the pre-trained GNN using only unlabeled ID data, where each filter tunes the receptive field and spatial relationships to capture salient features of ID graphs. At test time, apply the learned filter bank to the test graphs to extract sensitive features through layer-wise spatial-temporal dependencies, which can distinguish ID graphs from OOD samples.
CONTROLS: Compare against GOODAT, a baseline using pre-trained GNN with a learnable graph masker, and an ablation where the filter bank is not used.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to outperform GOODAT in terms of OOD detection accuracy on ID graphs and provide a more interpretable feature representation, but could fail on scenarios with complex graph layouts due to over-smoothing.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Equity Equivariant Graph Attention for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a test-time OOD detector using graph attention networks (GATs) that incorporate equity equivariance, enabling the model to focus on meaningful structural elements of the test graph while being invariant to redundant components. This can be achieved by adding a learnable scale invariant layer on each attention head, and using a dynamically gated output to prioritize structural features based on local graph contexts.
CONTROLS: Test the detector against the pre-trained baseline with its standard architecture, and an ablation of the equity equivariance ingredient, as well as a comparison with other GAT variants.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to show a significant boost in OOD detection accuracy by more effectively capturing graph structural variations and tolerating redundant component presence, but could fail for networks with highly variable graph topologies due to the difficulty in estimating the learning rate for equity equivariance penalties.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Unsupervised Graph Filter Learning for Test-Time OOD Detection with Structural Clique Ranking
PROPOSAL: Revise the previous proposal to not only learn the filter bank for feature extraction but also incorporate a structural clique ranking mechanism to locally identify informative sub-structures within the test graph, which can provide contextual cues to the model for distinguishing between ID and OOD graphs.
CONTROLS: Modify the original ablation study to compare against the updated model, as well as extending it to tests involving domains with highly variable graph topologies.
COST: 120 GPU-hours, increase from the pre-revision cost due to the introduction of additional training components
PREDICTION: Expected to not only maintain the previous results and potential benefits of the filter bank but also demonstrate improved robustness and interpretability when identifying relevant components in the graph, but could fail on graphs with locally low-dimensional features leading to clique detection difficulties.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Architecture-Agnostic Layer-Wise Importance Estimation for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel method to estimate the layer-wise importance of features extracted by the pre-trained GNN for OOD detection, by training a separate module that can adapt to different architectures and can work across various tasks and datasets. Use the learned importance estimator to identify and prune irrelevant or redundant features from the test graph, enabling the model to focus on critical components.
CONTROLS: Test the detector against variants of the pre-trained model, where features of different importance levels are removed or retained, as well as the GOODAT detector with a graph masker.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate improved OOD detection accuracy by adaptively focusing the model on meaningful components of the input graph, while avoiding over úpravิตภased analysis that leads to local minimal features that are inherently very small.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Transferable Hyperbolic Graph Networks for Out-of-Distribution Detection on Molecular Properties
PROPOSAL: Propose the use of hyperbolic graph networks (HGNs) and transfer learning to leverage knowledge from pre-trained models and adapt to molecular property prediction tasks with small OOD datasets. This involves mapping the graph-structured molecular data to a hyperbolic space, where the structural relationships can be better captured, and evaluating the effectiveness of the HGN-based OOD detector in identification of out-of-distribution samples.
CONTROLS: Test the HGN-based model on real-world molecular property prediction benchmarks and compare its performance with the state-of-the-art detectors on that specific domain, using a predefined dataset such as QM9 or MoleculeNet.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to show improved robustness and generalizability on molecular property prediction tasks due to the ability of HGNs to better capture the structural relationships, but may require domain adaptation techniques due to the unique chemical space of OOD samples in that domain.

ACTION: ADD 5

PROPOSAL: Develop a test-time OOD detector by adapting the graph contrastive learning (GCL) paradigm to the OOD detection problem. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Graph-SPLINE: An Efficient Test-Time Detector for Capturing Essential Structures
PROPOSAL: Graph-SPLINE is a test-time detector that learns to selectively project input graphs onto lower-dimensional representations, emphasizing essential structural components and suppressing irrelevant ones. This is achieved by optimizating the parameters of a set of graph convolutional filters over a learned spline-like basis that enables smooth interpolation between graph representations. By adaptively adjusting the focus on different parts of the graph, Graph-SPLINE captures the prominent structural motifs of input graphs while discarding misleading structural redundancy.
CONTROLS: We compare Graph-SPLINE against the current state-of-the-art test-time method, GOODAT, on three graph classification benchmarks in the molecular property prediction domain: ZINC, MIMIC, and MUV. We record the OOD detection accuracy and examine the per-class performance on both ID and OOD test sets.
COST: 
PREDICTION: We predict that Graph-SPLINE will achieve a significantly higher OOD detection accuracy than GOODAT, with up to a 25% improvement in the presence of large structural redundancy between ID and OOD graphs. We also expect that the method will be generally more robust to varying levels of structural noise and outliers, leading to a lower rate of incorrect predictions.

ACTION: REVISE 1 
TITLE: Graph-SPLINE: Adaptive Filtering Mechanism for Structural Importance Estimation
PROPOSAL: We refine Graph-SPLINE to incorporate an adaptive filtering mechanism that evaluates the relative importance of different graph components. This mechanism computes a per-structural-element importance score based on the uncertainty of the pre-trained model when making predictions over subgraphs. The importance scores are then combined with the learned spline-like basis to selectively emphasize or de-emphasize different structural components during the projection stage. By adaptively considering both the structural motifs and their importance, the method better captures the essential structural information of input graphs while discarding distracting structural redundancy.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised Graph-SPLINE against the previous baseline, GOODAT, as well as an ablation within Graph-SPLINE that constrains the adaptive filtering mechanism to be constant across all structural elements.
COST: 
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the adaptive filtering mechanism will improve the OOD detection accuracy of Graph-SPLINE by an average of 15% across the three graph classification benchmarks compared to the original model, with a notable gain in robustness to high levels of structural noise and outliers. Nevertheless, the ablation study will reveal limitations of the importance estimation when it is imposed to be constant across all structural elements.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Graph-Based Embedding Dilution (GED): A Novel Approach for Removing Structural Relevance
PROPOSAL: We devise Graph-Based Embedding Dilution (GED), a novel approach for removing structural relevance in input graphs. GED works by iteratively diluting the node and edge representations of the input graph using a learned smoothing function, which weakens the correlations between the selective projections of different graph components. By selectively removing the dependencies between graph components, GED allows for the efficient pruning of distracting structural redundancy that leads to incorrect OOD predictions.
CONTROLS: Empirically, we compare the performance of GED-Graph-SPLINE (Graph-SPLINE with GED integrated into the optimization stage) against Graph-SPLINE without GED, as well as against GOODAT on the same set of graph classification benchmarks.
COST: 
PREDICTION: We predict that GED-Graph-SPLINE will yield OOD detection accuracy improvements of up to 30% compared to its non-GED version, and up to 10% improvement when compared against GOODAT on challenging datasets. The semi-supervised property of GED will help to maintain a lower computational cost compared to fully-supervised alternative approaches.

ACTION: REVISE 2 
TITLE: Graph-Based Embedding Dilution (GED): Incorporating Dominant Pattern Invariance
PROPOSAL: We refine GED to incorporate a dominant pattern invariance approach that leverages the robustness of learned graph embeddings to various structural transformations. Specifically, we add a subset of significant transformations (e.g. , node/edge permutations, edge orientations) to the GED procedure and enforce the learned embeddings to remain consistent under these operations. By augmenting GED with the dynamic tracking of dominant patterns, the refined approach, denoted as GED-DPI, enhances the structural robustness of the input graphs, thereby capturing the recurrent topological features in real-world graphs and significantly improving OOD detection.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the effectiveness of GED-DPI in conjunction with Graph-SPLINE against GOODAT on three real-world datasets: Tencent Collaborative Filtering, BlogCatalog, and PPI.
COST: 
PREDICTION: We anticipate that GED-DPI-Graph-SPLINE will achieve an average 25% improvement in OOD detection accuracy over GOODAT and a 5% improvement compared to standard GED-Graph-SPLINE on moderately complex real-world graphs, revealing significant resilience to topological variations, and relatively robust performance alongside good parameter sensitivity.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Structure-Relevance Graph Contrast (SRGC): A Novel Test-Time Contrastive Learning for Essential Structure Capture
PROPOSAL: We introduce Structure-Relevance Graph Contrast (SRGC), a novel test-time contrastive learning method aimed at capturing the essential structures in input graphs by selectively emphasizing the contrast between relevant and irrelevant structural components. SRGC learns an self-similarity preservation function, via co-encoders, that estimates the reliance of each graph component on the entire graph structure and then learns to amplify the shared structural motifs across relevant components while ignoring the distracting structural redundancy. SRGC enables more accurate OOD detection by progressively amplifying essential structural information while effectively suppressing irrelevant details.
CONTROLS: We 실험ally compare the performance of SRGC-Graph-SPLINE against GED-DPI-Graph-SPLINE and GOODAT, as well as against an ablation of SRGC-Graph-SPLINE that disables the self-similarity preservation function.
COST: 
PREDICTION: We predict that SRGC-Graph-SPLINE will achieve a greater than 30% OOD detection accuracy improvement over GOODAT, with a 10% gain compared to GED-DPI-Graph-SPLINE on challenging datasets such as Tencent Collaborative Filtering and BlogCatalog. We also expect that SRGC-Graph-SPLINE will effectively identify and amplify the dominant patterns and essential structural motifs, leading to improved robustness against varying levels of structural noise and outliers.

ACTION: REVISE 1 
TITLE: Graph-SPLINE: Amplified Structural Importance Estimation via Multi-Information Gain
PROPOSAL: We refine Graph-SPLINE by incorporating a multi-information gain framework, which jointly evaluates the importance of different structural components based on multiple information gain metrics. The multi-information gain framework utilizes a weighted combination of mutual information, conditional mutual information, and information-theoretic metrics that quantify the conditional dependences among graph components and the entire graph structure. By incorporating a diversified set of importance metrics, the refined Graph-SPLINE approach, denoted as Graph-SPLINE-MIG, tends to identify more intrinsic structural importance, rejecting noisy or distracting structural features that contribute to OOD detection errors. We predict that Graph-SPLINE-MIG will perform better than previous Graph-SPLINE variants on the graph classification benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the performance of Graph-SPLINE-MIG using a comprehensive set of evaluative metrics, including OOD detection accuracy, graph reconstruction loss, and influential structural component identification. We also perform an ablation study to uncover the contribution of each importance metric to the multi-information gain.
COST:  
PREDICTION: We anticipate that Graph-SPLINE-MIG will achieve state-of-the-art OOD detection performance on challenging graph benchmarks such as Tencent Collaborative Filtering and BlogCatalog, yielding superiorly robust and accurate detection results over previous approaches, including GED-DPI-Graph-SPLINE and SRGC-Graph-SPLINE.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Graph-Hybrid: A Progressive Hybridization of GNN-based OOD Detection and Graph-based Inliers/Outliers Identification
PROPOSAL: We present Graph-Hybrid, a novel GNN-based OOD detection approach that progressively integrates both pre-trained GNN features and graph-based inliers/outliers identification mechanisms. Graph-Hybrid leverages a graph-augmentation framework to progressively highlight structurally significant features that are predictive of outliers while filtering out meaningless patterns present in the graph. The graph-augmentation steps adaptively enhance the structural representation of input graphs, allowing Graph-Hybrid to determine both the graph's structural normality and its OOD likelihood through a information convergence approach.

PROPOSAL 2: Graph-Based Embedding Dilution (GED): Incorporating Dominant Pattern Invariance
We refine GED to incorporate a dominant pattern invariance approach that leverages the robustness of learned graph embeddings to various structural transformations. Specifically, we add a subset of significant transformations (e.g. , node/edge permutations, edge orientations) to the GED procedure and enforce the learned embeddings to remain consistent under these operations. By augmenting GED with the dynamic tracking of dominant patterns, the refined approach, denoted as GED-DPI, enhances the structural robustness of the input graphs, thereby capturing the recurrent topological features in real-world graphs and significantly improving OOD detection.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Pre-Training Adaptation in SciML
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) technique for pre-trained LOMs in the context of SciML. Specifically, we will use the LoRA variant that embeds a low-rank update into the frozen weights of a pre-trained Fourier Neural Operator (FNO). This will be done on a large synthetic dataset of PDE solutions, with both compressible Navier-Stokes equations and the shallow-water equations being considered.
CONTROLS: We will compare our LoRA-based adaptation method to full-model fine-tuning and to a baseline of pre-training a separate FNO for each downstream task. Additionally, we will perform ablations to understand the impact of the LoRA embedding size and the number of parameters updated.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our LoRA-based adaptation method to outperform full-model fine-tuning in terms of parameter efficiency, while achieving comparable or better downstream performance. The adaptation size and embedding size of LoRA may play a crucial role in determining the success of our method, and we anticipate that smaller models may be more amenable to adaptation using LoRA. The method may fail if the pre-trained LOM has a very different spectral structure from the target PDE, or if the downstream task requires a significant shift in the underlying physics of the system.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Spectral Impact of LoRA on Pre-Trained LOMs
PROPOSAL: We will analyze the effect of LoRA on the spectral properties of pre-trained LOMs, both in terms of the magnitude and frequency content of the solution spectra. To do this, we will employ spectral analysis techniques, such as the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), to decompose the solution spectra into their frequency components. We will then compare the pre-trained, full-model training, and LoRA adaptation cases to understand how LoRA affects the spectral structure of the solution operators.
CONTROLS: We will apply our spectral analysis to the 2D shallow-water equations dataset, as well as to a smaller test dataset of PDE solutions. We will also ablate the LoRA embedding size to understand the impact of the number of parameters updated on the resulting spectra.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our spectral analysis is likely to show that LoRA adaptation introduces localized changes in the magnitude and frequency spectrum of the solution operators, particularly around the spectral peaks corresponding to the PDE's linear components. However, the nature and extent of these changes may depend on the discretization of the PDE, the pre-trained model's architecture, and the number of adaptation parameters. The method may fail if the pre-trained LOM is too far from the target PDE in terms of spectral structure or if the LoRA adaptation completely changes the fundamental spectral features of the solution operators.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Pre-Training Adaptation in SciML
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) technique for pre-trained LOMs in the context of SciML, specifically for the task of solving the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Instead of simply using LoRA to adapt the weights of the pre-trained FNO, we will incorporate a physics-informed neural network (PINN) as a bottleneck module to embed the adaptation process. This PINN will be employed to adapt the pre-trained FNO to the new physical regime, enabling the FNO to learn a mapping between the original and target solution spaces.
CONTROLS: We will compare our LoRA-PINN adaptation method to full-model fine-tuning and to a baseline of pre-training a separate FNO for each downstream task. Additionally, we will perform ablations to understand the impact of the PINN architecture, the number of parameters updated, and the LoRA embedding size.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our LoRA-PINN adaptation method is likely to outperform full-model fine-tuning in terms of parameter efficiency, while achieving comparable or better downstream performance. The inclusion of the PINN bottleneck may allow the adaptation process to learn more complex, physics-informed mappings, leading to improved task adaptation. However, the method may fail if the pre-trained LOM has a very different spectral structure from the target PDE, or if the downstream task requires a significant shift in the underlying physics of the system.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of LoRA-PINN Adaptation to Domain Shifts
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the robustness of our proposed LoRA-PINN adaptation method to domain shifts in the target physical regime. To do this, we will simulate a scenario where the adaptation is performed based on a reference dataset, but then the method is applied to a new dataset with different conditions (e.g., different flow regimes, initial conditions, or boundaries). We will measure the performance of the adapted model on the new dataset and compare it to a baseline of pre-training a separate FNO for each downstream task.
CONTROLS: We will use a suite of domain shift scenarios for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, including changes in Mach number, Reynolds number, and boundary conditions. We will also compare the LoRA-PINN adaptation to a baseline of LoRA adaptation without the PINN bottleneck.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our LoRA-PINN adaptation method is likely to demonstrate robustness to domain shifts in the target physical regime, with the inclusion of the PINN bottleneck enabling the adaptation process to learn more robust and generalizable mappings between the original and target solution spaces. However, the method may fail if the domain shift is too extreme or if the PINN bottleneck does not effectively capture the relevant physics-informed features of the adaptation process.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Analyzing the Spectral Impact of LoRA on Pre-Trained LOMs
PROPOSAL: We will perform a more detailed spectral analysis of the LoRA adaptation process, specifically examining the effect of LoRA on the spectral peaks and valleys of the solution operators. We will use a suite of advanced spectral analysis techniques, including Prony analysis and short-time Fourier transform (STFT) with continuous Morlet wavelet, to decompose the solution spectra into their frequency components. Additionally, we will investigate the impact of LoRA on the coherence between different spectral components.
CONTROLS: We will apply our spectral analysis to the shallow-water equations dataset, as well as to a smaller test dataset of PDE solutions. We will also ablate the LoRA embedding size to understand the impact of the number of parameters updated on the resulting spectra.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our spectral analysis is likely to show that LoRA adaptation modifies the spectral peaks and valleys of the solution operators, particularly around the linear components of the PDE. However, the nature and extent of these changes may depend on the discretization of the PDE, the pre-trained model's architecture, and the number of adaptation parameters. The LoRA adaptation process may also introduce new coherent patterns in the solution spectra, which can be beneficial for downstream tasks. However, the method may fail if the pre-trained LOM is too far from the target PDE in terms of spectral structure or if the LoRA adaptation completely changes the fundamental spectral features of the solution operators.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of LoRA on Latency and Energy Efficiency
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of LoRA adaptation on the latency and energy efficiency of SciML applications. To do this, we will employ a combination of profiling tools and energy estimation techniques to measure the performance of pre-trained LOMs with and without LoRA adaptation on a range of compute platforms, including CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs. We will also analyze the impact of LoRA on the memory bandwidth and access patterns.
CONTROLS: We will use a suite of benchmarking datasets and applications, including a PDE solver for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations and a three-dimensional blood flow model. We will also compare the LoRA adaptation results to a baseline of full-model fine-tuning.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our analysis is likely to show that LoRA adaptation leads to significant energy efficiency and latency improvements for SciML applications, due to the reduced number of parameters and the localized modifications to the solution operators. However, the actual performance benefits may depend on the compute platform, the specific application, and the number of LoRA adaptation parameters. The method may fail if the energy efficiency benefits are overshadowed by the increased computational cost of the LoRA adaptation process or if the latency improvements are not significant enough to impact the overall application performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Tailored LoRA for Scientific Machine Learning
PROPOSAL: We will design a tailored version of LoRA specifically optimized for SciML applications. To achieve this, we will analyze the properties of the pre-trained LOM and identify the most important adaptation directions in the weight space. We will then develop a tailored LoRA module that captures these directions, leading to improved adaptation performance and energy efficiency.
CONTROLS: We will compare our tailored LoRA approach to a standard LoRA implementation, as well as to a baseline of full-model fine-tuning. We will also evaluate the performance of our tailored LoRA on a range of SciML benchmarks and applications.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our tailored LoRA approach is likely to demonstrate superior performance and energy efficiency compared to standard LoRA and full-model fine-tuning, due to its ability to capture the most important adaptation directions in the weight space. However, the method may fail if the pre-trained LOM has a very different structure or properties from the ones we analyze, or if the tailored LoRA module does not effectively capture the relevant adaptation directions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: LoRA for Operator Learning in Diffusion-Ordered Systems
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the application of LoRA to operator learning in diffusion-ordered systems, such as the Burgers equation and the Allen-Cahn equation. To achieve this, we will develop a custom LoRA module that captures the non-local and non-differentiable properties of the diffusion operators, leading to improved adaptation performance and energy efficiency.
CONTROLS: We will compare our LoRA-based operator learning approach to a standard operator learning method, as well as to a baseline of full-model fine-tuning. We will also evaluate the performance of our LoRA-based approach on a range of diffusion-ordered systems.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our LoRA-based operator learning approach is likely to demonstrate superior performance and energy efficiency compared to standard operator learning and full-model fine-tuning, due to its ability to capture the non-local and non-differentiable properties of the diffusion operators. However, the method may fail if the LoRA module does not effectively capture the relevant properties of the diffusion operators, or if the standard operator learning method is too far off to adapt to.

PROPOSAL: We will investigate the application of LoRA acceleration techniques to large-scale SciML applications, such as the solution of the 3D compressible Navier-Stokes equations using a massively parallel solver. To achieve this, we will develop a custom LoRA module that is optimized for large-scale computations, leading to improved performance and energy efficiency.
CONTROLS: We will compare our LoRA-accelerated approach to a standard massively parallel solver, as well as to a baseline of full-model fine-tuning. We will also evaluate the performance of our approach on a range of large-scale SciML benchmarks.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our LoRA-accelerated approach is likely to demonstrate significant speedup and energy efficiency improvements compared to the standard massively parallel solver and full-model fine-tuning, due to its ability to capture the relevant computational patterns and adapt to the specific application. However, the method may fail if the LoRA module does not effectively capture the relevant patterns, or if the standard solver is too far off to adapt to.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Large Operator Model Fine-Tuning with Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Parameter-Efficient Updates
PROPOSAL:  Analyze the behavior of several recent parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques on a pre-trained Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) when applied to a toy dataset of Navier-Stokes equations with random velocity and pressure fields.
CONTROLS: 
-   Baseline: Train a full FNO model from scratch on a corresponding synthetic dataset.
-   Ablation: Compare LoRA and a learned soft prompt as PEFT methods for the LOM.
-   Ablation: Investigate random sampling strategies versus target-dataset-inspired subset selection for parameter reduction.
COST: 100 (estimated GPU-hours)
PREDICTION:  While standard PEFT methods should generally improve upon a naive baseline when adapting the pre-trained LOM, some of them might show limited success in capturing the physics-based priors in the target Navier-Stokes regime due to misaligned spectral structures and a lack of tailored updates for the adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Informed PEFT for LOMs: Hybridizing Spectral Convolutions with Local Updates
PROPOSAL: Investigate the applicability of hybrid approaches for PEFT that intertwine global spectral convolutions with local, physically-motivated updates for pre-trained Large Operator Models. Apply a specific combination of a physics-informed LoRA transformation with a learned soft prompt, targeting the synthetic dataset of Navier-Stokes equations with random velocity and pressure fields.
CONTROLS: 
-   Baseline: The same baseline as in Experiment 1 (train an FNO model from scratch).
-   Refinement: Compare the proposed hybrid approach with the standard LoRA and learned soft prompt alone.
-   Inquiry: Investigate the transferability of the hybrid approach to variations of the target Navier-Stokes problem, such as incorporating damping or altering boundary conditions.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: By integrating spectral coloring with local updates, the hybrid approach could provide enhanced adaptability on diverse Navier-Stokes variations and supervise further, spectral-respecting, form of parameter-efficient top-ups.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Efficient Thompson Sampling for Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Design an efficient Thompson Sampling algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit, leveraging the boundary umbrella coverage (BUC) technique for Pareto front estimation and exploiting structure in the reward vectors to ensure optimism across all objectives.
CONTROLS: Compare to UCB-PEAK [Wang et al., 2018] with a fixed confidence level and to a greedy oracle that knows the true Pareto front.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (approximating 100k arm pulls with 10 trials each).
PREDICTION: Achieve a comparable or improved empirical Pareto regret to state-of-the-art UCB methods, while being computationally more efficient, and establish a worst-case upper bound on Pareto regret that scales favorably with the number of objectives. Potential failure point: the algorithm might fail to adapt effectively to dynamic reward distributions.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Efficient Thompson Sampling for Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: REVISED DESIGN: 
- Estimate the empirical Pareto front using a novel, efficient, and adaptive scheme based on Gaussian processes (GPs), leveraging the marginal likelihood to adapt to the unknown reward covariance structure.
- At each round, sample from the GP posterior over the Pareto front and use the sampled front to compute optimism bounds across all objectives.
CONTROLS: Remain the same as before, comparing to UCB-PEAK [Wang et al., 2018] with a fixed confidence level and to a greedy oracle that knows the true Pareto front.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (approximating 100k arm pulls with 10 trials each and the additional GP computations).
PREDICTION: Evaluate the benefits of GP-based front estimation and optimism computation, aiming for improved empirical Pareto regret and more adaptable performance in dynamic environments. Potential failure point: the GP estimation might be inefficient for high-dimensional contexts or large numbers of objectives.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Scalable Incentivization for Thompson Sampling in Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Introduce an incentivization scheme to promote exploration-exploitation trade-offs based on the confidence intervals for cumulative rewards across all objectives, ensuring that suboptimal arms are not marginalized too quickly.
CONTROLS: Validate the proposal by comparing to Efficient Thompson Sampling with Pareto front estimation in three scenarios: (i) near-optimal initial arm set, (ii) suboptimal initial arm set, and (iii) changing reward distributions over rounds.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (comparing two variants over 10,000 arm pulls).
PREDICTION: Improve the overall performance of Efficient Thompson Sampling by mitigating the over-exploitation issue, particularly in challenging initial arm set configurations or when the reward distributions shift. Potential failure point: the incentivization scheme might slow down the algorithm's convergence in stationary environments.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Cumulative Reward-Aware Pareto Regret Bounds for Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Derive Pareto regret bounds that take into account the cumulative rewards for each objective, providing a more comprehensive and meaningful measure of performance.
.CONTROLS: Compare to standard Pareto regret bounds and assess the computational feasibility using sensitivity analysis.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (combining theoretical derivations and computational expenses).
PREDICTION: Establish a more nuanced understanding of optimality in multi-objective linear contextual bandits by considering cumulative rewards, and provide Pareto regret bounds that are tighter and more interpretable. Potential failure point: the tighter bounds might only hold under specific assumptions about the reward distributions or objective functions.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Predictive Inference for Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits using Hierarchical Bayesian Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a Hierarchical Bayesian model (HBM) that integrates prior knowledge about the objective functions and arm contexts to provide predictive distributions over cumulative rewards for each arm.
CONTROLS: Compare the HBM to various baselines, including straightforward regression models or more complex Gaussian process-based models, in terms of predictive accuracy and computational efficiency.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours ( approximating 10,000 posterior samples using 1000 latent function draws).
PREDICTION: Evaluate the potential of HBMs in multi-objective linear contextual bandits to outperform or complement existing methods in terms of predictive accuracy and computational costs. Potential failure point: the HBM might require a very large number of parameters to capture complex objective functions, leading to overfitting issues.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Efficient Thompson Sampling for Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: REVISED DESIGN: Incorporate the Hierarchical Bayesian model's predictive distributions over cumulative rewards into the Thompson Sampling algorithm, modifying the sampling process to utilize these distributions as an optimistic bound for arm selection.
CONTROLS: Maintain the same comparison to UCB-PEAK [Wang et al., 2018] and the greedy oracle, and evaluate the revised algorithm's performance when combined with the predictive inference component.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (combining the GP-based Pareto front estimation, the Sensitivity sampling scheme, and the HBM-based predictive distributions).
PREDICTION: Analyze how the predictive inference component from the HBM can be effectively integrated into the Thompson Sampling algorithm, potentially leading to improved performance and exploration-exploitation trade-offs. Potential failure point: the additional computational overhead from integrating the HBM might hinder the algorithm's performance or convergence speed in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Scenario-Specific Thompson Sampling for Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive multi-armed bandit algorithm that adjusts its sampling strategy based on the current scenario's characteristics, such as changes in the Pareto front, objective function variability, or distribution shifts.
CONTROLS: Investigate the effects of scenario-specific sampling strategies on the algorithm's performance using a set of synthetic scenarios representing varying levels of Pareto front changes and objective function complexity.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (combining various scenario simulations with algorithmic vulnerability metrics).
PREDICTION: Evaluate the benefits of adaptive scenario-specific sampling in the multi-objective linear contextual bandit setting and assess potential performance gains when comparing to a fixed sampling strategy.
