actions.texte:
ADD
TITLE: Worst-Case Pareto Regret Guarantees for Thompson Sampling
PROPOSAL: Establish a framework for analyzing Thompson Sampling in the multi-objective linear contextual bandit problem, focusing on development of a novel worst-case upper bound on Pareto regret that generalizes existing results from the single-objective setting. Leverage a regret-amplification approach to bound the Pareto regret by the sum of the individual regrets for each objective, while accounting for the crosstalk between objectives. Utilize a novel drift-based argument to bound the suboptimality gap between the observed rewards and their expected values, conditional on the beliefs maintained by Thompson Sampling.
CONTROLS: Compare against upper-confidence-bound (UCB) algorithms, as well as a variant of Thompson Sampling without optimism that randomizes arms based solely on historical rewards.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The worst-case upper bound will be a function of the number of objectives, with an additional logarithmic factor that captures the disparity between objectives. Further improvements to the bound require development of a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between objectives.

Note: This first proposal focuses on establishing a theoretical foundation, addressing the first research question by deriving worst-case Pareto regret guarantees for Thompson Sampling. The subsequent proposals will explore computational efficiency and extending these results to cumulative rewards-based optimality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: On the Pareto Regret of Thompson Sampling in Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Derive a theoretical analysis of Thompson Sampling for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit problem, focusing on a specific regime where the number of objectives L is fixed and the number of rounds T is sufficiently large. Employ techniques from Bayesian regret analysis, exploiting the structure of the linear reward model to obtain a closed-form expression for the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling.
CONTROLS: Establish a lower bound on Pareto regret for Thompson Sampling by leveraging a novel adversarial example and comparing against the performance of a Pareto-optimal arm.
COST: 1.5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis will show that the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling scales logarithmically with the number of rounds T, while the constants hidden in the logarithm will depend on the number of objectives L, the dimensionality d, and the noise level in the rewards. This result will shed light on the performance of Thompson Sampling in this setting, providing insights into its strengths and limitations.

Note: This second proposal builds upon the first one by providing a specific analysis of the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling in a particular regime, establishing both upper and lower bounds on its performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: On the Pareto Regret of Thompson Sampling in Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Refine the theoretical analysis of Thompson Sampling for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit problem, extending the regime from fixed L and sufficient T to consider a more general setup where L and d are allowed to grow with T at certain rates. To accommodate this increased complexity, add additional technical lemmas that bound the suboptimality gap and exploit structural properties of the linear reward model, leading to improved Pareto regret guarantees.
CONTROLS: Compare against UCB algorithms in this extended regime to demonstrate the robustness of the analysis.
COST: 3 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised analysis will show that the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling can be bounded in terms of the number of objectives L, the dimensionality d, and the noise level in the rewards, while also accounting for the dependence on the number of rounds T. This refined analysis will provide a better understanding of the performance of Thompson Sampling in more general settings.

Note: This revised proposal extends the scope of the initial analysis, addressing a more realistic and complex scenario, and providing improved theoretical guarantees.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Thompson Sampling for Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Develop a computationally efficient variant of Thompson Sampling that leverages the linear structure of the rewards to reduce the computational complexity of maintaining the multivariate Gaussian posterior distribution. Employ a dimensionality reduction technique, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), to project the high-dimensional context and reward spaces onto lower-dimensional subspaces, enabling faster computations while maintaining the accuracy of the policy.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original Thompson Sampling algorithm and UCB methods, evaluating the trade-off between computational efficiency and Pareto regret performance.
COST: 4 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The efficient variant of Thompson Sampling will achieve significant speedups compared to the original algorithm, while maintaining competitive Pareto regret performance, especially in high-dimensional settings where traditional Thompson Sampling becomes computationally expensive.

Note: This proposal focuses on addressing the computational efficiency of Thompson Sampling, a crucial aspect in practice, and explores ways to reduce the computational burden while maintaining its performance guarantees.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cumulative Rewards-Based Optimality in Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel optimality criterion that incorporates both the Pareto regret and cumulative rewards, allowing for a more comprehensive evaluation of policy performance. Define the Cumulative Pareto Regret (CPR) as the sum of Pareto regret and a term that penalizes the cumulative rewards gap between the chosen and optimal arms. Develop a theoretical framework to analyze the CPR of Thompson Sampling and UCB algorithms, providing insights into their performance in terms of both immediate and cumulative rewards.
CONTROLS: Compare against the Pareto regret-based optimality and evaluate the trade-off between immediate and cumulative rewards performance.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The CPR metric will capture the trade-offs between immediate and cumulative rewards, revealing that Thompson Sampling can achieve superior cumulative rewards performance, even when its Pareto regret is high, due to its ability to adapt to changing contextual information.

Note: This proposal extends the scope of the analysis to incorporate cumulative rewards, addressing the second research question and providing a more comprehensive understanding of policy performance in multi-objective linear contextual bandits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Minimax Regret in Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Investigate the minimax regret framework, which provides a worst-case optimal guarantee for the best policy in hindsight. Derive a lower bound on the minimax regret in the multi-objective linear contextual bandit setting and provide a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves this lower bound. Compare against the CPR metric and Pareto regret-based optimality, evaluating the trade-off between regret minimization and cumulative rewards maximization.
CONTROLS: Assess the performance of the minimax-regret algorithm in terms of both Pareto regret and CPR, and compare it to Thompson Sampling and UCB methods.
COST: 6 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The minimax-regret algorithm will achieve a sharp trade-off between regret minimization and cumulative rewards maximization, providing a robust and adaptive policy that adapts to the changing contextual information and the number of objectives.

Note: This proposal explores the minimax regret framework, providing a worst-case optimal guarantee for the best policy in hindsight, and develops a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves this lower bound.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Exploration in Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits with Unknown Objectives' Order
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive exploration strategy that discovers the order of the objectives and adjusts the exploration-exploitation trade-off accordingly. Introduce a novel Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates a probabilistic latent variable representing the order of the objectives. Update the model online using Thompson sampling and BALD (Bayesian Active Learning by Discrepancy) to optimize the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Evaluate the performance of the designed algorithm in terms of Pareto regret, CPR, and the average ratio of cumulative rewards obtained when the objectives' order is correctly inferred versus when it is not.
CONTROLS: Compare against the CPR metric, Thompson Sampling, and UCB methods in both cases where the objectives' order is known and unknown.
COST: 8 GPU-hours (high computational demanding due to optimization and inference procedures)
PREDICTION: The designed algorithm will adaptively explore the objectives and infer their order, leading to significant performance gains in CPR and cumulative rewards when the objectives' order is correctly inferred, and reduced performance degradation when it is not.

Note: This proposal focuses on adaptive exploration and order discovery in multi-objective linear contextual bandits, providing a novel solution for scenarios where the objectives' order is initially unknown.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sample Complexity of Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: Investigate the sample complexity of multi-objective linear contextual bandits and derive sharp bounds on the required number of samples to achieve a desired level of Pareto regret and CPR performance. Develop a novel simulation-based approach to efficiently estimate the sample complexity of Thompson Sampling and UCB methods, leveraging recent advances in statistical learning theory and complex function approximation.
CONTROLS: Compare against the empirical performance of Thompson Sampling, UCB, and the adaptive exploration algorithm on various synthetic and simulation-based scenarios.
COST: 3 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The sample complexity analysis will reveal that the required number of samples to achieve a desired level of performance grows logarithmically with the number of objectives, while the constants hidden in the logarithm will depend on the dimensionality d, the noise level in the rewards, and the desired level of performance.

Note: This proposal focuses on understanding the sample complexity of multi-objective linear contextual bandits, providing a fundamental insight into the required number of samples to achieve a desired level of performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extension to Non-Linear Contextual Bandits with Multi-Objective Rewards
PROPOSAL: Explore the extension of the proposed algorithms and analysis to the more challenging setting of non-linear contextual bandits with multi-objective rewards. Introduce a novel neural network architecture that incorporates a probabilistic output and is trained using a multi-objective version of the policy gradient method. Develop a theoretical framework to analyze the performance of the proposed algorithm, leveraging techniques from Bayesian neural networks and multi-objective optimization.
CONTROLS: Compare against the performance of UCB methods and Thompson Sampling in both linear and non-linear settings.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (high computational demanding due to the training and inference procedures)
PREDICTION: The proposed algorithm will provide state-of-the-art performance in the challenging setting of non-linear contextual bandits with multi-objective rewards, while maintaining competitive performance in the easier linear setting.

Note: This proposal focuses on extending the proposed algorithms and analysis to the more challenging setting of non-linear contextual bandits with multi-objective rewards, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the complexity of the problem.

ACTION: REVISE 7
TITLE: Extension to Non-Linear Contextual Bandits with Multi-Objective Rewards
PROPOSAL: Revising the extension to non-linear contextual bandits with multi-objective rewards, focus on development of a new neural network architecture that incorporates a probabilistic output conditioned on the context and rewards, leveraging information-theoretic techniques to derive lower bounds on the minimax regret in the non-linear setting. Evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm in terms of Pareto regret, CPR, and cumulative rewards, and compare against the performance of UCB methods and Thompson Sampling in both linear and non-linear settings.
CONTROLS: Assess the performance of the proposed algorithm in simulated scenarios, and evaluate its robustness to changes in the reward functions and contextual information.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (remains high due to the training and inference procedures)
PREDICTION: The revised extension will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the performance of the proposed algorithm in the challenging setting of non-linear contextual bandits with multi-objective rewards, while also providing insights into the fundamental limits of multi-objective optimization in this setting.

Note: This revised proposal focuses on development of a new neural network architecture and lower bounds on the minimax regret in the non-linear setting, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the performance of the proposed algorithm in this challenging setting.

TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Existing Feature Matchers on Orthophoto and Digital Surface Model Data

This will likely lead to unsatisfactory feature matching performance, specifically in oblique views.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Benchmark Dataset for UAV 6-DoF Visual Localization with Orthophoto and Elevation Map Data
PROPOSAL: Create a large-scale, cross-domain benchmark dataset that contains orthophotos, elevation maps, and paired 6-DoF camera poses from actual UAV flight datasets. The dataset should encompass various environments, include a range of viewpoints (nadir to oblique), and have different resolution and quality levels of the geodata. This dataset will enable the validation of the effectiveness of various algorithms for bridging the gap between UAV imagery and geodata.
CONTROLS: Utilize existing UAV flight datasets, such as the VIO-Dataset or the UAV-hd. Include more than one orthophoto and elevation map per scene to allow for analysis of viewpoint, resolution, and geodesign requirements.
COST: Estimated 800 GPU-hours (initial data collection), 100 GPU-hours (dataset preparation)
PREDICTION: The new dataset will significantly improve the reproducibility of research in UAV 6-DoF visual localization with orthophoto and elevation map data, enabling better comparison and evaluation of different approaches, especially on challenging oblique views. However, the development of the dataset will require significant effort to collect, process, and annotate the data.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of State-of-the-Art Feature Matchers with Orthographic Geodata
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of four state-of-the-art feature matchers (DeepLabCut, RaFT, SIFT, and SuperPoint) on a bespoke UAV dataset consisting of orthographic geodata (orthophotos and elevation maps) and aerial imagery taken from various viewpoints.
CONTROLS: Investigate various matchers with different resolutions of orthophotos (e.g., 0.5m, 1m, 2m) and their effects on matching performance, ablate the contribution of depth information, and compare to a handcrafted Oracle matcher serving as a strong baseline (around an active baseline).
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: State-of-the-art feature matchers will exhibit varying performance levels with orthographic geodata, with some showing high accuracy while others fail entirely. High-resolution orthophotos might offer better matching performance than lower resolution ones. The ablated Oracle matcher will serve as a strong reference point for understanding performance constraints. 
   Where it could fail: this is a first step to identify potential candidates for subsequent fine- tuning and fine-tuning might bring  state-of-the-art feature matchers up to speed with the handcrafted Oracle.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards a Benchmark for UAV Localization with Orthographic Geodata
PROPOSAL: Propose a real-world benchmark dataset, "AerialCity", consisting of paired aerial images and aligned aerial geodata (orthophotos and digital surface models) captured by UAVs over various cities, providing rich diversity in scenes, viewpoints, and illumination conditions. 
CONTROLS: The dataset will be split into a main 80% split for training and a 20% split for testing; ablate the effects of resolution, domain shifts, and preprocesssing methods (e.g., downsampling) on performance; collect a smaller set of sequences where camera intrinsic are available to estimate camera intrinsic.
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours (including data collection and pre-processing)
PREDICTION: AerialCity will become a widely adopted standard benchmark for UAV localization with orthographic geodata, fostering improvements in related AI research; benchmarking and experiments will confirm the difficulty of current solutions and motivate the development of new approaches capable of motivating the development of new methods that can take full advantage of the information contained in the orthophotos and elevation maps. 
   Where it could fail: challenges in data collection, data quality, or data diversity may limit the benchmark's performance and usability.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of State-of-the-Art Feature Matchers with Orthographic Geodata
PROPOSAL: Refine and expand proposal 1 to incorporate the recently proposed benchmark AerialCity and a more diverse set of feature matchers (DeepLabCut, RaFT, SIFT, SuperPoint, and LoFTR). Additionally, investigate how different data augmentations (e.g., color jittering, blurring, and realistic texture replacement) impact feature matcher performance with orthographic geodata. 
CONTROLS: Evaluate the feature matchers with various settings of AerialCity, train with augmented data, use ablated versions without data augmentation or finer matchers, and compare performance on various metrics (e.g., accuracy, speed, recall).
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours (using existing dataset and some collected from AerialCity)
PREDICTION: Feature matchers will exhibit varying robustness to different types of augmentations, while some showing a small improvement, others degrade significantly, thereby indicating the trade-offs between generalizability and performance. Some feature matchers might adapt poorly to a wider variety of augmentations, and this could explain why the divergent results across experiments will pinpoint this source of difficulty as being conclusively identifiable.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Temporal Domain Shifts on UAV Localization
PROPOSAL: Design and conduct experiments to simulate temporal domain shifts by introducing differences in acquisition time between the query UAV image and the reference geodata in the AerialCity benchmark. This involves creating various versions of the dataset with, for example, cloud cover, scene changes, or differently-looking vegetation and comparing the performance of state-of-the-art localization algorithms under different temporal domain shifts.
CONTROLS: Compare performance when using reference data (and associated geodata) collected at the same acquisition time as the query image versus when using reference data collected at a later or earlier time point; ablate the effects of temporal domain shifts on performance by investigating partial and full domain shifts; include standard deviation metrics quantifying the temporal shifts, and relocation mismatches within images.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating the temporal domain shifts in a domain-anomaly-aware approach could potentially help for initial estimates and populate the vast uncertain areas while identifying sub-par performance from view perspective changes due to distinct sub-structures local solved from geological mission data.
   Where it could fail: problems may arise with the paramount degree of prior assumptions under the guise of preprocessing for robust image payloads in unstable aerial capture that lack/almost flown-on-foot redundant data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exemplar-Based Georeferencing for UAV Localization with Orthographic Geodata
PROPOSAL: Design a novel exemplar-based method for georeferencing that leverages the AerialCity benchmark. This method learns a feature space to embed both the query UAV image and the orthographic geodata, allowing for efficient retrieval of a small set of relevant examples (exemplars) from the reference set. Georeferencing is then performed by finding the exemplar that best matches the query image and using its associated projection information to determine the camera pose.
CONTROLS: Investigate the effect of varying the number and diversity of exemplars on performance; ablate the importance of similarity search and alternative optimization-based methods for feature embedding; include standard metrics, sample complexity, and Rosenblattian variations; prove convergence of approximations; add orthorectification handling between superficial discrepancies.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Exemplar-based georeferencing could provide a efficient and computationally lightweight solution for bridging the domain gap between UAV imagery and orthographic geodata, achieving a good trade-off between accuracy and computational complexity. The effectiveness of this approach may depend on the quality and representativeness of the learned embeddings.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Temporal Domain Shifts on UAV Localization
PROPOSAL: Refine proposal 3 to incorporate the exemplar-based georeferencing method from proposal 4, which can efficiently retrieve relevant examples from the reference set. Investigate whether the exemplar-based method can mitigate the effect of temporal domain shifts by learning a feature space that captures the differences between the query image and the reference geodata collected at different times.
CONTROLS: Compare performance of the exemplar-based method and a state-of-the-art feature matcher when dealing with temporal domain shifts; ablate the importance of similarity search, feature embedding, and exemplar diversity in addressing temporal domain shifts; include standard metrics for robustness to temporal shifts, sample complexity and ROC analysis.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: The exemplar-based method may outperform state-of-the-art feature matchers when dealing with temporal domain shifts, as it can learn a feature space that captures the temporal differences and adapt to changes in the scene, leading to better robustness and accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Camera Intrinsic Parameter Estimation for UAVs with Orthographic Geodata
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of estimating camera intrinsic parameters for UAVs using orthographic geodata as the sole reference, without requiring ground truth camera intrinsic parameters or additional external sensors. Design a novel method that integrates the exemplar-based georeferencing from proposal 4 with a camera intrinsic parameter estimation framework.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the method on the AerialCity benchmark, comparing it to state-of-the-art camera intrinsic parameter estimation methods; ablate the importance of different components (exemplar-based georeferencing, camera intrinsic parameter estimation framework) in estimating camera intrinsic parameters; include standard metrics for accuracy and robustness.
COST: Estimated 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Estimating camera intrinsic parameters for UAVs using orthographic geodata as the sole reference is a challenging task, but the novel method integrating exemplar-based georeferencing and camera intrinsic parameter estimation framework may provide a promising solution, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a good balance between accuracy and robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust UAV Localization with Orthographic Geodata under Adversarial Conditions
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of state-of-the-art localization methods, including those presented in the previous proposals, to adversarial attacks and outliers that might be present in real-world scenarios, such as faulty sensors, weather conditions, or human-made attacks. Design a defense mechanism that can detect and mitigate the effects of these attacks.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed defense mechanism using synthetic data and a testbed of real-world scenarios with different types of attacks (e.g., perspective-invariant point removal, noise injection, physical object occlusion); compare the performance of the defense mechanism to state-of-the-art methods; ablate the importance of different components in the defense mechanism.
COST: Estimated 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The robustness of UAV localization methods to adversarial attacks and outliers is a critical challenge for the adoption of these systems in real-world scenarios. A robust defense mechanism can mitigate the effects of these attacks and ensure reliable localization, making the system more secure and trustworthy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: System Integration and Real-World Deployment of a Full-Pose UAV Localization System
PROPOSAL: Design and implement a comprehensive system that integrates the proposed localization methods (feature matchers, exemplar-based georeferencing, camera intrinsic parameter estimation, and robust defense mechanisms) and evaluates the system's performance in real-world deployments using actual UAVs and orthographic geodata. Conduct experiments in diverse environments, such as urban, rural, and mixed areas, and gather insights on the system's accuracy, robustness, and scalability.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the integrated system to existing state-of-the-art methods; perform thorough ablations to understand the contribution of each individual component; document the system's architecture and deployment steps for reproducibility and further improvements.
COST: Estimated 1500 GPU-hours (including data collection, system integration, and deployment)
PREDICTION: The system integration and real-world deployment of the full-pose UAV localization system will demonstrate its potential to achieve high accuracy, robustness, and scalability, thereby facilitating widespread adoption in various applications, including aerial mapping, surveillance, and disaster response.

propositions.titre: Evaluating the Effectiveness of State-of-the-Art Feature Matchers with Orthographic Geodata

propositions.controles: The dataset will be split into a main 80% split for training and a 20% split for testing; ablate the effects of resolution, domain shifts, and preprocesssing methods (e.g., downsampling) on performance; collect a smaller set of sequences where camera intrinsic are available to estimate camera intrinsic.

AerialCity will become a widely adopted standard benchmark for UAV localization with orthographic geodata, fostering improvements in related AI research; benchmarking and experiments will confirm the difficulty of current solutions and motivate the development of new approaches capable of motivating the development of new methods that can take full advantage of the information contained in the orthophotos and elevation maps. 
   Where it could fail: challenges in data collection, data quality, or data diversity may limit the benchmark's performance and usability.
propositions.texte: Propose a real-world benchmark dataset, "AerialCity", consisting of paired aerial images and aligned aerial geodata (orthophotos and digital surface models) captured by UAVs over various cities, providing rich diversity in scenes, viewpoints, and illumination conditions.
propositions.titre: Towards a Benchmark for UAV Localization with Orthographic Geodata

propositions.controles: Compare performance of the exemplar-based method and a state-of-the-art feature matcher when dealing with temporal domain shifts; ablate the importance of similarity search, feature embedding, and exemplar diversity in addressing temporal domain shifts; include standard metrics for robustness to temporal shifts, sample complexity and ROC analysis.
propositions.prediction: The exemplar-based method may outperform state-of-the-art feature matchers when dealing with temporal domain shifts, as it can learn a feature space that captures the temporal differences and adapt to changes in the scene, leading to better robustness and accuracy.
propositions.texte: Refine proposal 3 to incorporate the exemplar-based georeferencing method from proposal 4, which can efficiently retrieve relevant examples from the reference set. Investigate whether the exemplar-based method can mitigate the effect of temporal domain shifts by learning a feature space that captures the differences between the query image and the reference geodata collected at different times.
propositions.titre: Investigating the Impact of Temporal Domain Shifts on UAV Localization

propositions.controles: Investigate the effect of varying the number and diversity of exemplars on performance; ablate the importance of similarity search and alternative optimization-based methods for feature embedding; include standard metrics, sample complexity, and Rosenblattian variations; prove convergence of approximations; add orthorectification handling between superficial discrepancies.
propositions.prediction: Exemplar-based georeferencing could provide a efficient and computationally lightweight solution for bridging the domain gap between UAV imagery and orthographic geodata, achieving a good trade-off between accuracy and computational complexity. The effectiveness of this approach may depend on the quality and representativeness of the learned embeddings.
propositions.texte: Design a novel exemplar-based method for georeferencing that leverages the AerialCity benchmark. This method learns a feature space to embed both the query UAV image and the orthographic geodata, allowing for efficient retrieval of a small set of relevant examples (exemplars) from the reference set. Georeferencing is then performed by finding the exemplar that best matches the query image and using its associated projection information to determine the camera pose.
propositions.titre: Exemplar-Based Georeferencing for UAV Localization with Orthographic Geodata

propositions.controles: Evaluate the performance of the method on the AerialCity benchmark, comparing it to state-of-the-art camera intrinsic parameter estimation methods; ablate the importance of different components (exemplar-based georeferencing, camera intrinsic parameter estimation framework) in estimating camera intrinsic parameters; include standard metrics for accuracy and robustness.
propositions.prediction: Estimating camera intrinsic parameters for UAVs using orthographic geodata as the sole reference is a challenging task, but the novel method integrating exemplar-based georeferencing and camera intrinsic parameter estimation framework may provide a promising solution, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a good balance between accuracy and robustness.
propositions.texte: Investigate the feasibility of estimating camera intrinsic parameters for UAVs using orthographic geodata as the sole reference, without requiring ground truth camera intrinsic parameters or additional external sensors. Design a novel method that integrates the exemplar-based georeferencing from proposal 4 with a camera intrinsic parameter estimation framework.
propositions.titre: Camera Intrinsic Parameter Estimation for UAVs with Orthographic Geodata

A robust defense mechanism can mitigate the effects of these attacks and ensure reliable localization, making the system more secure and trustworthy.
propositions.texte: Investigate the robustness of state-of-the-art localization methods, including those presented in the previous proposals, to adversarial attacks and outliers that might be present in real-world scenarios, such as faulty sensors, weather conditions, or human-made attacks. propositions.titre: Robust UAV Localization with Orthographic Geodata under Adversarial Conditions

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tractable Lower Bounds on Score Error in the Small-$\sigma$ Regime
PROPOSAL: We develop a framework to derive lower bounds on the score error for a wide class of smoothed probability measures $\mu_\sigma$, assuming the smoothed density $p_\sigma$ is $$ p_\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{d/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left\lvert\lvert{x - x^\star}\right\rvert\right)^2 \right) $$where $x^\star = X^\star + Z$, $X^\star \sim \mu_{\mathrm{data}}$, $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$, and $\sigma > 0$ denotes the noise level. We leverage the/variance-preserving smoothing/$the smoothed density is related to the density of the data distribution through the Fourier transform.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Accuracy Requirements of Score-Based Geometric Sampling
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the accuracy requirements of learning the target distribution induced by Langevin dynamics driven by a learned score function, specifically for geometric sampling tasks such as computing geodesic and diffusion distances. We propose an experiment where we train a score model on a given dataset using Langevin dynamics and then use the learned score to sample from the uniform distribution on the data manifold. We'll use the (statistical) distance between the sampled distribution and the ground-truth uniform distribution as a proxy for the quality of geometric sampling. We'll experiment with different score models, training procedures, and datasets to investigate how the accuracy requirements of the score function scale with the noise level $\sigma$.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our results to using the classical graph-based normalizations for sampling, as well as a recent alternative method that fine-tunes diffusion models for uniform sampling.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the accuracy requirements of the score function increase with decreasing $\sigma$, and that the learned score function needs to achieve a larger precision in the small-$\sigma$ regime to support high-quality geometric sampling. We may also observe that the score-based method is more robust to score errors than the classical graph-based normalizations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Accuracy Requirements of Score-Based Geometric Sampling
PROPOSAL: We refine our experiment by incorporating WKB-type expansions of the stationary Fokker-Planck equation to analyze the stationary distributions produced by the learned score function driven by Langevin dynamics. This will provide insight into how the score errors affect the concentration of the distribution on the manifold. We'll also investigate the efficacy of different boundary layer expansions to correct for the asymptotic deficiency of the leading-order WKB approximation near the manifold. This will allow us to better understand how the accuracy requirements of the score function correlate with the number of stable points of the Langevin dynamics near the manifold.
CONTROLS: As before, we'll compare our results to using the classical graph-based normalizations for sampling, as well as a recent alternative method that fine-tunes diffusion models for uniform sampling.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (accounting for the additional computational cost of implementing WKB-type expansions)
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the WKB-type expansions provide a more refined understanding of how score errors affect the concentration of the distribution on the manifold, and that the boundary layer expansions can effectively improve the accuracy of the WKB approximation in certain cases.

TITLE: Investigating the Accuracy Requirements of Score-Based Geometric Sampling

We use the neural score model D Noon to sample from the uniform distribution on the data manifold. We'll then measure the quality of the sampled distribution using the mismatch with the uniform distribution on the manifold and compare this with the case where we sample directly from the uniform distribution using a classical graph-based normalization method.

COST: 70 GPU-hours

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Prior Choice in Plug-and-Play Methods for Bayesian Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical analysis of the effect of prior choice in plug-and-play methods for Bayesian inverse problems. We prove that the choice of prior affects the score accuracy needed for correct posterior sampling. Specifically, we show that the required accuracy of the learned prior score depends on the "smoothness" of the prior distribution. We derive upper bounds on the required accuracy of the learned prior score in terms of the smoothness of the prior distribution and the noise level in the measurement.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our results to existing guarantees that require the learned prior score to be exact.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the choice of prior significantly impacts the required accuracy of the learned prior score, and that the derived upper bounds provide a practical guideline for selecting priors in plug-and-play methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiments on Plug-and-Play Methods with Imperfect Prior Scores
PROPOSAL: We conduct experiments on plug-and-play methods for Bayesian inverse problems with imperfect prior scores. We'll implement a plug-and-play method using a neural score model to learn a prior score from a dataset of noisy measurements. We'll then use the learned prior score to sample from the posterior distribution of the latent signal. We'll evaluate the quality of the sampled posterior distribution using metrics such as KL divergence and mean squared error. We'll also investigate the effect of prior smoothness and score accuracy on the quality of the sampled posterior.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our results to existing methods that use exact prior scores, and to the ground-truth posterior distribution obtained using MCMC methods.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the plug-and-play method with an imperfect prior score produces a sampled posterior distribution that is close to the ground-truth posterior, and that the quality of the sampled posterior improves as the accuracy of the learned prior score increases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Recovery of Intrinsic Dimension and Data Support
PROPOSAL: We conduct experiments to investigate the recovery of intrinsic dimension and data support using score-based methods. We'll train a neural score model on a dataset and use the learned score to sample from the smoothed probability measure. We'll then estimate the intrinsic dimension of the sampled points and the geometry of the data support using techniques such as PCA and GPE. We'll evaluate the accuracy of these estimates using metrics such as silhouette score and mean squared error. We'll also compare our results to existing methods that use other generative models.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our results to the ground-truth intrinsic dimension and data support, and to the estimates obtained using other generative models such as DGMs and GANs.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the score-based method can recover the intrinsic dimension and data support of the dataset with high accuracy, and that the quality of the estimates improves as the accuracy of the learned score increases.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Recovery of Intrinsic Dimension and Data Support
PROPOSAL NUMBER: 5
ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Recovery of Intrinsic Dimension and Data Support
REVISED PROPOSAL: We modify our experiment to focus on the specific case of text-to-image generation, a task that is known to be challenging for score-based methods. We'll use the recently released text-to-image dataset CLEVR, which consists of images and text descriptions of objects in different scenes. We'll train a neural score model on this dataset and use the learned score to sample new images and captions. We'll then evaluate the quality of the generated images and captions using metrics such as inception score and BLEU score. We'll also investigate the recovery of intrinsic dimension and data support in this task.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our results to the ground-truth images and captions, and to the results obtained using other generative models such as GANs and VAEs.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the score-based method can generate realistic images and captions, but may struggle with recovering the intrinsic dimension and data support in this task due to the complexity of the text-to-image mapping.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Approximability of the Ground-Truth Distribution from an Imperfect Score
PROPOSAL: We investigate the approximability of the ground-truth distribution from an imperfect score function. We'll consider a scenario where the score function is learned using a neural network and is not exact, but rather an approximation of the true score function. We'll study the effect of score errors on the generative power of the score-based method and derive bounds on the variational distance between the output distribution of the score-based method and the ground-truth distribution. We'll also provide insights into the conditions under which the score-based method can recover the ground-truth distribution approximately.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our results to existing bounds on the variational distance between the output distribution of the score-based method and the ground-truth distribution.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the approximability of the ground-truth distribution from an imperfect score depends on the magnitude and properties of the score errors, and that the derived bounds provide a useful characterization of the trade-offs involved in this scenario.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Proving accuracy and concentration rates for the variance-preserving smoothing
PROPOSAL: Use the Malliavin-Sobolev calculus to identify the regime of $\sigma$ where the score function of the variance-preserving smoothed measure $p_{\sigma}$ accurately recovers the geometry of the data manifold. Specifically, we aim to prove quantitative bounds for the approximation error of the score, expressed in terms of $\sigma$ and derivatives of the true manifold geometry, and investigate the dimensionality threshold beyond which these bounds degrade.
CONTROLS: Compare to the existing convergence theory for diffusion and score-based samplers, which treats geometry and density together in the score error.
COST: Estimated to be low, around 0.01 GPU-hours for a Mathematica proof.
PREDICTION: The derived bounds will reveal a power-law dependence on $\sigma$ for the recovery of manifold geometry, with minimal degradation up to moderate dimensions. However, we expect the theoretical analysis to fail to capture the behavior in extremely high-dimensional settings.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Comparing learned scores in variance-exploding and variance-preserving smoothing
PROPOSAL: Investigate the difference in learned scores for the variance-exploding and variance-preserving smoothed measures on a set of real-world image datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, LSUN). We aim to compare the accuracy of the learned scores, the convergence rates of the generated samples to the manifold, and the resulting samples themselves. Utilizing techniques from density estimation (e.g., kernel density estimation) and manifold learning (e.g., diffusion maps), we will analyze the effect of different smoothing variance on the learned scores.
CONTROLS: Compare the two smoothing techniques on naive (no-signal-processing), classical signal-processing and  fine-tuned Generative adversarial networks (GAN) as a prior.
COST: Estimated to be around 100 GPU-hours to train the models and generate samples.
PREDICTION: While variance-preserving smoothing shows better convergence rates and more accurate samples on lower-dimensional manifolds, variance-exploding smoothing yields more realistic results for high-dimensional images.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Investigating the effect of score accuracy on uniform sampling
PROPOSAL: Train a diffusion model on a dataset of text-to-image pairs (e.g., COCO) and manipulate its parameters to produce uniform samples on the learned manifold. We will investigate the impact of score accuracy on the uniformity of the generated samples and compare the results to those obtained by fine-tuning a pre-trained diffusion model (as previously proposed). By using tools from random measure theory and desingularized kernels, we aim to quantify the relative influence of the data's geometry and density on the resulting samples.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard non-uniform sampling methods, gradient-based fine-tuning methods, and fixed uniform sampling.
COST: Estimated to be around 500 GPU-hours to tune the model's parameters and collect the necessary data.
PREDICTION: Score accuracy is critical to producing uniform samples on the manifold, with a degradation in sampling quality observable when the score error exceeds a certain threshold.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating manifold hypothesis convergence rates for diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Establish convergence bounds on the induced measure $\mu_\sigma$ using a score-matching approximation under the manifold hypothesis. By analyzing the spectrum of the diffusion operator, we will derive a rate of convergence for $\mu_\sigma$ as $\sigma \to 0$. Specifically, we consider the cases where the manifold's mean curvature, diffusion tensor, and anisotropic diffusion coefficients are slowly varying in the small-$\sigma$ regime.
CONTROLS: Baseline convergence rate for $\mu_\sigma$ without the manifold hypothesis, Langevin dynamics driven by the true score instead of an approximation.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Under the manifold hypothesis, the rate of convergence of $\mu_\sigma$ as $\sigma \to 0$ should improve upon the baseline results, but we expect the error bounds to worsen as the manifold's curvature increases, since a better score approximation can be expected on more regular parts of the manifold.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sampling from data supports using partially accurate low-noise score models
PROPOSAL: We will analyze the behavior of Langevin dynamics and predictor-corrector samplers under the manifold hypothesis when a partially accurate low-noise score model is employed. We aim to derive conditions on the score accuracy and the manifold's geometry that ensure the generated samples concentrate on the data support.
CONTROLS: Same baseline as in proposal 1, as well as an ablation study of the specific predictor-corrector scheme used and the effect of manifold dimensionality on sampler performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that even with significant score errors, samples from the data support can still be recovered as long as the score is sufficiently accurate at the manifold boundary, which may not be the case for highly accurate scores at the center of the manifold; in particular, we anticipate that there is a trade-off between the quality of the recovered support and the intra-manifold distributional detail.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uniform sampling on the data manifold using imperfect score models
PROPOSAL: We will develop a theory for generating the uniform distribution on the data manifold using a non-uniformly trained score model, under various assumptions on the manifold's regularity and the sampling density. Our goal is to derive bounds on the accuracy of the resulting uniform samples and identify the relationship between the required score accuracy and the characteristics of the data manifold.
CONTROLS: Theoretical results from proposals 1 and 2, as well as the results of using classical normalization techniques for uniform sampling; we will also explore the effect of the manifold's intrinsic dimensionality on the required score accuracy.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that imperfect score models can still produce near-uniform samples on the manifold, albeit with reduced accuracy, and that the manifold's curvature and intrinsic dimensionality play a critical role in determining the required score accuracy; in particular, we anticipate that highly irregular manifolds may require more accurate score models to achieve uniform sampling.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating manifold hypothesis convergence rates for diffusion models
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will extend the analysis of proposal 1 to consider the effects of score errors on the induced measure $\mu_\sigma$ under the manifold hypothesis. By including terms representing the error in the score approximation, we will derive more precise bounds on the convergence rate of $\mu_\sigma$ as $\sigma \to 0$. This will provide insight into how score errors propagate through the diffusion model and affect the induced measure.
CONTROLS: The original baseline comparison with the exact score approximation, as well as the analysis of score accuracy for uniform sampling from proposal 3, which will help us understand the conditions under which score errors become significant.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (approximately, due to additional computational complexity)
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the inclusion of score errors in the analysis leads to a more nuanced understanding of the trade-offs between score accuracy and convergence rates, and that highly accurate score models may not be necessary for achieving good convergence rates, especially on manifolds with low curvature.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Sampling from data supports using partially accurate low-noise score models
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will perform an empirical study of the behavior of Langevin dynamics and predictor-corrector samplers under the manifold hypothesis using real-world text-to-image datasets, with a focus on the distribution of samples across different parts of the manifold as a function of the score model's accuracy and noise level. We will compare our results to the theoretical predictions from proposals 1 and 3.
CONTROLS: A baseline study using Langevin dynamics with an oracle score, as well as an ablation study of different predictor-corrector schemes and noise levels.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to confirm the theoretical results from proposals 1 and 3, and provide further insight into the behavior of diffusion models on real-world data; we may also discover additional effects or challenges in the small-$\sigma$ regime that are not captured by our theoretical analysis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effect of prior choice on score accuracy in Bayesian inverse problems
PROPOSAL: We will analyze the impact of different prior choices on the required score accuracy in plug-and-play methods for Bayesian inverse problems, and derive conditions under which a given prior requires higher score accuracy for correct posterior sampling. We will consider both smoothed data density priors and other common choices, and explore their effects on the trade-off between score accuracy and posterior convergence rate.
CONTROLS: A study of the convergence behavior of plug-and-play methods for different prior choices, as well as an empirical comparison of the required score accuracy for different priors using a set of realistic Bayesian inverse problems.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that certain prior choices (e.g., smoothed data density) require lower score accuracy than others, and that the convergence rate of the posterior distribution can be sensitive to the prior choice, even with accurate scores; we may also discover prior choice-dependent strategies for balancing score accuracy and posterior convergence rate.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Effect of prior choice on score accuracy in Bayesian inverse problems
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will extend the analysis in proposal 4 to consider the case of textured priors, which are common in applications such as image de-noising and compressive sensing. We will derive conditions under which textured priors require higher score accuracy for correct posterior sampling, and explore the propagation of texture information through the plug-and-play method.
CONTROLS: Same empirical study as in the revised proposal 4, as well as a theoretical comparison with the case of smoothed data density priors.
COST: 220 GPU-hours (approximately, due to additional theoretical analysis)
PREDICTION: We expect to find that textured priors indeed require higher score accuracy than smoothed data density priors, and that the propagation of texture information can lead to a richer posterior distribution, but also makes the method more sensitive to score errors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Warm-starting diffusion models with imperfect scores for sampling from the ground truth data distribution
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of imperfect score models as a warm-start for diffusion models, to initialize the training process of a more accurate score model. By leveraging the structure of the data manifold and the partial knowledge provided by the imperfect score, we hope to accelerate the convergence of the diffusion model and improve the quality of the generated samples.
CONTROLS: A baseline comparison with plain diffusion model training, as well as an ablation study to identify the key factors that influence the effectiveness of the warm-start strategy.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that warm-starting diffusion models with imperfect scores can lead to significant improvements in convergence speed and sample quality, especially in scenarios where the ground truth data distribution is complex or high-dimensional.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Connections between imperfect score models and graph-based normalization techniques
PROPOSAL: We will explore the connection between imperfect score models and graph-based normalization techniques, with a focus on understanding how graph-based methods can be used as a preprocessing step to improve the accuracy of imperfect score models. By analyzing the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian and the diffusion operator, we hope to derive conditions under which graph-based normalization can be effective in improving score accuracy.
CONTROLS: A theoretical comparison with existing results on the accuracy of imperfect score models, as well as an empirical study to validate the effectiveness of graph-based normalization techniques in improving sample quality and convergence speed.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that graph-based normalization techniques can indeed improve the accuracy of imperfect score models, especially in scenarios where the data manifold has a clear graph structure; however, we may also discover limitations and challenges associated with applying graph-based methods to high-dimensional or large-scale datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive evaluation of diffusion models on text-to-image generation benchmarks
PROPOSAL: We will perform a comprehensive evaluation of diffusion models on a set of text-to-image generation benchmarks, with a focus on comparing the performance of different score approximations (e.g., imperfect scores, graph-based normalized scores) and evaluating the generalization ability of diffusion models to diverse datasets and task settings. We aim to provide a thorough assessment of the strengths and limitations of diffusion models in the context of text-to-image generation.
CONTROLS: A baseline comparison with existing text-to-image generation models, as well as an evaluation of the proposed techniques in proposals 5 and 6.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that diffusion models are a promising approach for text-to-image generation, and that the proposed techniques can improve their performance and generalization ability, but we also anticipate that there may be remaining challenges and open research questions in this area that require further exploration.

TITLE:  Non-Asymptotic Sample-Complexity Bounds for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We establish the first non-asymptotic sample-complexity bounds for KernelSHAP, providing insights into its accuracy and sampling efficiency. By leveraging lemmas on the probabilistic recovery of constrained systems and combinatorial moments, we prove that with $\widetilde{\Omega}(\max\{d\log d, \log p\})$ samples, KernelSHAP achieves a constant-factor approximation to the true Shapley values. These results also lay the groundwork for provable analyses of other randomized estimators related to KernelSHAP.

TITLE: Analyzing the Empirical Efficiency of KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: Experimental study to investigate the empirical efficiency and accuracy of KernelSHAP on a range of real-world datasets, focusing on its performance with different kernel types, subset sampling methods, and subsample sizes. This will involve comparing KernelSHAP to other popular Shapley value estimators such as LeverageSHAP and Unbiased KernelSHAP, and analyzing the results through metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and the coefficient of determination R2.
CONTROLS: Implementing three SHAP-based methods - KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP, and the vanilla algorithm, all re-implemented in the open-source SHAP library.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tractable Bounds for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We provide non-asymptotic sample complexity guarantees for KernelSHAP, showing that its error is bounded by a function of the number of samples, the inverse of the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the kernel matrix, and the dimensionality of the feature space. The proof relies on a novel use of matrix concentration inequalities and a careful analysis of the sampling distribution used by KernelSHAP.
CONTROLS: 
- Considering a smaller number of features to demonstrate the effect of dimensionality on the error bound.
- Comparing the error bound to that of LeverageSHAP, a known estimator with strong theoretical guarantees.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (focusing on theory requires less computational resources)
PREDICTION: Our bounds will reveal that, surprisingly, KernelSHAP requires a polynomial number of samples in the dimensionality to achieve a certain level of accuracy, and may struggle in high-dimensional settings. This could help explain why LeverageSHAP appears to outperform KernelSHAP in some scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Sampling Distribution of KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We conduct a detailed empirical analysis of the sampling distribution used by KernelSHAP, with the goal of understanding its properties and implications. We investigate how the sampling distribution changes as a function of the dimensionality of the feature space, the choice of kernel, and the number of samples used. This analysis will help identify potential sources of systematic bias in KernelSHAP and shed light on its limitations.
CONTROLS: 
- Using synthetic data to isolate the effects of dimensionality and kernel choice.
- Comparing the results to those of LeverageSHAP, which uses a different sampling distribution.
- Considering the effect of subsampling and reweighting on the sampling distribution.
COST: 500 GPU-hours ( this analysis requires more computational resources)
PREDICTION: Our results will show that the sampling distribution used by KernelSHAP is not as well-behaved as previously thought, and that it may introduce significant biases in certain regimes. This could help explain some of the observed differences between KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Baseline for Randomized Estimators: Theoretical Guarantees for Random Subsampling
PROPOSAL: We develop a framework for analyzing the properties of randomized estimators, including KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP. We show that, in general, randomized estimators can be viewed as approximately solving a constrained weighted least-squares problem, and that their error can be bounded using standard matrix concentration inequalities. This result provides a common theoretical foundation for understanding the behavior of these estimators.
CONTROLS: 
- Considering a simple randomized estimator, such as random subsampling, to demonstrate the generality of our results.
- Comparing the error bounds for our baseline estimator to those of KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (this proposal is relatively light computationally)
PREDICTION: Our results will provide a new perspective on the design and analysis of randomized estimators, and will help to identify the key factors that contribute to their error. This may shed light on why some estimators, such as LeverageSHAP, are more accurate than others.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Tighter Bounds for KernelSHAP via the Baseline Estimator
PROPOSAL: We apply our framework for analyzing randomized estimators to KernelSHAP, and derive tighter error bounds than our initial tractable bounds. By taking advantage of the specific structure of the KernelSHAP estimator, we are able to obtain improved concentration inequalities and a more refined understanding of its behavior. This will provide a more accurate picture of the tradeoffs between KernelSHAP and other estimators, such as LeverageSHAP.
CONTROLS: 
- Comparing the new bounds to the original bounds for KernelSHAP.
- Evaluating the effect of the tighter bounds on our understanding of the estimator's behavior.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (modifying the existing code to apply the new framework)
PREDICTION: Our revised bounds will reveal that KernelSHAP is more accurate than previously thought, but still has its limitations. This will help inform the choice between KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP in practical applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: LeverageSHAP Meets the Baseline: A Comparison of Sampling Distributions
PROPOSAL: We conduct an empirical comparison of the sampling distributions used by LeverageSHAP and our baseline estimator. By analyzing the properties of these distributions, we aim to understand what contributes to the improved performance of LeverageSHAP and whether our baseline estimator is a suitable proxy for other randomized estimators.
CONTROLS: 
- Evaluating the effect of different sampling distributions on the estimator's accuracy.
- Comparing the results to those obtained with KernelSHAP.
- Investigating whether the improvements in LeverageSHAP can be replicated using our baseline estimator.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (running experiments to compare the estimators)
PREDICTION: Our results will provide insights into the design of sampling distributions for randomized estimators and help identify the key factors that contribute to their performance. This may inform the development of new estimators that combine the strengths of LeverageSHAP and other methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Estimating Shapley Values with Gradient-based Methods
PROPOSAL: We explore the use of gradient-based methods for estimating Shapley values. Building on recent advances in gradient-based explanations, we develop a new approach that leverages the gradients of the model's output with respect to its inputs to efficiently estimate Shapley values. This approach has the potential to be much faster and more scalable than traditional Shapley value estimators, making it more practical for high-dimensional settings.
CONTROLS: 
- Comparing the accuracy of the gradient-based estimator to traditional estimators.
- Evaluating the effect of different gradient-based methods on the estimator's accuracy.
- Investigating whether the gradient-based estimator can be used to improve the performance of LeverageSHAP and other methods.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (developing and testing the gradient-based estimator)
PREDICTION: Our results will demonstrate the potential of gradient-based methods for estimating Shapley values and provide insights into their strengths and limitations. This may lead to new approaches for explaining complex models in high-dimensional settings.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Tighter Guarantees for Randomized Estimators via Uniform Concentration
PROPOSAL: We refine our baseline estimator's theoretical guarantees by leveraging uniform concentration inequalities. This provides tighter bounds on the estimator's error and allows us to better understand the tradeoffs between the number of samples, the dimensionality of the feature space, and the accuracy of the estimator. This improved analysis will provide more precise insights into the behavior of randomized estimators and their limitations.
CONTROLS: 
- Applying uniform concentration inequalities to derive tighter bounds on the estimator's error.
- Evaluating the effect of the improved bounds on our understanding of the estimator's behavior.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (refining the existing analysis)
PREDICTION: Our revised bounds will provide a more nuanced understanding of the tradeoffs between different design choices for randomized estimators, and will help inform the development of more accurate and efficient explanation methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Shapley Values for Time Series Data: Challenges and Opportunities
PROPOSAL: We investigate the challenges and opportunities of applying Shapley values to time series data. We discuss the difficulties of accurately explaining time-varying models and the potential benefits of using Shapley values to analyze the contributions of different features and interactions in these models. We also propose a methodology for estimating Shapley values in time series contexts and evaluate its performance using synthetic and real-world data.
CONTROLS: 
- Evaluating the impact of temporal dependencies on Shapley value estimation.
- Comparing the performance of our proposed methodology to existing explanation methods for time series data.
- Investigating the potential applications of Shapley values in time series analysis, such as feature selection and model interpretability.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (developing and testing the methodology for Shapley values in time series data)
PREDICTION: Our results will provide new insights into the challenges and opportunities of applying Shapley values to time series data and will help establish the potential of this approach for understanding complex, dynamic systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Unified Framework for Model Interpretability via Shapley Values
PROPOSAL: We develop a unified framework for model interpretability via Shapley values, which subsumes and generalizes existing explanation methods. Our framework enables the estimation of Shapley values for arbitrary models, datasets, and applications, and provides a common language for comparing and combining different explanation methods. We demonstrate the versatility and power of our framework using a range of model families, including linear regression, decision trees, and neural networks.
CONTROLS: 
- Evaluating the performance of our unified framework on a comprehensive set of models and datasets.
- Comparing the results to existing explanation methods and discussing the advantages of our framework.
- Investigating potential applications and extensions of our framework, such as noisy or scaled data.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours (developing and testing the unified framework)
PREDICTION: Our results will provide a fundamental shift in the way we approach model interpretability, enabling more accurate, flexible, and scalable explanation methods for a wide range of applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Real-World Evaluation of Model Interpretability via Shapley Values
PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive real-world evaluation of our unified framework and explanation methods for Shapley values. We apply our methods to a range of real-world datasets and models, including those from healthcare, finance, and aerospace, and assess their performance using various metrics, such as accuracy, interpretability, and model fairness. We also survey domain experts and practitioners to understand the practical implications of our results and identify opportunities for further research.
CONTROLS: 
- Selecting a diverse range of real-world datasets and models for evaluation.
- Using a combination of objective metrics and subjective assessments from domain experts.
- Investigating the impact of model complexity, dataset size, and other factors on the performance of our methods.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours (evaluating the methods on real-world data)
PREDICTION: Our results will provide a robust evaluation of our unified framework and explainability methods in real-world settings, facilitating their adoption, and highlighting opportunities for further research in model interpretability and fairness.
