actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Accelerated Flow Matching using Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Implement a speculative decoding approach for FM that uses a token-based draft generator to sample velocities in parallel. This draft generator will be trained to mimic the velocity output of the full FM model. The full model will then selectively verify the drafted trajectories, using a lightweight evaluation metric to filter out poorly performing trajectories. The filtered trajectories will be integrated to produce the final output, reducing the number of full-step integrations required for a given output quality.
CONTROLS: Train the draft generator using a self-supervised learning objective, comparing drafted and ground-truth velocities. Compare against a standard baseline where the full FM model is run sequentially without speculative decoding. Compare also against a random draft approach, where drafted velocities are selected randomly.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (estimating 5000 batch size, 2000 steps of FD training, and 500 steps of self-supervised training)
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant reduction in inference latency (x2-x3 reduction) with minimal loss of output quality. However, we anticipate that the draft generator may accumulate drift over long integration paths, leading to occasional failures in generating coherent samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improved Draft Generation through proxy objectives
PROPOSAL: Introduce an additional proxy objective during draft generator training to improve its ability to mimic the full FM model's velocity output. Specifically, we will use a variant of mean squared error (MSE) that emphasizes the importance of velocity components that contribute most to the generated sample. This proxy objective will be combined with the self-supervised learning objective used in the initial draft generator. We hypothesize that this additional objective will allow the draft generator to better model the high-variance components of the velocity output.
CONTROLS: Compare against the initial speculative decoding approach with no proxy objective, and against a baseline where the full FM model is run sequentially without speculative decoding. Also, investigate the impact of different weights assigned to the proxy objective relative to the self-supervised objective.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (estimating an additional 500 epochs of FD training with proxy objective)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvements in the quality of drafted trajectories, leading to reduced failure rates in generating coherent samples. However, the added complexity of the proxy objective may increase training time and computational cost.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Improved Draft Generation through proxy objectives
REVISED PROPOSAL: Instead of using a simple proxy objective, incorporate an attention-based mechanism that selectively focuses the draft generator's attention on the most relevant components of the velocity output. This mechanism will be implemented using a sparse attention mechanism, which will dynamically weight the importance of different velocity components based on their impact on the generated sample. We hypothesize that this attention-based approach will allow the draft generator to better capture the complex relationships between velocity components and generated samples.
CONTROLS: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with attention mechanism, and against the initial approach with proxy objective. Also, investigate the impact of different attention mechanisms (e.g., standard attention, sparse attention) and the weight assigned to the attention mechanism relative to the self-supervised objective.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (estimating an additional 750 epochs of FD training with attention mechanism)
PREDICTION: We expect to see further improvements in the quality of drafted trajectories, leading to reduced failure rates in generating coherent samples. However, the added complexity of the attention mechanism may increase training time and computational cost, and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Improved Draft Generation through proxy objectives
REVISED PROPOSAL: Replace the sparse attention mechanism with a mechanism that learns to compress the velocity output into a fixed-size, lower-dimensional vector. This compressed vector will then be used as the input to the full FM model for selective verification. The compression mechanism will be implemented using a learnable encoder-decoder pair, and will be trained jointly with the self-supervised objective and the bottleneck of the selective verification process. We hypothesize that this compression mechanism will allow the draft generator to effectively summarize the most relevant information in the velocity output, reducing the drift of the drafted trajectories.
CONTROLS: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with compression mechanism, and against the initial approach with proxy objective. Also, investigate the impact of different compression mechanisms (e.g., PCA, Autoencoders) and the size of the compressed vector.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (estimating an additional 750 epochs of FD training with compression mechanism)
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant reductions in the drift of drafted trajectories, leading to improved generation quality and reduced failure rates. However, the effectiveness of the compression mechanism may depend on the specific properties of the velocity output.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Complexity Reduction using Group Invariance
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether group invariance can be used to reduce the complexity of the FM model during selective verification. Specifically, we will apply a group Fourier transform to the compressed velocity vector and remove high-frequency components before feeding it to the full FM model for verification. We hypothesize that this will reduce the model's sensitivity to minor variations in the velocity output, improving the quality of drafted trajectories.
CONTROLS: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with compression mechanism, and investigate the impact of different group invariance mechanisms (e.g., group Fourier transforms, wavelet transforms).
COST: 250 GPU-hours (estimating an additional 500 epochs of FD training with group invariance)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved generation quality and reduced failure rates due to the reduction in model complexity. However, the effectiveness of the group invariance mechanism may depend on the specific characteristics of the velocity output.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Drafting for Variable Velocity Stability
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive drafting mechanism that adjusts the drafting rate based on the stability of the velocity output. When the velocity output is stable, the drafting rate can be increased to reduce latency, while when the velocity output is unstable, the drafting rate can be decreased to maintain generation quality. We will use a stability metric, such as the L2 norm of the velocity output, to determine the drafting rate. We hypothesize that this adaptive mechanism will improve generation quality and reduce latency.
CONTROLS: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with adaptive drafting mechanism, and against the initial approach with fixed drafting rate. Also, investigate the impact of different stability metrics and drafting rate adjustment policies.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (estimating an additional 400 epochs of FD training with adaptive drafting mechanism)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved generation quality, reduced latency, and flexibility in handling variable velocity stability. However, the effectiveness of the adaptive mechanism may depend on the specific characteristics of the velocity output and the drafting rate adjustment policy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Visualization of Velocity Output for Drafting
PROPOSAL: Develop a visualization tool to efficiently display the velocity output and aid in the debugging and understanding of the drafting mechanism. The visualization tool will be based on a dimensionality reduction technique, such as PCA or t-SNE, to reduce the complexity of the high-dimensional velocity output. We will also incorporate interactive features, such as hover-over annotations and brushing, to facilitate exploration and investigation of the velocity output. We hypothesize that this visualization tool will enable researchers to better understand the behavior of the drafting mechanism and identify potential issues.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of different visualization tools and techniques, and compare against a baseline with no visualization tool.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (estimating 200 epochs of FD training with visualization tool)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved understanding and debugging of the drafting mechanism, and increased efficiency in identifying and addressing issues. However, the effectiveness of the visualization tool may depend on the expertise and experience of the researchers using it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Drafting for Enhanced Generation Quality
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether multi-task learning can be applied to the drafting mechanism to improve generation quality. Specifically, we will train a single model to generate both images and videos, using a shared velocity output. We will also investigate using different loss functions, such as multi-scale SSIM or structural similarity, to aggregate the losses from different tasks. We hypothesize that this multi-task approach will lead to improved generation quality and reduced failure rates.
CONTROLS: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with single-task drafting mechanism, and investigate the impact of different task combinations and loss functions.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (estimating 1000 epochs of FD training with multi-task drafting mechanism)
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in generation quality and reduced failure rates due to the multi-task learning approach. However, the effectiveness of the multi-task mechanism may depend on the specific tasks and loss functions used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Transfer Learning for FM Drafting
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether transfer learning can be applied to the drafting mechanism to improve performance on different domains. Specifically, we will initialize the draft generator with pre-trained weights from a related task, such as text-to-image generation. We will also investigate using different initialization methods, such as using a pre-trained language model or a pre-trained image model. We hypothesize that this transfer learning approach will lead to improved performance and reduced training time.
CONTROLS: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with randomly initialized draft generator, and investigate the impact of different initialization methods and domains.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (estimating 600 epochs of FD training with transfer learning)
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in performance and reduced training time due to the transfer learning approach. However, the effectiveness of the transfer learning mechanism may depend on the specific domains and initialization methods used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Evaluation of FM Drafting
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the FM drafting mechanism on a large and diverse set of real-world tasks, including image synthesis, video generation, and image editing. We will use a range of evaluation metrics, including pixel accuracy, SSIM, and Inception score, to assess the performance of the FM drafting mechanism. We will also conduct an ablation study to investigate the contributions of each component of the FM drafting mechanism. We hypothesize that the FM drafting mechanism will demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on these tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art methods in each task, and investigate the impact of different evaluation metrics and ablation study components.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (estimating 2000 epochs of FD training with large-scale evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect to see state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated tasks, and a comprehensive understanding of the contributions and trade-offs of each component of the FM drafting mechanism.

The full model will then selectively verify the drafted trajectories, using a lightweight evaluation metric to filter out poorly performing trajectories. The filtered trajectories will be integrated to produce the final output, reducing the number of full-step integrations required for a given output quality.
propositions.titre: Accelerated Flow Matching using Speculative Decoding

propositions.controles: Compare against the initial speculative decoding approach with no proxy objective, and against a baseline where the full FM model is run sequentially without speculative decoding. Also, investigate the impact of different weights assigned to the proxy objective relative to the self-supervised objective.
propositions.cout_texte: 200 GPU-hours (estimating an additional 500 epochs of FD training with proxy objective)
propositions.prediction: We expect to see improvements in the quality of drafted trajectories, leading to reduced failure rates in generating coherent samples. However, the added complexity of the proxy objective may increase training time and computational cost.
propositions.texte: Introduce an additional proxy objective during draft generator training to improve its ability to mimic the full FM model's velocity output. Specifically, we will use a variant of mean squared error (MSE) that emphasizes the importance of velocity components that contribute most to the generated sample. This proxy objective will be combined with the self-supervised learning objective used in the initial draft generator. We hypothesize that this additional objective will allow the draft generator to better model the high-variance components of the velocity output.
propositions.titre: Improved Draft Generation through proxy objectives

propositions.controles: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with compression mechanism, and investigate the impact of different group invariance mechanisms (e.g., group Fourier transforms, wavelet transforms).
propositions.cout_texte: 250 GPU-hours (estimating an additional 500 epochs of FD training with group invariance)
propositions.prediction: We expect to see improved generation quality and reduced failure rates due to the reduction in model complexity. However, the effectiveness of the group invariance mechanism may depend on the specific characteristics of the velocity output.
propositions.texte: Investigate whether group invariance can be used to reduce the complexity of the FM model during selective verification. Specifically, we will apply a group Fourier transform to the compressed velocity vector and remove high-frequency components before feeding it to the full FM model for verification. We hypothesize that this will reduce the model's sensitivity to minor variations in the velocity output, improving the quality of drafted trajectories.
propositions.titre: Exploring Complexity Reduction using Group Invariance

propositions.controles: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with adaptive drafting mechanism, and against the initial approach with fixed drafting rate. Also, investigate the impact of different stability metrics and drafting rate adjustment policies.
propositions.cout_texte: 200 GPU-hours (estimating an additional 400 epochs of FD training with adaptive drafting mechanism)
propositions.prediction: We expect to see improved generation quality, reduced latency, and flexibility in handling variable velocity stability. However, the effectiveness of the adaptive mechanism may depend on the specific characteristics of the velocity output and the drafting rate adjustment policy.
propositions.texte: Develop an adaptive drafting mechanism that adjusts the drafting rate based on the stability of the velocity output. When the velocity output is stable, the drafting rate can be increased to reduce latency, while when the velocity output is unstable, the drafting rate can be decreased to maintain generation quality. We will use a stability metric, such as the L2 norm of the velocity output, to determine the drafting rate. We hypothesize that this adaptive mechanism will improve generation quality and reduce latency.
propositions.titre: Adaptive Drafting for Variable Velocity Stability

propositions.controles: Evaluate the effectiveness of different visualization tools and techniques, and compare against a baseline with no visualization tool.
propositions.cout_texte: 100 GPU-hours (estimating 200 epochs of FD training with visualization tool)
propositions.prediction: We expect to see improved understanding and debugging of the drafting mechanism, and increased efficiency in identifying and addressing issues. However, the effectiveness of the visualization tool may depend on the expertise and experience of the researchers using it.
propositions.texte: Develop a visualization tool to efficiently display the velocity output and aid in the debugging and understanding of the drafting mechanism. The visualization tool will be based on a dimensionality reduction technique, such as PCA or t-SNE, to reduce the complexity of the high-dimensional velocity output. We will also incorporate interactive features, such as hover-over annotations and brushing, to facilitate exploration and investigation of the velocity output. We hypothesize that this visualization tool will enable researchers to better understand the behavior of the drafting mechanism and identify potential issues.
propositions.titre: Efficient Visualization of Velocity Output for Drafting

propositions.controles: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with single-task drafting mechanism, and investigate the impact of different task combinations and loss functions.
propositions.cout_texte: 500 GPU-hours (estimating 1000 epochs of FD training with multi-task drafting mechanism)
propositions.prediction: We expect to see significant improvements in generation quality and reduced failure rates due to the multi-task learning approach. However, the effectiveness of the multi-task mechanism may depend on the specific tasks and loss functions used.
propositions.texte: Investigate whether multi-task learning can be applied to the drafting mechanism to improve generation quality. Specifically, we will train a single model to generate both images and videos, using a shared velocity output. We will also investigate using different loss functions, such as multi-scale SSIM or structural similarity, to aggregate the losses from different tasks. We hypothesize that this multi-task approach will lead to improved generation quality and reduced failure rates.
propositions.titre: Multi-Task Drafting for Enhanced Generation Quality

propositions.controles: Compare against the revised speculative decoding approach with randomly initialized draft generator, and investigate the impact of different initialization methods and domains.
propositions.cout_texte: 300 GPU-hours (estimating 600 epochs of FD training with transfer learning)
propositions.prediction: We expect to see significant improvements in performance and reduced training time due to the transfer learning approach. However, the effectiveness of the transfer learning mechanism may depend on the specific domains and initialization methods used.
propositions.texte: Investigate whether transfer learning can be applied to the drafting mechanism to improve performance on different domains. Specifically, we will initialize the draft generator with pre-trained weights from a related task, such as text-to-image generation. We will also investigate using different initialization methods, such as using a pre-trained language model or a pre-trained image model. We hypothesize that this transfer learning approach will lead to improved performance and reduced training time.
propositions.titre: Exploring Transfer Learning for FM Drafting

propositions.controles: Compare against state-of-the-art methods in each task, and investigate the impact of different evaluation metrics and ablation study components.
propositions.cout_texte: 1000 GPU-hours (estimating 2000 epochs of FD training with large-scale evaluation)
propositions.prediction: We expect to see state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated tasks, and a comprehensive understanding of the contributions and trade-offs of each component of the FM drafting mechanism.
propositions.texte: Evaluate the FM drafting mechanism on a large and diverse set of real-world tasks, including image synthesis, video generation, and image editing. We will use a range of evaluation metrics, including pixel accuracy, SSIM, and Inception score, to assess the performance of the FM drafting mechanism. We will also conduct an ablation study to investigate the contributions of each component of the FM drafting mechanism. We hypothesize that the FM drafting mechanism will demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on these tasks.
propositions.titre: Large-Scale Evaluation of FM Drafting

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Low-Latency Flow Matching via Chunked Inference
PROPOSAL: We propose a chunked inference algorithm that breaks the ODE integration into smaller chunks, allowing for parallelization and reducing the number of explicit function evaluations. We will use the accurate and efficient `sdm-lg` (strongly-conditioned disentangled mixture approximate likelihood generative model) diffusion model as a baseline for flow modeling and compare its inference performance with our proposed optimized implementation.
CONTROLS: Baseline: `sdm-lg` diffusion model with full-step ODE integration; Ablations: different chunk sizes, number of evaluation points per chunk, and parallelization strategies.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our chunked inference algorithm should reduce inference latency by 40-50% with minimal loss in output quality. However, we expect issues with breaking the sequential integration process, especially with fine-grained generation, which could result in decomposition artifacts if the chunk size is too large.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Drafted Flow Inference via Generative Dream Team (GDT)
PROPOSAL: Building on the idea of speculative decoding from language models, we propose to use a smaller-draft version of the flow model, dubbed the "Dream Team", to generate proposals in parallel. The Draft Team will be trained to mimic the full model's velocity output, but with reduced capacity and parasitic loss. We will then use a small, parallelized version of the full model, dubbed the "Verifier", to evaluate and select the best draft proposals, which are then used to guide the full ODE integration.
CONTROLS: Baseline: full-step ODE integration; Ablations: different Dream Team and Verifier capacities, draft proposal sampling rates, and selection thresholds.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our GDT approach should reduce inference latency by 60-70% with minimal loss in output quality. However, the challenge of learning a viable Draft Team that Coupled with the full model's trajectory will require significant optimization effort and hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Drafted Flow Inference via Generative Dream Team (GDT)
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal by incorporating residual learning from the Dream Team to the Verifier. This allows us to fine-tune the Verifier to a corrected proposal, rather than simply sampling a single proposal. By leveraging residual learning, we can improve the quality and fidelity of the draft proposals and their guided trajectory.
CONTROLS: Baseline: full-step ODE integration; Ablations: different Dream Team and Verifier capacities, draft proposal sampling rates, and selection thresholds; Additional control: ablation on residual learning from the Dream Team to the Verifier.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised GDT approach should reduce inference latency by 70-80% with minimal loss in output quality. However, the introduction of residual learning might increase the stability challenges of training the Verifier, which could be difficult to optimize for.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised Drafted Flow Inference via Generative Dream Team (GDT)
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal by outlining the specific architecture and training procedures for the Dream Team and Verifier. The Dream Team will be a smaller-draft version of the flow model, with 25-50% of the capacity, and trained on a self-supervised objective of predicting velocities from the full model. The Verifier will be a small, parallelized version of the full model, with 5-10% of the capacity, and trained on evaluating and correcting draft proposals. We will explore different architectures and training procedures to optimize the performance of both components.
CONTROLS: Baseline: full-step ODE integration; Ablations: different capacities of the Dream Team and Verifier, different training procedures, and selection thresholds.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised GDT approach should reduce inference latency by 70-80% with minimal loss in output quality. However, we anticipate that complex hyperparameter tuning and selection might be required to optimize the Dream Team and Verifier architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Flow Inference via Segmentation and Drafting (HFID)
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical approach to flow inference that first segment the input data into smaller regions and then apply the GDT method to each region separately. This allows us to reduce the complexity of ODE integration by dividing the process into multiple smaller steps, each with a reduced search space. We will use a novel segmentation method based on a masked convolutional neural network to identify coherent regions in the input data.
CONTROLS: Baseline: full-step ODE integration; Ablations: different segmentation thresholds, number of regions, and GDT capacities for each region.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our HFID approach should reduce inference latency by 50-60% with minimal loss in output quality. However, we anticipate that the segmentation step might introduce additional artifacts or boundary effects, especially when the number of regions is large.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised Drafted Flow Inference via Generative Dream Team (GDT)
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal by incorporating a novel loss function that combines the fidelity of the draft trajectory with its similarity to the full model's trajectory. This will allow us to better balance the trade-off between accuracy and speed in the GDT method. We will use a weighted combination of L2 distances between the two trajectories, with a weight that adapts based on the similarity between the draft and full model outputs.
CONTROLS: Baseline: full-step ODE integration; Ablations: different weights for the fidelity and similarity terms, different architecture types for the Dream Team and Verifier.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised GDT approach should maintain or even improve the output quality while reducing inference latency by 70-80%. However, the novel loss function might be unstable to optimize, especially when the similarity between the draft and full model outputs is low.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Flow Inference via Incremental Verification (TFIV)
PROPOSAL: We propose a temporal-based approach to flow inference that verifies and refines the draft proposal at each time step individually. This will allow us to accurately capture dynamic changes in the input data and reduce the overall latency by verifying only the local flow corrections. We will use a novel incremental verification method based on a temporal convolutional neural network to evaluate the draft proposal at each time step.
CONTROLS: Baseline: full-step ODE integration; Ablations: different TCN architectures, verification rates, and verification thresholds.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our TFIV approach should reduce inference latency by 80-90% with minimal loss in output quality. However, we anticipate that the incremental verification process might introduce temporal artifacts or inconsistency across the time steps, especially when the verification rate is too high.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Automated Adaptive Redundancy in Flow Inference (AARI)
PROPOSAL: We propose to automatically adjust the redundancy level of the flow inference process based on the input data's complexity and model's accuracy. This will allow us to adaptively optimize the trade-off between latency and quality. We will use a novel predictive model based on a dimensional-aware neural network to estimate the risk of over-redundancy and under-redundancy at each inference step and adjust the verification rate accordingly.
CONTROLS: Baseline: fixed verification rate; Ablations: different dimensional-aware architectures, predictive models, and overhead ratios for redundancy trade-off.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our AARI approach should achieve optimal trade-off between latency and quality, reducing latency by 50-80% depending on the input data and model. However, we anticipate that the predictive model might require significant training data to achieve reliable performance and handle diverse scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Co-training Flow Models with Approximate and Exact Inference (CFAME)
PROPOSAL: We propose a co-training framework that simultaneously learns an approximate model (AM) for fast inference and an exact model (EM) for high-quality results. We will use a novel dual-learning approach to minimize the discrepancy between the two models and encourage them to collaborate. This will allow us to leverage the strengths of both models and adaptively switch between them to achieve real-time performance without sacrificing quality.
CONTROLS: Baseline: using a pre-trained EM; Ablations: different dual-learning approaches, co-training schedules, and approximation ratios for AM.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our CFAME approach should achieve real-time inference performance while maintaining high-quality results, reducing latency by 80-90% depending on the input data and model. However, we anticipate that the co-training process might require careful design of the dual-learning objective and scheduling to avoid over-fitting or attribute imbalances between the AM and EM.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ex-FM: Exit Flow Matching for Early Time Steps
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach that finds an early exit point for the flow matching process where the deviations from the target distribution are minimized. We will use a novel reachability-based analysis to identify the early exit point and develop a framework for early exit flow matching (Ex-FM). This approach can significantly reduce the latency of flow matching while maintaining high-quality results.
CONTROLS: Baseline: full flow matching process; Ablations: different exit point identification methods, reachability-based analysis techniques, and Ex-FM threshold values.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our Ex-FM approach should significantly reduce latency by 70-80% while maintaining high-quality results. However, we anticipate that the approach might require careful tuning of the exit point identification method and reachability-based analysis parameters to avoid divergences or over-approach of the target distribution.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Draft Connection Flow Matching
PROPOSAL: Implement a draft connection mechanism in FM that uses a lightweight, cascade-style ODE-Net initialized with a small fraction (e.g., 10%) of the full model's weights and learns to approximate the velocity field through local interpolation on the input space. This approach will allow drafts to leverage the pre-trained features of the full model to facilitate speculative decoding.
CONTROLS: Compare draft connection FM to standard FM on four text-to-image benchmarks (e.g., LSUN, Places, COCO, CelebA), evaluating both quantitative quality metrics (e.g., FID, IS) and qualitative properties (e.g., output diversity, smoothness of trajectories).
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Draft connection FM is likely to show substantial improvements in inference latency while maintaining output quality comparable to standard FM. However, we anticipate potential difficulties in scaling this approach to high-dimensional cases like video generation due to the complexity of the ODE field and the limited capacity of the draft network.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bound-Guided Velocity Estimation
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework to provide tight bounds on the velocity output in Flow Matching by leveraging properties of the ODE and the underlying probability distributions. Introduce a stochastic Dykstra-type algorithm to estimate velocity bounds in practice, allowing for efficient evaluation of draft velocities and facilitating speculative decoding in high-dimensional cases like video generation.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed bound-guided velocity estimation to a naive, uniform-bound method on the standard FM model, evaluating both accuracy (e.g., bound tightness) and computational efficiency.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The bound-guided approach is expected to show significant improvements in computational efficiency for draft velocity evaluation, enabling more scalable and parallelizable speculative decoding in both image and video generation. However, maintaining tight bounds might require additional model computation or learning steps that may introduce additional latency.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Improved Bound-Guided Velocity Estimation for FM
PROPOSAL: Refine the bound-guided velocity estimation framework by introducing a regularization term during the stochastic Dykstra-type algorithm to ensure that the estimated velocity bounds are close to the true velocity field, thus improving bound tightness. Additionally, incorporate a learned controller using a neural network to adaptively select the number of iterations for the Dykstra-type algorithm based on the input data and model complexity.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the revised bound-guided approach by comparing it to the original formulation and a naive, uniform-bound method on three FM models with varying complexity (e.g., Text-to-Image, Image-to-Image, Text-to-Video) using metrics such as bound tightness, computational efficiency, and generation quality.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined bound-guided approach is expected to demonstrate improved bound tightness, higher computational efficiency, and comparable or improved generation quality, making it more suitable for real-time and interactive applications. However, the added learnable controller might require additional training, leading to potential overfitting or increased latency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quality-Aware Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel quality-aware decoding strategy for Flow Matching that combines speculative decoding withBound-Guided Velocity Estimation. Introduce a probabilistic framework to evaluate the reliability of draft samples and adaptively select the best velocity fields and number of steps based on the predicted quality of the generated samples.
CONTROLS: Evaluate Quality-Aware Speculative Decoding on a range of benchmarks (e.g., text-to-image, image-to-image, text-to-video) and compare its performance to standard FM, Draft Connection FM, and the Bound-Guided approach using metrics such as FID, IS, and computational efficiency.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Quality-Aware Speculative Decoding is likely to show significant improvements in inference efficiency while maintaining high-quality outputs comparable to standard FM. However, the increased complexity of the approach may require careful tuning of hyperparameters, and the adaptive choice of velocity fields and steps may lead to differences in output quality that are difficult to predict.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Adaptive Composition of Speculative Decoding Strategies

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Efficacy of Adapter Modules in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of a pre-trained forecasting model with and without an adapter module in online traffic flow forecasting. The adapter module is a small multi-layer perceptron that modifies the output of the pre-trained model. We will use a batch of recent samples to estimate the gradient and update the adapter module.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Pre-trained forecasting model without adapter module. Ablation: Pre-trained forecasting model without the latest few time steps.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (training for 1000 time steps with a batch size of 100)
PREDICTION: We expect the adapter module to improve performance, but the improvement might be marginal due to the limited capacity of the adapter module.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Gradient Estimation Methods on Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of online gradient descent with different gradient estimation methods, including using a batch of recent samples, experience replay, and a combination of recent and past samples. We will use the M4 dataset for multi-step electricity consumption forecasting.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Online gradient descent with a single sample. Ablation: Different batch sizes or replay buffer sizes.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (training for 5000 time steps with different batch sizes and replay buffer sizes)
PREDICTION: We expect online gradient descent with experience replay to perform best, but the difference between the methods might be small due to the limited impact of gradient estimation on the performance in online time series forecasting.

ACTION: REVISE 1
 TITLE: Investigating the Efficacy of Adapter Modules in Online Time Series Forecasting with Concept Drift
PROPOSAL: Extend the experiment in proposal 1 to evaluate the adapter module's performance on concept drift, where the relationship between the input and target changes over time. We will use a dataset that simulates concept drift in traffic flow forecasting, such as the PEMS-BAY dataset with a shifted regime for a certain period.
CONTROLS: Same as before, but with an additional control comparing the performance in the pre-drift and post-drift periods.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (additional training with the drifted dataset)
PREDICTION: We expect the adapter module to adapt poorly to concept drift due to its small capacity and lack of information about the changing relationship between the input and target.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Online Incremental Learning via Ensembling with Delayed Feedback
PROPOSAL: Investigate ensembling-based online incremental learning strategies that incorporate delayed feedback, which can help to mitigate the effects of delayed gradient updates and improve adaptability to evolving patterns. Specifically, we will consider dynamically weighted ensembling, i.e., assigning higher weights to models trained on more recent data.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Standard online gradient descent. Ablation: Different weights for ensembling or different ensemble methods (e.g., bagging, boosting).
COST: 400 GPU-hours (training for 5000 time steps with ensembling, bagging, and boosting)
PREDICTION: We expect ensembling with delayed feedback to significantly improve performance, as it can effectively combine the knowledge from models trained on different time steps and adapt to concept drift.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Regularization-based Strategies for Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of regularization techniques to improve the stability and adaptability of online time series forecasting models. Specifically, we will explore L1 and L2 regularization, as well as dropout and early stopping in the context of online gradient descent on electricity transformer temperature forecasting data from the CIGRE dataset.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Standard online gradient descent without regularization. Ablation: Different regularization strengths, dropout rates, and early stopping criteria.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (training for 3000 time steps with different regularization and dropout settings)
PREDICTION: We expect regularization-based strategies to improve the resistance to concept drift and noise in the data, but they might come at the cost of slightly decreased accuracy in forecasting.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Gradient Estimation Methods on Online Time Series Forecasting with Multi-Step Scenarios
PROPOSAL: Extend the experiment in proposal 2 to evaluate the gradient estimation methods under multi-step scenarios, where the model needs to forecast multiple time steps ahead. We will use the same M4 dataset for multi-step electricity consumption forecasting, with the added complexity of forecasting H steps ahead.
CONTROLS: Same as before, but with an additional control comparing the performance of different gradient estimation methods under different multi-step forecasting scenarios.
COST: 350 GPU-hours (training for 5000 time steps with different gradient estimation methods and multi-step forecasting)
PREDICTION: We expect the performance of online gradient descent with experience replay to degrade under multi-step scenarios, as the delayed feedback may cause cascading errors. However, the effect may be mitigated by using more advanced gradient estimation methods, such as those that incorporate information from past samples.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Offline Rehearsal for Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of offline rehearsal, where the model is trained on a small batch of data from the new distribution before being deployed online. This can help to adapt the model to the changing data distribution and reduce the impact of delayed feedback. We will evaluate offline rehearsal on traffic flow forecasting data from the Inrix Flex dataset.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Standard online gradient descent without offline rehearsal. Ablation: Different sizes of offline rehearsal batches and different rehearsal intervals.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (training for 5000 time steps with offline rehearsal)
PREDICTION: We expect offline rehearsal to improve the adaptability of online time series forecasting models, especially under concept drift scenarios. However, it may also introduce additional computational costs and require careful tuning of the rehearsal batch size and interval.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Online Incremental Learning via Ensembling with Delayed Feedback and Concept Drift
PROPOSAL: Extend the experiment in proposal 3 to evaluate the performance of ensembling-based online incremental learning strategies under concept drift scenarios, where the relationship between the input and target changes over time. We will use the same setup as in proposal 1, but with the additional complexity of delayed feedback and concept drift.
CONTROLS: Same as before, but with an additional control comparing the performance of ensembling with and without concept drift.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (training for 5000 time steps with concept drift and delayed feedback)
PREDICTION: We expect ensembling with delayed feedback to be more robust to concept drift, as it can effectively combine the knowledge from models trained on different time steps and adapt to changing relationships between the input and target. However, the performance may degrade if the concept drift is severe or rapid.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Online Time Series Forecasting with Auxiliary Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of multi-task learning, where the model is trained to predict multiple related time series tasks in parallel. This can help to improve the generalization and adaptability of the model to changing data distributions. We will evaluate multi-task learning on a dataset with multiple related time series tasks for traffic flow and electricity consumption forecasting.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Standard online gradient descent without multi-task learning. Ablation: Different numbers of auxiliary tasks and task weights.
COST: 450 GPU-hours (training for 5000 time steps with multi-task learning)
PREDICTION: We expect multi-task learning to improve the adaptability of online time series forecasting models, especially under concept drift scenarios. However, it may also require careful tuning of the task weights and number of auxiliary tasks.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: A Unifying Framework for Online Time Series Forecasting with Concept Drift
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework that unifies the various online time series forecasting approaches, including online gradient descent, ensembling, regularization, and multi-task learning. This framework will provide a deeper understanding of the relationships between these approaches and their strengths and weaknesses under different concept drift scenarios.
CONTROLS: None (theoretical comparison).
COST: N/A (theoretical)
PREDICTION: We expect the unified framework to provide insights into the trade-offs between different online time series forecasting approaches and help guide the design of more robust and adaptable models for real-world applications.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Updating Different Model Components in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We conduct an experiment where we update different components of a pre-trained deep forecasting model (e.g., final prediction layer, ensemble weights, low-rank scaling coefficients, adapters on input and output) and evaluate their effect on online performance on real-world datasets (e.g., traffic flow, electricity consumption) using metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE) and mean squared error (MSE). We compare these to updating all model parameters and to not updating the model at all, serving as a baseline. We also explore different update frequencies to see how often the model should be updated for each component update type.
CONTROLS: Updating all model parameters at every time step, not updating the model at all, and updating only the final prediction layer using OGD
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect updating the final prediction layer to lead to significant performance gains, especially in traffic flow forecasting, whereas updating ensemble weights or low-rank scaling coefficients will have limited effect. Updating adapters on input and output will also improve performance, but to a lesser extent than updating the final layer. We may find that updating too frequently leads to overfitting, while updating too infrequently leads to slow adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Delayed Feedback in Online Gradient Descent for Multi-Step Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We conduct an experiment to study the impact of delayed feedback on online time series forecasting in the multi-step setting, where we forecast H steps in advance and have access to the true values only after H steps. We test Online Gradient Descent (OGD) with different gradient computation schemes: using the full output of the H-step forecast, using only the one-step ahead forecast, and using a gradient approximation method that corrects for the delayed feedback. We compare these methods to a baseline that uses OGD but is trained with early stopping to avoid lag. We evaluate performance on real-world multi-step forecasting datasets (e.g., electricity consumption with H=6 steps).
CONTROLS: OGD with early stopping to avoid lag, OGD with delayed feedback correction, not updating the model at all
COST: 300 GPU-hours (considering two real-world datasets for evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect methods that account for delayed feedback (e.g., delayed feedback correction) to significantly outperform the baseline OGD with early stopping. We may also find that the full output of the H-step forecast is more informative than the one-step ahead forecast, but at the cost of higher variance. We anticipate that correcting for delayed feedback leads to faster convergence and better adaptability to evolving patterns.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Evaluating the Impact of Updating Different Model Components in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We expand upon our previous proposal by incorporating a more comprehensive set of evaluation metrics and experiments. In addition to mean absolute error (MAE) and mean squared error (MSE), we will also evaluate the performance of the pre-trained forecasting model under different online update frequencies and component update types using metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score, as well as average precision and recall. Furthermore, we incorporate a new ablation study to evaluate the importance of each component update by examining the impact of disabling or removing individual components from the pre-trained model on online forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: Updating all model parameters at every time step, not updating the model at all, and updating only the final prediction layer using OGD, with a new ablation study to evaluate the importance of individual components
COST: 250 GPU-hours (considering additional computational requirements for evaluating diverse metrics and ablation study)
PREDICTION: We expect our revised proposal to provide a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between model components, online update frequencies, and forecasting performance. The added ablation study is likely to reveal which components have the most significant impact on online forecasting and are worthy of further exploration in future research.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Investigating the Effect of Delayed Feedback in Online Gradient Descent for Multi-Step Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We modify the delayed feedback correction method used in our previous proposal to incorporate historical gradient information from previous steps as well as the current step's gradient, which could further improve the effectiveness of correcting for delayed feedback. Furthermore, we include an extrinsic evaluation to examine the impact of delayed feedback on the model's ability to adapt to changing patterns and seasonality in the data, beyond just its immediate performance. This will involve evaluating the model's performance on a sequence of different seasons or patterns recorded in historical data.
CONTROLS: OGD with early stopping to avoid lag, original delayed feedback correction method for comparison, not updating the model at all
COST: 350 GPU-hours (considering additional computational requirements for evaluating the extrinsic model adaptation and including historical gradient information)
PREDICTION: We expect the revised delayed feedback correction method to yield improved performance commitments and enhanced adaptability to changing patterns in the data, indicating the method's robustness and reliability in practical forecasting scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Online Time Series Forecasting Models to Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: We investigate the robustness of online time series forecasting models to distribution shift by evaluating their performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) data generated by artificially introducing concept drift in the data. We will use datasets with various types of real-world distribution shifts (e.g., traffic flow forecasting with changes in daily traffic patterns) to assess the performance of online models (e.g., OGD) under different simulation scenarios, and compare the results to strong baselines. We will also explore the application of robustification techniques, such as ensemble methods, to mitigate the impact of distribution shift on online forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: OOD testing with artificially introduced concept drift, baselines including existing robust online time series forecasting methods
COST: 400 GPU-hours (considering computational requirements for generating OOD data and evaluating robustification techniques)
PREDICTION: We expect the performance of standard online time series forecasting models to degrade under OOD conditions, while robustification techniques (e.g., ensemble methods) can lead to improved robustness and adaptability to changing distributions in real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Normalization for Online Time Series Forecasting under Concept Drift
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel normalization technique, adaptive normalization, that adjusts the normalization statistics online as the data distribution shifts. We integrate this technique with an existing online time series forecasting model and evaluate its performance on real-world datasets (e.g., traffic flow forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting) with artificial concept drift. We compare this approach to other normalization techniques and baselines, and investigate its ability to mitigate the impact of concept drift on online forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: Comparison to state-of-the-art normalization methods, baselines including existing online time series forecasting methods
COST: 280 GPU-hours (considering computational requirements for online evaluation and comparison to baselines)
PREDICTION: We expect adaptive normalization to improve online forecasting performance under concept drift conditions by effectively adapting to changing data distributions, and outperform baselines in scenarios where normalization plays a critical role. However, we also anticipate potential challenges in tuning the normalization parameters and its integration with existing model architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying Key Features and Patterns for Online Time Series Forecasting Model Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We investigate the identification of key features and patterns from high-dimensional time series data that can facilitate effective online model adaptation under distribution shift. We propose a novel approach that combines dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE) and feature selection methods (e.g., mutual information, L1 regularization) to extract informative and relevant features from the data. We evaluate this approach on real-world datasets (e.g., traffic flow forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting) and compare its performance to other dimensionality reduction methods.
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing dimensionality reduction methods, baselines including existing online time series forecasting methods
COST: 320 GPU-hours (considering computational requirements for feature extraction and evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to improve online forecasting performance by identifying key features and patterns that are most relevant to the changing distribution, and providing insights into the underlying factors driving distribution shift. However, we also anticipate potential challenges in selecting the optimal dimensionality reduction method and feature selection technique for different datasets and scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Online Gradient Descent for Time Series Forecasting under Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical analysis of Online Gradient Descent (OGD) for time series forecasting under distribution shift, focusing on the impact of concept drift on the convergence rate and generalization error of the model. We derive bounds on the expected regret and expected error, and investigate the effect of different update frequencies and convergence rates on the model's ability to adapt to changing distributions. We also discuss the implications of these results for the design of online time series forecasting algorithms and model architectures.
CONTROLS: Derivations of existing theoretical results on OGD and online learning
COST: 120 GPU-hours (considering computational requirements for theoretical derivations)
PREDICTION: We expect this theoretical analysis to provide valuable insights into the behavior of OGD under distribution shift and guide the development of more robust and effective online time series forecasting algorithms. However, we also anticipate challenges in translating the theoretical results into practical implementation and real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multitask Learning for Online Time Series Forecasting under Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: We explore the use of multitask learning to improve online time series forecasting performance under distribution shift. We propose a new multitask learning framework that leverages the relationships between multiple related time series to improve forecasting accuracy and adaptability under changing distributions. We will investigate various multitask learning techniques (e.g., joint optimization, shared weights) and evaluate their performance on real-world datasets (e.g., traffic flow forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting).
CONTROLS: Comparison to existing multitask learning methods, baselines including existing online time series forecasting methods
COST: 380 GPU-hours (considering computational requirements for evaluating multitask learning techniques and comparing to baselines)
PREDICTION: We expect multitask learning to improve online forecasting performance and adaptability under distribution shift by leveraging the shared relationships between multiple related time series, but we also anticipate potential challenges in choosing the right multitask learning technique and evaluating its performance on different datasets and scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implementation and Deployment of Online Time Series Forecasting Systems
PROPOSAL: We develop and deploy real-world online time series forecasting systems that integrate the various techniques and components evaluated in the previous proposals. We will create a scalable and flexible architecture that allows for easy integration of new techniques and datasets, and provide a user-friendly interface for data scientists and practitioners to experiment with different models and parameters. We will also conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the deployed systems in real-world scenarios and gather feedback from users to refine and improve the systems.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparison with existing online time series forecasting systems and methodologies
COST: 500 GPU-hours (considering computational requirements for deployment and testing of the system)
PREDICTION: We expect the developed systems to be highly effective and adaptable to changing distributions in real-world scenarios, providing value to a wide range of users and industries. However, we also anticipate challenges in ensuring the stability and scalability of the systems, as well as addressing potential security and data privacy concerns.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Distribution Shift on Adapter-based Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the effect of distribution shift on the performance of adapter-based online time series forecasting models on traffic flow forecasting datasets, specifically hpa-2013 and peMS-pu, using metrics such as MAE and RMSE. We will train a pre-trained forecasting model with an adapter and evaluate its performance on both stationary and non-stationary data under various distribution shifts.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results against a baseline model that uses online gradient descent to update all model parameters and another baseline that freezes the pre-trained model and uses a fixed adapter for all time steps.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results will show that the adapter-based model outperforms the baseline models under distribution shift, but its performance will degrade when the distribution shift is large. We expect the MAE to increase by up to 30% under significant distribution shifts.

PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of various update strategies for online time series forecasting under delayed feedback on solar power forecasting datasets, specifically the Germany solar power dataset, using metrics such as MAE and MASE. We will train a pre-trained forecasting model with different update strategies, including online gradient descent, delayed gradient descent, and gradient aggregation methods, and evaluate their performance under delayed feedback.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results against a baseline model that uses online gradient descent to update all model parameters.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results will show that delayed gradient descent and gradient aggregation methods outperform online gradient descent under delayed feedback, but may suffer from increased computational cost. We expect the MAE to decrease by up to 20% using delayed gradient descent compared to online gradient descent.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Revised Pseudo-Label Encoding for Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: 
Propose to investigate a revised pseudo-label encoding approach that utilizes a soft-max distribution rather than a one-hot encoding, where the pseudo-label for each class is represented as a probability distribution over all classes. This approach can express the shared attributes among confusing classes and provide a more robust supervision signal for pixels with incorrect class decisions.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with one-hot encoding on fully supervised setting
- Compare with existing pseudo-label learning methods (e.g. hard pseudo-labels, confidence-based filtering)
- Evaluate robustness to label noise
COST: 
500 GPU-hours (using a moderate-sized image segmentation dataset like Cityscapes)
PREDICTION: 
The soft-max encoding should match one-hot encoding in the fully supervised setting, but show improved robustness to label noise in pseudo-label learning. 

(Soft-max encoding might be less effective in several-sided segmentation tasks with clear inter-class clusters, where one-hot speaks to fact : for example, across different street signs which are visually low-level abstract & nothing that relate.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Soft-Max-based Pseudo-Label Generation
PROPOSAL: 
Propose a method to generate soft-max based pseudo-labels for unlabeled data using a temporal smoothing technique. Specifically, we suggest using a weighted moving average of the teacher model's predictions, where the weights are calculated based on the prediction confidence. This can help regularize the pseudo-label generation process and improve the quality of pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with exponential moving average (EMA) based pseudo-label generation
- Evaluate the effect of different weight initialization strategies and confidence thresholds on pseudo-label quality
- Compare with using only the most recent teacher model prediction
COST: 
300 GPU-hours (running multiple epochs on a moderately-sized image segmentation dataset)
PREDICTION: 
The soft-max based pseudo-label generation approach should improve pseudo-label quality and lead to better segmentation performance in semi-supervised learning, especially for high-confidence predictions.

(Rationale: Soft-max is well aligned w/ EMA with Confidence thresh = –∞ -> hard max ; –∞ -> one-hot )

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Confidence Guided Joint Loss for Semi-Supervised Segmentation
PROPOSAL: 
Develop a confidence guided joint loss function that combines the supervised cross-entropy loss with a semi-supervised Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss. The loss function would incorporate a confidence-based weighting scheme to promote better pseudo-label learning and stabilize training. The teacher model's confidence would be used to assign different weights to the supervised and semi-supervised losses, effectively combining the strengths of both.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with the standard cross-entropy loss function for semi-supervised segmentation
- Evaluate the effect of different confidence threshold and weighting schemes on performance
- Compare with existing joint loss functions
COST: 
700 GPU-hours (running multiple epochs on a larger image segmentation dataset like PASCAL VOC)
PREDICTION: 
The proposed confidence guided joint loss should improve segmentation accuracy and convergence speed in semi-supervised settings by providing a more robust supervision signal. 

(inspired by confidence calibrated info-theoretic bound (c) discriminative transfer)

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Confidence Guided Joint Loss for Semi-Supervised Segmentation
PROPOSAL: 
 REVISED 3. Confidence Guided Joint Loss for Semi-Supervised Segmentation
 Introduce an adaptive parameter to adjust the balance between the supervised cross-entropy loss and the semi-supervised KL divergence loss. This adaptive parameter would be a function of the teacher model's confidence and the distribution of pseudo-labels. The goal is to automatically adjust the weighting of the supervised and semi-supervised losses based on the confidence and accuracy of the pseudo-labels, promoting better convergence and segmentation accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with fixed-weight joint loss functions
- Evaluate the effect of different adaptive parameter formulations on performance
- Compare with existing adaptive weighting schemes
COST: 
400 GPU-hours (running multiple epochs on a medium-sized image segmentation dataset)
PREDICTION: 
The revised loss function should adaptively regulate the weighting of the supervised and semi-supervised losses, leading to better segmentation accuracy and faster convergence in semi-supervised settings. 

(Dynamic loss weighting schemes already distant from any weight shared metrics)

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Improved Class Encoding for Pseudo-Label Learning
PROPOSAL: 
REVISED 1. Revised Pseudo-Label Encoding for Semantic Segmentation
 Propose to investigate an improved pseudo-label encoding approach that incorporates class hierarchy and shared attributes among classes. The encoding would represent each class as a combination of its own identity and its similarity to other classes, enabling the model to learn from pseudo-labels even when the class decision is incorrect. This can be achieved by introducing a new encoding layer that learns to represent classes in a compact and informative manner.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with one-hot encoding for classes with and without shared attributes
- Evaluate the effect of different class hierarchy and similarity measures on pseudo-label quality
- Compare with the original soft-max based pseudo-label encoding
COST: 
800 GPU-hours (running multiple epochs on a larger image segmentation dataset)
PREDICTION: 
The improved class encoding should provide a more robust supervision signal for pixels with incorrect class decisions, especially for classes with shared attributes, and lead to better segmentation accuracy in semi-supervised settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Automatic Selection of Pseudo-Label Filtering Thresholds
PROPOSAL: 
Propose an automatic method to select pseudo-label filtering thresholds using a curriculum learning approach. The idea is to start with a low threshold and gradually increase it during training, guiding the model to focus on more confident pseudo-labels at early stages and shifting to less confident ones as it becomes more robust. This approach should allow the model to adapt to the level of noise in the pseudo-labels and produce better segmentation accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with fixed pseudo-label filtering thresholds
- Evaluate the effect of different curriculum learning schedules on performance
- Compare with other pseudo-label filtering methods
COST: 
600 GPU-hours (running multiple epochs on a medium-sized image segmentation dataset)
PREDICTION: 
The automatic threshold selection method should produce better segmentation accuracy by adapting to the level of noise in the pseudo-labels and by effectively leveraging the curriculum learning approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Consistency based Consistency Regularization for SSL
PROPOSAL: 
Propose a novel consistency regularization method for semi-supervised learning that enforces self-consistency of the model's predictions under different transformations. Specifically, the method would learn to predict the same output given different views of the same input, indirectly promoting the model to produce consistent and accurate predictions. This approach can be used in conjunction with existing consistency regularization methods to improve segmentation accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with existing consistency regularization methods (e.g. mean teacher, debacle)
- Evaluate the effect of different transformation types and ratios on performance
- Compare with self-training based methods
COST: 
1000 GPU-hours (running multiple epochs on a larger image segmentation dataset)
PREDICTION: 
The self-consistency based consistency regularization method should improve segmentation accuracy by promoting consistent and accurate predictions, and can be combined with other methods to produce even better results.

(This builds on extra developments not previously reported)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning using Synthetic Data and Real-world Adaptation for Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: 
Propose a transfer learning framework for semantic segmentation that leverages synthetic data and real-world adaptation. The framework would involve training a model on a synthetic dataset and then adapting it to a real-world dataset using a novel domain adaptation approach that combines data augmentation and consistency regularization. This approach can help reduce the need for large amounts of real-world labeled data and improve segmentation accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with traditional transfer learning methods
- Evaluate the effect of different data augmentation techniques and consistency regularization methods on performance
- Compare with domain adaptation methods that do not use synthetic data
COST: 
1200 GPU-hours (running multiple epochs on a large image segmentation dataset and a corresponding synthetic dataset)
PREDICTION: 
The transfer learning framework should improve segmentation accuracy by leveraging synthetic data and real-world adaptation, and can significantly reduce the need for large amounts of real-world labeled data. 

(This capitalizes on recent work leveraging synthetic data)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness Analysis of Semi-Supervised Segmentation Methods against Label Noise and Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: 
conduct a comprehensive robustness analysis of the proposed semi-supervised segmentation methods, focusing on their performance under label noise and distribution shift scenarios. The analysis would involve evaluating the methods on various synthetic and real-world datasets with different levels of label noise and distribution shift, and comparing their robustness with state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation methods
- Evaluate the effect of different levels of label noise and distribution shift on performance
- Compare with robustness-enhancing methods used in other contexts
COST: 
1500 GPU-hours (running multiple experiments on various datasets and label noise scenarios)
PREDICTION: 
The robustness analysis should provide valuable insights into the performance of the proposed semi-supervised segmentation methods in real-world scenarios, helping to identify their strengths and weaknesses. 

(This adds a reality check by assessing parameter stability )

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Deployment and Explainability of Semi-Supervised Segmentation Models
PROPOSAL: 
Propose a real-world deployment and explainability framework for semi-supervised segmentation models, focusing on transparent and interpretable models that can provide insights into their decision-making processes. The framework would involve evaluating the models on real-world datasets, conducting human evaluation studies, and developing techniques for visualizing and interpreting the models' outputs.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare with state-of-the-art explainability techniques for deep learning models
- Evaluate the effect of different explainability techniques on user understanding and model trustworthiness
- Compare with other deployment and evaluation frameworks for semi-supervised segmentation models
COST: 
2000 GPU-hours (running multiple experiments on various real-world datasets and conducting human evaluation studies)
PREDICTION: 
The real-world deployment and explainability framework should provide valuable insights into the performance and interpretability of semi-supervised segmentation models in real-world scenarios, helping to improve their trustworthiness and adoption in practical applications.

(This sets a high bar for practical models)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Proposal: Modified Pseudo-Label Encoding for Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel soft pseudo-label encoding where each pixel's label is represented by a weighted combination of top k predicted classes, instead of relying on a single hard class assignment from the argmax. Use a curriculum learning approach to iteratively increase the number of classes considered for soft encoding as the model improves.
CONTROLS: Compare to UDA-SSL baselines using Soft-Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (Soft-ASPP) decoder architecture and cross-entropy training objective. Ablate pseudo-label confidence threshold selection and examine the effects of varying k values (3,5,7).
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improve over UDA baselines but retain some noise from soft pseudo-labels. Empirically demonstrate soft encoding superiority in SSL scenarios where target domain contains ambiguous classes. Potential failure: convergence may be sensitive to choice of k and learning rate schedules.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiment: Comparison with Phantom Classes
PROPOSAL: Introduce artificially created "phantom" classes during training that correspond to the confusing classes (e.g., for sheep, cow, and horse, create a single phantom class). Assign large weights to phantom classes when computing the weighted combination of top k predicted classes. Investigate whether the model learns to distinguish the true classes from the phantom classes and thereby reduces the impact of incorrect class assignments.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing soft pseudo-label encoding variant that does not consider phantom classes. Measure the effect on the model's ability to correctly classify pixels from the target domain dataset.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improve over existing soft pseudo-label encoding by leveraging phantom classes to demarcate confusing classes.
