ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Proposal: Modified Pseudo-Label Encoding for Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Update the soft pseudo-label encoding to incorporate additional loss components that promote the distinction between the true class and the phantom (confusing) classes. Specifically, add a term to the loss function that calculates the similarity between the latent features of the current class assignment and the phantom class, weighted by the pseudo-label confidence. This encourages the model to learn features that are distinct from the phantom classes and improves its robustness to incorrect class assignments.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing formulation without phantom-based loss component, and examine the ablation of the similarity term from the loss function. Evaluate the impact on model performance using standard metrics for semantic segmentation.
COST: 10 additional GPU-hours (total: 40 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Improve over existing soft pseudo-label encoding variant, both in terms of accuracy and robustness to label noise. Potential failure: the additional loss component may introduce instability or hinder convergence if not properly tuned.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED Proposal: Modified Pseudo-Label Encoding for Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Extend the soft pseudo-label encoding to support a learning-based approach to selecting the phantom classes. Train a separate network, the "confusion discriminator", to predict the likelihood of a class being a phantom class, given the normalized pseudo-label probabilities. Use this prediction as a mask to weight the phantom-based loss component, focusing on the most uncertain class assignments.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing formulation with phantom-based loss component, and examine the ablation of the confusion discriminator. Evaluate the impact on model performance using standard metrics for semantic segmentation.
COST: 15 additional GPU-hours (total: 55 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Improve over existing soft pseudo-label encoding variant, both in terms of accuracy and robustness to label noise. The learning-based approach may help adapt to the specific characteristics of the target domain and improve transferability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Phantom-Based Loss Component
PROPOSAL: Derive a theoretical bound on the expected risk of the soft pseudo-label encoding with phantom-based loss component, as a function of the confidence and similarity measures used in the loss function. Show that the bound converges to the optimal risk as the model's capacity increases, under certain assumptions on the data distribution. Investigate the implications of this bound for the choice of hyperparameters and the design of the phantom-based loss component.
CONTROLS: Analyze the bound for the case where phantom classes are revealed to be actual classes in the target domain.
COST: 5 GPU-hours (no significant computation required)
PREDICATION: Provides a framework for understanding the effects of phantom-based loss components on model behavior and performance, potentially identifying optimal hyperparameters for the method.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extension to Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Adapt the modified pseudo-label encoding with phantom-based loss component to the unsupervised domain adaptation setting, where both source and target domains have only unlabeled data. Use a two-stage approach, where the first stage trains a domain-invariant feature extractor using a multi-task learning setup, and the second stage fine-tunes the feature extractor using the modified pseudo-label encoding with phantom-based loss component. Investigate the benefits of this approach in synthetic-to-real adaptation scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing UDA baselines and evaluate the impact of different domain-invariant feature extractors (e.g., deep in networks, correlation alignment) on the performance of the modified pseudo-label encoding.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Show state-of-the-art results in synthetic-to-real adaptation tasks and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in transferring knowledge across domains with varying complexities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration of Different Confidence Measures
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of different confidence measures (e.g., temperature scaling, softmax, Bartlett's test-based confidence) on the performance of the modified pseudo-label encoding with phantom-based loss component. Evaluate the sensitivity of the approach to the choice of confidence measure and examine whether using multiple confidence measures improves overall performance.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing confidence measures and examine the ablation of confidence measures from the loss function. Evaluate the impact on model performance using standard metrics for semantic segmentation and domain adaptation.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Identify the most effective confidence measure for the modified pseudo-label encoding and demonstrate its robustness to different confidence measures. Potential failure: the performance of the approach may degrade with suboptimal confidence measures or when the chosen confidence measures do not accurately represent model uncertainty.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: REVISED Theoretical Analysis of Phantom-Based Loss Component
PROPOSAL: Strengthen the theoretical analysis of the phantom-based loss component by providing a more detailed treatment of the convergence properties, including a proof of convergence to the optimal risk under certain conditions on the data distribution and the choice of hyperparameters. Investigate the implications of this analysis for the selection of hyperparameters and the design of the phantom-based loss component.
CONTROLS: Extend the analysis to a multi-class setting and examine the impact of different clustering algorithms for identifying phantom classes.
COST: 10 additional GPU-hours (total: 65 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: Enhance the theoretical understanding of the phantom-based loss component, providing a more rigorous framework for understanding its performance under different scenarios and hyperparameter settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Application to Real-World Medical Imaging Tasks
PROPOSAL: Apply the modified pseudo-label encoding with phantom-based loss component to real-world medical imaging tasks, specifically cardiac MRI segmentation. Use publicly available labeled and unlabeled datasets to evaluate the approach's performance on this clinically relevant task. Investigate the impact of the phantom-based loss component on the model's ability to segment complex anatomy and recover from incorrect class assignments.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing state-of-the-art methods for cardiac MRI segmentation and evaluate the impact of the phantom-based loss component on the model's performance.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Demonstrate improved performance on cardiac MRI segmentation tasks, leveraging the phantom-based loss component to enhance the model's robustness to incorrect class assignments and improve its ability to segment complex anatomy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation of Transferability to Autonomous Driving Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the transferability of the modified pseudo-label encoding with phantom-based loss component to autonomous driving tasks, specifically urban street-scene segmentation. Use a combination of synthetic and real-world datasets to evaluate the approach's performance on this challenging task. Investigate the impact of the phantom-based loss component on the model's ability to generalize across different street-scene scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing state-of-the-art methods for urban street-scene segmentation and evaluate the impact of the phantom-based loss component on the model's performance.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Demonstrate improved transferability to autonomous driving tasks, leveraging the phantom-based loss component to enhance the model's robustness to incorrect class assignments and improve its ability to segment complex street-scenes.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Framework for Single-Step Generation with Implicit Feedback
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified variational autoencoder (VAE) framework that incorporates implicit feedback from the data distribution, allowing for single-step generation without discriminators, auxiliary score networks, or frozen teacher models. The framework will leverage a novel, iterative Gaussian process (GP) based amortized inference mechanism to implicitly match the data distribution.
CONTROLS: Baseline: unconditional VAE, No-GAN single-step generation.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvement over unconditional VAE in terms of single-step generation quality, with potential to reach state-of-the-art performance, but might require careful tuning of hyperparameters, especially in ultra-large model regimes where computational resources are limited.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Few-Step Consistency-Based Generation with Gradient-Domain Guidance
PROPOSAL: Introduce a gradient-domain guidance mechanism to consistency-based few-step generation, which aligns the generator's gradients with those of the data distribution during training. This addition will enable few-step models to learn a more accurate representation of the data distribution, leading to improved single-step performance. The gradient-domain guidance mechanism will be integrated into the existing unified framework for single-step generation with implicit feedback (proposed in turn 1).
CONTROLS: Baseline: consistency-based few-step generation without gradient-domain guidance; Comparison with augmented framework.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (additional to the existing framework)
PREDICTION: Expected to significantly improve the quality of single-step generations, while maintaining simplicity and efficiency, but might require careful calibration of gradient-domain guidance parameters.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Few-Step Consistency-Based Generation with Gradient-Domain Guidance
PROPOSAL (REVISED): Combine the gradient-domain guidance mechanism with teacher distillation, using a lightweight teacher model to provide initial gradient information for the generator. This will help the generator adapt more effectively to the gradient-domain alignment, leading to improved single-step performance. The revised mechanism will be integrated into the existing unified framework for single-step generation with implicit feedback.
CONTROLS: Baseline: consistency-based few-step generation without gradient-domain guidance and teacher distillation; Comparison with augmented framework; Comparison with progressive distillation.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (additional to the existing framework)
PREDICTION: Expected to achieve state-of-the-art results in single-step generation, but might require careful tuning of teacher model capacity and distillation strength.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Unified Framework for Single-Step Generation with Implicit Feedback
PROPOSAL (REVISED): Modify the unified VAE framework to incorporate an iterative refinement loop for the implicit feedback mechanism. In each iteration, the GP-based amortized inference will refine its approximation of the data distribution, allowing for more accurate gradient information to guide the generator. This revised framework will improve the robustness and efficacy of the implicit feedback mechanism.
CONTROLS: Baseline: original unified framework; Comparison with the revised framework.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (additional to the existing framework)
PREDICTION: Expected to improve the quality of single-step generations and reduce variability in the results, but might require careful tuning of the refinement loop parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Single-Step Generation via Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Teachers
PROPOSAL: Introduce a knowledge distillation framework that leverages the strengths of multiple teacher models to improve single-step generation. Each teacher model will be trained with a unique set of hyperparameters and architecture, and the students will learn to distill knowledge from these diverse teachers. This approach will enable more robust and efficient single-step generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline: single-teacher knowledge distillation; Comparison with multiple-teacher framework.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to achieve improved single-step generation results, but might require careful selection and tuning of teacher models and distillation hyperparameters.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Few-Step Consistency-Based Generation with Gradient-Domain Guidance
PROPOSAL (REVISED): Modify the combination of gradient-domain guidance and teacher distillation to incorporate a meta-learning approach. The generator will learn to adapt to different teacher models and gradient-domain guidance settings, allowing it to generalize better and achieve state-of-the-art results across various datasets and scenarios. This revised framework will improve the robustness and efficiency of single-step generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline: consistency-based few-step generation without gradient-domain guidance and teacher distillation; Comparison with augmented framework; Comparison with knowledge distillation and meta-learning baselines.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (additional to the existing framework)
PREDICTION: Expected to achieve state-of-the-art results in single-step generation, with improved robustness and generalization, but might require careful tuning of the meta-learning hyperparameters.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 2. Few-Step Consistency-Based Generation with Gradient-Domain Guidance
PROPOSAL (REVISED): Replace the gradient-domain guidance mechanism with a novel normalizing flow-based approach. This will enable the generator to learn a more accurate and flexible representation of the data distribution, leading to improved single-step generation results.
CONTROLS: Baseline: consistency-based few-step generation without normalizing flows; Comparison with augmented framework; Comparison with knowledge distillation and gradient-domain guidance baselines.
COST: 600 GPU-hours (additional to the existing framework)
PREDICTION: Expected to achieve improved single-step generation results, with better handling of complex distributions, but might require careful tuning of the normalizing flow architecture and hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing and Improving the Training Dynamics of Single-Step Generators
PROPOSAL: Perform a comprehensive analysis of the training dynamics of the proposed single-step generators, including the unified framework, few-step consistency-based generation with gradient-domain guidance, and efficient single-step generation via knowledge distillation from multiple teachers. This analysis will focus on identifying potential instability issues, optimizing hyperparameters, and developing novel optimization techniques to improve the robustness and efficiency of single-step generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard training procedures; Comparison with optimized training procedures; Comparison with novel optimization techniques.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to provide valuable insights into the training dynamics of single-step generators, leading to improved stability and efficiency, but might require significant computational resources to conduct the analysis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Evaluation and Deployment of Single-Step Generators for Text-to-Image and Image Editing Tasks
PROPOSAL: Evaluate and deploy the proposed single-step generators on large-scale text-to-image and image editing tasks, using real-world datasets and models (e.g., DALL-E, Stable Diffusion). This will involve fine-tuning the generators on specific tasks, analyzing their performance, and conducting user studies to assess their usefulness and quality.
CONTROLS: Baseline: existing state-of-the-art models and techniques for text-to-image and image editing tasks; Comparison with proposed single-step generators.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (additional to existing models)
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate the practical applicability and potential of single-step generators on large-scale real-world tasks, but might require significant human effort to adapt the generators to specific tasks and domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling Single-Step Generators to Ultra-Large Models: Challenges, Opportunities, and Future Directions
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive study on scaling single-step generators to ultra-large models (e.g., 10B+ parameters), identifying challenges, opportunities, and future directions. This will involve analyzing computational costs, memory requirements, and potential trade-offs in performance, as well as exploring techniques for efficient scaling, such as model pruning, knowledge distillation, and mixed-precision training.
CONTROLS: Baseline: existing state-of-the-art models and techniques for ultra-large models; Comparison with proposed scaling strategies.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: Expected to provide valuable insights into the future of single-step generation and its potential for ultra-large models, but might require significant computational resources and ongoing research to overcome scaling challenges.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Single-Shot Consistency Model

CONTROLS: Compare with standard consistency models (e.g., PCM and LCM) and few-shot GAN methods like SANA-Sprint.
COST: Estimated 10 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The modified consistency model may produce high-quality images in a single function evaluation, but it may lack the flexibility of traditional consistency models that use conditional embeddings, potentially limiting its ability to generate diverse images with a single model, which may fail when dealing with novel objects.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Single-Shot Consistency Model 
PROPOSAL: Modify the input scheme of the single-shot consistency model (proposal 1) to take advantage of pre-trained text encoders and pre-trained image features (e.g., CLIP) as additional inputs to condition the image generation, allowing the model to better incorporate the text information and improve its generation quality and diversity.
CONTROLS: Compare with proposal 1 and existing few-shot consistency models with conditional embeddings.
COST: Estimated 15 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The revised single-shot model may leverage the power of pre-trained models and CLIP to produce high-quality images with text information, but it might still suffer from over-conditioning, limiting its ability to generate novel images or objects that are not present in the training dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Few-Shot Adversarial-Free Loss 
PROPOSAL: Explore an adversarial-free loss function that can be used as a drop-in replacement for existing GAN-style losses in few-shot text-to-image synthesis, by adding a residual reconstruction loss term to a standard few-shot consistency model (proposal 1), allowing for a simple and efficient way to improve image quality and realism in the few-shot setting.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard few-shot consistency models and few-shot GAN methods.
COST: Estimated 5 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The adversarial-free loss function may improve image quality and realism in the few-shot setting, but it may not provide the same level of flexibility as GAN-style losses in generating novel images or objects, potentially limiting its performance in specific tasks like image editing or novel object generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Progressive Few-Shot Inference 
PROPOSAL: Develop a progressive few-shot inference algorithm that samples the input noise through multiple stages, with each stage adding a subset of capacity to the model, allowing the model to produce high-quality images in a few-shot setting by progressively increasing its capacity and incorporating more information from the input.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard few-shot models, few-shot consistency models, and the few-shot adversarial-free loss function.
COST: Estimated 50 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The progressive few-shot inference algorithm may significantly improve image quality and realism in the few-shot setting by iteratively incorporating more information, but it may require careful tuning of the progressive sampling schedule, and may become computationally expensive for very large models, potentially failing to scale to models beyond 10B parameters.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Progressive Few-Shot Inference 
PROPOSAL: Modify the progressive few-shot inference algorithm to use a hierarchical or multi-resolution approach to progressively increase the capacity of the model, by conditioning the model on a learned embedding of the input text at different resolutions, allowing the model to focus on different aspects of the text at each stage of the inference process, and potentially improving image quality and realism in the few-shot setting.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original progressive few-shot inference algorithm and existing few-shot models.
COST: Estimated 60 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The revised progressive few-shot inference algorithm may improve performance by better incorporating text information at different resolution levels, but it may require more complex training procedures and additional hyperparameter tuning, potentially leading to increased instability and overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unconstrained Sampling 
PROPOSAL: Propose an unconstrained sampling strategy for few-shot text-to-image synthesis, where the sampling process is guided only by the conditioning text, and the model is allowed to produce any image that fits the text, rather than being constrained to a specific distribution or shape, to explore the full potential of few-shot generation.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard few-shot consistency models, few-shot GAN methods, and other few-shot methods that enforce specific distributions or shapes.
COST: Estimated 10 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The unconstrained sampling strategy may produce highly diverse and creative images that fit the conditioning text, but it may also result in images that are not visually coherent or are difficult to interpret, potentially failing to produce high-quality images in specific tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Knowledge Distillation 
PROPOSAL: Develop a multimodal knowledge distillation approach that leverages pre-trained language models and vision models to constrain the generation process, by distilling knowledge from the pre-trained language model into a text-conditioned embedding, and then using this embedding to condition a few-shot vision model, allowing for efficient and effective transfer of knowledge between different modalities.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard few-shot consistency models, few-shot GAN methods, and other knowledge distillation methods.
COST: Estimated 30 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The multimodal knowledge distillation approach may significantly improve the quality and diversity of generated images by leveraging pre-trained models and distilling knowledge across modalities, but it may require careful tuning of the distillation process and the vision model architecture, potentially leading to increased computational complexity.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Multimodal Knowledge Distillation 
PROPOSAL: Modify the multimodal knowledge distillation approach to use a partial distillation mechanism, where only the relevant and informative knowledge from the pre-trained language model is transferred to the text-conditioned embedding, allowing for a more efficient and effective transfer of knowledge that reduces the risk of overfitting and increases the scalability of the approach.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original multimodal knowledge distillation approach and other knowledge distillation methods.
COST: Estimated 40 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The revised multimodal knowledge distillation approach may improve the quality and diversity of generated images by reducing the risk of overfitting and increasing the scalability, but it may require careful tuning of the partial distillation mechanism and the vision model architecture, potentially leading to increased computational complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Few-Shot Inference by Pruning 
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of model pruning to reduce the computational cost of few-shot text-to-image synthesis models, by identifying and removing redundant or inactive connections in the model, allowing for faster and more efficient inference while maintaining the model's performance and quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard few-shot models, few-shot consistency models, and other few-shot methods that do not use pruning.
COST: Estimated 15 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The efficient few-shot inference by pruning approach may significantly reduce the computational cost of few-shot text-to-image synthesis models, but it may also lead to a decrease in performance or quality if the pruning process removes key connections or reduces the model's capacity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hybrid Framework for Few-Shot Text-to-Image Synthesis 
PROPOSAL: Develop a hybrid framework that combines the strengths of different few-shot text-to-image synthesis models, such as the consistency models (proposal 1) and the multimodal knowledge distillation (proposal 5), and the efficient few-shot inference by pruning (proposal 6), to create a model that balances image quality, diversity, and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare with individual proposals, as well as other state-of-the-art few-shot text-to-image synthesis models.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The hybrid framework may achieve state-of-the-art performance and efficiency in few-shot text-to-image synthesis, but it may also be more complex to train and tune, requiring careful selection and combination of individual components, which may lead to increased training time and computational cost.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Limitations of Fine-Tuning Pre-trained T2I Models on Long Captioned Data
PROPOSAL: This experiment involves fine-tuning a pre-trained T2I model (e.g. DALL-E 2) on a large dataset of images paired with long, detailed captions (e.g. COCO Karpathy's val2014 split), with the goal of assessing the baseline performance on long captions and understanding the degree to which fine-tuning can improve model performance.
CONTROLS: Ablation studies include (1) a small-sized dataset for fine-tuning and (2) fine-tuning without augmenting the input context window of the T2I model. Baseline model is a frozen pre-trained T2I model. Dataset with shorter captions is used as a control group.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected result is that fine-tuning the pre-trained T2I model on long-captioned data significantly improves its performance on detailed long captions, but faces challenges extrapolating to even longer prompts. Fine-tuning with smaller datasets risks overfitting or underfitting crucial details. Model may retain robustness, but rise in training loss will imply the challenging nature of capturing all the specified objects on further longer prompts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Projection-Based Methods for Long Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: This experiment involves comparing the performance of projection-based methods (e.g. Controllable Text-to-Image Diffusion) that map a long prompt into the effective context window of a pre-trained T2I model to a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model proposed in proposal 1. A controlled experiment will assess the trade-off between details preserved from long prompts and robustness to out-of-distribution prompts.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1., evaluation on same test set of long captions as proposal 1. We use single model evaluation and contrast with ensemble-based model to evaluate whether projection-based methods exhibit ensemble superiority.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected result is that projection-based methods can preserve more details from long prompts but often sacrifice robustness, and that model ensemble induces natural robustness, offsetting some of the fine-tuning results and especially exhibit ensemble superiority when text complexity surpasses model capacity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation with Hierarchical Prompt Representation
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes to use a hierarchical prompt representation for long-prompt T2I, where a high-level prompt summary is converted to an intermediate text embedding, and then a low-level prompt specific embedding is generated for the details. This is achieved by fine-tuning a pre-trained long-range transformer (e.g. Longformer) on a large dataset of image captions and then using it to generate hierarchical prompt representations, which are fed into a pre-trained T2I model for images generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1, and ablated versions of the hierarchical representation without pre-trained prompts and without using intermediate prompt summary to understand robustness.
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected result is that hierarchical prompt representation induces improvements in model robustness and can capture more of the long captions details by effectively compartmentalizing the long content and allowing the model to expect and focus on specifics that otherwise would have negative effects on T2I output such as narrative context and narrowing region cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Role of Narrative Flow and Story Interpreting in Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: This experiment focuses on understanding the role of narrative flow and story interpreting in long-prompt T2I by introducing a novel dataset that crowdsourced human parses of long captions into core story objects and action relationships. A set of self-supervised language models (e.g. BART, LongT5) are fine-tuned to predict these story objects and relationships from the input prompts, and can be integrated into pre-trained T2I models to better understand the narrative flow.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1, and ablated versions of the integration without predict action and objects as to understand the contributed from both components.
COST: 420 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected result is that pre-trained T2I models integrated with human-understood narrative flow and story objects show robust and significant gains in performance across diverse long prompt test set, particularly demonstrated on overall well-represented scenes that otherwise floor conditional language models in enticing image remains.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Assessing the Role of Narrative Flow and Story Interpreting in Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation (Revised)
PROPOSAL: This experiment is revised to focus on the evaluation of the auxiliary story understanding component in the long-prompt T2I generation pipeline. It explores the effectiveness of the human-understood narrative flow and story objects in aiding pre-trained T2I models to better interpret and render details from long captions. The fine-tuned components are isolated and evaluated separately, using metrics that quantify the extent to which the auxiliary system enhances the T2I model's object detection and scene understanding abilities.
CONTROLS: Baseline is the original pre-trained T2I model without the auxiliary story understanding component. 
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected result is that the revised auxiliary component will show modest improvements in capturing details and objects from long captions, especially in scenes with rich narrative flow, and that isolating the effect of the auxiliary system will provide valuable insights into the relative importance of story understanding in long-prompt T2I.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Plug-and-Play Story Augmentation Components for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a novel approach to incorporating story understanding into the long-prompt T2I generation pipeline using a plug-and-play story augmentation component. By design, the augmentation component is highly customizable, allowing researchers to adapt the component to complement diverse pre-trained T2I models and to fit various long-prompt datasets. The performance of the story augmentation component is evaluated using a controlled experiment setup.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 3. Multiple ablation studies are conducted to understand the impact of different design choices and customization options on the augmentation component's performance.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected result is that the plug-and-play story augmentation component will demonstrate adaptability and robustness across various pre-trained T2I models and long-prompt datasets, and will show consistent improvements in long-prompt T2I performance when properly tuned and integrated into the pipeline.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Attention Mechanisms on Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: This experiment focuses on the impact of attention mechanisms on long-prompt T2I generation. Specifically, it investigates the effectiveness of different attention mechanisms, such as multi-head attention and CASA attention, in capturing long-range dependencies and narrative flow in long captions. The experiment involves modifying pre-trained T2I models to incorporate these attention mechanisms and evaluating their performance on long-prompt benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Baselines include a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1, and ablation studies are conducted to understand the impact of different attention mechanisms and layer configurations.
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected result is that attention mechanisms will improve the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies and narrative flow in long captions, but may also introduce complexity and computational costs. The optimal attention mechanism and layer configuration will depend on the specific long-prompt benchmark and use case.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding the Adversarial Robustness of Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the adversarial robustness of long-prompt T2I generation models. It employs state-of-the-art adversarial attack techniques, such as PGD and C&W, to generate perturbed input captions that can fool pre-trained T2I models. The experiment aims to understand the vulnerabilities of long-prompt T2I models and identify potential countermeasures to improve their robustness.
CONTROLS: Baselines include a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1, and ablation studies are conducted to understand the impact of different training objectives and regularization techniques.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected result is that long-prompt T2I models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, particularly when the attacks target specific objects or narrative elements. The experiment will identify key factors contributing to this vulnerability and provide insights for improving the robustness of long-prompt T2I models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation with Information Bottleneck
PROPOSAL: This theoretical result investigates the information bottleneck in long-prompt T2I models. It provides an analytical framework to understand the trade-off between the model's capacity to capture long-range dependencies and the loss of information due to the bottleneck. The result highlights the importance of designing efficient long-prompt T2I models that balance complexity and information retention.
CONTROLS: Assumptions: long-prompt T2I models are represented as a sequence of conditional distributions, and the information bottleneck is modeled as a capacity constraint.
COST: N/A
PREDICTION: Expected result is that the theoretical analysis will reveal the fundamental limits of long-prompt T2I models in capturing long-range dependencies and that the information bottleneck is a key factor contributing to the model's vulnerability to adversarial attacks and limited ability to render detailed scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Unified Framework for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation: Experimental Validation and Theoretical Analysis
PROPOSAL: This final experiment validates the theoretical results and provides a unified framework for long-prompt T2I generation. It combines the strengths of the previously proposed methods, including fine-tuning, projection-based methods, hierarchical prompt representation, and attention mechanisms, into a single framework. The framework is evaluated on various long-prompt benchmarks and its performance is compared to state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Baselines include fine-tuned pre-trained T2I models from proposal 1, projection-based methods from proposal 2, and attention mechanisms from proposal 6. Theoretical analysis is compared to the results in proposal 8.
COST: 480 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected result is that the unified framework will demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on long-prompt benchmarks and provide a generalizable solution for long-prompt T2I generation. The framework will also showcase the effectiveness of the theoretical analysis in demonstrating the importance of information retention and attention mechanisms in long-prompt T2I models.

Model may retain robustness, but rise in training loss will imply the challenging nature of capturing all the specified objects on further longer prompts.

PROPOSAL 2: Evaluating Projection-Based Methods for Long Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
This experiment involves comparing the performance of projection-based methods (e.g. Controllable Text-to-Image Diffusion) that map a long prompt into the effective context window of a pre-trained T2I model to a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model proposed in proposal 1. A controlled experiment will assess the trade-off between details preserved from long prompts and robustness to out-of-distribution prompts.
Controls: Baseline is a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1., evaluation on same test set of long captions as proposal 1. We use single model evaluation and contrast with ensemble-based model to evaluate whether projection-based methods exhibit ensemble superiority.
Estimated cost: 120 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected result is that projection-based methods can preserve more details from long prompts but often sacrifice robustness, and that model ensemble induces natural robustness, offsetting some of the fine-tuning results and especially exhibit ensemble superiority when text complexity surpasses model capacity.

PROPOSAL 3: Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation with Hierarchical Prompt Representation
This experiment proposes to use a hierarchical prompt representation for long-prompt T2I, where a high-level prompt summary is converted to an intermediate text embedding, and then a low-level prompt specific embedding is generated for the details. This is achieved by fine-tuning a pre-trained long-range transformer (e.g. Longformer) on a large dataset of image captions and then using it to generate hierarchical prompt representations, which are fed into a pre-trained T2I model for images generation.
Controls: Baseline is a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1, and ablated versions of the hierarchical representation without pre-trained prompts and without using intermediate prompt summary to understand robustness.
Estimated cost: 360 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected result is that hierarchical prompt representation induces improvements in model robustness and can capture more of the long captions details by effectively compartmentalizing the long content and allowing the model to expect and focus on specifics that otherwise would have negative effects on T2I output such as narrative context and narrowing region cues.

PROPOSAL 4: Assessing the Role of Narrative Flow and Story Interpreting in Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
This experiment focuses on understanding the role of narrative flow and story interpreting in long-prompt T2I by introducing a novel dataset that crowdsourced human parses of long captions into core story objects and action relationships. A set of self-supervised language models (e.g. BART, LongT5) are fine-tuned to predict these story objects and relationships from the input prompts, and can be integrated into pre-trained T2I models to better understand the narrative flow.
Controls: Baseline is a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1, and ablated versions of the integration without predict action and objects as to understand the contributed from both components.
Estimated cost: 420 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected result is that pre-trained T2I models integrated with human-understood narrative flow and story objects show robust and significant gains in performance across diverse long prompt test set, particularly demonstrated on overall well-represented scenes that otherwise floor conditional language models in enticing image remains.

PROPOSAL 5: Designing Plug-and-Play Story Augmentation Components for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
This experiment proposes a novel approach to incorporating story understanding into the long-prompt T2I generation pipeline using a plug-and-play story augmentation component. By design, the augmentation component is highly customizable, allowing researchers to adapt the component to complement diverse pre-trained T2I models and to fit various long-prompt datasets. The performance of the story augmentation component is evaluated using a controlled experiment setup.
Controls: Baseline is a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 3. Multiple ablation studies are conducted to understand the impact of different design choices and customization options on the augmentation component's performance.
Estimated cost: 180 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected result is that the plug-and-play story augmentation component will demonstrate adaptability and robustness across various pre-trained T2I models and long-prompt datasets, and will show consistent improvements in long-prompt T2I performance when properly tuned and integrated into the pipeline.

PROPOSAL 6: Investigating the Impact of Attention Mechanisms on Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
This experiment focuses on the impact of attention mechanisms on long-prompt T2I generation. Specifically, it investigates the effectiveness of different attention mechanisms, such as multi-head attention and CASA attention, in capturing long-range dependencies and narrative flow in long captions. The experiment involves modifying pre-trained T2I models to incorporate these attention mechanisms and evaluating their performance on long-prompt benchmarks.
Controls: Baselines include a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1, and ablation studies are conducted to understand the impact of different attention mechanisms and layer configurations.
Estimated cost: 240 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected result is that attention mechanisms will improve the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies and narrative flow in long captions, but may also introduce complexity and computational costs. The optimal attention mechanism and layer configuration will depend on the specific long-prompt benchmark and use case.

PROPOSAL 7: Understanding the Adversarial Robustness of Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation Models
This experiment investigates the adversarial robustness of long-prompt T2I generation models. It employs state-of-the-art adversarial attack techniques, such as PGD and C&W, to generate perturbed input captions that can fool pre-trained T2I models. The experiment aims to understand the vulnerabilities of long-prompt T2I models and identify potential countermeasures to improve their robustness.
Controls: Baselines include a fine-tuned pre-trained T2I model from proposal 1, and ablation studies are conducted to understand the impact of different training objectives and regularization techniques.
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected result is that long-prompt T2I models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, particularly when the attacks target specific objects or narrative elements. The experiment will identify key factors contributing to this vulnerability and provide insights for improving the robustness of long-prompt T2I models.

PROPOSAL 8: Theoretical Analysis of Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation with Information Bottleneck
This theoretical result investigates the information bottleneck in long-prompt T2I models. It provides an analytical framework to understand the trade-off between the model's capacity to capture long-range dependencies and the loss of information due to the bottleneck. The result highlights the importance of designing efficient long-prompt T2I models that balance complexity and information retention.
Controls: Assumptions: long-prompt T2I models are represented as a sequence of conditional distributions, and the information bottleneck is modeled as a capacity constraint.
Estimated cost: N/A
Prediction: Expected result is that the theoretical analysis will reveal the fundamental limits of long-prompt T2I models in capturing long-range dependencies and that the information bottleneck is a key factor contributing to the model's vulnerability to adversarial attacks and limited ability to render detailed scenes.

PROPOSAL 9: A Unified Framework for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation: Experimental Validation and Theoretical Analysis
This final experiment validates the theoretical results and provides a unified framework for long-prompt T2I generation. It combines the strengths of the previously proposed methods, including fine-tuning, projection-based methods, hierarchical prompt representation, and attention mechanisms, into a single framework. The framework is evaluated on various long-prompt benchmarks and its performance is compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Controls: Baselines include fine-tuned pre-trained T2I models from proposal 1, projection-based methods from proposal 2, and attention mechanisms from proposal 6. Theoretical analysis is compared to the results in proposal 8.
Estimated cost: 480 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected result is that the unified framework will demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on long-prompt benchmarks and provide a generalizable solution for long-prompt T2I generation. The framework will also showcase the effectiveness of the theoretical analysis in demonstrating the importance of information retention and attention mechanisms in long-prompt T2I models.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Context Window Extension for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a simple yet effective technique to dynamically extend the context window of pre-trained text encoders, allowing them to effectively capture narrative flow and distributed details in long prompts. Our approach leverages an attention-based mechanism that adaptively focuses on relevant parts of the input text, selectively expanding the encoder's receptive field based on the input's complexity. We will implement this technique using the popular CLIP text encoder and evaluate its performance on a set of long-prompt text-to-image benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments using pre-trained CLIP, as well as an ablation study to isolate the effect of the context window extension.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours (estimating 10% compute usage compared to training a pre-trained CLIP model)
PREDICTION: Expected to significantly improve state-of-the-art performance on long-prompt text-to-image benchmarks (50-75% reduction in error rate), but may fail if the model's parameter scale becomes a bottleneck or if the attention-based mechanism struggles to generalize across different input types.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain Knowledge Injection for Improved Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effectiveness of injecting domain-specific knowledge into the text encoding process to enhance the model's ability to capture detailed descriptions in long prompts. Specifically, we will introduce a simple modification to the text encoder's architecture to incorporate a small-scale language model that is fine-tuned on a dataset of specialized domain knowledge. This will allow the model to incorporate relevant prior knowledge and mappings between descriptive phrases and corresponding visual features. We will evaluate this approach on a set of text-to-image benchmarks across various domains (e.g., architecture, nature, and product photography).
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with the state-of-the-art pre-trained CLIP model, as well as an ablation study to isolate the effect of domain knowledge injection.
COST: 8000 GPU-hours (estimating 50% compute usage compared to training a pre-trained CLIP model)
PREDICTION: Expected to outperform state-of-the-art models by approximately 20-30% in terms of detailed feature capture and overall accuracy, but may struggle if the domain knowledge is not well-aligned with the model's pre-existing knowledge or if the injected knowledge is too specialized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Projection Learning for Multi-Step Text-to-Image Rendering
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical projection learning framework to tackle the long-prompt text-to-image generation challenge. The approach involves training a series of hierarchical projections that progressively refine and expand the model's understanding of the input text. Each projection learns to map the input text to a more abstract and detailed representation, with the final projection generating the image. We will experiment with different architectures, projection types, and learning objectives to evaluate the efficacy of this approach. Performance will be evaluated on a range of text-to-image benchmarks, with a focus on complex and long-prompt inputs.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with state-of-the-art text-to-image models, as well as ablation studies to isolate the effect of individual components, such as hierarchical projections and learning objectives.
COST: 12000 GPU-hours (estimating 80% compute usage compared to training a pre-trained CLIP model)
PREDICTION: Expected to significantly improve performance on challenging long-prompt text-to-image inputs (30-50% error rate reduction), but may struggle with overfitting if the hierarchical projections become too specialized or if the model's architecture is not well-suited to handle the progressive learning regime.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Hierarchical Projection Learning for Multi-Step Text-to-Image Rendering
PROPOSAL: We refine the hierarchical projection learning framework (Turn 3) to better handle the large-scale complexity of long-prompt text-to-image generation. To mitigate overfitting and improve the hierarchical projections' generalizability, we introduce a curriculum learning strategy that progressively increases the difficulty of the text prompts and corresponding image generation tasks. Specifically, early training phases focus on simpler, short-prompt inputs, while later phases address increasingly complex and long-prompt inputs. This adaptive learning regime will be implemented using a teacher-student learning framework, with the teacher model guiding the student model's learning process at each hierarchical projection layer.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with the original hierarchical projection learning framework (Turn 3), as well as ablation studies to isolate the effect of curriculum learning and the teacher-student learning framework.
COST: 15000 GPU-hours (estimating 100% compute usage compared to training a pre-trained CLIP model)
PREDICTION: Expected to further reduce the error rate by 20-30% compared to the original hierarchical projection learning framework, and better handle the complex long-prompt inputs.

PROPOSAL: We investigate sharing a common latent space across different long-prompt text-to-image models, leveraging pre-trained knowledge to improve transfer learning and generate more accurate images. This approach involves training multiple pre-trained models on the same dataset, then aligning their latent spaces using a novel latent space alignment module. TITLE: Adaptive Context Window Extension for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Models
PROPOSAL: We refine the adaptive context window extension for the CLIP model to better capture complex narrative flow in long prompts. By incorporating a sequence-aware mechanism to monitor the output of the attention module, the extended context window will adaptively expand or shrink based on the relevance of the input text. This update allows the model to discard irrelevant information and maintain coherence across longer, more intricate prompts.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with the original adaptive context window extension, as well as ablation studies to isolate the effect of the sequence-aware mechanism.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (estimating 10% compute usage compared to training a pre-trained CLIP model)
PREDICTION: Expected to improve coherence and relevance in long-prompt text-to-image generation by 15-25%, reducing model's shift towards incorrect or distressed components

TITLE: Regularization via Discriminative Image Patch Relevance
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel regularization technique, Image Patch Relevance (IPR), to encourage the model to generate more precise and relevant details in long-prompt text-to-image generation. IPR involves training a discriminative patch selection module to identify relevant image patches, then assigning weights to the input text tokens based on their relevance to these patches. This promotes the model to selectively focus on the most relevant information in the input text, resulting in more accurate and coherent images.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with state-of-the-art text-to-image models, as well as ablation studies to isolate the effect of IPR.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours (estimating 25% compute usage compared to training a pre-trained CLIP model)
PREDICTION: Expected to improve the accuracy of image generation by 15-25% by focusing on relevant details and reducing noise, but may struggle if the IPR module is not effectively trained or if the weights assignment is not well-calibrated.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach to train a model that can adapt to diverse text prompts and learn to generate high-quality images. Our approach involves training a meta-model using a mix of prompt-specific learning objectives and a general text-to-image generation task. This meta-model can then be fine-tuned for specific long-prompt text-to-image generation tasks, leveraging its learned meta-knowledge to quickly adapt to novel prompts.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with state-of-the-art text-to-image models, as well as ablation studies to isolate the effect of the meta-learning mechanism.
COST: 10000 GPU-hours (estimating 50% compute usage compared to training a pre-trained CLIP model)
PREDICTION: Expected to improve the adaptability and flexibility of the model, allowing it to generate high-quality images from unfamiliar long prompts, but may struggle if the meta-model is not effectively trained or if the fine-tuning process takes too long to converge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Vision-Language Alignment via Temporal Consistency
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to align the vision and language modalities in long-prompt text-to-image generation, leveraging temporal consistency across different levels of abstraction. Our approach involves training a Gaussian process to model the temporal dependencies between tokens in the input text, and then using this model to align the corresponding visual representations. This alignment enables the model to learn more robust and coherent vision-language representations, leading to improved image generation quality.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with state-of-the-art text-to-image models, as well as ablation studies to isolate the effect of the temporal consistency approach.
COST: 9000 GPU-hours (estimating 40% compute usage compared to training a pre-trained CLIP model)
PREDICTION: Expected to improve the coherence and robustness of the vision-language representations, leading to better image generation quality, but may struggle if the temporal dependencies are not accurately modeled or if the alignment process is computationally expensive.

This hybrid approach combines the adaptive context window extension with the meta-learning mechanism, further enhancing the model's ability to adapt to diverse text prompts and learn to generate high-quality images. Additionally, the temporal consistency mechanism is used to align the vision and language modalities, ensuring more robust and coherent vision-language representations.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with the original adaptive context window extension, as well as ablation studies to isolate the effect of the hybrid approach.

PREDICTION: Expected to achieve state-of-the-art performance in long-prompt text-to-image generation, with improved adaptability, flexibility, and coherence, but may struggle with computational efficiency and the potential for overfitting.

PROPOSAL 5: Regularization via Discriminative Image Patch Relevance
We propose a novel regularization technique, Image Patch Relevance (IPR), to encourage the model to generate more precise and relevant details in long-prompt text-to-image generation. IPR involves training a discriminative patch selection module to identify relevant image patches, then assigning weights to the input text tokens based on their relevance to these patches. This promotes the model to selectively focus on the most relevant information in the input text, resulting in more accurate and coherent images.

PROPOSAL 6: Meta-Learning for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
We propose a meta-learning approach to train a model that can adapt to diverse text prompts and learn to generate high-quality images. Our approach involves training a meta-model using a mix of prompt-specific learning objectives and a general text-to-image generation task. This meta-model can then be fine-tuned for specific long-prompt text-to-image generation tasks, leveraging its learned meta-knowledge to quickly adapt to novel prompts.

We propose a novel approach to align the vision and language modalities in long-prompt text-to-image generation, leveraging temporal consistency across different levels of abstraction. Our approach involves training a Gaussian process to model the temporal dependencies between tokens in the input text, and then using this model to align the corresponding visual representations. This alignment enables the model to learn more robust and coherent vision-language representations, leading to improved image generation quality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration of Long-Prompt Adapters for Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: 
Develop a collection of adapter modules that can be inserted into the text encoder of a pre-trained T2I model to improve its ability to process long prompts. These adapters will be trained on a combination of the pre-trained model's original training data and synthetic-long-prompt datasets. We explore the impact of using different types of adapters, such as self-attention, position-wise feeding-forward networks, or hierarchical text encoding modules, on the model's performance.
CONTROLS: 
 Baseline: Pre-trained T2I model without adapters, fine-tuned on original training data
    - startPosition: a simple adaptation of short-prompt training data to learn a positional embedding which is later added on to the short input and covered by a position-encoder. )
        Baseline-startSimplePosition): 
        Simple Baseline- baseline-Alternative): Please See Tech Report : one simply selects all of words - surround this with absolute value tokens
    Ablation study: Adapters trained on different subsets of the pre-trained model's training data

COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The adapter modules significantly improve the T2I model's performance on long prompts, with the best-performing adapter achieving a 20-30% increase in F1 score compared to the baseline model. We also observe that using a hierarchical text encoding module yields better results than the other adapter types, but with high variance across different prompts and domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Long-Prompt Fine-Tuning via Iterative Conditional Refining
PROPOSAL: 
Propose a new fine-tuning method for long-prompt text-to-image generation by iteratively refining the input to the pre-trained T2I model. In each iteration, the model takes as input a refined version of the original prompt, modified by a conditioned transformer that iteratively masks and fills in the least confident regions of the input based on the model's previous predictions. The refined prompt is then fed through the pre-trained model to generate a refined image. We study the effect of different refinement architectures and iteration numbers on the final performance.

Combining the two methods further improves the results and is robust to the choice of refinement architecture and iteration numbers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: 
Introduce a meta-learning approach to train a T2I model to adapt to new long prompts by learning a meta-learner that generates an initial policy for image synthesis based on the prompt, and a learner that refines the policy based on the generated image. The meta-learner is trained to learn how to adapt to different prompts and image synthesis tasks, while the learner is trained to refine the policy based on the generated image. We explore different types of meta-learners and learners, and study their performance on long prompts.
CONTROLS: 
 Baseline: standard fine-tuning on original training data
 Baseline-Single Shot): pre-trained model with meta-learner and learner
 Ablation study: removing either the meta-learner or learner

COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The meta-learning approach significantly improves the T2I model's performance on long prompts, especially when the meta-learner and learner are combined. We observe that the meta-learner is able to adapt to new prompts effectively, and the learner is able to refine the policy based on the generated image. This approach is particularly useful when the pre-trained model is paired with the refinement modules from our previous proposals.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Memory-Augmented Reasoning for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: 
Introduce a memory-augmented reasoning module to the T2I model to enable it to reason about the long prompt more effectively. The module consists of a memory bank and a memory reader, which are trained to retrieve relevant information from the memory bank and use it to reason about the prompt. We explore different types of memory banks, such as graph-based memory and slot-based memory, and study their performance on long prompts.
CONTROLS: 
 Baseline: standard fine-tuning on original training data
 Baseline-Memory Augmented): pre-trained model with memory-augmented reasoning module
 Ablation study: removing either the memory bank or the memory reader

COST: 140 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The memory-augmented reasoning module significantly improves the T2I model's performance on long prompts, especially when the memory bank is graph-based. We observe that the module is able to reason about the prompt more effectively, and retrieve relevant information from the memory bank. This approach is particularly useful when combined with the refinement modules from our previous proposals.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: 
Modify the meta-learning approach to use a more advanced meta-learner architecture, such as a transformer-based meta-learner, to better capture the complex relationships between prompts and image synthesis tasks. Additionally, we add a self-supervised pre-training stage to the meta-learning approach, where the model is trained to predict the next token in a sequence of tokens from the prompt, using a mask-based prediction task. This self-supervised pre-training stage is designed to improve the model's ability to reason about the structure and semantics of the prompt.
CONTROLS: 
 Baseline: standard fine-tuning on original training data
 Baseline-Meta Learner-Augmented): pre-trained model with transformer-based meta-learner and self-supervised pre-training stage
 Ablation study: removing either the transformer-based meta-learner or the self-supervised pre-training stage

COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The revised meta-learning approach significantly improves the T2I model's performance on long prompts, especially when the transformer-based meta-learner and self-supervised pre-training stage are combined. We observe that the approach is able to reason about the prompt more effectively, and capture complex relationships between prompts and image synthesis tasks. This revised approach is particularly useful when combined with the refinement modules from our previous proposals.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Prompt Decomposition and Re-Composition for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: 
Introduce a prompt decomposition and re-composition module to the T2I model, which decomposes the long prompt into multiple sub-prompts, generates an image for each sub-prompt, and then re-composes the images into a final image. We explore different types of prompt decomposition and re-composition methods, such as BERT-based decomposition and VAE-based re-composition, and study their performance on long prompts.
CONTROLS: 
 Baseline: standard fine-tuning on original training data
 Baseline- Decomposition-Recomposition): pre-trained model with prompt decomposition and re-composition module
 Ablation study: removing either the prompt decomposition module or the re-composition module

COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The prompt decomposition and re-composition module significantly improves the T2I model's performance on long prompts, especially when the BERT-based decomposition and VAE-based re-composition methods are combined. We observe that the approach is able to generate more coherent and complete images for long prompts. This module is particularly useful when combined with the refinement modules from our previous proposals.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Long-Prompt Fine-Tuning via Iterative Conditional Refining
PROPOSAL: 
Modify the iterative conditional refining method to incorporate the prompt decomposition and re-composition module from our previous proposal. The method will first decompose the long prompt into multiple sub-prompts, and then refine each sub-prompt iteratively using the conditional refining approach. We study the effect of combining the prompt decomposition module with the iterative conditional refining method on the performance of the T2I model on long prompts.
CONTROLS: 
 Baseline: standard fine-tuning on original training data
 Baseline-Incorporating Prompt Decomposition): pre-trained model with prompt decomposition and re-composition module, and iterative conditional refining method
 Ablation study: removing either the prompt decomposition module or the iterative conditional refining method

COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The revised approach significantly improves the T2I model's performance on long prompts, especially when the prompt decomposition module and iterative conditional refining method are combined. We observe that the approach is able to generate more coherent and complete images for long prompts, and the prompt decomposition module helps to reduce the computational cost of the iterative refining method.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hybrid Approach for Long-Prompt Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: 
Introduce a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of multiple methods proposed in this research, including the long-prompt adapters, meta-learning, memory-augmented reasoning, and prompt decomposition and re-composition. The hybrid approach will use a weighted ensemble of multiple models, each trained using a different method, to generate a single image for a long prompt. We study the effect of combining multiple methods on the performance of the T2I model on long prompts.
CONTROLS: 
 Baseline: standard fine-tuning on original training data
 Baseline-Hybrid): pre-trained model with weighted ensemble of multiple models, each trained using a different method
 Ablation study: removing one or more models from the ensemble

COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: 
The hybrid approach significantly improves the T2I model's performance on long prompts, especially when the ensemble includes models trained using meta-learning, memory-augmented reasoning, and prompt decomposition and re-composition. We observe that the hybrid approach is able to generate more coherent and complete images for long prompts, and the weighted ensemble helps to improve the overall performance of the model. This approach is particularly useful when the pre-trained model is paired with the refinement modules from our previous proposals.

propositions.prediction: The revised meta-learning approach significantly improves the T2I model's performance on long prompts, especially when the transformer-based meta-learner and self-supervised pre-training stage are combined.  Baseline-Memory Augmented): pre-trained model with memory-augmented reasoning module

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lower Bound on Long-term Fairness Regularizer
PROPOSAL: We propose to establish a fundamental lower bound on the performance of any online algorithm for the fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs. Specifically, we will show that for an instance of this problem, the optimal dynamic offline benchmark (obtained via linear programming) has a lower bound on its competitive ratio that decreases at least as fast as O(1(/\sqrt{T})) as the horizon T increases. We achieve this result by demonstrating a general lower bound for online learning problems with adversarially selected sequence rewards and a finite memory of adversarially chosen actions.
CONTROLS: We will compare our lower bound against the competitive ratio achieved by several known methods, such as Primedual, REPTILE, and HOPO, under two sources of richness, randomly selected M dimensions or A_t, to verify the finite variants capture the general phenomenon found in our lower bound and inform the study of convergent methods.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our lower bound will indicate challenges in overcoming the O(1(/\sqrt{T})) barrier for achieving finite performance against the dynamic offline optimum, and, specifically, our lower bound regime specializes to the real-world domains of geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and predict that lower bounds may be hard toLt exactly there even when switching costs can be simplified to being equal to the 1-norm.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Finite Competitive Ratio for Easy Instances
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop an efficient algorithm that achieves a finite competitive ratio for a specific, easy instance of the fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs, where the per-round objective functions have a simple dependency on the past actions and the fairness cost decays polynomially with respect to time. Specifically, we provide an efficient-forward-backward method that combines the strengths of existing algorithms, such as federated learning and offline–online gradient proximal augmented Lagrangian algorithm. This provides an initial result on achieving finite competitive ratios for fair online optimization problems.
CONTROLS: We will test the efficiency of our algorithm on small-scale synthetic data, analyzing its performance against the robust Baseline primal-dual approach (PDB) algorithm in such 'easy' instances and extensive ablation studies.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our finite competitive ratio guarantee may motivate researchers to push forward toward more generalizable methods by relaxing regret minimization for the specific, overly restrictive assumptions and competing restrictions, and leveraging new variants such as greedy improved algorithms over simple components to deliver a higher finite competitive ratio.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Switching Cost for Fair Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive approach to reconcile the tension between minimizing the hitting cost, the switching cost, and the long-term fairness cost. Specifically, we introduce a learned adaptive switching cost (LASC) that dynamically adjusts the switching cost based on the agent's past actions, the fairness cost incurred, and the current hitting cost. The LASC is learned using a reinforcement learning framework that balances the trade-off between short-term and long-term performance.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate LASC against two baselines: a fixed switching cost algorithm and a state-of-the-art adaptive algorithm for online optimization without fairness constraints. We will test LASC on a variety of instances in the domains of geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and LLM inference workload serving.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our adaptive approach will outperform the baselines in terms of long-term fairness and overall performance, demonstrating the benefits of dynamically adjusting the switching cost to balance competing objectives. However, the performance of LASC may degrade when the fairness cost is high, indicating a need for further investigation into the interplay between fairness and switching costs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-world Validation for Fair Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We propose a real-world validation of the proposed methods by applying them to public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation in the United States. We will use real-world data on power plants, air quality, and population demographics to evaluate the performance of the three proposed methods: Lower Bound, Finite Competitive Ratio, and Adaptive Switching Cost. We will compare their performance against a baseline approach that ignores fairness considerations and measures their ability to reduce health disparities and improve overall population health outcomes.
CONTROLS: We will use real-world data from the EPA's National Emissions Inventory and the 2010 U.S. Census to evaluate the performance of the proposed methods. We will also compare their performance against a state-of-the-art fairness-aware optimization algorithm for reducing health disparities.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our real-world validation will demonstrate the value of the proposed methods in reducing health disparities and improving overall population health outcomes, highlighting the potential for fair online optimization to make a positive impact on real-world problems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration of Domain-specific Fairness Metrics
PROPOSAL: We propose to explore domain-specific fairness metrics for the geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and LLM inference workload serving domains. In particular, we will investigate the use of metrics such as data locality fairness, latency fairness, and cost fairness, which are relevant to the specific application domains. We will also develop new fairness metrics that capture the unique characteristics of these domains, such as fairness of access to shared resources and fairness of model calibration.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed domain-specific fairness metrics against traditional fairness metrics such as demographic parity and equalized odds. We will also evaluate the impact of these metrics on the performance of the proposed methods, including the Lower Bound, Finite Competitive Ratio, and Adaptive Switching Cost.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our exploration of domain-specific fairness metrics will provide a more nuanced understanding of fairness in the context of online optimization and will enable the development of more effective fairness-aware optimization algorithms specifically tailored to the needs of the geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and LLM inference workload serving domains.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED 5 
PROPOSAL: We refine our exploration of domain-specific fairness metrics by incorporating the geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and LLM inference workload serving domains into the Adaptive Switching Cost for Fair Online Optimization framework. Specifically, we will introduce a new fairness-aware objective function that incorporates the domain-specific fairness metrics and learn an adaptive switching cost that balances the trade-off between fairness and other objective functions.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of the revised Adaptive Switching Cost framework against the original framework and a baseline approach that ignores fairness considerations. We will also compare its performance against state-of-the-art fairness-aware optimization algorithms for reducing health disparities.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our refined exploration of domain-specific fairness metrics will demonstrate the effectiveness of fairness-aware optimization algorithms specifically tailored to the needs of the geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and LLM inference workload serving domains, while maintaining competitive performance in the public health domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Catastrophic Forgetting in Fair Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: We investigate the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting in fair online optimization, where the algorithm forgets previously learned fairness-aware solutions when faced with new and different data distributions. We propose methods to prevent catastrophic forgetting, including iterated retraining, knowledge distillation, and meta-learning. We will evaluate the performance of these methods in the context of fair online optimization for geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and LLM inference workload serving domains.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the proposed methods against a baseline approach that ignores fairness considerations and state-of-the-art fairness-aware optimization algorithms. We will also analyze the effect of catastrophic forgetting on fairness metrics and overall performance.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our investigation of catastrophic forgetting in fair online optimization will highlight the importance of addressing this phenomenon in fairness-aware optimization algorithms, and our proposed methods will provide a foundation for developing more robust and reliable fairness-aware optimization algorithms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation of Fairness-Aware Optimization Algorithms for Real-world Imitation
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the performance of the fairness-aware optimization algorithms developed in this work for real-world imitation, using publicly available datasets and simulated environments. We will assess the algorithms' ability to learn fairness-aware policies and compare their performance against state-of-the-art fairness-aware optimization algorithms.
CONTROLS: We will use datasets from the geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and LLM inference workload serving domains to evaluate the performance of the algorithms. We will also assess the algorithms' robustness to distribution shifts and biases.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our evaluation of fairness-aware optimization algorithms for real-world imitation will highlight the potential of these algorithms for practical applications and provide insights into their strengths and weaknesses, enabling further improvements and refinements in fairness-aware optimization.
