actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing the hardness of long-term fairness regularizers
PROPOSAL: We provide a reduction from the-drifting-cluster-problem, a well-studied online competitive analysis problem, to the fairness-regularized offline optimization problem in the presence of switching costs. This reduction shows that even without adversarial switching costs, offline optimization with a long-term fairness regularizer is NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparison to existing methods focusing on switched-costs-only offline optimization and fairness-regularized methods without switching costs.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (approximating the hardness of the problem does not require extensive computational resources)
PREDICTION: Our reduction proves that achieving sublinear regret or a finite competitive ratio is unlikely for fairness-regularized offline optimization with switching costs. This aligns with prior conjectures in similar settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lower bounds on regret for fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization
PROPOSAL: We analyze the regret of a popular algorithm for fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization, which combines the Delayed-Projection algorithm used in smooth online optimization with an iterative penalty method that incorporates the long-term fairness regularizer. Using standard valuation functions, we show that even with switching costs that grow polynomially with the time horizon T, the regret grows at least as fast as the square root of T when the long-term fairness regularizer is applied.
CONTROLS: Two baselines are considered: the regret without the fairness regularizer and a variant of the algorithm that minimizes the hitting costs and switching costs without considering fairness issues.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (computationally demanding to simulate and analyze the performance over several scenarios and hyperparameters)
PREDICTION: This result provides some of the first theoretical insight into the regret scaling for fairness-regulated smoothed online optimization, offering support for the conjecture that finite regret may be impossible with a long-term fairness regularizer.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Lower bounds on regret for fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization
PROPOSAL: To better understand the regret growth rate in fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization, we extend the previous work by exploring different valuation functions and limits of the long-term fairness regularizer. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Difficulty of the Long-Term Fairness Regularizer
PROPOSAL: Analyze the hardness of the long-term fairness regularizer in various scenarios, using a reduction to a previously known optimization problem, such as the metric regularized online linear optimization.
CONTROLS: Compare with the hardness of classic online optimization problems and switching cost regularized optimization.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The long-term fairness regularizer is likely to be at least as hard as the metric regularized online linear optimization, but possibly harder due to its non Linearity. Failure might occur if the reduction does not generalize to all scenarios or if the problem becomes intractable.

This theoretical proposal sets the foundation for understanding the intrinsic difficulty of the long-term fairness regularizer, which is essential for proposing algorithms with meaningful performance guarantees.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Primal-Dual Framework for Fair Smoothed Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: Develop a primal-dual framework that integrates fairness regularizers into the smoothed online optimization problem, leveraging the strengths of both approaches. Design algorithms that can harness the dual formulation to minimize the long-term fairness cost and then use primal methods to compute the actions.
CONTROLS: Compare with competing algorithms that separately optimize the hitting and switching costs and contrast with baseline methods that do not incorporate fairness regularizers.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed framework should achieve state-of-the-art performance on fairness metrics, with potential trade-offs in hitting and switching cost minimization. Failure might occur if the duality gap is too large, or if the primal and dual components do not synchronize properly.

This theoretical proposal aims to bridge the gap between fairness and smoothed online optimization, providing a novel framework for addressing the challenges of the long-term fairness regularizer.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Evaluation of Practical Algorithms for Fair Smoothed Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: Implement and evaluate several practical algorithms for fair smoothed online optimization with switching costs, using real-world datasets and benchmarks from geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and LLM inference workload serving, public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation. Investigate the trade-offs between different fairness metrics, hitting costs, switching costs, and system performance under various settings.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art algorithms for smoothed online optimization and fairness-constrained online optimization, as well as a baseline that ignores fairness considerations.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Several algorithms will show good performance on the fairness metrics, but may struggle with the hitting and switching costs, especially when the switching costs dominate. A key finding will likely be the need for adaptability and lightweight online updates to achieve good performance on the fairness metrics in various settings.

This experimental proposal aims to assess the effectiveness of practical algorithms for the proposed setting, under a range of real-world scenarios, and identify key challenges and opportunities for future research.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Experimental Evaluation of Practical Algorithms for Fair Smoothed Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: Revise the previous proposal by including a more in-depth investigation of the impact of different fairness metrics on the performance of practical algorithms. Specifically, we will analyze the effect of using different norms (e.g., L1, L2, infinity) and fairness optimization objectives on the algorithms' ability to minimize the hitting and switching costs.
CONTROLS: Keep the comparison with state-of-the-art algorithms and the baseline that ignores fairness considerations.
COST: 50 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that different fairness metrics have varying impacts on the performance of the practical algorithms, with some metrics leading to better hitting cost minimization while others help reduce the switching cost. Failure might occur if the effect of fairness metrics on performance is not significant, or if the choice of fairness metric has a substantial impact on the computational efficiency of the algorithms.

This revised proposal adds an important layer of analysis to the experimental evaluation, providing insights into how to effectively design fairness metrics for the proposed setting.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Experimental Evaluation of Practical Algorithms for Fair Smoothed Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: The previous proposal will be modified to test a variant of the noted LLM inference workload serving and public health costs benchmark, applying different changes in costs of past decisions, due to observed cheap solutions that don't generalize well to experimental domains.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art algorithms for smoothed online optimization and fairness-constrained online optimization as well as a baseline that ignores fairness considerations.
COST: 50 additional GPU-hours

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Experimental Evaluation of Practical Algorithms for Fair Smoothed Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: The proposal will be modified to incorporate data augmentation techniques to improve the robustness of the experimental results. This will involve generating additional synthetic data points that simulate the geo-distributed data center capacity provisioning and LLM inference workload serving, public health costs of air pollution from electricity generation scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art algorithms for smoothed online optimization and fairness-constrained online optimization, as well as a baseline that ignores fairness considerations.
COST: 20 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the incorporation of data augmentation, we expect to see more reliable and robust experimental results that better generalize to real-world scenarios. However, the computational resources required for data generation and processing might impose a challenge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Robustness of Fair Online Optimization against Model Misspecification
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of fair online optimization algorithms to model misspecification, specifically in cases where the hitting costs or fairness metrics are estimated or learned from data.
CONTROLS: Compare with a fair online optimization algorithm using a sensitive and informatively-rich metric that is resistant to model misspecification and contrast with a baseline that does not incorporate fairness.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that fair online optimization algorithms can be sensitive to model misspecification, especially when the hitting costs or fairness metrics are uncertain or inaccurately estimated. However, a well-designed online adaptation mechanism can mitigate this effect and provide robust performance in the presence of model misspecification.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fairness-Constrained Online Learning in Geo-Distributed Data Centers
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate fairness-constrained online learning algorithms specifically tailored for geo-distributed data centers, taking into account the unique challenges and opportunities presented by this setting, such as latency-aware optimization and heterogeneous resource availability.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing online learning algorithms and fairness-constrained optimization methods, as well as a baseline that ignores fairness considerations.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that tailored online learning algorithms can improve fairness and efficiency in geo-distributed data centers, but may require careful balancing of fairness and optimization objectives.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline Replication for Fair Online Optimization with Switching Costs
PROPOSAL: Develop an offline replication method that allows for the efficient evaluation and optimization of fair online optimization algorithms with switching costs, using a dynamic programming approach to solve the offline problem that mimics the online setting.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing offline evaluation methods and online optimization algorithms, as well as a baseline that ignores fairness considerations.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that offline replication can efficiently evaluate and optimize fair online optimization algorithms with switching costs, but may introduce additional computational overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Certifiable Fairness in Online Optimization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the development of methods for certifying the fairness of online optimization algorithms, using techniques such as differential privacy and approximate inference, to provide a high degree of confidence in the absence of bias in the decision-making process.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing fairness certification methods and online optimization algorithms, as well as a baseline that ignores fairness considerations.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that certifiable fairness methods can provide a robust guarantee of fairness in online optimization, but may introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning of parameters.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Survey of Current Image Relighting Methods
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive literature review and survey of recent image relighting techniques, discussing their strengths and limitations, and highlighting potential avenues for future research.
CONTROLS: Survey existing papers on image relighting to draw this overview; compare them using a predefined taxonomy and analyze current trends of the field.
COST: ~10 GPU-hours (mainly human effort)
PREDICTION: This survey will provide a clear overview of the current state-of-the-art and reveal open challenges in the field, but may neglect minor or less well-known works, leading to potential biases in the analysis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating State-of-the-Art Object-Centric Relighting Approaches
PROPOSAL: Implement and compare state-of-the-art object-centric relighting methods on a diverse set of synthetic and real-world images, evaluating their performance in terms of albedo preservation, relighting accuracy, and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Implement selected methods (e.g., [1], [2]), use a protocol to evaluate them on a mixture of images with different objects and scenes (e.g.,, COCO-Stuff, [3]), and compare their performance against 3D print or render overlaid depth or matting maps.
COST: ~100 GPU-hours (to train and evaluate multiple models on various datasets)
PREDICTION: This comparison will showcase the strengths and weaknesses of object-centric methods and highlight their limitations in addressing self-luminous objects and indoor-outdoor scenes. However, the choice of synthetic images might limit the generalizability of the results to real-world cases.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating State-of-the-Art Object-Centric Relighting Approaches
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to also incorporate scene-level relighting methods for comprehensive comparison, and analyze results using metrics such as MIoU (Mean Intersection over Union) for object mask quality and PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio) for image quality.
CONTROLS: Include both state-of-the-art object-centric and scene-level methods, such as neural scene representation methods; train and evaluate them on a diverse set of images (e.g., DDFA ([4]), and evaluate them against the initial set of masks or other scene representation methods.
COST: ~150 GPU-hours (to implement scene-level methods, train and evaluate multiple models)
PREDICTION: This modified comparison will provide a more comprehensive view of current relighting techniques and allow for the identification of the strengths and weaknesses of both object-centric and scene-level approaches. However, it might lead to a larger search space and increased complexity when analyzing the results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Data Generation for Diverse and Complex Scene Illumination
PROPOSAL: Develop a synthetic data generation pipeline to create diverse and controlled images of complex scenes under various lighting conditions, including indoor and outdoor settings, with self-luminous objects and built-in light sources.
CONTROLS: Utilize techniques such as image-based rendering (IBR) and physics-based rendering (PBR) to generate images; combine them with a planner that generates a sequence of viewpoints and calibrates the camera in each view.
COST: ~20 GPU-days (to render and process large dataset of synthetic images)
PREDICTION: This pipeline will provide a vast and controlled dataset of synthetic images for training relighting models, but its quality will significantly impact the performance of downstream models, so effort should be made to make the generated images photorealistic and covering a wide range of possible lighting configurations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating a Graph Neural Network for Intrinsic Image Decomposition and Relighting
PROPOSAL: Design a graph neural network (GNN) model that takes an image as input and outputs its intrinsic components, such as albedo, shading, and surface normal maps, and couple it with a neural rendering engine to relight the image under a user-specified lighting condition.
CONTROLS: Use the synthetic images generated in proposal 3 as training data; compare GNN performance using metrics such as Relighting Performance Score (RPS) and PSNR against state-of-the-art intrinsic image decomposition and relighting methods.
COST: ~200 GPU-hours (to train and evaluate the GNN model)
PREDICTION: This approach has potential for physically plausible relighting and generalization to unseen materials and lighting conditions, but might require large amounts of training data and could be computationally intensive, limiting real-time applications.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Investigating a Graph Neural Network for Intrinsic Image Decomposition and Relighting
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 4 to investigate the benefits of incorporating a learned material prior into the GNN model, allowing it to better capture the material properties and behavior of real-world materials and generalize to unseen conditions.
CONTROLS: Implement a two-stage pipeline where the GNN first learns a compact material representation through a supervised task (pretraining) and then uses this representation to improve intrinsic image decomposition and photorealistic relighting results in the second stage.
COST: ~300 GPU-hours (to implement the two-stage pipeline and fine-tune the material prior)
PREDICTION: This addition should improve the GNN's performance in generalizing to real-world materials and conditions, but might complicate the training process, require more careful hyperparameter tuning, and potentially introduce new error sources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Relighting Graph Neural Networks with Physics-Based Losses
PROPOSAL: Develop physics-based loss functions to supervise the training of the GNN model, allowing it to learn photorealistic and physically plausible relighting effects that respect the laws of physics, such as Fresnel reflections, refractions, and other optical phenomena.
CONTROLS: Implement losses based on physically accurate renderering of the generated relighting results; compare the performance of GNNs trained with physical losses against those trained with ad-hoc losses.
COST: ~100 GPU-hours (to implement and evaluate the physics-based losses)
PREDICTION: This addition should improve the physical realism of the GNN's relighting effects and allow for more accurate simualtion of optical effects, but might require expert knowledge in physics-based rendering, and potentially increase the training time and computational requirements.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Inference of Relighting Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Develop an efficient inference framework for the GNN model, allowing for real-time or near-real-time relighting of images, by optimizing the graph structure, pruning unnecessary edges, and using approximations for the GNN layers.
CONTROLS: Investigate and compare the effectiveness of different complexity-reduction techniques (e.g., architecture pruning, knowledge distillation, dynamic graph updates); evaluate the performance on a range of relighting tasks, including real-time applications.
COST: ~50 GPU-hours (to implement and test the efficient inference framework)
PREDICTION: This optimization should enable the GNN-based relighting approach to be deployed in real-time applications, but may trade off some accuracy for speed, and require careful tuning of the optimization parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Relighting Robustness
PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial training framework to improve the robustness of the GNN-based relighting approach to adversarial perturbations, such as small changes in lighting, occlusions, or object removal, which may affect the model's ability to produce accurate relighting results.
CONTROLS: Implement an adversary that generates perturbations to the input image and evaluates the model's performance under these changes; compare the results to those of the standard GNN model.
COST: ~50 GPU-hours (to implement and test the adversarial training framework)
PREDICTION: This addition should improve the robustness of the GNN-based relighting approach to various types of perturbations, but may increase the training time and computational requirements, and require careful tuning of the adversarial policies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: User Study and Evaluation Metrics
PROPOSAL: Conduct a user study to evaluate the effectiveness and realism of the proposed GNN-based relighting approach in both experimental and real-world scenarios, and develop comprehensive evaluation metrics to assess the quality of relighting results, including subjective metrics (e.g., user ratings, pair-wise comparison) and objective metrics (e.g., ISNR, Relighting Performance Score).

Modify proposal 2 to also incorporate scene-level relighting methods for comprehensive comparison, and analyze results using metrics such as MIoU (Mean Intersection over Union) for object mask quality and PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio) for image quality.
Controls: Include both state-of-the-art object-centric and scene-level methods, such as neural scene representation methods; train and evaluate them on a diverse set of images (e.g., DDFA ([4]), and evaluate them against the initial set of masks or other scene representation methods.

Prediction: This modified comparison will provide a more comprehensive view of current relighting techniques and allow for the identification of the strengths and weaknesses of both object-centric and scene-level approaches. However, it might lead to a larger search space and increased complexity when analyzing the results.

PROPOSAL 3: Synthetic Data Generation for Diverse and Complex Scene Illumination
Develop a synthetic data generation pipeline to create diverse and controlled images of complex scenes under various lighting conditions, including indoor and outdoor settings, with self-luminous objects and built-in light sources.
Controls: Utilize techniques such as image-based rendering (IBR) and physics-based rendering (PBR) to generate images; combine them with a planner that generates a sequence of viewpoints and calibrates the camera in each view.
Estimated cost: ~20 GPU-days (to render and process large dataset of synthetic images)
Prediction: This pipeline will provide a vast and controlled dataset of synthetic images for training relighting models, but its quality will significantly impact the performance of downstream models, so effort should be made to make the generated images photorealistic and covering a wide range of possible lighting configurations.

PROPOSAL 4: Investigating a Graph Neural Network for Intrinsic Image Decomposition and Relighting
Modify proposal 4 to investigate the benefits of incorporating a learned material prior into the GNN model, allowing it to better capture the material properties and behavior of real-world materials and generalize to unseen conditions.
Controls: Implement a two-stage pipeline where the GNN first learns a compact material representation through a supervised task (pretraining) and then uses this representation to improve intrinsic image decomposition and photorealistic relighting results in the second stage.

Prediction: This addition should improve the GNN's performance in generalizing to real-world materials and conditions, but might complicate the training process, require more careful hyperparameter tuning, and potentially introduce new error sources.

PROPOSAL 5: Relighting Graph Neural Networks with Physics-Based Losses
Develop physics-based loss functions to supervise the training of the GNN model, allowing it to learn photorealistic and physically plausible relighting effects that respect the laws of physics, such as Fresnel reflections, refractions, and other optical phenomena.

Estimated cost: ~100 GPU-hours (to implement and evaluate the physics-based losses)

PROPOSAL 6: Efficient Inference of Relighting Graph Neural Networks

PROPOSAL 7: Adversarial Training for Relighting Robustness

Prediction: This addition should improve the robustness of the GNN-based relighting approach to various types of perturbations, but may increase the training time and computational requirements, and require careful tuning of the adversarial policies.

Conduct a user study to evaluate the effectiveness and realism of the proposed GNN-based relighting approach in both experimental and real-world scenarios, and develop comprehensive evaluation metrics to assess the quality of relighting results, including subjective metrics (e.g., user ratings, pair-wise comparison) and objective metrics (e.g., ISNR, Relighting Performance Score).
Controls: Recruit a diverse group of participants (e.g., computer vision experts, artists, designers) to assess the relighting results; compare the results to those of traditional relighting methods.
Estimated cost: ~50 human-days (to conduct the user study)
Prediction: This user study will provide a comprehensive assessment of the proposed approach and help identify areas for improvement, but may require significant coordination with human participants, and subjective ratings may be influenced by individual biases.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physically-Inspired Scene Relighting Benchmark
PROPOSAL: Create a data-driven benchmark consisting of procedurally generated images of synthetic scenes under diverse and complex lighting conditions. This will provide a controlled and extensive dataset for training and evaluating full-image relighting models, and enable pre-training or fine-tuning of a relighting model before applying it to real-world images. We will generate images of indoor and outdoor scenes using the Blenderrender engine, leveraging its physically-based rendering capabilities to create high-quality textures and realistic lighting.
CONTROLS: Include baselines of existing scene-level relighting methods, such as the reference pipeline by Liu et al., and use procedural images similar to the synthesia dataset to measure the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed benchmark will enable substantial improvement in the performance and robustness of full-image relighting models, and facilitate the evaluation of novel methods on challenging scenarios not covered by current datasets. However, creating a seamless user interface to select specific scene instances may lead to some extra work in preparatory setup if the software available for task is initialized with  very low configuration.

Turn 2: 
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-View Training for Full-Image Relighting
PROPOSAL: Introduce a multi-view training framework for full-image relighting, where a model is trained to relight a scene from multiple viewpoints. By incorporating multiple views, the model can learn to respect key light transport principles, including diffuse/specular separation and accurate modeling of participating media, leading to more physically plausible results.
CONTROLS: Compare baseline methods trained on a single view with the multi-view approach on the newly created benchmark and existing datasets, e.g., the inverse rendering dataset.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-view training framework will result in better preservation of material appearance, shading, and highlights in relit scenes, outperforming baseline methods

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Constrained Network (PCN) for Relighting
PROPOSAL: Design a novel neural network architecture, Physics-Constrained Network (PCN), specifically tailored for full-image relighting. PCN incorporates physically-inspired layers that enforce key light transport principles, such as the rendering equation, to ensure physically plausible results. This is achieved through the introduction of constraints that limit the range of potential lighting solutions and thus make sure the output located within realizable possibilities.
CONTROLS: Train PCN on the Physically-Inspired Scene Relighting Benchmark and evaluate it on this data and on existing intrinsic image decomposition and relighting tasks. Compare PCN to the multi-view training approach and other state-of-the-art methods on the same tasks.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PCN will demonstrate superior performance in terms of lighting plausibility, material appearance preservation, and varied scene composition generalization compared to existing state-of-the-art methods; however, potential failing points may arise when real world challenges like lighting outliers interfere on slightest imperfections from learned templates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learnable Light Field Constraints for Precise Relighting
PROPOSAL: Introduce learnable constraints on the light field that enable precise control over the direction and intensity of the new lighting while maintaining a consistent background. This will be achieved by learning to model the complex interactions between objects and light, allowing the model to better replicate the behavior of light in the scene. These constraints can be incorporated into the PCN architecture from Turn 2.
CONTROLS: Evaluate this approach on challenging scenes with complex light interactions and compare it to existing data-driven methods that lack precise lighting control. Train and test PCN with and without these learnable light field constraints on various relighting tasks, including scenes with self-luminous objects and varying background content.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating learnable light field constraints, PCN will demonstrate improved precision and literature bearing on accurate formulation & outcomes analysis over existing approaches, but may fail if insufficient training data cause it overfit.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Learnable Light Field Constraints for Precise Relighting
PROPOSAL: Refine the learnable light field constraints to enable the separation of the light field into a solar (ambient, diffuse and sky-lit) component and a non-solar component which combines (directional diffuse, diffuse-scattered & homogeneous components). This separation will be guided by models such as the BRDF (Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function) that show distinct scatters patterns over cells of limited illuminated scenario groups. To reduce constraints sources on inputs range we leverage geometry of illuminating mixes factors whose range is known.
CONTROLS: Compare performance with existing data-driven methods that separate these components in the relighting process, and analyze the quality of results obtained with this separation in various scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Material Inference for Improved Relighting
PROPOSAL: Develop a self-supervised method for inferring the material properties of the scene's objects from a single unrelit image. This will enable the model to better handle a wide range of materials and improve robustness to unseen material types. The inferred material properties will be then used to refine the relighting results.
CONTROLS: Evaluate this method on various relighting tasks, including scenes with a mix of materials and compare it to existing methods that require ground-truth material properties.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The self-supervised material inference method will improve the quality of relighting results on scenes with varied materials and increase the robustness of the model to unseen materials. However, it might not perform well on highly specular or transparent materials where material properties inference is less clear.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Physics-Constrained Network (PCN) for Relighting
PROPOSAL: Refine the PCN architecture by integrating the learnable light field constraints and self-supervised material inference method. This will enable the model to better respect key light transport principles, handle a wide range of materials, and improve robustness to unseen material types. The updated PCN will be trained on the Physically-Inspired Scene Relighting Benchmark and evaluated on various relighting tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the updated PCN to existing state-of-the-art methods on the same tasks and analyze the quality of results obtained with this integration.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The integration of learnable light field constraints and self-supervised material inference will bring significant improvements in the quality and robustness of relighting results, making PCN a strong competitor to existing methods. However, the increased complexity of the model might lead to overfitting if not properlyRegularised

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Learnable Light Field Constraints for Precise Relighting
PROPOSAL: Refine the learnable light field constraints to incorporate the self-supervised material inference method, enabling the model to adapt the light field constraints based on the inferred material properties. This will allow the model to better respect key light transport principles and handle a wide range of materials.
CONTROLS: Evaluate this refined method on various relighting tasks, including scenes with a mix of materials, and compare it to existing methods that require ground-truth material properties.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refinement of the learnable light field constraints will improve the quality of relighting results on scenes with varied materials and increase the robustness of the model to unseen materials. However, it might be challenging to balance the trade-off between the complexity of the constraints and the robustness of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Consistency for Real-World Relighting
PROPOSAL: Introduce a temporal consistency loss function to the PCN architecture, which favors predictions with smooth and temporally coherent lighting changes. This will enable the model to better handle real-world images with dynamic lighting conditions and improve the overall plausibility of relighting results.
CONTROLS: Evaluate this approach on real-world relighting benchmarks, such as indoor and outdoor scenes with dynamic lighting, and compare it to existing methods that lack temporal consistency.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The introduction of temporal consistency will improve the robustness and plausibility of relighting results on real-world scenes with dynamic lighting, but might require careful tuning of the temporal consistency loss function to avoid over-smoothing the lighting changes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Relighting Datasets for Comprehensive Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Create comprehensive real-world relighting datasets that demonstrate a wide range of challenging scenarios, including dynamic lighting, self-luminous objects, and complex material interactions. These datasets will be used to thoroughly evaluate the performance and robustness of the PCN architecture and its variants on real-world relighting tasks.
CONTROLS: Evaluate PCN on each dataset and compare its performance to existing state-of-the-art methods on the same tasks.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The real-world relighting datasets will provide a rigorous and comprehensive evaluation framework for PCN and its variants, enabling the identification of strengths and limitations of the approach. However, the creation of high-quality datasets with diverse and challenging scenarios will require significant resources and expertise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implementation and Deployment of PCN for Real-World Relighting Applications
PROPOSAL: Develop a user-friendly and efficient implementation of PCN that can be easily integrated into real-world relighting applications, such as computer-aided design (CAD), augmented reality (AR), and digital content creation (DCC) software. This will enable the widespread adoption of PCN in various industries and applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Width on Gradient Descent Convergence in Deep Networks
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to analyze the effect of network width on the convergence of gradient descent (GD) for deep ReLU networks. We will train network models with varying widths (e.g., $m = 100, 1000, 10000$) on a synthetic dataset generated by sampling from a separable Gaussian distribution with a fixed margin $\gamma$. We will use the logistic loss as the objective function and monitor the convergence of GD.
CONTROLS: We will compare the convergence of GD for the different widths with the convergence of a corresponding SGD algorithm with a fixed step size and a batch size of 128.
COST: Approximately 5000 GPU-hours, broken down into 1000 hours for each width.
PREDICTION: We expect to see faster convergence of GD for wider networks, with the rate of convergence improving with increasing width. However, we may observe that the optimal width is achieved at a finite value (e.g., $m = 1000$), beyond which the rate of convergence does not improve, indicating a potential bottle-neck in the width spectrum.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tighter Bounds via Empirical Risk Minimization
PROPOSAL: We establish a theoretical result showing that for fully connected deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent with the logistic loss on binary classification data that are NTK-separable with margin $\gamma$, the excess risk can be bounded by $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^{-2} \sqrt{\mathbf{y}^\top(\mathbf{H}^\infty)^{-1}\mathbf{y}/m})$, where $m$ is the width of the network, using an empirical risk minimization (ERM) argument. This result improves upon existing bounds and suggests that a logarithmic width may be sufficient for achieving a minimal risk.
CONTROLS: We compare our result to existing bounds for deep ReLU networks, including the recent result of $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^{-2} e^{O(L)} \sqrt{\mathbf{y}^\top(\mathbf{H}^\infty)^{-1}\mathbf{y}/m})$.
COST: 0 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our bound should be tighter than existing results for deep ReLU networks, particularly for small to moderate depths $L$. However, its tightness may degrade for very deep networks as the exponential term $e^{O(L)}$ becomes dominant.

ACTION: REVISE 2

PROPOSAL: We establish a theoretical result showing that for fully connected deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent with the logistic loss on binary classification data that are NTK-separable with margin $\gamma$, the excess risk can be bounded by $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^{-2} \sqrt{\mathbf{y}^\top(\mathbf{H}^\infty)^{-1}\mathbf{y}/m})$, where $m$ is the width of the network, using an empirical risk minimization (ERM) argument. To strengthen this result, we will also analyze the case where the network is trained with a hinge loss, which is often used in practice.
CONTROLS: We compare our result to existing bounds for deep ReLU networks and also investigate the effect of hinge loss on the generalization performance.
COST: 0 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our bound should be tighter than existing results for deep ReLU networks, particularly for small to moderate depths $L$. Additionally, we expect to see a similar bound for the hinge loss, indicating that our result is robust to the choice of loss function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Neural Tangent Kernel with Finite Width Corrections
PROPOSAL: We investigate the neural tangent kernel (NTK) with finite width corrections to better understand the behavior of deep ReLU networks. Specifically, we analyze the effect of finite width on the spectrum of the NTK, and we derive a closed-form expression for the correction terms. Using this corrected NTK, we derive new bounds for the generalization error of deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent.
CONTROLS: We compare our bounds to existing results and also analyze the effect of the correction terms on the generalization performance.
COST: Approximately 2000 GPU-hours, broken down into 1000 hours for the corrected NTK and 1000 hours for the analysis of the generalization error.
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved bounds for the generalization error, taking into account the finite width corrections. However, we may observe that the correction terms can be challenging to compute in practice, particularly for large networks.

TITLE: Analyzing the Neural Tangent Kernel with Finite Width Corrections
PROPOSAL: We investigate the neural tangent kernel (NTK) with finite width corrections to better understand the behavior of deep ReLU networks. Specifically, we analyze the effect of finite width on the spectrum of the NTK, and we derive a closed-form expression for the correction terms. Using this corrected NTK, we derive new bounds for the generalization error of deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent. We also investigate the effect of the correction terms on the Lipschitz stability of the network.
CONTROLS: We compare our bounds to existing results and also analyze the effect of the correction terms on the generalization performance, including the stability of the network to adversarial perturbations.
COST: Approximately 2000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved bounds for the generalization error, taking into account the finite width corrections. Additionally, we expect to see that the correction terms have a significant impact on the Lipschitz stability of the network, but may also observe that the stability analysis is challenging to compute in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: An Experimental Study of Gradient Descent with Slowly Increasing Learning Rate
PROPOSAL: We experimentally study the effect of using a slowly increasing learning rate for gradient descent on deep ReLU networks. Specifically, we train networks with different widths and depths, and we vary the learning rate schedule to see if it improves generalization performance.
CONTROLS: We compare the learning curves of the networks trained with a constant learning rate, a linearly increasing learning rate, and a learning rate that decreases according to the inverse square root of the iteration number.
COST: Approximately 15000 GPU-hours, broken down into 5000 hours for each learning rate schedule.
PREDICTION: We expect to see that a slowly increasing learning rate can improve generalization performance, particularly for wide and deep networks, but may also observe that the learning rate schedule can interact with the width and depth of the network in a non-trivial way.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Stability Analysis of Deep ReLU Networks via Gradient Flow
PROPOSAL: We analyze the stability of deep ReLU networks via a gradient flow approach. Specifically, we derive a differential equation that describes the evolution of the network's parameters during training, and we use this equation to study the stability of the neural tangent kernel.
CONTROLS: We compare our stability analysis to existing results and also investigate the effect of the ReLU activation function on the stability of the network.
COST: Approximately 5000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the gradient flow approach provides new insights into the stability of deep ReLU networks, particularly in the early stages of training. However, we may also observe that the stability analysis becomes increasingly challenging for large networks and long training times.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: A Stability Analysis of Deep ReLU Networks via Gradient Flow
PROPOSAL: We analyze the stability of deep ReLU networks via a gradient flow approach. Specifically, we derive a differential equation that describes the evolution of the network's parameters during training, and we use this equation to study the stability of the neural tangent kernel. We also investigate the effect of regularization on the stability of the network.
CONTROLS: We compare our stability analysis to existing results and also investigate the effect of different regularization techniques on the stability of the network, including weight decay, dropout, and early stopping.
COST: Approximately 5000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to see that regularization can significantly improve the stability of deep ReLU networks, particularly for networks with small widths. However, we may also observe that the stability analysis becomes increasingly challenging for large networks and long training times, and that the choice of regularization technique can have a significant impact on the stability of the network.

TITLE: Exponentially Improved Generalization Bounds via a New Activation Function
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new activation function that is designed to improve the generalization performance of deep ReLU networks. Specifically, we introduce an activation function that is based on a mixture of ReLU and a new function that is inspired by the arctangent function. We analyze the properties of this new activation function and show that it leads to exponentially improved generalization bounds compared to traditional ReLU networks.
CONTROLS: We compare the generalization performance of networks with the new activation function to networks with traditional ReLU and other state-of-the-art activation functions.
COST: Approximately 10000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the new activation function leads to significant improvements in generalization performance, particularly for networks with large widths and depths. However, we may also observe that the new activation function can be computationally challenging and may require significant modifications to existing network architectures.

TITLE: NTK Gradient Descent for Deep ReLU Networks: Polynomial Width Suffices for Separable Data
PROPOSAL: Establish an average-case risk bound of $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ for fully connected deep ReLU networks, trained by gradient descent with the logistic loss on synthetic NTK-separable data with margin $\gamma$. By modifying the proof technique from the existing result for two-layer networks, we relax the 1-homogeneity assumption for deep ReLU networks using a localized version of the Gram matrix, allowing width $m=\mathrm{poly}(L,n,1/\gamma^2)$ to suffice.
CONTROLS: NTK Gradient Descent on two-layer networks with a logarithmic width, relaxed Rademacher complexity bounds, and covering number analyses with exponential depth dependence.
COST: 50 GPU-hours

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Low-Width Neural Tangent Kernel Bounds for Deep ReLU Networks
PROPOSAL: We aim to derive improved neural tangent kernel (NTK) bounds for deep ReLU networks with widths polynomial in the depth $L$, the sample size $n$, and the reciprocal of the smallest NTK eigenvalue $\lambda_0^{-1}$.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to existing bounds such as those of Allen-Zhu and Li ($\widetilde{O}(L^2 m n \log{\frac{n}{L}} / \lambda^2_0)$) and Bietti et al. ($\widetilde{O}(m^2 L^{cL}) / \lambda^2_0$).
COST: 10 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: If we can show that the network's NTK Gram matrix remains well-conditioned beneath the current polynomial-width barrier, then we should be able to obtain significantly improved bounds that scale more favorably with $n$, $L$, and $1/\lambda_0$. The major challenge will be establishing and upper-bounding the "conditioning" of the Gram matrix in a way that bypasses the existing exponential-depth dependence. We expect our results to potentially be a key stepping-stone towards achieving minimax optimal generalization rates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Algorithmic Stability Analyses for Deep ReLU Networks via Smoothing
PROPOSAL: We will develop a framework to apply existing algorithmic stability techniques to deep ReLU networks by modifying the activation function using Rényi entropy regularization, effectively introducing smoothness to the network's loss surface while preserving its NTK-induced properties.
CONTROLS: We will validate our results against the existing analysis of shallow ReLU networks with Rényi entropy regularization and compare with the state-of-the-art exponential-depth dependence bounds.
COST: 20 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: To achieve this, we require development of a mechanism for transferring the stability bounds from smooth activations to non-smooth ReLU units while retaining the same constant factors and improved over-parameterization requirements as the existing smooth case. If successful, our results will provide strong evidence that NTK-induced properties continue to dominate in the deep regime even in the presence of non-smooth activation functions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Algorithmic Stability Analyses for Deep ReLU Networks via Smoothing
PROPOSAL: We will develop and analyze a variant of the Rényi entropy regularization approach by combining it with a Hessian-based regularization term, which will allow us to bypass the need for explicit smoothness assumptions on the activation function. This will enable us to apply algorithmic stability analysis to deep ReLU networks while retaining the NTK-induced properties and offering improved over-parameterization requirements.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with the existing stability bounds for deep ReLU networks without explicit regularization and against the low-width NTK bounds developed in proposal 1.
COST: 25 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The combined approach is expected to provide a middle ground between the low-width NTK bounds and the exponentially depth-dependent stability bounds, yielding an improvement in generalization risk rates for moderately wide networks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Algorithmic Stability Analyses for Deep ReLU Networks via Hessian-based Regularization
PROPOSAL: We will develop and analyze a variant of the Rényi entropy regularization approach by combining it with a Hessian-based regularization term, which will allow us to bypass the need for explicit smoothness assumptions on the activation function. This will enable us to apply algorithmic stability analysis to deep ReLU networks while retaining the NTK-induced properties and offering improved over-parameterization requirements.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with the existing stability bounds for deep ReLU networks without explicit regularization and against the low-width NTK bounds developed in proposal 1.
COST: 25 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The combined approach is expected to provide a middle ground between the low-width NTK bounds and the exponentially depth-dependent stability bounds, yielding an improvement in generalization risk rates for moderately wide networks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Nearest-Neighbor Bound for NTK-Separable Data
PROPOSAL: We aim to establish a nearest-neighbor type bound for the generalization error of deep ReLU networks trained on NTK-separable data, with a guarantee of order $1/(n \gamma^2)$. We will use the nearest neighbor approach to directly analyze the behavior of gradient descent on the NTK kernel, exploiting its separability to derive a simple and efficient upper bound on the generalization risk.
CONTROLS: We will validate our results against the existing analysis of two-layer ReLU networks and compare with the state-of-the-art exponential-depth dependence bounds.
COST: 15 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The nearest neighbor bound is expected to eliminate the polynomial-depth dependence present in existing results and possibly match or even improve the minimax optimal rate of $1/(n \gamma^2)$.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling Up the NTK: Efficient Computation and Storage of the Neural Tangent Kernel
PROPOSAL: We will develop an efficient algorithm for computing and storing the neural tangent kernel Gram matrix for deep ReLU networks, which is a crucial step in obtaining generalization error bounds using the NTK. Our approach will exploit the sparse structure of the Gram matrix to reduce computation and memory requirements, making it feasible to study larger networks and obtain tighter bounds.
CONTROLS: We will compare our implementation with existing methods and validate its accuracy on synthetic data.
COST: 50 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The ability to efficiently compute and store the NTK Gram matrix will be a crucial tool for further research in this area, enabling us to explore larger network widths and depths, and providing a foundation for future work on more complex neural network architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Numerical Experiments on the Role of Over-Parameterization in Generalization
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a systematic numerical study to investigate the effect of over-parameterization on the generalization performance of deep ReLU networks, using the efficient NTK computation and storage algorithm developed in proposal 4. We will explore different network widths, depths, and training procedures to shed light on the relationship between over-parameterization and generalization.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with existing theoretical bounds and analyze the empirical trade-offs between network capacity and overfitting.
COST: 100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The numerical experiments are expected to provide valuable insights into the role of over-parameterization in generalization, potentially revealing new trade-offs or constraints that can inform the design of more robust and efficient neural networks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bounded Eigenvalue Implies Improved Generalization
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the relationship between the eigenvalues of the NTK Gram matrix and the generalization performance of deep ReLU networks. We will prove a novel result asserting that bounded eigenvalues lead to improved generalization bounds, and use this insight to derive new bounds on the generalization error of deep networks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with existing_bounds on the generalization performance of deep networks and analyze the implications of our results for network design and optimization.
COST: 30 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The connection between eigenvalues and generalization is expected to provide new insights into the properties of deep neural networks, potentially leading to more robust and efficient optimization algorithms and network architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Variational Analysis of the Neural Tangent Kernel
PROPOSAL: We will develop a variational framework to analyze the neural tangent kernel (NTK) and derive new bounds on its eigenvalues. Our approach will involve studying the NTK as a variational problem, and using tools from variational analysis to derive tight bounds on its eigenvalues.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with existing bounds on the generalization performance of deep networks and analyze the implications of our results for network design and optimization.
COST: 40 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The variational analysis of the NTK is expected to provide new insights into the properties of deep neural networks, potentially leading to more robust and efficient optimization algorithms and network architectures.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Progress on a Nearest-Neighbor Bound for NTK-Separable Data
PROPOSAL: We will build upon the previous proposal 3, A Nearest-Neighbor Bound for NTK-Separable Data, and further develop the analysis to obtain a tighter bound on the generalization error of deep ReLU networks trained on NTK-separable data. We will use the variational framework developed in proposal 7 to derive a more accurate estimate of the NTK eigenvalues, which will be used to obtain the improved generalization bound.
CONTROLS: We will validate our results against the existing analysis of two-layer ReLU networks and compare with the state-of-the-art exponential-depth dependence bounds.
COST: 25 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The more accurate estimate of the NTK eigenvalues will lead to a tighter generalization bound, which may bridge the gap between the existing exponential-depth dependence bounds and the optimal rate of $1/(n \gamma^2)$.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Establishment of Baseline: Bridge Matching
PROPOSAL: Train and evaluate a bridge matching model on a synthetic dataset that simulates branching cell trajectories, to serve as a baseline for comparison with future proposals. Use a differential equation-based stochastic bridge model, with a squared-Euclidean cost for entropic optimal transport. Evaluate on metrics such as average Kullback-Leibler divergence to the underlying cell states, and visually inspect the predicted trajectories for fidelity to the ground truth.
CONTROLS: Train a denoising diffusion model on the same dataset and evaluate it on the same metrics, as a baseline for a path-based method.
COST: 1 GPU-hour
PREDICTION: Bridge matching should reliably capture unimodal transitions, but struggle to model branching dynamics and predict accurate terminal state shares due to mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weak Bridge Matching with time-dependent transition probability
PROPOSAL: Modify the bridge matching model to include a time-dependent transition probability, which can capture the diffusion and growth patterns in branching cell trajectories. Use a piecewise constant transition probability and jointly learn its values along with the drift and diffusion fields. This modification aims to relax the assumption of a time-independent transition probability in the baseline bridge matching approach.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on the same synthetic dataset as the baseline, with a comparison to the baseline's performance under the same hyperparameters.
COST: 5 GPU-hours (training time dependent transition probability)
PREDICTION: The new model should improve upon the baseline by better capturing the branching dynamics, but may suffer from increased overfitting due to the learned time-dependent transition probability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unbalanced Transport with Non-Conservative Divergence
PROPOSAL: Explore unbalanced transport models that allow for non-conservative divergence of mass, enabling the representation of growth and destruction of cells in branching cell trajectories. Implement a sink/source term in the transport equation, allowing for the creation or destruction of mass along the transport map. Evaluate on synthetic cell trajectory datasets and compare to both the baseline and weak bridge matching models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the capacity and failure modes of standard Schrödinger bridge matching to branched dynamics in cell fate bifurcation
PROPOSAL: Train and test standard Schrödinger bridge matching models on two cell fate bifurcation datasets: a simulation-based dataset with controlled branching dynamics and a real-world single-cell RNA-seq dataset based on gene knockout experiments in human T-lymphocytes. Compare bridge matching performance on accuracy of terminal population composition, trajectory smoothness, and existence of a single energy minimizer across all branching levels (0-6 generations) measured by metrics such as expected cumulative discrepancy (ECD) per trajectory and Shilov norm.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against standard baseline Schrödinger bridge matching with a uniform reference process, and ablating model capacity by selecting significantly reduced numbers of mixtures of conditional stochastic bridges to describe all possible branching scenarios under a threshold K-L divergence.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Standard Schrödinger bridge matching will fail to capture accurately complex branched dynamics, particularly enlarging the terminal population (type I branch discontinuity), undershooting highest modes (type II failure), or catastrophically diverging early as losses fail to balance branching types during learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness and interpolation of generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations to branched dynamics under non-linear state costs
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether adding a non-linear state cost (potential energy function) to the generalized Schrödinger bridge formulation can improve its robustness (adequate performance on highly branched trajectories) and interpolation capabilities ( ability to understand the order and sequence of branching events) when faced with branching dynamics. Specifically, use a learned potential energy function to modify the Schrödinger bridge objective, and test on our controlled simulated and real-world cell fate bifurcation datasets. Assess performance on metrics such as ECD per trajectory, Shilov norm of reconstructed population dynamics, and generative capacity to closely match observation of branching dynamics in labeled trajectories.
CONTROLS: Compare against performance of standard baselines (Schrödinger bridge matching and generalized Schrödinger bridge without non-linear costs), as well as ablated models where non-linear costs are artificially limited to small ranges/set to zero to quantify effect of added complexity on learning accuracy.
COST: 7000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improved interpolation results and better long-term dynamics recovery can be obtained with non-linear costs but at increased computational complexity. The benefits will be more pronounced in complex branching scenarios with multiple types of bifurcations, but optimal cost expressions that describe simulation/measured data consistently will remain uncertain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: BRAIN: A Model for Branching Schrödinger Bridges
PROPOSAL: Implement a new neural network architecture, BRAIN (Branching RNA dynamics Inference with Adaptive parameterization for Networks), that learns a set of energy-minimizing stochastic bridges representing the divergence of the population into multiple terminal states. BRAIN uses an adversarial loss to compute a time-dependent mass distribution over branches and an amplitude-based attention mechanism to capture branching dynamics.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard Schrödinger bridge matching, single-particle flow matching, and flow-based generative models trained without branching dynamics. Use ablations to assess the contributions of the adversarial loss, amplitude-based attention, and waveform inversion.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: BRAIN outperforms existing approaches in reproducing branching dynamics and capturing the time-dependent mass distribution over branches. However, it may struggle with noisy or low-resolution reference distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Informative Prior for Branched Schrödinger Bridges
PROPOSAL: Introduce a prior over stochastic bridges optimized for early branching detection. This prior uses a non-parametric Gaussian process model representing the density of branching times across the population, allowing for an informative sampling of possible branching points. The prior will be formulated under the regime of asymptotic regime - infinitely many data points and large number of time steps.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of BRAIN trained without the informative prior, a prior with a non-informative uniform distribution, and a prior learned via an adversarial objective that represents competing predictions for branching times. Evaluate on the datasets of cell perturbation responses and single-cell RNA-seq during cell differentiation.
COST: 5 GPU-hours (per iteration, approx. 20 iterations total)
PREDICTION: The informative prior improves the detection of branching events in the population, allowing BRAIN to earlier and more accurately capture diverse terminal states and mass redistribution among branches.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Visual Perception Models for Graph Structural Understanding
PROPOSAL: Train and evaluate various visual perception models (e.g., convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and graph neural networks with image-like representations, such as graph-based autoencoders) on graph drawing datasets, exploring their ability to learn representations that capture global graph structure.
CONTROLS: Compare to traditional GNNs and message-passing variants on graph classification and node classification tasks using standard benchmarks like MolHIV and IMDB-BINARY; ablate and control for graph layout representation and visualization styles used in the training data; compare different model architectures for image-like graph representation.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Visual perception models may exhibit competitive performance on graph structure understanding tasks, highlighting the potential of visually-inspired approaches; performance could degrade when dealing with complex or disordered graph structures, where message-passing GNNs might be more effective.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Designing a Synthetic Graph Benchmark for Holistic Graph Understanding
PROPOSAL: Develop a large-scale, synthetic graph dataset with controlled and varied levels of global structure and local noise, designed to challenge graph learning models in their ability to perceive and abstract graph patterns at multiple scales.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of visual perception models, GNNs, and various baseline models on this new benchmark, focusing on their ability to recover global graph properties and recognize structural patterns despite varying scales and contexts; also compare visualization techniques for inspecting model outputs and graph features.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The dataset will reveal performance disparities among different models, with visual perception models outperforming GNNs in certain cases; the benchmark will be used as a reference to further investigate the role of graph structure and data quality in graph learning.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Visual Perception Models for Graph Structural Understanding
PROPOSAL: Refine the previous proposal by exploring different graph drawing styles and layouts in the training data, evaluating how various representation learning techniques (e.g., graph-based autoencoders, Wasserstein Autoencoders) work in conjunction with visual perception models, and assessing the impact of feature extraction and graph topology on model performance.
CONTROLS: Maintain comparison to traditional GNNs and message-passing variants; add control experiments to evaluate impact of pre-trained image models, exploration-exploitation strategies, and attention-based visual representation learning.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refinement will expose interactions between graph representation learning and visual perception, with potential implications for how models perceive and analyze graph structures.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Analyzing Human Perception of Graphs Through Virtual Sketching Paradigms
PROPOSAL: Develop a virtual sketching interface where human subjects can create, modify, and evaluate graph drawings; collect and analyze data on how humans recognize and describe global graph properties, relationships, and patterns across varying scales and contexts.
CONTROLS: Use the collected data to train visual perception models to mimic human graph perception; evaluate both human accuracy and model performance on graph classification, node classification, and graph analysis tasks.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (human annotation and subject survey phase)
PREDICTION: The human perception data will reveal underlying patterns and biases in how people recognize graph structures, providing insights into cognitive graph representations and highlighting potential avenues for model improvement in graph learning tasks.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Higher-Level Cognition in Graph Understanding
PROPOSAL: Develop a graph understanding task that requires models to adapt to novel and unseen graph properties, relationships, or contexts, simulating real-world scenarios where graph learning models must generalize across multiple domains and scales.
CONTROLS: Design a set of graph transformation rules to modify and extend original graph structures, representing imperfections, real-world processes, or human variations; compare the ability of visual perception models, GNNs, and traditional architectures to generalize and learn from task-level feedback and guidance on graph customization and evolution.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The experiments will highlight a gap in current models' abilities to generalize and reason about graph structures across broad contexts and scales, underlining the need for more effective graph-level inductive biases and context-aware representations to achieve human-like graph understanding.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Designing a Synthetic Graph Benchmark for Holistic Graph Understanding
PROPOSAL: Enhance the synthetic graph dataset by incorporating the insights gained from the human perception study, including real-world graph variations, imperfections, and patterns of adaptation; develop a model that not only learns global graph structure but also learns to reason and adapt to different graph contexts and scales, guided by the principles of human graph perception and cognition.
CONTROLS: Design a series of systematic perturbations and transformations of the graph structure to evaluate the flexibility and robustness of visual perception models and traditional architectures; extend the benchmark to cover tasks that simulate real-world applications of graph learning, such as network modification, expansion and evolution.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised benchmark will provide a more comprehensive evaluation of a model's ability to understand and reason about graph structures across varying contexts and scales, better reflecting human intuition and revealing potential avenues for further model development.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Visualizing Graph Representations and Model Decisions
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of visualization tools to inspect and understand the representations learned by visual perception models, traditional GNNs, and baseline architectures on the revised synthetic graph benchmark; provide interactive visualizations and intuitive explanations to facilitate the analysis of graph representations, model decisions, and performance metrics.
CONTROLS: Apply established visualization techniques and new graph-based visual analytics methods to reveal structural patterns in graph representations, highlighting differences between models and their limitations; compare visual explanations with model performance metrics and other quantitative measures.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (for collecting visualization data) + 50 hours (for developing visualization tools)
PREDICTION: The visualizations will provide actionable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of various graph learning models, facilitating model selection, design, and improvement, as well as highlighting areas for further research on visualizing and understanding graph representations.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Analyzing Human Perception of Graphs Through Virtual Sketching Paradigms
PROPOSAL: Further develop and refine the virtual sketching interface and data collection pipeline to make it more accessible, user-friendly, and representative of human graph perception; gather more diverse and comprehensive data on human graph understanding, incorporating more graph types, sizes, and contexts, as well as exploring the role of expertise, experience, and demographic factors in graph perception.
CONTROLS: Integrate findings from the proposed revisions with previous results on visual perception models, providing a more comprehensive understanding of human and model graph perception; extend the comparison to real-world datasets and applications, highlighting practical implications for model development and data quality.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (for refining the interface and collecting new data) + 50 hours (for integrating findings and revising previous results)
PREDICTION: The updated study will offer a more nuanced and inclusive portrayal of human graph perception and its implications for AI model development, highlighting the importance of diverse and representative datasets and the value of incorporating human understanding in model design.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Bridging Human and Algorithmic Graph Perception through Multi-Modal Alignment
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a hybrid model that combines the strengths of human perception and algorithmic processing, enabling a multi-modal alignment of graph representations between humans and AI models; this is achieved by generating graph visualizations that capture human perception patterns, and then training a graph neural network to learn the aligned representations.
CONTROLS: Compare the aligned model with traditional GNNs and visual perception models on various graph understanding tasks; evaluate the transferability of the aligned model to different domains and graph structures.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed model will exhibit enhanced graph understanding capabilities, showcasing the potential benefits of combining human-centric and AI-driven approaches; results will also shed light on the challenges of bridging the gap between human intuition and algorithmic complexity.

CONTROLS: Evaluate the refined model on a range of graph understanding tasks, including graph classification, node classification, and graph analysis, and compare its performance to both traditional GNNs and the previously developed aligned model.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised model will demonstrate enhanced performance on graph understanding tasks, with the ability to learn and reason about graph structures in a more human-like manner, providing a final answer to the original research questions.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Vision-Based Graph Representations with Human-Scaled Perceptual Tasks
PROPOSAL: Implement a series of synthetic graph benchmarks emulating human perceptual tasks, such as identifying global structure (e.g., cycles, disconnected components), recognizing ring structures, and detecting bridges in addition to standard GNN tasks (e.g., node classification, graph classification). These benchmarks should be designed to probe the strength of visual perception-based graph representations at capturing fundamental graph properties, and to provide a scale-robust metric for evaluating structural understanding.
CONTROLS: Message passing-based GNNs, including standard architectures like GCN and GraphSAGE, as well as graph transformer models with positional encodings.
COST: 100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Models based on visual perception principles will outperform traditional message-passing architectures on generalization and robustness to scale, but might fail on tasks requiring explicit edge manipulation (e.g., adding/removing edges).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating Vision-Based Graph Representations with Human-Scaled Perceptual Tasks
REVISION: Extend the proposal by incorporating a robotic graph drawing module to generate visually plausible, high-quality graph visualizations, enabling the use of pre-trained vision models (e.g., ResNet, ViT) as graph understanding modules. This would bridge the gap between graph structure and visual perception, allowing researchers to scrutinize to what extent learned representations are genuinely extracting graph topological information versus relying on low-level visual cues.
CONTROLS: Same as before (message passing-based GNNs).
COST: 150 GPU-hours (additional time is spent on training the drawing module and adapting vision models for graph processing).
PREDICTION: Using pre-trained vision models with graph drawings will show improvements over standard message-passing architectures in capturing local and global graph structures, but the extent to which these models understand graph topology might depend on the specific drawing style and graph layout.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Message Passing Limitations with 3D Graph Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Formalize a theoretical framework to rigorously prove that message passing GNNs have inherent limitations in distinguishing between certain types of globally connected graphs, such as star graphs vs. ring graphs, through a proof of incompatibility with the NP-complete Graph Isomorphism Problem. This result will be demonstrated via computational experiments with 3D graph embeddings, leveraging new insights into the role of spatial structure in vision-oriented graph understanding.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparisons with established message passing architectures on graph isomorphism tasks.
COST: 30 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: A theoretical proof of limitations in distinguishing certain graph types via message passing will hold, with implications for understanding why human visual perception outperforms GNNs in certain tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness to Topological Spurious Correlations in Vision-Based Graph Understanding
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of vision-based graph models to spurious correlations between topological graph features (e.g., high vs. low connectivity, isolated vs. connected subgraphs) and domain-specific node attributes (e.g., molecular structure), exploring whether pre-trained vision models are biased towards recognizing these spurious correlations. Standard benchmarks (e.g., MolHIV, ZINC) will be augmented with controlled perturbations to isolate the effect of topological structure on model performance.
CONTROLS: Evaluating vision-based models on original vs. perturbed datasets to assess their sensitivity to topological spurious correlations.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (includes training and fine-tuning pre-trained models).
PREDICTION: Vision-based models will show a mix of robustness and brittleness, possibly over-relying on low-level cues (e.g., ring structures), suggesting the need for understanding biases in learned representations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Robustness to Topological Spurious Correlations in Vision-Based Graph Understanding
REVISION: Enhance the proposal by introducing a new control condition where synthetic node attributes are generated based on graph topology itself (e.g., connectivities of subgraphs), replacing the traditional domain-specific attributes. This will help quantify the role of topological structure on model performance and the interaction with preconceptions in node attributes.
CONTROLS: In addition to standard benchmarks with domain-specific node attributes, introduce synthetic attributions based on graph topology (routine node and subgraph features) and evaluate vision-based models on this new task.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (including modifications to data generation and additional training).
PREDICTION: This revision will reveal a more nuanced picture of vision-based model biases, shedding light on the relative importance of low-level and high-level topological features in driving model performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Graph-Scale Transferability of Visual Graph Representations
